# Custom MMO Engine — Rendering Architecture
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Technical Research · Phase 01 · October 2026</text>

For this engine, I'd target a **GPU-driven, GPU-resident, bindless, meshlet-based, virtualized rendering architecture** designed for enormous persistent worlds, extreme entity counts, and minimal CPU involvement.

Not a conventional game renderer with GPU optimizations bolted on. A renderer designed from the beginning around GPU ownership of scene processing.

Our guiding principle:

**The CPU owns authoritative state, networking, persistence, and resource orchestration. The GPU owns visibility, geometry selection, rendering, shading, and as much visual simulation as practical.**

One important distinction: GPU-driven rendering does not mean literally zero CPU work. Vulkan submission, memory allocation, synchronization, streaming I/O, and swapchain management still require host participation. The objective is to remove CPU work that scales with visible objects, draw calls, and scene complexity.

## 1. Cutting-edge rendering techniques

These are the major technologies I'd evaluate for the engine.

| Technique | What it gives us | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| **GPU-driven rendering** | GPU builds and executes visible work with minimal CPU submission | Foundational |
| **Mesh shaders + task shaders** | GPU-generated geometry workloads and meshlet amplification/culling | Foundational |
| **Virtualized geometry (Nanite-class)** | Extremely dense geometry with continuous GPU-selected LOD | Foundational |
| **Bindless rendering** | Massive texture/material/resource tables without per-object binding | Foundational |
| **GPU scene database** | Persistent SoA entity, transform, material, and geometry buffers | Foundational |
| **GPU hierarchical Z-buffer (HZB)** | Large-scale occlusion culling | Foundational |
| **Morton-coded spatial hierarchy** | GPU-friendly spatial locality, sorting, and hierarchical traversal | High |
| **GPU radix sorting + prefix scans** | Parallel compaction, material sorting, visibility processing | High |
| **Visibility buffer rendering** | Compact geometry pass, deferred material evaluation | High |
| **Virtual texturing** | Massive texture datasets with bounded physical residency | High |
| **Sparse resource residency** | Stream huge worlds without allocating all assets physically | High |
| **GPU work graphs** | GPU-generated and scheduled dependent workloads | Experimental/strategic |
| **GPU-driven animation** | Skeletal evaluation, crowd animation, skinning on GPU | High |
| **GPU procedural generation** | Terrain, vegetation, decals, and detail generation | High |
| **Virtual shadow maps** | High-resolution, demand-driven shadow pages | High |
| **GPU-driven terrain clipmaps** | Huge terrain with camera-relative detail | High |
| **Ray tracing / ray queries** | Selective reflections, GI, shadows, and visibility | Optional high-end |
| **ReSTIR DI/GI** | Spatiotemporal reuse of lighting samples | Experimental/high-end |
| **Neural rendering / reconstruction** | Learned denoising, super-resolution, frame reconstruction | Strategic |
| **GPU render graph** | Explicit resource lifetime, dependencies, and synchronization | Foundational |

The strongest approach is not to implement every technique simultaneously. It's to build an architecture in which the advanced techniques can coexist without requiring major rewrites.

## 3. Advanced techniques worth investigating

Beyond the main pipeline, these are particularly interesting for a next-generation MMO.

| Technology | Architectural opportunity |
|---|---|
| Software + hardware hybrid rasterization | Nanite-style handling of microtriangles |
| GPU persistent kernels | Reduce repeated dispatch overhead for suitable workloads |
| Compressed GPU scene representations | Reduce memory bandwidth and VRAM pressure |
| GPU-generated indirect commands | GPU determines rendering work and supported pipeline selections |
| Shader execution reordering | Improve coherence in divergent ray-tracing workloads |
| Radiance caches / DDGI | Scalable dynamic indirect illumination |
| Reservoir-based light sampling | Handle large numbers of dynamic lights |
| Neural material compression | Reduce texture storage and bandwidth |
| Foveated / variable-rate shading | Reduce shading cost in less important image regions |
| GPU-driven impostors | Render huge distant crowds and settlements |
| Temporal LOD and stochastic rendering | Distribute expensive visual detail over frames |
| GPU particle and volumetric simulation | High-density effects without CPU-per-particle work |

A critical new development: the September 2026 Direct3D **Work Lists** proposal describes GPU-selected rendering pipelines within a single submission. It is still early-stage, with implementations not yet ready. This makes it a research target, not a shipping dependency. <Cite refs={["turn676349search6","turn676349search0"]}/>

## 4. Technology stack recommendation

| Domain | Recommended direction |
|---|---|
| Rendering API | Vulkan-first, explicit backend abstraction |
| Engine core | Rust |
| Low-level GPU utilities | Zig where beneficial |
| Shaders | Slang/HLSL with SPIR-V compilation, subject to validation |
| Server networking | Go |
| Authoritative simulation | Rust, with Go for services and orchestration |
| Rendering scheduling | GPU compute + indirect dispatch |
| Geometry | Mesh shaders + compressed hierarchical meshlets |
| Scene indexing | Morton-coded linear BVH / spatial hierarchy |
| Materials | Bindless, data-driven, visibility-buffer resolve |
| Asset residency | Sparse buffers/images and virtualized resources |
| World precision | CPU 64-bit world coordinates, GPU camera-relative coordinates |

I'd avoid hardwiring the entire engine to work graphs immediately. Vulkan already supports GPU-driven scene processing and indirect rendering, while its device-generated-command facilities provide an evolution path. <Cite refs={["turn676349search1","turn676349search2"]}/>

## 5. Five architectural decisions to settle first

My proposed north star is **a GPU-resident virtualized world renderer**, with a persistent GPU scene database, GPU-selected hierarchical geometry, visibility-buffer shading, and demand-driven resource residency.

For an MMO, the most interesting differentiator isn't simply rendering billions of triangles. It's efficiently handling **millions of potentially relevant entities, thousands of visible characters, large terrain, dynamic structures, and constant world-state updates** without CPU draw-call or scene-traversal bottlenecks.

That's the rendering architecture I'd build toward.

## 007 — Assistant

Message ID: `6431cbea-f010-47d3-946e-1f44c9fc56b8` · 2026-10-08T01:09:25.637178+00:00

Yes—let’s make those explicit architectural requirements:

**Mesh/task-shader geometry, a GPU-resident retained-mode UI, and text rendered directly from Bézier outlines—not bitmap or signed-distance-field glyph atlases.**

The important distinction is that **mesh shaders would generate the geometry covering a glyph; fragment or compute shaders would evaluate its curves.** We do not need to turn every letter into a densely tessellated mesh. Direct outline rendering with a small bounding primitive is an established GPU technique, demonstrated by Slug; Loop–Blinn is another foundational approach to shader-based curve rendering. citeturn667641view0turn513686search3

Here is how I would refine the renderer around that direction.

## 1. Mesh + task shaders as the geometry foundation

For our Vulkan backend, I would require `VK_EXT_mesh_shader` and explicitly enable the mesh/task features. Mesh shaders generate primitives directly, while task shaders can cull or expand work before launching mesh workgroups. The extension also provides indirect mesh draws with GPU-supplied draw counts. citeturn513686search4

Our proposed division of work would be:

| GPU stage | World rendering | UI rendering |
|---|---|---|
| **Compute** | Scene updates, hierarchy traversal, visibility lists, animation | Dirty-node processing, layout, animation, clipping preparation, hit testing, ordered work lists |
| **Task** | Cull meshlet groups and select geometry work | Cull UI chunks, text runs, and batches of glyph instances |
| **Mesh** | Decode/generate visible meshlet geometry | Generate glyph bounds, panel geometry, and vector-path covering primitives |
| **Fragment** | Visibility output or surface shading | Bézier coverage, fills, images, gradients, and clip evaluation |
| **Compute / graphics composition** | Lighting and image processing | Layer composition, masks, blur, and other UI effects |

**Supporting task shaders does not mean requiring a task stage for every pass.** Vulkan permits mesh-only pipelines, and Khronos explicitly cautions that mesh/task shaders are not automatically a performance improvement. I would benchmark task amplification against direct mesh dispatch for already-compacted UI batches. Both remain GPU-driven. citeturn513686search4

That gives us a consistent geometry architecture without forcing every operation through the same shader stages.

## 2. Bézier text: outlines remain the source of truth

### Representation

TrueType outlines use straight segments and quadratic Bézier curves; CFF2 outlines use straight segments and cubic Bézier curves. Our font representation should account for both rather than assuming every font contains quadratics. citeturn669700view4turn669700view0

I would separate **shared glyph geometry** from **individual glyph instances**:

| Persistent GPU data | Proposed contents |
|---|---|
| **Glyph records** | Bounds, contour references, curve ranges, acceleration references |
| **Curve storage** | Line, quadratic, and cubic control points |
| **Curve acceleration** | Per-glyph bands or spatial bins selecting relevant curve segments |
| **Glyph instances** | Glyph reference, transform, paint reference, clip reference, ordering information |
| **Text runs** | Glyph-instance ranges, layout constraints, language/style metadata, dirty flags |

A thousand instances of the same glyph would reference the same curve data. Moving or recolouring text would change instance state—not regenerate its outline.

For cubic support, I would initially preserve the original curves. A quadratic-only runtime could instead use error-bounded conversion, but that introduces a maximum acceptable approximation error that must remain valid over our supported zoom range.

### Rendering

My preferred starting point is **direct outline evaluation over glyph bounds**.

A mesh shader emits a quad or tighter covering polygon. The fragment shader maps the pixel footprint into glyph space, retrieves relevant curves, determines the filled region, and calculates antialiased coverage. Slug demonstrates this architecture using quadratic outlines, bounding primitives, and spatial acceleration rather than precomputed glyph images or distance fields. Its library has a C++ interface, so it is a technical reference here—not our proposed runtime dependency. citeturn667641view0

For our implementation, the important requirements would be robust contour winding, correct holes and overlaps, stable treatment of curve endpoints, and coverage-aware antialiasing.

**Evaluating an exact curve boundary is not the same as calculating exact pixel coverage.** We should avoid promising “perfect text at every size” merely because the source is mathematical. Small text still needs a deliberate legibility policy; TrueType’s grid-fitting machinery exists to address issues such as inconsistent stems and disappearing details at small sizes. citeturn669700view4

Our acceptance tests should therefore include tiny chat text, fractional scaling, scrolling, rotated labels, and distant world-space text—not just large, attractive glyphs.

## 3. All UI on the GPU means a persistent UI database

I would not build a conventional CPU UI renderer and merely upload its triangles.

The proposed model is:

**The host supplies state changes and input events. The GPU maintains and executes the visual UI representation.**

That representation would contain parent/child relationships, layout constraints, resolved rectangles, transforms, paints, clipping relationships, text runs, interaction state, and animation state.

The key architectural choices would be:

| Area | Proposed approach |
|---|---|
| **Updates** | Apply compact changes to persistent buffers instead of rebuilding a complete draw list each frame |
| **Layout** | Compute-based measure/arrange passes over dirty subtrees |
| **Animation** | GPU evaluation of transitions, scrolling, fades, and transforms |
| **Visibility** | Cull entire panels and text runs before processing individual primitives |
| **Clipping** | Rectangular clip intersections as a fast path; GPU masks or analytic evaluation for complex clips |
| **Interaction** | GPU hit testing against resolved geometry and clipping |
| **Rendering** | GPU-generated work lists feeding mesh and fragment stages |
| **Caching** | Retain geometry, shaped runs, and optionally expensive composited layers until their dependencies change |

For layout, I would start with a deliberately bounded engine model—stacks, grids, anchors, and explicit sizing rules—rather than attempting arbitrary browser-style layout immediately. Parent/child size dependencies would be handled through explicit passes, not an assumption that the whole tree resolves in one dispatch.

### Morton order is not UI draw order

For UI, we must keep **spatial locality** separate from **compositing order**.

Morton ordering could help organise spatial bins or hit-test candidates. It must not replace the ordering of overlapping translucent UI elements: drawing A over B generally produces a different result from drawing B over A.

I would therefore give UI nodes a stable compositing order and preserve it during GPU compaction and batching. Locality optimisation would operate only where it does not change the result.

## 4. Text shaping is a separate GPU subsystem

This is the largest scope item hidden inside “all UI on GPU.”

Rendering a glyph outline does not determine which glyphs a string needs. Shaping selects and positions glyphs using the text, font, script, language, and font features. Bidirectional ordering and paragraph line breaking are additional responsibilities beyond shaping itself. citeturn785504view0turn785504view1

For the literal all-GPU target, I would include:

**GPU text processing → GPU shaping → GPU line layout → GPU glyph instances → GPU outline rendering.**

But I would classify full GPU Unicode/OpenType processing as a **separate research and engineering workstream**, not something mesh shaders give us automatically. We would need to implement and validate those compute kernels, including caret and selection mappings back to the original text.

The implementation strategy I would choose is to process only dirty text runs and cache the results. Scrolling unchanged chat history should not cause the same strings to be shaped again.

The host would still retain the semantic state and platform bridge: input events, text-editing state, clipboard integration, input-method integration, accessibility information, and application actions. That fits the CPU-as-state/orchestration boundary without making it responsible for drawing the UI.

For GPU hit testing, I would also explicitly budget the feedback path. GPU-local hover feedback can remain on the GPU; a click result consumed by host logic becomes available only after the relevant GPU work completes. We should avoid a synchronous CPU wait in the normal frame path and use event-sequenced results instead.

## 5. One UI system, specialised rendering paths

“All GPU” should not mean “everything is a Bézier curve.”

I would give the UI renderer several specialised primitive types sharing the same retained state, clipping, ordering, and composition infrastructure:

| UI content | Proposed rendering path |
|---|---|
| **Text and vector icons** | Direct Bézier-outline coverage |
| **Panels, borders, rounded rectangles** | Specialised analytic primitives |
| **Complex vector illustrations** | GPU path processing with an appropriate coverage backend |
| **Portraits, item artwork, minimaps** | Bindless image sampling |
| **Blurred panels and group opacity** | Explicit intermediate layers and GPU composition |
| **World-space labels** | Shared glyph data with world transforms and a deliberate depth/occlusion policy |

For general vector rendering research, Vello is relevant, but the distinction between its implementations matters: its current documentation separates an experimental compute-centric renderer from a GPU renderer that performs path preprocessing on the CPU. Neither should be casually described as a turnkey all-GPU UI implementation for our architecture. citeturn667641view1

For the screen-space HUD, my default would be to render at output resolution after world temporal reconstruction, with explicit colour-space handling during final composition. World-space text would use a separately defined integration point depending on whether it should behave like physical scene content or an overlay.

## Updated rendering target

**A GPU-resident world and UI renderer, using compute for state-dependent processing, mesh/task shaders for geometry work, and direct Bézier-outline evaluation for vector text.**

The three things I would lock now are **persistent GPU UI state, shared curve-based glyph storage, and no CPU-generated per-widget draw stream**. Task-stage granularity, curve acceleration, coverage algorithms, and GPU text-layout scheduling remain benchmarked implementation choices—not assumptions that “more GPU” automatically means faster.

## 011 — Assistant

Message ID: `b2727449-9113-4c63-ab98-e5d728a322a5` · 2026-10-08T01:23:10.925928+00:00

Yes. **The world/scene split and ECS model should come before the individual rendering techniques.** They determine how simulation, streaming, networking, rendering, and UI fit together.

My proposed direction is:

> **A persistent logical world, partitioned simulation ECS, and a GPU-resident presentation ECS—connected through stable entity identities and incremental state changes.**

That gives us a full ECS architecture without forcing the server, client state, GPU renderer, and persistence layer to share one enormous data structure.

I’m assuming a seamless overworld with support for separate instances, interiors, and independently streamed content.

## 1. Separate “world,” “scene,” and “view”

For our engine, I would give these terms explicit meanings:

| Concept | What it means in our architecture |
|---|---|
| **Logical world** | The persistent game reality: entities, ownership, rules, world time, and durable state. It can span multiple server processes. |
| **Runtime ECS world** | A local entity/component store with its own systems and execution schedule. A server simulation partition and a client replica would have separate stores. |
| **Scene asset / scene instance** | A composable content package and its runtime instantiation: a settlement, building, dungeon, vehicle, or encounter. |
| **Streaming cell** | A spatial unit used to decide which content and resources should be resident. It is not automatically a server partition or ECS world. |
| **GPU scene** | The persistent, GPU-resident representation used for visual processing: geometry instances, poses, lights, effects, and presentation relationships. |
| **View** | A camera or presentation output with its own visibility, LOD, and rendering state. Multiple views can use the same GPU scene. |

**These are related concepts, not a mandatory containment tree.**

A city could contain many scene instances and streaming cells, be simulated by several workers, and appear in one client GPU scene. The main camera, minimap, and another camera could then use different views of that resident scene.

The most important distinction is:

**The world describes what exists. The GPU scene describes how the locally relevant portion is presented.**

For example, a chest’s contents and ownership belong to world state. Its mesh, lid pose, highlight, and shadow participation belong to presentation. Unloading its visual representation must not mean deleting the chest.

Separating simulation state from rendering state is an established architecture; Bevy, for example, explicitly extracts data from a main world into a render world. Our design would extend that separation with persistent GPU storage and incremental updates rather than assume a complete per-frame reconstruction. citeturn896075search6

## 2. “Full ECS” should mean the engine’s programming model

I would use ECS for gameplay, scene membership, transforms, relationships, animation state, lights, cameras, UI state, and streaming metadata—not just for renderable objects.

But **full ECS does not mean every byte becomes an entity**. My design would keep mesh data, texture pages, font curves, terrain samples, and navigation data in specialised resource stores, referenced by components.

The ECS foundation I would scope is:

| Technology | Proposed role |
|---|---|
| **Archetype-based component storage** | Group entities with matching component compositions for bulk processing. |
| **Chunked columnar storage** | Store component columns in bounded allocation/processing units rather than individual heap objects. |
| **Hybrid storage policies** | Use dense storage for frequently processed data and appropriate side stores or bitsets for other workloads. |
| **First-class entity relationships** | Represent attachment, ownership, containment, targeting, and scene membership explicitly. |
| **Dependency-aware system scheduling** | Schedule work from declared reads, writes, and ordering requirements. |
| **Deferred structural changes** | Batch entity creation, destruction, and composition changes at controlled boundaries. |
| **Incremental change streams** | Feed replication, persistence, GPU updates, and tooling without rebuilding everything. |
| **Versioned component schemas** | Define serialization, replication, GPU representation, inspection, and migration rules. |
| **Multiple execution domains** | Keep a common ECS model while supporting different CPU and GPU storage and system implementations. |

### Archetype-first, not archetype-only

An archetype groups entities with the same component set. Changing that set can move an entity to another archetype. Table storage favours iteration, while sparse-set storage makes different tradeoffs around component insertion and removal. These distinctions are explicit in current ECS implementations. citeturn368375view1turn910405view2

For our engine, I would keep frequently processed component compositions relatively stable. Rapidly changing conditions—selected, recently damaged, temporarily hidden, awaiting streaming—would not automatically become components that are repeatedly inserted and removed.

Some should be values or bitsets. Others genuinely deserve separate components. We would choose based on query patterns and mutation frequency.

### Relationships instead of one universal scene tree

I would distinguish relationships such as `AttachedTo`, `OwnedBy`, `ContainedIn`, and `MemberOfScene`.

A sword can be owned by a player, attached to a hand, and associated with a streamed content instance. Those are different relationships with different lifetime rules.

A transform hierarchy would remain useful, but it would be **one relationship structure within the ECS**, not the structure that dictates all storage, simulation, and ownership. Relationship components are already a first-class ECS technique; Bevy’s implementation, for example, represents links and their reverse collections explicitly. citeturn190078view1

For our design, unloading a scene would therefore follow explicit lifetime policies—not recursively destroy everything that happens to be transform-parented underneath its root.

## 3. Full ECS across CPU and GPU—not a single shared memory layout

I would divide execution into three main domains.

### Authoritative simulation ECS

This owns the accepted gameplay state: movement rules, combat, interactions, NPC decisions, and other simulation responsibilities.

**Authority and processor choice are separate decisions.** We can execute suitable authoritative systems on a server GPU without giving authority to the client GPU.

My recommendation is to define authority per component family or subsystem. A movement simulation worker and an inventory service should not accidentally both be treated as unrestricted writers of every component on a player.

### Client state ECS

This maintains the relevant replicated state, local input state, and whatever prediction/reconciliation the game needs.

It would not be a complete copy of the server world. Selective entity/component replication, per-client visibility, and priority are established mechanisms; client and server entity handles also commonly require explicit mapping. citeturn775835view4turn775835view3

For the GPU-first target, we would explicitly assign which client systems remain host-side and which execute on the GPU. We should not silently recreate a CPU scene traversal and draw-list builder here.

### GPU presentation ECS

This is where I would go beyond a conventional render cache.

The proposed GPU ECS would own persistent presentation components and run systems for transforms, animation, bounds, visibility preparation, visual effects, and the retained UI we discussed. Mesh/task shaders would consume its generated geometry work.

It could also create **GPU-only entities**: cosmetic particles, procedural detail, temporary highlights, and other visual objects that do not need a persistent world identity or server replication.

GPU ECS is a demonstrated research direction. Madrona implements GPU-accelerated ECS for batched simulation, but its workload is many independent environments—not a demonstration of a seamless distributed MMO. Its current implementation also requires predefined archetypes and does not support arbitrary dynamic component addition/removal. Its C++ implementation would be a research reference, not our runtime dependency. citeturn910405view1turn775835view5

For our custom implementation, I would therefore treat **GPU structural mutation**—creation, destruction, composition changes, allocation, and compaction—as an explicit subsystem to prototype.

The unifying principle would be:

> **Shared component semantics and tooling; specialised storage and executable systems for each domain.**

Not “write an arbitrary Rust system and assume it can automatically run on either processor.”

## 4. Morton codes belong beside the ECS, not inside its identity model

This is a particularly important architectural decision.

**An archetype answers “what components does this entity have?”**

**A spatial index answers “where is this entity, and what is nearby?”**

Those are different query dimensions.

Morton ordering is useful for spatial locality and GPU hierarchy construction. A common linear BVH construction approach assigns Morton codes, radix-sorts the objects, and constructs a hierarchy over that ordering. It is a strong building block, but not a complete ECS design. citeturn190078view0

For our engine, I would propose:

**Coarse world cells → region-local spatial indexes → object bounds → geometry/meshlet hierarchies.**

The exact index would depend on the workload. I would evaluate GPU LBVHs for dynamic object bounds, grids or spatial hashes for suitable neighbourhood queries, and separately built hierarchies for static content.

Crucially, I would **sort spatial references or specialised processing streams**, rather than continually reorder every component of the entire ECS into one global Morton sequence.

Under that design, when an entity moves:

- Its persistent identity remains unchanged.
- Its archetype remains unchanged unless its component composition changes.
- Its spatial membership and relevant acceleration structures are updated.

That separation keeps movement from becoming an unnecessary structural operation throughout the engine.

I would also keep static and dynamic spatial data separate where useful. Rebuilding and refitting have different costs and quality tradeoffs; refitted BVHs can deteriorate as objects move, so neither “rebuild everything” nor “refit forever” should be a universal policy. citeturn190078view0

## 5. Split the world in several independent ways

I would not make one grid responsible for all scaling concerns.

### Content and residency partitioning

This decides what assets, scene instances, collision data, and visual representations are loaded.

I would use stable, hierarchical content cells, with support for scene packages that span several cells. A large building or moving vehicle should not have to be artificially broken into gameplay entities merely to match the streaming grid.

### Simulation authority partitioning

This decides which worker is responsible for particular simulation state.

I would allow a worker to own multiple cells and make the ownership mapping independent of the authored content layout. That leaves room for later load balancing without rewriting the world’s content packaging.

For migration, the design would need explicit handoff, neighbouring-state exchange, and authority versions that let us reject stale updates from a former owner. Those are separate distributed-systems responsibilities—not something an ECS or Morton code solves automatically.

**I would design for movable ownership now, but prototype live repartitioning separately.** A crowded battle is not guaranteed to scale simply because we divide its coordinates into smaller boxes; interactions still have to cross those boundaries.

### Replication interest

This decides what each client is allowed and needs to know.

I would combine spatial relevance with semantic relevance: party membership, an ongoing interaction, a tracked objective, or other game-specific relationships.

This is distinct from rendering visibility. Replication systems already expose client-specific visibility and prioritisation independently of rendering. citeturn775835view3

For our game, an enemy behind the camera may still need simulation updates. Conversely, the client should not receive secret state merely because it is geographically nearby. GPU visibility feedback could inform presentation or streaming priorities, but would not be the authority for information access.

**Shared coarse coordinates are useful. Identical boundaries and policies are not required.**

## 6. Stable identities and incremental updates are foundational

I would use a persistent entity identity that is separate from local ECS handles and GPU storage slots.

A chest should remain the same chest when its server ownership changes, its client representation unloads, or its GPU allocation moves.

This separation matters even with existing ECS libraries: Bevy documents that its entity handles are local to a world and that their serialized representation does not provide long-term wire-format compatibility. citeturn368375view2

For our architecture:

**Persistent identity identifies the thing. Local handles locate its current representation.**

The same distinction should apply to updates. I would build explicit change streams for component changes, entity lifecycle events, and relationship changes, with versioning and consumer-specific policies.

Those streams would feed networking, persistence, GPU state updates, and debugging—but they would not all consume the same fields or run at the same cadence.

### Change detection is not automatically incremental work

A subtle trap is assuming a “changed components” query avoids scanning unchanged entities. That is implementation-dependent. Bevy’s `Changed<T>` documentation explicitly states that it can inspect every matching entity even when none changed. citeturn752370view3

For our large-world target, I would scope **dirty-chunk tracking and explicit mutation queues**, with a dense-processing fallback when most of a dataset changes.

The goal is not a universal promise that every operation costs only the number of changed entities. It is to avoid making a full-world scan the default way to discover a small update.

## 7. Two more high-level choices I would lock early

### Large-world coordinates with local reference frames

I would use a coarse integer cell coordinate plus a bounded local position, then derive camera-relative GPU coordinates.

The canonical position should not change just because the camera moves. Integer-grid and floating-origin designs demonstrate this separation between stable world position and reduced-precision rendering transforms. citeturn910405view0

I would also support local reference frames for moving assemblies, such as ships or large vehicles. That would be distinct from server ownership and ordinary scene membership.

### Independent clocks and active sets

I would give authoritative simulation, replication, persistence, presentation, and UI their own schedules and explicit exchange points.

Likewise, I would distinguish **persistent**, **actively simulated**, **replicated**, **resident**, and **visible**. These would be independent properties, not one `Active` flag.

For example, our proposed engine could keep an unloaded object’s durable state without allocating its full GPU representation. A distant NPC could use a lower-frequency simulation policy where gameplay permits it, while a nearby combatant remains in the high-frequency active set.

Dependency-aware scheduling is an established ECS capability; the important additional work for us is defining dependencies across these different execution domains and clocks. citeturn368375view0

## The architecture I would choose

**A custom, archetype-first ECS with specialised GPU execution, composable scene instances, independent spatial indexes, and explicit authority/residency boundaries.**

The rendering side remains fully aligned with our mesh/task-shader and GPU UI direction. But the engine’s central abstraction would not be a draw object or a scene-tree node—it would be **an entity with typed state, explicit relationships, and well-defined ownership**.

The most valuable next decision is the **component ownership model**: which component families are authoritative, replicated, predicted, derived, or GPU-only. That will make the world/scene split concrete before we choose storage layouts or implementation libraries.

## 013 — Assistant

Message ID: `20d4519d-4fa3-44cc-ab79-53507fc57f5f` · 2026-10-08T01:31:28.875136+00:00

Absolutely. In fact, **contiguous, data-oriented memory should be a foundational requirement of our custom ECS**, not merely an optimization.

For our MMO engine, I'd push this further:

**Archetype ECS + Structure of Arrays (SoA) + chunked contiguous storage + GPU-coalesced layouts + Morton-ordered spatial processing.**

The objective is to make almost every major system process contiguous streams of exactly the data it needs, minimizing cache misses, pointer chasing, and unnecessary memory transfers.

## 1. Traditional objects vs contiguous ECS

Consider updating 100,000 entities.

  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Object-oriented layout**
      <badge color="danger">Poor locality</badge>
    </row>
    <svg viewBox="0 0 330 90" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
      {#each [0,1,2,3] as i}
        <rect x={8+i*82} y="7" width="72" height="53" rx="5" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeOpacity=".4"/>
        <rect x={14+i*82} y="14" width="19" height="14" rx="2" fill="#D68B6D"/>
        <rect x={36+i*82} y="14" width="27" height="14" rx="2" fill="#8CA9BD"/>
        <rect x={14+i*82} y="32" width="49" height="19" rx="2" fill="#9CA7AC" fillOpacity=".5"/>
        <path d={`M ${44+i*82} 62 l ${i%2===0?14:-9} 13`} stroke="#D68B6D" strokeWidth="1.5" strokeDasharray="3 3"/>
      {/each}
      <text x="165" y="86" fontSize="10" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Scattered objects · mixed data · pointer traversal</text>
    </svg>
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Each entity mixes position, health, inventory, rendering state, and references. Iterating positions may bring unrelated data into cache.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Contiguous SoA layout**
      <badge color="success">High locality</badge>
    </row>
    <svg viewBox="0 0 330 111" width="100%">
      {#each [{name:"Position",c:"#4E9DCD",y:5},{name:"Velocity",c:"#56AA8A",y:40},{name:"Health",c:"#C69A54",y:75}] as r}

        {#each Array.from({length:8},(_,i)=>i) as i}

</box>

In a well-designed data-oriented ECS, the important unit of work is no longer an individual entity. It is a **batch of components**.

For example, a movement system can iterate `Position[]` and `Velocity[]` without reading inventories, rendering resources, or unrelated entity metadata.

This approach is compatible with the established column-oriented ECS model used by Bevy, although we'd implement our own engine-specific storage and scheduling. <Cite refs={["turn817091search6"]}/>

## 3. Push beyond SoA: different layouts for different workloads

I'd investigate three layouts rather than mandate one everywhere.

| Layout | Best use |
|---|---|
| **SoA** (Structure of Arrays) | Bulk movement, transforms, animation, simple component processing |
| **AoSoA** (Array of Structures of Arrays) | SIMD kernels, GPU workgroup-sized tiles, processing fields together |
| **Packed immutable arrays** | Meshlets, geometry clusters, font curves, static spatial acceleration |

AoSoA is particularly interesting. We can tile tightly coupled values into blocks sized according to SIMD or compute-kernel requirements, reducing the downsides of maintaining many globally separate component arrays.

However, a CPU cache line, CPU SIMD width, and GPU subgroup are not necessarily the same size. I would benchmark their storage configurations independently.

## 4. GPU memory needs its own layout

CPU cache efficiency and GPU memory coalescing are related but not identical.

On GPUs, neighbouring shader invocations should ideally access neighbouring memory addresses. Poorly arranged loads can require substantially more memory transactions than coalesced loads. <Cite refs={["turn817091search1","turn817091search4"]}/>

I would propose a GPU presentation ECS with dense streams for:

- Transforms and bounds
- Mesh and material references
- Animation/pose state
- Visibility and LOD metadata
- Lights, particles, and procedural instances
- GPU UI nodes and text instances

Those streams would be laid out for the GPU systems that consume them, not copied byte-for-byte from the authoritative ECS.

**The GPU should receive compact changes to persistent data, not a complete ECS snapshot every frame.**

## 5. Combine dense storage with Morton locality

This is where the architecture becomes especially interesting.

For spatial processing, we can compute Morton keys, radix-sort entity references, and build spatially coherent processing lists.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **Proposed spatial processing path**

  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} align="center">Dense ECS component chunks</box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} align="center">Spatial keys (cell + Morton code)</box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} align="center">GPU radix sort / spatial binning</box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} align="center">Compact locality-ordered work lists</box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} align="center">GPU culling / LOD / collision broad phase</box>
</box>

The important design choice is that **we sort references or derived streams when necessary, not continuously physically reorder the entire ECS**.

That avoids excessive data movement, handle invalidation, and cache churn whenever entities move.

For relatively static spatial regions, actual component reordering could still be worthwhile. For rapidly moving crowds, incremental spatial bins or sorted reference arrays may be better.

## 6. Additional optimizations I'd investigate

| Technique | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Hot/cold component splitting** | Keep rarely accessed metadata out of frequently processed memory |
| **Generational handles** | Stable references while compacting or relocating data |
| **Dirty bitsets per chunk** | Skip unchanged data without inspecting every entity |
| **Bulk structural mutations** | Amortize archetype migrations, spawning, and despawning |
| **SIMD-friendly padding/alignment** | Improve vectorised CPU processing |
| **GPU subgroup operations** | Efficient filtering, ballot operations, and local compaction |
| **Prefix scans / stream compaction** | Generate dense active-work arrays |
| **Read/write phase separation** | Reduce synchronization, contention, and false sharing |
| **NUMA-aware allocation** | Preserve locality across high-core-count server machines |
| **Software prefetching** | Worth exploring for unavoidable indirect lookups, after profiling |
| **Column compression / quantization** | Reduce memory footprint and bandwidth when accuracy permits |

I would not assume that more aggressive compression or sorting is always faster. Decompression, data movement, and synchronization all have costs.

## 7. What I'd lock into the design

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{name:"Archetype-first ECS",desc:"Dense storage grouped by component composition"},{name:"Chunked SoA / AoSoA",desc:"Configurable layouts according to workload and processor"},{name:"GPU-native component streams",desc:"Persistent GPU buffers optimized for coalesced processing"},{name:"Morton-ordered spatial work lists",desc:"Spatial locality without making Morton codes entity identities"},{name:"Stable indirection",desc:"Generational local handles and persistent world identities"},{name:"Incremental synchronization",desc:"Dirty-chunk tracking and batched component updates"}] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success" size="lg"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{item.name}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{item.desc}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

One further consideration: **the fastest ECS is not necessarily the one with the most contiguous data; it's the one that minimizes total memory traffic for the actual systems being run.** Overpacking unrelated components, unnecessary data transformations, and excessive archetype migrations can defeat the benefits.

For our MMO, I would make **data-oriented architecture and bandwidth-efficient execution** a core engine design principle across simulation, networking, streaming, rendering, and UI.

The next high-level question is whether we want the **GPU to own and mutate the primary client-side ECS**, with the CPU acting mainly as an authoritative-state and I/O bridge, or whether the GPU should have a specialised ECS derived from a host-side store.

Given your goal of CPU-as-state/database-only, I'd lean toward GPU-primary for presentation and GPU-suitable local simulation, while keeping server authority and synchronization explicitly separate.

Agreed. Let's establish **GPU-first execution with data-oriented ECS** as a core architectural principle of the custom MMO engine.

The rule should be:

> **If a workload is massively parallel, data-oriented, and can remain GPU-resident across multiple processing stages, it should default to GPU execution.**

The CPU becomes primarily responsible for authoritative state, orchestration, networking, persistence, I/O, and workloads that are inherently sequential or latency-sensitive.

Importantly, this doesn't mean sending everything to the GPU. It means minimizing total computation, memory traffic, synchronization, and CPU↔GPU transfers.

## Proposed execution ownership

| Subsystem | Primary execution |
|---|---|
| GPU ECS component processing | GPU compute |
| Transform hierarchy updates | GPU compute |
| Spatial indexing and Morton sorting | GPU compute |
| Visibility, culling, LOD | GPU compute + task shaders |
| Meshlet generation/selection | GPU compute + mesh shaders |
| Character animation and skinning | GPU compute |
| Particles, vegetation, environmental simulation | GPU compute |
| UI layout, animation, rendering | GPU compute + mesh/fragment shaders |
| Text outline rendering | GPU mesh + Bézier evaluation |
| Terrain generation and detail | GPU compute |
| Lighting, shadows, rendering | GPU |
| Client prediction | GPU where latency and reconciliation permit |
| Gameplay simulation | CPU or GPU, depending on dependencies and authority |
| Networking, database, persistence | CPU/server |
| Asset I/O and GPU resource management | CPU orchestration + GPU processing |

## The next foundational decision: three data domains

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Server / authoritative world ECS**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs" textAlign="center">Persistent world state · Simulation ownership · Database · Network replication</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/> <text size="xs" color="secondary">Interest-filtered state deltas</text></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Client / host state bridge**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs" textAlign="center">Input · Networking · Asset I/O · Resource allocation · GPU uploads</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/> <text size="xs" color="secondary">Batched state changes + asynchronous feedback</text></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text textAlign="center" weight="medium">GPU-PRIMARY CLIENT WORLD</text>
    <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
      {#each ["Persistent ECS arrays","GPU simulation systems","Spatial hierarchies","Animation + transforms","GPU UI ECS","Mesh/task rendering"] as label}
        <grid-item>
          <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2} minHeight="48px" justify="center">
            <text size="xs" textAlign="center">{label}</text>
          </box>
        </grid-item>
      {/each}
    </grid>
  </box>
</box>

The server may eventually use GPU acceleration for suitable large-scale simulations, but **server authority must not depend on the client GPU**.

## Design principles to lock

1. **GPU-first, not GPU-exclusive.** Choose execution based on total workload cost, not processor ideology.
2. **Persistent contiguous data.** Chunked SoA/AoSoA ECS with independent GPU-resident component storage.
3. **No per-entity CPU rendering work.** GPU-generated work lists and mesh/task shader dispatch. Vulkan supports indirect mesh task commands, including device-supplied draw counts. <Cite refs={["turn862269search0","turn862269search2"]}/>
4. **No routine GPU-to-CPU readback.** Use asynchronous results only when host-side decisions need them.
5. **Incremental state movement.** Stream changed component ranges rather than rebuilding complete scenes.
6. **Spatial locality without identity coupling.** Morton codes accelerate queries, not determine entity ownership or identity.
7. **Explicit synchronization.** GPU work remains asynchronous, with declared dependencies between simulation, animation, visibility, and rendering.
8. **Benchmark-driven placement.** Small sequential jobs, irregular pointer-heavy algorithms, and urgent CPU-consumed decisions might remain faster on the CPU.

### What this means for the engine

We are building something closer to a **GPU-resident simulation and presentation runtime with a distributed authoritative world behind it**, rather than a conventional CPU game engine that submits graphics commands.

I would investigate one particularly interesting next step: **GPU-native ECS scheduling**, where systems operate directly on dense component streams and generate subsequent work on the GPU.

That potentially eliminates much of the per-frame CPU system scheduling and dispatch management, although synchronization and platform command submission still need explicit handling.

The next major high-level area I'd scope is **GPU memory architecture**: unified component pools, archetype chunks, allocation, compaction, sparse residency, and how we organize potentially millions of entities without fragmentation or excessive synchronization.

## 022 — Assistant

Message ID: `9af80ceb-7b30-4073-918a-01890aac055a` · 2026-10-08T01:37:37.523797+00:00

# GPU-Native ECS Scheduling
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Core Architecture · Feasibility Assessment</text>

**Yes. GPU-native ECS scheduling is feasible, and we can design it so synchronization does not become the primary bottleneck.**

However, I would not build a traditional CPU ECS scheduler and simply port it to a compute shader.

For our architecture, the stronger approach is a **GPU-resident, dependency-driven, bulk-parallel execution system** with GPU-generated work queues, persistent component storage, and explicit synchronization boundaries.

The key architectural idea:

> Schedule groups of systems and contiguous data streams, not millions of individual entities.

## 1. Feasibility by technology

| Technique | Feasibility | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| GPU-resident ECS component arrays | Proven primitives | Core |
| GPU indirect dispatch scheduling | Supported in Vulkan | Core |
| GPU work queues and stream compaction | Established techniques | Core |
| GPU-side spawn/despawn and compaction | Feasible, complex | Core, phased |
| GPU dependency DAG execution | Feasible with constraints | Core |
| GPU work graphs / shader enqueue | Hardware/API dependent | Advanced backend |
| Persistent-kernel ECS scheduler | Feasible with occupancy risks | Experimental |
| Fully dynamic GPU-defined system graph | Much harder | Research |
| Zero host submission or synchronization | Not realistic | Not a goal |

Vulkan's indirect dispatch mechanism allows the GPU to write the size of a subsequent compute workload without the CPU reading back the result. Device-generated commands extend this to more complex command generation, including supported compute-dispatch and shader-selection capabilities. <Cite refs={["turn998014search1","turn998014search2"]}/>

That is sufficient to build the first generation of our scheduler without depending on experimental work-graph functionality.

## 2. Proposed architecture

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1} align="center">
    **HOST / RUST**

    <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Input · Network deltas · Resource management · Submit frame graph</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text weight="medium" textAlign="center">GPU ECS RUNTIME</text>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
      **Persistent Component Database**

      <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">SoA / AoSoA · Archetype chunks · Entity handles · GPU allocation tables</text>
    </box>
    <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
      **Work Discovery + Scheduling**

Each system declares:

- Which component streams it reads and writes.
- Which resource ranges it accesses.
- Whether it may change ECS structure.
- Which active set or query it processes.
- Whether it needs current-frame or previous-frame results.

The graph compiler derives a safe ordering.

Message ID: `fdcd451f-1a73-4637-8ca6-c01f6e471891` · 2026-10-08T01:38:03.571153+00:00

## 4. Can we synchronize without bottlenecks?

**Yes, if we minimize synchronization frequency and scope.** We cannot eliminate dependencies, but we can avoid making the CPU wait for each GPU operation.

I would use four synchronization levels.

| Level | Synchronization strategy | Expected cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Within workgroup** | Shared memory + subgroup/workgroup barriers | Low, when used carefully |
| **Within one kernel** | Atomics, partition ownership, local queues | Variable; contention-sensitive |
| **Between GPU dispatches** | Vulkan Synchronization2 barriers | Depends on dependency scope and GPU work |
| **Between GPU queues / CPU** | Timeline semaphores, asynchronous completion | Potentially expensive if waited on unnecessarily |

The critical distinction is between **a GPU execution dependency and a CPU stall**.

A GPU compute pass can finish writing position data before a later pass reads it, using a GPU-side dependency. The CPU does not need to wait for either pass.

Vulkan's synchronization model explicitly supports these dependencies, including compute-to-compute barriers. <Cite refs={["turn909031search3","turn909031search5"]}/>

### My five rules for avoiding synchronization bottlenecks

**1. Never synchronize per entity.**

Process whole chunks or dense batches. One boundary between two large processing stages is generally preferable to thousands of tiny dependent operations.

**2. Double- or triple-buffer data when useful.**

Rendering can consume a completed state snapshot while the next simulation state is being prepared. Use versioned buffers for frame-sensitive data and explicit ownership for mutable resources.

We don't necessarily triple-buffer every ECS component—only where concurrent reads and writes would otherwise cause contention.

**3. Prefer single-writer ownership.**

Assign a component range or chunk to one kernel invocation group where possible. If one workgroup exclusively owns a chunk, most writes need no global atomic synchronization.

**4. Fuse systems when profitable.**

Instead of dispatching:

`PositionUpdate → Barrier → VelocityUpdate → Barrier → BoundsUpdate`

we can sometimes fuse compatible operations into one processing kernel.

But fusion has limits: if downstream work requires the completed results of *all* workgroups, a normal workgroup barrier is insufficient. That dependency usually still needs a separate dispatch or a supported device-wide execution mechanism.

**5. Synchronize at declared phase boundaries.**

The graph compiler should emit barriers only where dependency analysis requires them.

Overly broad barriers can unnecessarily serialize GPU work, and Khronos specifically recommends careful stage and access scopes. <Cite refs={["turn909031search1"]}/>

## 5. A practical GPU scheduler design

I would build a **two-level scheduler**.

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={2}>
      <icon name="workflow" size="lg"/>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Level 1 — Compiled execution graph**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Determines system ordering, dependencies, barriers, shader pipelines, and dispatch slots. Established on the host and reused across frames.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="center" padding={{left:3}}>
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={2}>
      <icon name="cpu" size="lg"/>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Level 2 — GPU dynamic work scheduler**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Determines which chunks, entities, and workgroups execute. Maintains dense work queues, dispatch counts, free lists, and active-set data.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

This gives us GPU autonomy without paying the cost of building and validating an entirely new execution graph every frame.

### Example frame execution

| Phase | Systems | Dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| A | Apply state deltas, process input | Upload completion |
| B | Movement, independent animation jobs | Affected component dependencies |
| C | Transform propagation, bounds | Previous relevant outputs |
| D | Spatial structures, visibility preparation | Updated bounds |
| E | Mesh/task geometry rendering | Visibility and LOD results |
| F | Lighting, composition, GPU UI | Relevant rendering dependencies |

Independent work within or across these groups should overlap where the hardware and hazards allow.

We should not hardcode this exact ordering universally. For example, animation that feeds movement or root motion needs different edges.

## 6. Persistent kernels vs indirect dispatch vs work graphs

This is an important choice.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Indirect dispatch chains**
      <badge color="success">Recommended baseline</badge>
    </row>
    <text size="sm">One GPU pass generates work counts for subsequent GPU passes. The host records the command structure, while workload sizing stays GPU-controlled.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Advantages: relatively portable Vulkan foundation, clear barriers, easier profiling, and predictable execution.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Device-generated commands / work graphs**

    <text size="sm">More dynamic GPU-side work generation and, where supported, pipeline selection. Attractive for irregular processing and adaptive work expansion.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Limitations: feature and hardware variability, additional preprocessing or scratch requirements, and less predictable performance.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Persistent compute kernels**

    <text size="sm">A long-running kernel uses resident workers to pull jobs from GPU queues instead of repeatedly launching separate kernels.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Advantages: can reduce launch overhead for appropriate fine-grained workloads. Risks: occupancy pressure, starvation, queue contention, and deadlocks from unsafe cross-workgroup waits.</text>
  </box>
</box>

Vulkan now specifies `VK_EXT_device_generated_commands` and execution-graph mechanisms through `VK_AMDX_shader_enqueue`, but they have different constraints and available feature sets. I would not assume feature parity across vendors. <Cite refs={["turn998014search6","turn998014search10"]}/>

**My choice:** indirect dispatch for the general ECS scheduler, selective work-graph acceleration when supported, and persistent kernels only for specific workloads that prove faster.

A persistent kernel should never assume that all launched workgroups are simultaneously resident. A workgroup waiting for another unscheduled workgroup can deadlock.

# GPU-Native ECS Scheduling
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Core Architecture · Feasibility Assessment</text>

**Yes. GPU-native ECS scheduling is feasible, and we can design it so synchronization does not become the primary bottleneck.**

However, I would not build a traditional CPU ECS scheduler and simply port it to a compute shader.

For our architecture, the stronger approach is a **GPU-resident, dependency-driven, bulk-parallel execution system** with GPU-generated work queues, persistent component storage, and explicit synchronization boundaries.

The key architectural idea:

> Schedule groups of systems and contiguous data streams, not millions of individual entities.

## 1. Feasibility by technology

| Technique | Feasibility | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| GPU-resident ECS component arrays | Proven primitives | Core |
| GPU indirect dispatch scheduling | Supported in Vulkan | Core |
| GPU work queues and stream compaction | Established techniques | Core |
| GPU-side spawn/despawn and compaction | Feasible, complex | Core, phased |
| GPU dependency DAG execution | Feasible with constraints | Core |
| GPU work graphs / shader enqueue | Hardware/API dependent | Advanced backend |
| Persistent-kernel ECS scheduler | Feasible with occupancy risks | Experimental |
| Fully dynamic GPU-defined system graph | Much harder | Research |
| Zero host submission or synchronization | Not realistic | Not a goal |

Vulkan's indirect dispatch mechanism allows the GPU to write the size of a subsequent compute workload without the CPU reading back the result. Device-generated commands extend this to more complex command generation, including supported compute-dispatch and shader-selection capabilities. <Cite refs={["turn998014search1","turn998014search2"]}/>

That is sufficient to build the first generation of our scheduler without depending on experimental work-graph functionality.

## 7. Where the real bottlenecks will be

The biggest threats aren't necessarily dispatch overhead. They are memory traffic, contention, and dependencies.

| Bottleneck | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Global atomic contention | Per-chunk counters, local aggregation, parallel prefix scans |
| Scattered memory access | SoA/AoSoA storage, spatial work ordering |
| Excessive barriers | Graph-based synchronization, system fusion |
| Frequent archetype migrations | Batch structural changes at designated boundaries |
| GPU allocator contention | Per-chunk allocation pools and batched free lists |
| Read-after-write dependencies | Versioned state, independent work overlap |
| Divergent GPU workloads | Classify and compact entities into coherent batches |
| CPU readback stalls | Asynchronous event queues and timeline completion |
| GPU overloaded by simulation | Explicit budgets and scheduling priorities |
| Highly irregular gameplay logic | Keep unsuitable work on CPU |

One particularly important issue for our MMO: **rendering and simulation share the same GPU resources**.

A million GPU ECS entities might be inexpensive to process individually, but a heavy simulation pass can still compete with mesh shaders, fragment shaders, and memory bandwidth.

We should not let low-priority vegetation simulation delay critical player rendering.

## 8. Proposed scheduler priorities

I'd establish distinct workload classes:

    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

These are scheduling priorities, not guarantees of GPU hardware preemption. Dispatch granularity and critical-path ordering still matter.

Before building the full ECS, I would benchmark a minimal scheduler with synthetic but realistic workloads.

I'd capture GPU execution time, critical-path latency, memory bandwidth, cache behavior, atomic contention, barrier costs, CPU submission overhead, and frame-time stability.

We should compare against both a conventional CPU-scheduled Vulkan baseline and a GPU-indirect implementation without our custom ECS scheduler. Otherwise, we risk attributing speedups to the scheduler that actually came from contiguous data layout or eliminating CPU readbacks.

  - **CPU:** Compile/record execution graph, manage resources, handle authoritative and external state.
  - **GPU:** Select active entities, build work lists, process ECS component streams, and generate downstream work.
  - **Synchronization:** GPU-local dependency barriers, cross-queue timeline semaphores, no per-entity host waits.
  - **Memory:** Persistent chunked SoA/AoSoA, single-writer partitions, versioned snapshots where beneficial.
  - **Advanced scheduling:** Work graphs and persistent kernels as measured optimizations rather than mandatory dependencies.
</box>

**My assessment:** This is an achievable architecture with current Vulkan primitives. Efficient GPU-side work generation is supported today; fully arbitrary GPU runtime scheduling is not necessary to deliver the benefits we're targeting.

The biggest remaining design question is **whether ECS structural changes—entity creation, destruction, component addition/removal, archetype migration, and allocation—should also be GPU-native**.

I recommend yes for GPU-owned entities, with batched mutation, deferred publication, generational handles, and a dedicated GPU allocator. That's the natural next layer of the architecture, and one of the hardest parts to implement well.

## 7. Where the real bottlenecks will be

The biggest threats aren't necessarily dispatch overhead. They are memory traffic, contention, and dependencies.

| Bottleneck | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Global atomic contention | Per-chunk counters, local aggregation, parallel prefix scans |
| Scattered memory access | SoA/AoSoA storage, spatial work ordering |
| Excessive barriers | Graph-based synchronization, system fusion |
| Frequent archetype migrations | Batch structural changes at designated boundaries |
| GPU allocator contention | Per-chunk allocation pools and batched free lists |
| Read-after-write dependencies | Versioned state, independent work overlap |
| Divergent GPU workloads | Classify and compact entities into coherent batches |
| CPU readback stalls | Asynchronous event queues and timeline completion |
| GPU overloaded by simulation | Explicit budgets and scheduling priorities |
| Highly irregular gameplay logic | Keep unsuitable work on CPU |

One particularly important issue for our MMO: **rendering and simulation share the same GPU resources**.

A million GPU ECS entities might be inexpensive to process individually, but a heavy simulation pass can still compete with mesh shaders, fragment shaders, and memory bandwidth.

We should not let low-priority vegetation simulation delay critical player rendering.

## 8. Proposed scheduler priorities

I'd establish distinct workload classes:

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{name:"Latency-critical",sub:"Input response, essential transforms, visible UI",p:1},{name:"Frame-critical",sub:"Animation, culling, meshlet generation, rendering dependencies",p:2},{name:"Simulation",sub:"Particles, physics subsets, crowd updates",p:3},{name:"Background",sub:"Spatial hierarchy maintenance, procedural generation, streaming preparation",p:4}] as x}
    <row align="center" gap={3}>
      <box background="surface-tertiary" radius="md" size="40px" align="center" justify="center">
        <title size="md" color="default" tabularNums>{x.p}</title>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{x.name}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.sub}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

These are scheduling priorities, not guarantees of GPU hardware preemption. Dispatch granularity and critical-path ordering still matter.

## 9. How we prove it works

Before building the full ECS, I would benchmark a minimal scheduler with synthetic but realistic workloads.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Proposed benchmark configurations</text>
  {@body const [entities,setEntities] = DIL.useState("1000000")}
  {@body const [mode,setMode] = DIL.useState("indirect")}
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Active entity count</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={entities} onChange={setEntities}>
      <radio value="100000">100,000</radio>
      <radio value="1000000">1 million</radio>
      <radio value="10000000">10 million</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Scheduler approach</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={mode} onChange={setMode}>
      <radio value="indirect">Compiled graph + GPU indirect dispatch</radio>
      <radio value="workgraph">Work graphs / device-generated commands</radio>
      <radio value="persistent">Persistent-kernel work queues</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <button block color="primary" onClick={()=>GenUI.issueNewTurn("Design a detailed GPU ECS scheduling benchmark for "+Number(entities).toLocaleString("en-US")+" active entities, using "+({indirect:"compiled graph and indirect dispatch",workgraph:"device-generated commands/work graphs",persistent:"persistent-kernel work queues"})[mode]+". Specify data layouts, test workloads, instrumentation, correctness tests, synchronization measurements, and pass/fail thresholds. No C++.")}>Develop benchmark specification <icon name="arrow-right" inline/></button>
</box>

I'd capture GPU execution time, critical-path latency, memory bandwidth, cache behavior, atomic contention, barrier costs, CPU submission overhead, and frame-time stability.

We should compare against both a conventional CPU-scheduled Vulkan baseline and a GPU-indirect implementation without our custom ECS scheduler. Otherwise, we risk attributing speedups to the scheduler that actually came from contiguous data layout or eliminating CPU readbacks.

Agreed. We'll lock **GPU-native ECS structural mutation** into the engine architecture.

This means GPU-owned entities can be created, destroyed, migrated between archetypes, and compacted without CPU involvement in individual operations.

### Core design decisions

- **GPU-native allocation:** Pooled chunk allocators, free lists, and generational handles.
- **Deferred structural mutations:** Spawn, despawn, and component-change requests enter GPU-resident command queues.
- **Batched archetype migrations:** Compact and relocate component data using parallel scans and GPU compute.

- **GPU-managed spatial membership:** Incremental Morton/spatial-index updates.
- **Epoch-based publication:** Systems see consistent entity/component state at defined synchronization boundaries.

One important constraint: memory reclamation must respect in-flight GPU readers. Generational handles alone don't make immediate reuse safe.

Message ID: `a11e99d0-a3fa-4361-9c83-65629234f9b7` · 2026-10-08T01:48:54.888870+00:00

# GPU Memory Architecture — Phase 04
<text color="secondary" size="sm" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · GPU-Native ECS · Memory, Allocation & Residency</text>

We now have the core direction: a **GPU-primary ECS with contiguous storage, GPU-native entity mutations, GPU-driven scheduling, and mesh/task-shader rendering**.

The next challenge is making millions of entities practical without memory fragmentation, expensive allocations, scattered reads, or synchronization stalls.

My recommended architecture is:

**Virtual GPU memory arenas + chunked archetype SoA + generational entity handles + GPU allocation pools + deferred compaction + hierarchical residency management.**

One crucial distinction: the ECS must own *logical* memory allocation, but Vulkan and the host still manage *physical* GPU memory allocation and binding. Shader code cannot simply create arbitrary new Vulkan allocations.

## 1. Split GPU memory into specialized arenas

I would not put the entire engine inside one massive universal memory allocator.

Instead, establish several GPU memory domains, each with its own lifetime and access patterns.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU VIRTUAL MEMORY / RESOURCE MANAGER**

    <caption>Vulkan allocations · Resource tables · Budgets · Device addresses</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{t:"ECS component arena",d:"Dense SoA / AoSoA chunks"},{t:"Entity metadata arena",d:"Handles, generations, locations"},{t:"Spatial arena",d:"Morton keys, bounds, BVHs"},{t:"Geometry arena",d:"Meshlets, clusters, instances"},{t:"Dynamic work arena",d:"Queues, counters, scans, sorting"},{t:"UI + typography arena",d:"UI nodes, glyphs, Bézier curves"},{t:"Streaming arena",d:"Upload staging and resource pages"},{t:"Transient frame arena",d:"Temporary pass resources"}] as a}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={3} minHeight="92px" gap={1}>
          <text weight="medium" size="sm">{a.t}</text>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{a.d}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

This separation matters because each type of memory behaves differently.

For example, ECS component chunks experience entity creation, destruction and migration, whereas compressed mesh geometry is relatively static. Sorting scratch buffers are short-lived, while font Bézier curves can remain resident for long periods.

One allocator strategy cannot efficiently serve all those requirements.

Vulkan's own guidance favours larger allocations with application-managed suballocation rather than an excessive number of small device-memory allocations. <Cite ref="turn138358search8"/>

## 2. Chunked archetype storage

Our ECS should primarily use **dense, fixed-capacity component chunks**.

Each archetype represents a component composition, and each chunk contains contiguous columns for entities belonging to that archetype.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Example: moving character archetype</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Archetype 017**
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Chunk capacity: 256 entities</text>
    </row>
    {#each [{n:"Entity slot IDs",c:"#91A4BA"},{n:"Positions",c:"#4B96D1"},{n:"Rotations",c:"#AF8BD8"},{n:"Velocities",c:"#46A58B"},{n:"Animation state",c:"#D0A35A"},{n:"Render references",c:"#D98278"}] as column}
      <row align="center" gap={2}>
        <box width="105px">
          <text size="2xs">{column.n}</text>
        </box>
        <row flex="1" gap="2px">
          {#each Array.from({length:12},(_,i)=>i) as i}
            <box flex="1" height="17px" radius="2xs" background={column.c}/>
          {/each}
        </row>
      </row>
    {/each}
  </box>
  <caption>The diagram illustrates logical SoA columns. Their byte sizes and alignments differ in physical storage.</caption>
</box>

### Why fixed-capacity chunks?

They give us predictable allocation units, efficient parallel processing, simple indexing, bounded compaction work, and a natural granularity for scheduling GPU jobs.

But I would **not lock a universal 16 KB, 32 KB, or 64 KB ECS chunk size** yet.

Different archetypes have dramatically different row widths. A character with animation state and a projectile with position and velocity should not necessarily use the same capacity.

Instead, define chunk classes and select them by measured workload.

| Proposed chunk class | Intended workload |
|---|---|
| Small | Frequently changing compositions and low-population archetypes |
| Medium | General-purpose gameplay and visual entities |
| Large | Extremely dense, stable component streams |
| Specialized | Particles, procedural instances, and high-throughput simulation |

These are design categories, not yet fixed byte sizes.

### Physical layout

I would prefer each component column to be contiguous *within a chunk*, with a descriptor specifying its offset and stride.

That means a GPU system can access a chunk's position column directly without reading other components.

A simplified chunk descriptor:

```rust
struct ChunkDescriptor {
    archetype_id: u32,
    capacity: u32,
    live_count: u32,
    generation: u32,
    component_base_offsets: /* schema-defined */,
    occupancy_bits: /* separate arena reference */,
}
```

This is a conceptual host-side representation, not a finalized binary ABI. Actual GPU descriptors should be fixed-size and aligned for the target shader layout.

One important optimization: **do not load the chunk descriptor for every entity**. Resolve it per workgroup or batch, then perform sequential component accesses.
