## 031 — Assistant

Message ID: `c5a23bd1-bb31-427d-9276-af814bfdc525` · 2026-10-08T01:49:13.528782+00:00

## 3. Entity identity must never depend on physical memory

This is mandatory if we want GPU compaction and relocation.

A handle should refer to an entity slot, not a permanent byte address.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">GPU handle resolution</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Entity Handle**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Slot index + generation</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Entity Location Table**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Validate generation → Archetype + Chunk + Row</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Contiguous Component Arrays**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Access required component columns at resolved row</text>
  </box>
</box>

When an entity migrates to another archetype or moves during compaction, only its location mapping needs updating. References using its handle remain valid.

We should also distinguish:

- **Persistent World ID:** Identifies the entity across persistence, networking, and server migration.
- **Local GPU Entity Handle:** Efficiently identifies a resident entity on one GPU, with generation validation.
- **Archetype/Chunk/Row:** Temporary physical storage location.

For high-throughput systems, we avoid resolving handles repeatedly by operating directly on dense chunk rows. Handle resolution happens primarily at relationship boundaries or irregular accesses.

A generational handle does not solve every lifetime hazard. We still need generation-wrap policy, duplicate-free protection, and deferred reuse until previous readers have finished.

## 4. GPU-native memory allocation

I would implement a hierarchical allocation strategy rather than rely on one global atomic free list.

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">01</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Host-managed physical arena**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Rust/Vulkan creates large backing buffers, manages device allocation, and grows the available physical capacity when needed.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">02</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **GPU-managed chunk pool**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">GPU shaders claim/release fixed-capacity chunks from preallocated pools using scalable free-list structures.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">03</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Chunk-local slot allocation**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Spawns and migrations claim slots using occupancy bitsets, reserved ranges, or batched allocation counters.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">04</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Deferred reclamation**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Destroyed entities and emptied chunks return to free pools only after all relevant in-flight readers are finished.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

### Avoiding atomic contention

Imagine 100,000 particles spawning at once. We should not issue 100,000 independent atomic operations on one global allocator counter if a few bulk reservations can achieve the same result.

Instead:

1. Count allocation requests per chunk or workgroup.
2. Use parallel prefix sums to calculate output ranges.
3. Reserve destination capacity in batches.
4. Assign entity slots in parallel.
5. Publish new entities after their component initialization completes.

For small, low-frequency mutations, a simpler atomic allocator may be preferable. The scheduler should support both.

**Out-of-memory handling must be explicit.** If a GPU pool is exhausted, the allocation request returns a failure or capacity-request record. The host expands backing storage asynchronously where possible. Critical entities must never silently disappear because a GPU allocator ran out of slots.

## 5. Structural mutations should be transactional at epoch boundaries

This is how we avoid synchronization chaos.

A system does not immediately rearrange archetype storage while another system is reading it.

Instead, it emits structural commands:

```rust
enum StructuralCommand {
    Spawn { archetype: u32, payload_ref: u32 },
    Despawn { entity: u64 },
    AddComponent { entity: u64, component: u32 },
    RemoveComponent { entity: u64, component: u32 },
}
```

Conceptually these become packed GPU command records, not a direct Rust enum ABI.

### Proposed GPU mutation pipeline

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU systems emit mutation requests**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Validate + resolve conflicts**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Group by destination archetype**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Count + reserve destination slots**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Copy retained components + initialize new ones**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Publish location-table changes**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Retire old slots after reader completion**
  </box>
</box>

Multiple conflicting changes to the same entity must have deterministic resolution rules.

For example, a despawn and add-component command targeting the same entity cannot be applied in arbitrary order. We should define mutation priorities and, where necessary, stable command sequence numbers.

A useful distinction is **logical mutation atomicity**, which we can enforce at publication, versus globally deterministic execution, which is a stronger requirement and may require extra sorting and ordering costs.

We should also keep GPU-initiated structural mutations separate from authoritative network changes. A GPU-only particle may despawn immediately according to client simulation policy; an authoritative inventory entity cannot be destroyed locally just because a shader requested it.

```rust
    component_base_offsets: /* schema-defined */,
    occupancy_bits: /* separate arena reference */,
}
```

This is a conceptual host-side representation, not a finalized binary ABI. Actual GPU descriptors should be fixed-size and aligned for the target shader layout.

One important optimization: **do not load the chunk descriptor for every entity**. Resolve it per workgroup or batch, then perform sequential component accesses.

## 3. Entity identity must never depend on physical memory

This is mandatory if we want GPU compaction and relocation.

A handle should refer to an entity slot, not a permanent byte address.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">GPU handle resolution</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Entity Handle**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Slot index + generation</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Entity Location Table**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Validate generation → Archetype + Chunk + Row</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Contiguous Component Arrays**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Access required component columns at resolved row</text>
  </box>
</box>

When an entity migrates to another archetype or moves during compaction, only its location mapping needs updating. References using its handle remain valid.

We should also distinguish:

- **Persistent World ID:** Identifies the entity across persistence, networking, and server migration.
- **Local GPU Entity Handle:** Efficiently identifies a resident entity on one GPU, with generation validation.
- **Archetype/Chunk/Row:** Temporary physical storage location.

For high-throughput systems, we avoid resolving handles repeatedly by operating directly on dense chunk rows. Handle resolution happens primarily at relationship boundaries or irregular accesses.

A generational handle does not solve every lifetime hazard. We still need generation-wrap policy, duplicate-free protection, and deferred reuse until previous readers have finished.

## 4. GPU-native memory allocation

I would implement a hierarchical allocation strategy rather than rely on one global atomic free list.

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">01</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Host-managed physical arena**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Rust/Vulkan creates large backing buffers, manages device allocation, and grows the available physical capacity when needed.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">02</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **GPU-managed chunk pool**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">GPU shaders claim/release fixed-capacity chunks from preallocated pools using scalable free-list structures.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">03</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Chunk-local slot allocation**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Spawns and migrations claim slots using occupancy bitsets, reserved ranges, or batched allocation counters.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" size="44px" justify="center" align="center">
      <title size="md">04</title>
    </box>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Deferred reclamation**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Destroyed entities and emptied chunks return to free pools only after all relevant in-flight readers are finished.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

### Avoiding atomic contention

Imagine 100,000 particles spawning at once. We should not issue 100,000 independent atomic operations on one global allocator counter if a few bulk reservations can achieve the same result.

Instead:

1. Count allocation requests per chunk or workgroup.
2. Use parallel prefix sums to calculate output ranges.
3. Reserve destination capacity in batches.
4. Assign entity slots in parallel.
5. Publish new entities after their component initialization completes.

For small, low-frequency mutations, a simpler atomic allocator may be preferable. The scheduler should support both.

**Out-of-memory handling must be explicit.** If a GPU pool is exhausted, the allocation request returns a failure or capacity-request record. The host expands backing storage asynchronously where possible. Critical entities must never silently disappear because a GPU allocator ran out of slots.

## 5. Structural mutations should be transactional at epoch boundaries

This is how we avoid synchronization chaos.

A system does not immediately rearrange archetype storage while another system is reading it.

Instead, it emits structural commands:

```rust
enum StructuralCommand {
    Spawn { archetype: u32, payload_ref: u32 },
    Despawn { entity: u64 },
    AddComponent { entity: u64, component: u32 },
    RemoveComponent { entity: u64, component: u32 },
}
```

Conceptually these become packed GPU command records, not a direct Rust enum ABI.

### Proposed GPU mutation pipeline

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU systems emit mutation requests**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Validate + resolve conflicts**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Group by destination archetype**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Count + reserve destination slots**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Copy retained components + initialize new ones**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Publish location-table changes**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Retire old slots after reader completion**
  </box>
</box>

Multiple conflicting changes to the same entity must have deterministic resolution rules.

For example, a despawn and add-component command targeting the same entity cannot be applied in arbitrary order. We should define mutation priorities and, where necessary, stable command sequence numbers.

A useful distinction is **logical mutation atomicity**, which we can enforce at publication, versus globally deterministic execution, which is a stronger requirement and may require extra sorting and ordering costs.

We should also keep GPU-initiated structural mutations separate from authoritative network changes. A GPU-only particle may despawn immediately according to client simulation policy; an authoritative inventory entity cannot be destroyed locally just because a shader requested it.

## 6. Compaction without stalling the GPU

Even with contiguous chunks, spawning and despawning create holes.

I'd use two levels of compaction.

### Local compaction

Within a chunk, move live rows into unused slots and update their location-table entries.

This should be cheap enough for selected chunks, although moving rows still requires copying all retained component columns.

### Global compaction

When many chunks belonging to an archetype become underutilized, consolidate them and return empty chunks to their pools.

**Global compaction should be incremental and budgeted**, not a mandatory full-memory operation.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Interactive compaction policy example</text>
  {@body const [occupancy,setOccupancy] = DIL.useState(45)}
  {@body const [threshold,setThreshold] = DIL.useState(50)}
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <label>Chunk occupancy</label>
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{occupancy}%</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={0} max={100} step={5} value={occupancy} onChange={setOccupancy}/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <label>Compaction threshold</label>
    <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{threshold}%</text>
  </row>
  <slider min={10} max={90} step={5} value={threshold} onChange={setThreshold}/>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      <text weight="medium">Example decision</text>
      <badge color={occupancy<threshold?"warning":"secondary"}>{occupancy<threshold?"Candidate":"Retain"}</badge>
    </row>
    <text size="sm" color="secondary">{occupancy<threshold?"This chunk could be queued for compaction if suitable destination capacity exists and the expected memory benefit exceeds relocation cost.":"Keep the chunk in place; no occupancy-triggered compaction is indicated."}</text>
  </box>
  <caption>Illustrative policy only. Actual thresholds should account for mutation frequency, component width, relocation bytes, and memory pressure.</caption>
</box>

A critical optimization would be **compaction hysteresis**: we don't want an archetype repeatedly compacting and expanding because population fluctuates near a threshold.

I would also favour stable storage for certain GPU data structures. Not everything needs continuous compaction.

## 7. GPU memory addressing: buffer device addresses

For the core memory layer, I recommend Vulkan **Buffer Device Address (BDA)**.

It allows shaders to access buffers through GPU virtual addresses. It's core in Vulkan 1.2 and required in Vulkan 1.3, making it an excellent foundation for our target. <Cite ref="turn138358search1"/>

We can maintain a GPU-resident directory of chunk locations rather than bind a new storage buffer for every archetype.

For example:

```text
Archetype 17
    Chunk 0 → Buffer address + column offsets
    Chunk 1 → Buffer address + column offsets
    Chunk 2 → Buffer address + column offsets
```

However, **we should not expose raw device addresses as permanent component references**.

Addresses can become stale after allocation relocation or resource replacement. Handles and indirection tables remain the safer public representation.

BDA also requires strict adherence to shader memory alignment rules. Khronos documents that incorrect alignment declarations can produce invalid or inefficient accesses. <Cite ref="turn138358search0"/>

## 8. Sparse residency: powerful, but use selectively

Vulkan sparse resources let us reserve virtual resources and bind backing memory non-contiguously, changing those bindings over time. <Cite ref="turn138358search3"/>

That sounds ideal for a huge MMO, but I wouldn't make sparse allocation mandatory for every ECS buffer.

| Resource | Preferred strategy |
|---|---|
| Hot ECS components | Fully backed device-local chunks |
| Entity metadata | Persistent backed buffers |
| Work queues and scratch | Reusable transient arenas |
| Massive texture datasets | Virtual texturing / sparse images |
| Large geometry datasets | Paged geometry residency |
| Inactive world regions | Stream or evict GPU representations |
| Sparse ECS backing | Optional advanced implementation |

Why?

Sparse binding is not ordinary shader-side allocation. Vulkan sparse memory bindings are submitted as queue operations and must be synchronized with users of the affected memory. <Cite ref="turn138358search6"/>

For high-frequency entity allocation, preallocated GPU chunk pools should generally be simpler.

For enormous geometry, terrain, and texture resources, sparse residency becomes far more attractive.

## 9. Entity-scale memory model

Before choosing arena sizes, we should distinguish entities that need complete GPU state from those requiring only lightweight visual state.

The following is a **hypothetical storage scenario**, not a measured benchmark.

| Entity type | Example bytes/entity | 1 million entities |
|---|---:|---:|
| Minimal procedural instance | 32 B | ~30.5 MiB |
| Lightweight visual entity | 64 B | ~61 MiB |
| Moving gameplay replica | 128 B | ~122 MiB |
| Animated presentation entity | 256 B | ~244 MiB |
| Rich presentation entity | 512 B | ~488 MiB |

These estimates exclude many shared or auxiliary resources, including meshes, textures, skeletal palettes, spatial acceleration structures, allocator metadata, unused chunk capacity, and rendering buffers.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text weight="medium">GPU ECS capacity estimator</text>
  {@body const [count,setCount] = DIL.useState("1000000")}
  {@body const [bytes,setBytes] = DIL.useState("128")}
  {@body const [overhead,setOverhead] = DIL.useState(25)}
  {@body const total = Number(count)*Number(bytes)*(1+overhead/100)}
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Resident entities</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={count} onChange={setCount}>
      <radio value="100000">100,000</radio>
      <radio value="1000000">1 million</radio>
      <radio value="10000000">10 million</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Component bytes per entity</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={bytes} onChange={setBytes}>
      <radio value="64">64 bytes — lightweight</radio>
      <radio value="128">128 bytes — moderate</radio>
      <radio value="256">256 bytes — animation-heavy</radio>
      <radio value="512">512 bytes — rich</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    <row justify="between" align="center">
      <label>Reserved overhead allowance</label>
      <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{overhead}%</text>
    </row>
    <slider min={0} max={100} step={5} value={overhead} onChange={setOverhead}/>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Component storage</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{(Number(count)*Number(bytes)/1073741824).toFixed(2)} GiB</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Including allowance</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{(total/1073741824).toFixed(2)} GiB</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <caption>Excludes geometry, textures, render targets and other major GPU resources. Overhead is an adjustable planning assumption.</caption>
</box>

The conclusion is important: **storing millions of lightweight entities is not necessarily the hard part.**

Keeping millions of complex entities *actively processing* at real-time frequency while sharing the GPU with high-end rendering is much harder.

Our architecture must separate storage residency from active execution.

## 10. Synchronization and memory lifetime

I would use an epoch-oriented memory model.

Each published ECS epoch has a consistent location-table view and component data lifetime. Structural changes are prepared separately, then published at a defined dependency boundary.

Readers may continue accessing earlier snapshots where permitted. Allocations referenced by those readers cannot be reclaimed until the relevant GPU work has completed.

Two useful rules:

- **Publish metadata atomically at the appropriate granularity, after initialization and proper memory dependencies.**
- **Reclaim physical storage only after the last GPU reader has completed, not merely after an entity is marked dead.**

We can often avoid copying the entire ECS between epochs. Only resources that truly require overlapping mutable and immutable versions need versioned storage.

For synchronization, prefer declared compute-to-compute barriers and queue-level coordination, not a global device idle. Async compute is useful only when the hardware can overlap it profitably and memory dependencies allow it.

## 11. The memory architecture I'd lock

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{name:"Hierarchical GPU arenas",desc:"Separate allocators for ECS, geometry, spatial data, scratch, and UI."},{name:"Chunked SoA/AoSoA archetypes",desc:"Dense, processor-friendly storage with workload-specific chunk classes."},{name:"Generational identity and location indirection",desc:"Relocation without invalidating logical entity references."},{name:"GPU-native structural mutations",desc:"Batched allocation, migration, compaction, and publication."},{name:"BDA-backed buffer directories",desc:"Fast GPU access without making device pointers stable identities."},{name:"Selective sparse residency",desc:"Primarily for large streamable geometry, textures, and world resources."},{name:"Epoch-safe memory reclamation",desc:"Prevent relocation and reuse from racing GPU readers."},{name:"Incremental, budgeted maintenance",desc:"No mandatory full-world compaction or rebuilding per frame."}] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{item.name}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{item.desc}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 12. What comes next

The next major architectural problem is **world residency and streaming**.

This connects everything we've discussed:

- The persistent world may contain billions of logical entities.
- Server workers simulate relevant subsets.
- Each client maintains a smaller replicated world.
- The GPU stores only the presentation and simulation data it needs.
- Only a fraction of GPU-resident entities require processing every frame.

I'd scope **hierarchical world partitioning, spatial streaming, and active-set management** next, including how content cells, Morton hierarchies, ECS archetypes, networking interest, and GPU residency work together.

That will let us design a seamless world where total persistent world size is largely decoupled from per-frame rendering and simulation cost.

# World Partitioning & GPU Residency
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Phase 05 · October 2026</text>

The next major subsystem is **how we represent a virtually unlimited persistent world while keeping only the relevant portion active, replicated, GPU-resident, and rendered**.

Our target should be substantially more sophisticated than traditional distance-based loading.

I recommend a **hierarchical, Morton-addressed world with GPU-driven residency and active-set selection, independently partitioned server authority, and predictive asynchronous streaming**.

The central architectural rule:

> **World existence, simulation activity, client replication, GPU residency, and visual detail must be independently controlled.**

An entity should be able to exist permanently without being simulated every frame, replicated to every player, or allocated in local GPU memory.

## 1. The five independent views of the world

  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>

  </box>

      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} minHeight="88px">
          <text weight="medium" size="sm">{x.t}</text>

  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

  </box>
  <caption textAlign="center">Conceptual relationships, not a single strict subset hierarchy. Different views have different ownership and update policies.</caption>
</box>

A distant castle, for example, may be represented by a coarse visual proxy without the client receiving its individual interactive entities.

Likewise, an off-screen combat encounter may require authoritative simulation and replication even though none of its geometry is currently rendered.

This separation is foundational to MMO scalability.

## 2. Spatial architecture: hierarchical cells plus Morton codes

I would use a hierarchical spatial-addressing system over a very large, stable world coordinate space.

For an overworld, a sparse quadtree is often preferable to a full 3D octree when most content occupies a relatively thin terrain surface. We can use octrees or specialised 3D indexes for caves, vertical cities, underwater environments, and other volumetric areas.

Our general spatial key would conceptually contain:

`World ID + Spatial Level + Cell Coordinates`

Morton codes would accelerate indexing and locality within supported coordinate ranges.

### Proposed hierarchy

I would not force all spatial systems to use the exact same physical cell size.

| Spatial level | Purpose | Initial design direction |
|---|---|---|
| World / shard | Persistent world identity | Stable, non-spatial identity namespace |
| Region | World content and administrative locality | Large, stable regions |
| Streaming cell | Loadable scene/content metadata | Hierarchical cells, independent of server worker |
| Spatial leaf | Nearby-object indexing | Morton bins / grid / dynamic BVH |
| Geometry cluster | Fine-grained visual detail | GPU virtualized geometry hierarchy |
| Resource page | Actual VRAM residency | Allocator-dependent memory granularity |

We should also support content spanning cell boundaries. A large fortress or moving ship cannot be assumed to fit inside one leaf cell.

I would use a canonical owner plus multi-cell spatial references where needed, so crossing a cell boundary does not duplicate or destroy the entity.

## 3. Partitioning the simulation independently

This is the most important MMO-specific distinction.

**A streaming cell is not a simulation server.**

The world could have tens of thousands of small content cells, with a smaller number of active simulation workers responsible for subsets of their entities.

Our distributed authority directory would conceptually map:

`World region / simulation partition → authoritative worker + ownership epoch`

Ownership should be adjustable as population and workloads change.

For example, a quiet valley could be managed as one large simulation partition. A crowded capital could require finer assignment of responsibilities.

But spatial partitioning is not enough on its own. A 5,000-player encounter in a tiny area can still create heavy cross-partition interactions.

I would plan for:

- Authority transfer with explicit ownership versions.
- Neighbour-state exchange or ghost replicas for cross-partition simulation.
- Server-controlled replication interest.
- Load-aware partitioning rather than fixed-size worker grids.
- Explicit handling of interactions spanning simulation boundaries.

The GPU-primary **client ECS remains separate from these server authority boundaries**.

No client's GPU state should decide whether a character legitimately exists or whether an authoritative action succeeds.

## 4. GPU-driven world streaming: demand rather than distance alone

A simple distance threshold is not enough for a next-generation renderer.

I recommend a **hierarchical demand-driven residency system** that combines camera visibility, projected detail, occlusion history, player movement, gameplay importance, and network interest.

A world cell should progress through independently tracked states rather than one `Loaded` boolean.

| Residency state | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indexed** | Metadata and content references are known |
| **Requested** | Streaming demand has been registered |
| **Staged** | Asset data is available in a host-side staging buffer |
| **GPU-resident** | Required GPU data has been uploaded and published |
| **Active** | Content is included in relevant GPU processing lists |
| **Retiring** | No new users admitted; outstanding GPU readers complete |
| **Evicted** | GPU backing reclaimed; persistent world state remains |

A cell can also have partially resident geometry, textures, animation data, or entity state. Residency must therefore be tracked per resource family or page where finer control is needed.

### Proposed streaming process

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium" color="secondary" size="xs">GPU / CPU STREAMING LOOP</text>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU demand analysis**

    <caption>Camera motion · Hierarchical visibility · Screen-space error · Gameplay priorities</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU page requests + priority queue**

    <caption>Deduplicated missing resource IDs · Requested detail level</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust streaming service**

    <caption>Asynchronous feedback readback · Local storage / network I/O · Decompression planning</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Resource upload + residency publication**

    <caption>Staging transfers · GPU decompression where suitable · Page-table updates</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU scene / ECS activation**

    <caption>Update resident resource references · Generate active work lists</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="refresh-cw" color="secondary"/> <text size="xs" color="secondary">Continuous bounded feedback</text></row>
</box>

The GPU performs fine-grained demand generation, but the host handles filesystem I/O, network fetching, Vulkan allocation, and physical resource binding.

This is not a CPU-driven visibility pipeline: the host reads compact resource requests rather than traversing every world entity.

### Predictive streaming

I would support multiple streaming predictors simultaneously:

- Camera position, velocity, and direction.
- Player movement and likely traversal path.
- Known teleport destinations and portals.
- Gameplay transitions such as entering an interior.
- Server-provided relevance and imminent entity spawns.
- GPU visibility and missing-page feedback.

We should prioritize **latency-sensitive missing resources over speculative distant detail**, and reserve budget for unforeseen camera movements.

For very large content, coarser representations must be available before fine-grained pages. This prevents a single missing detail page from making an entire city disappear.

## 5. Hierarchical visual detail is not the same as world streaming

This is where our mesh/task shader architecture connects to world partitioning.

Consider a city with millions of source triangles and thousands of individual logical entities.

We should not require every source mesh or individual building component to reside in VRAM simultaneously.

Instead, build **a hierarchy of compressed geometry clusters with error-bounded LOD selection**.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **Proposed geometry hierarchy**

  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    Coarse regional representation
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="sm">City district clusters</text></box></grid-item>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="sm">Terrain clusters</text></box></grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={3} gap={2}>
    {#each ["Building groups","Vegetation groups","Rock / terrain detail"] as x}
      <grid-item><box border padding={2} radius="md" align="center" minHeight="61px"><text size="xs" textAlign="center">{x}</text></box></grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Visible meshlets and individual instances**
  </box>
</box>

The GPU can traverse the hierarchy, select appropriate detail, and generate missing-page requests.

Importantly, our content streaming hierarchy and geometry hierarchy can reference one another without sharing identical boundaries.

### Relevant cutting-edge precedent

NVIDIA's RTX Mega Geometry SDK now documents a Cluster LOD path using prebuilt triangle clusters, continuous LOD selection, and GPU-driven on-demand residency under fixed geometry budgets. Its implementation can raise the effective LOD error when pools are under pressure, choosing coarser detail instead of thrashing. <Cite refs={["turn864748search6","turn864748search8"]}/>

That is a particularly useful architectural reference for us, even though we are implementing our own engine and not adopting its native C++ implementation.

I would carry across the principle of **budget-aware detail selection**:

> If resource demand exceeds available memory, reduce detail gracefully before triggering uncontrolled eviction and reload cycles.

That should apply to geometry, textures, vegetation, and optional effects.

## 6. GPU-managed active sets

Every GPU-resident entity should not execute every system on every frame.

Instead, each system processes a compact **active work set** built from component queries, spatial relevance, dirty state, and scheduling policy.

For example:

| Active set | Selection policy |
|---|---|
| Critical characters | Relevant player and character state |
| Visible animation | Visible or soon-to-be-visible animated entities |
| Nearby effects | Distance, visibility and lifetime |
| Dynamic transforms | Dirty transform components and dependencies |
| Spatial updates | Entities whose spatial membership or bounds changed |
| GPU rendering | Frustum, occlusion and LOD selection |
| UI | Dirty nodes, animation, visible panels |

These sets are not all subsets of one another. A hidden transform can still need updating because it influences a visible child.

### Scheduling frequencies

I'd use **independent execution frequencies** rather than apply one frame rate to everything.

| Workload | Proposed policy |
|---|---|
| Player input and presentation-critical updates | Frame-critical |
| Authoritative simulation | Fixed server ticks, separate from render cadence |
| Nearby visual animation | Frame-frequency where necessary |
| Distant visual animation | Reduced frequency or analytic time evaluation |
| Stationary structures | Event-driven updates |
| Environmental effects | Variable frequency, quality-dependent |
| Spatial hierarchy maintenance | Incremental dirty-region updates |
| Background streaming | Budget-driven, asynchronous |

The important point is to avoid tying simulation correctness to client render frequency. Any reduced-frequency gameplay simulation must be a deliberate server-side rule, not a consequence of GPU visibility.

## 7. Budgeted residency: avoid the memory-thrashing problem

A streaming system can become unstable if it continuously evicts and reloads resources as the player moves.

I would use a **multi-budget residency manager**, with separate accounting for ECS data, geometry, textures, animation, spatial structures, and scratch memory.

  </box>
  <caption>Illustrative proportions only. Render targets, ray-tracing acceleration structures, driver reservations and other resources also need to be accounted for when defining actual heap budgets.</caption>
</box>

### Eviction policy

I would use a hybrid of priority, recency, predicted future use, resource cost, and reload latency.

Resource eviction should generally follow these principles:

1. Protect essential low-detail fallback pages.
2. Prefer evicting optional high-detail pages before complete scene representations.
3. Use hysteresis and residency minimum lifetimes.
4. Avoid evicting pages currently referenced by GPU work.
5. Track real available memory and reserve headroom for unpredictable activity.

Vulkan sparse resources support rebinding memory and partially resident images, but the residency system must synchronize binding changes with resource use. <Cite ref="turn864748search3"/>

## 8. Seamless world streaming and transitions

The architecture should handle more than walking across terrain.

| Scenario | Architectural requirement |
|---|---|
| Walking across cell boundaries | Overlapping residency windows; no entity recreation |
| High-speed vehicles | Velocity-aware streaming lookahead |
| Teleportation | Prewarm destination before revealing full scene where possible |
| Buildings and interiors | Portal- and relationship-aware streaming |
| Flying above the world | Larger coverage, coarser geometry and terrain |
| Crowded MMO city | Population-aware entity prioritization and simulation budgets |
| Moving ships and structures | Persistent scene instances with moving reference frames |
| Dynamic world destruction | Versioned changes and selective invalidation of visual proxies |
| Multiple cameras | Union of view demands, prioritized under one shared budget |

For moving ships or other mobile scene instances, I would separate their **local scene-space content** from the ship's global transform. That avoids reassigning every child to different world streaming cells simply because the ship moves.

For dynamic destruction, we need to invalidate stale aggregate representations. A distant proxy showing an intact bridge after the bridge has been destroyed would be a world-consistency problem, not just an LOD artifact.

## 9. World partitioning must be decoupled from ECS archetypes

This is an important refinement to our contiguous-memory architecture.

I would not store entities permanently in archetypes belonging to individual world cells.

If we did, an entity crossing a cell boundary could require copying every component into different memory, even though its component composition had not changed.

Instead:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Archetype Storage**
    <caption>Dense, contiguous component chunks</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Spatial Membership Index**
    <caption>Cell IDs → Entity handles / processing ranges</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Active-Set Lists**
    <caption>Compacted references to component rows</caption>
  </box>
</box>

That gives us three independent optimizations:

- Archetypes optimize component iteration.
- Spatial indexing optimizes locality and neighbourhood queries.
- Active-set compaction optimizes the amount of work performed.

For frequently processed spatial entities, we could periodically reorganize selected chunks to improve spatial locality—but this should be a measured optimization, not a requirement for every move.

## 10. Proposed complete world-streaming execution

The system can operate as a continuously updated pipeline:

| Phase | Main processor | Work |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Receive world changes | CPU / network | Receive authoritative state and asset metadata |
| 2. Update client ECS | GPU | Apply resident entity changes and structural mutations |
| 3. Update spatial structures | GPU | Dirty bounds, membership, Morton-ordered indexes |
| 4. Evaluate streaming demand | GPU | View-dependent demand, prediction, page feedback |
| 5. Process external requests | Rust host | Deduplicate requests, resolve assets, initiate I/O |
| 6. Upload resource data | Transfer queue / GPU | Transfer pages, prepare and validate resources |
| 7. Publish residency | GPU + synchronization | Make completed uploads available to GPU consumers |
| 8. Build active sets | GPU | Identify simulation, animation, and rendering workloads |
| 9. Execute systems | GPU | Scheduler dispatches relevant ECS operations |
| 10. Render | GPU mesh/task pipeline | Visibility, geometry, shading, UI |
| 11. Maintenance | GPU / host | Eviction, compaction, reclamation, budget adjustments |

These are logical dependencies, not eleven mandatory serial passes. Independent work can overlap, and many steps need not run every frame.

## 11. Architecture decisions I'd lock now

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{n:"Hierarchical world addressing",d:"Stable world/region/cell identity, with Morton locality and 2D/3D specializations."},{n:"Independent authority boundaries",d:"Server partitions can move and scale separately from content cells."},{n:"GPU-owned residency demand",d:"GPU generates fine-grained active sets, LOD decisions and asset-page requests."},{n:"Rust-managed external streaming",d:"Asynchronous I/O, decompression orchestration, Vulkan resource binding and uploads."},{n:"Virtualized geometry and textures",d:"Page-level streaming with protected fallback detail."},{n:"Residency-aware GPU ECS",d:"Contiguous archetype storage separate from spatial membership and streaming cells."},{n:"Incremental spatial updates",d:"Avoid entire-world Morton sorting or hierarchy rebuilding each frame."},{n:"Budget-driven execution",d:"Bound background work, allocate GPU time and memory explicitly, prevent thrashing."},{n:"Predictive streaming",d:"Use movement, portals, view feedback and gameplay signals to prepare content."}] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{x.n}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 12. The next architectural frontier

With world partitioning established, the next subsystem I'd tackle is **GPU-native spatial queries, physics, and world simulation**.

That means answering questions such as:

- Can one unified spatial infrastructure serve collision broad phase, proximity queries, visibility, and interaction selection?
- Should we use GPU LBVHs, hashed grids, hierarchical Morton bins, or a hybrid?
- How do we handle extremely crowded areas without excessive atomic contention?
- How do we manage GPU collision queries without introducing frame-latency penalties?
- Which simulation systems can be GPU-primary while preserving server authority, reproducibility, and player responsiveness?

I would specifically investigate **a unified spatial addressing layer with multiple specialized acceleration structures**, rather than one universal BVH for everything.

That would tie our GPU ECS, streaming, simulation, and mesh/task rendering into a coherent high-performance world architecture.

## 6. GPU-managed active sets

Every GPU-resident entity should not execute every system on every frame.

Instead, each system processes a compact **active work set** built from component queries, spatial relevance, dirty state, and scheduling policy.

For example:

| Active set | Selection policy |
|---|---|
| Critical characters | Relevant player and character state |
| Visible animation | Visible or soon-to-be-visible animated entities |
| Nearby effects | Distance, visibility and lifetime |
| Dynamic transforms | Dirty transform components and dependencies |
| Spatial updates | Entities whose spatial membership or bounds changed |
| GPU rendering | Frustum, occlusion and LOD selection |
| UI | Dirty nodes, animation, visible panels |

These sets are not all subsets of one another. A hidden transform can still need updating because it influences a visible child.

### Scheduling frequencies

I'd use **independent execution frequencies** rather than apply one frame rate to everything.

| Workload | Proposed policy |
|---|---|
| Player input and presentation-critical updates | Frame-critical |
| Authoritative simulation | Fixed server ticks, separate from render cadence |
| Nearby visual animation | Frame-frequency where necessary |
| Distant visual animation | Reduced frequency or analytic time evaluation |
| Stationary structures | Event-driven updates |
| Environmental effects | Variable frequency, quality-dependent |
| Spatial hierarchy maintenance | Incremental dirty-region updates |
| Background streaming | Budget-driven, asynchronous |

The important point is to avoid tying simulation correctness to client render frequency. Any reduced-frequency gameplay simulation must be a deliberate server-side rule, not a consequence of GPU visibility.

## 7. Budgeted residency: avoid the memory-thrashing problem

A streaming system can become unstable if it continuously evicts and reloads resources as the player moves.

I would use a **multi-budget residency manager**, with separate accounting for ECS data, geometry, textures, animation, spatial structures, and scratch memory.

## 041 — Assistant

Message ID: `4aa6b898-ca01-455e-b1bf-92d94ba8e418` · 2026-10-08T02:46:21.859425+00:00

Yes. You're likely thinking of a **flat uniform spatial grid using direct array indexing**, potentially combined with **Morton-order linearization**.

For a world with predefined dimensions, this can be substantially faster than an octree, quadtree, or BVH for certain spatial operations.

And for our GPU-native MMO ECS, it's an architecture worth seriously considering.

The key idea is:

> **If we already know the world's spatial bounds, we can calculate a cell's memory index directly from its coordinates—without traversing a tree or performing a hash-table lookup.**

## 1. Direct-addressed flat spatial grids

Imagine a world divided into fixed-size cells.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">2D flat grid — direct indexing</text>
  <svg viewBox="0 0 336 190" width="100%">
    {#each Array.from({length:6},(_,i)=>i) as y}
      {#each Array.from({length:10},(_,i)=>i) as x}
        <rect x={25+x*29} y={8+y*25} width="27" height="23" rx="2" fill={x===6&&y===2?"#329A79":(x+y)%2===0?"#8DA5BB":"#BAC9D4"} fillOpacity={x===6&&y===2?0.9:0.3} stroke="currentColor" strokeOpacity=".2"/>
      {/each}
    {/each}
    <text x="25" y="178" fontSize="11" fill="currentColor">index = y × gridWidth + x</text>
    <path d="M 215 70 L 275 165" stroke="#329A79" strokeWidth="1.6" strokeDasharray="4 3"/>
    <text x="272" y="177" fontSize="10" fill="#329A79" textAnchor="middle">O(1) lookup</text>
  </svg>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">Every spatial cell has a deterministic position in one contiguous array. No pointer-based tree traversal.</text>
</box>

For a 3D world:

\[
\text{index}=x+N_x(y+N_yz)
\]

The GPU calculates the index using a few integer operations, retrieves the cell metadata, and processes the associated contiguous entity range.

**This is especially attractive for collision broad-phase, nearby-entity queries, interest management, and spatial work scheduling.**

Message ID: `d6e6b9d7-476e-4730-93a4-859d6a3a4578` · 2026-10-08T02:46:21.867994+00:00

Yes. You're likely thinking of a **flat uniform spatial grid using direct array indexing**, potentially combined with **Morton-order linearization**.

For a world with predefined dimensions, this can be substantially faster than an octree, quadtree, or BVH for certain spatial operations.

And for our GPU-native MMO ECS, it's an architecture worth seriously considering.

The key idea is:

> **If we already know the world's spatial bounds, we can calculate a cell's memory index directly from its coordinates—without traversing a tree or performing a hash-table lookup.**

## 1. Direct-addressed flat spatial grids

Imagine a world divided into fixed-size cells.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">2D flat grid — direct indexing</text>
  <svg viewBox="0 0 336 190" width="100%">
    {#each Array.from({length:6},(_,i)=>i) as y}
      {#each Array.from({length:10},(_,i)=>i) as x}
        <rect x={25+x*29} y={8+y*25} width="27" height="23" rx="2" fill={x===6&&y===2?"#329A79":(x+y)%2===0?"#8DA5BB":"#BAC9D4"} fillOpacity={x===6&&y===2?0.9:0.3} stroke="currentColor" strokeOpacity=".2"/>
      {/each}
    {/each}
    <text x="25" y="178" fontSize="11" fill="currentColor">index = y × gridWidth + x</text>
    <path d="M 215 70 L 275 165" stroke="#329A79" strokeWidth="1.6" strokeDasharray="4 3"/>
    <text x="272" y="177" fontSize="10" fill="#329A79" textAnchor="middle">O(1) lookup</text>
  </svg>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">Every spatial cell has a deterministic position in one contiguous array. No pointer-based tree traversal.</text>
</box>

For a 3D world:

\[
\text{index}=x+N_x(y+N_yz)
\]

The GPU calculates the index using a few integer operations, retrieves the cell metadata, and processes the associated contiguous entity range.

**This is especially attractive for collision broad-phase, nearby-entity queries, interest management, and spatial work scheduling.**

## 2. The more powerful version: flat grid + CSR

The technique I'd particularly recommend is **Compressed Sparse Row (CSR)-style spatial indexing**, also called a *sorted uniform grid* or *cell start/count indexing*.

Instead of storing a dynamically allocated list for every spatial cell, maintain three flat arrays:

```text
CellOffsets[]    // Start of each cell's entity range
CellCounts[]     // Number of entities in each cell
EntityIndices[]  // Contiguous entity handles, grouped by cell
```

Then querying a cell becomes:

```rust
let cell = x + nx * (y + ny * z);

let start = cell_offsets[cell];
let count = cell_counts[cell];

for i in start..start + count {
    let entity = entity_indices[i];
    // Process entity
}
```

This is conceptual Rust code; the actual implementation would run in GPU compute shaders.

An NVIDIA GPU Gems implementation uses the same broad principle: generate cell/object IDs, sort by cell, and construct a cell-index table for parallel queries. <Cite ref="turn423975search0"/>

## 3. Flat grid vs Morton grid vs tree

| Structure | Cell access | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat dense grid | O(1) | Direct indexing, predictable memory | Empty-cell overhead |
| Flat CSR grid | O(1) cell header | Dense entity ranges, GPU-friendly | Rebuilding or updating membership |
| Morton-coded flat grid | O(1) encoding | Better spatial locality in some traversal patterns | More complicated indexing and padding |
| Spatial hash grid | Expected O(1) | Supports sparse/unbounded spaces | Collisions, irregular access |
| Quadtree/octree | O(depth) | Adaptive spatial resolution | Tree traversal and pointer/index chasing |
| Linear BVH | O(depth) | Strong for irregular geometry and variable object sizes | Hierarchy maintenance |

One clarification: **Morton order is a way to arrange cells, not a replacement for their membership structure**. You can use Morton codes with flat grids, sorted arrays, or trees.

## 4. The limitation: enormous empty grids

Even with predefined world boundaries, a dense high-resolution 3D grid can consume substantial memory.

A 4096 × 4096 × 256 grid contains approximately 4.3 billion cells. Even one 4-byte value per cell requires **16 GiB**.

So I would not allocate a full-resolution global 3D grid.

Instead, my preferred architecture is:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Predefined World Bounds**

    <caption>Integer world coordinates</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Flat 2D Region Directory**

    <caption>Direct index → region metadata</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Resident Region-Local Flat Grids**

    <caption>Optional 3D grids for caves, cities, aerial spaces</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **CSR Cell Ranges → Dense ECS Entity References**

    <caption>GPU compute · Spatial queries · Broad phase · Active sets</caption>
  </box>
</box>

This preserves direct addressing within allocated regions without paying for empty fine-resolution cells across the entire world.

## 5. My recommendation for our MMO

I'd make **flat indexed spatial grids the primary world spatial infrastructure**, reserving BVHs or other hierarchies for workloads where variable object sizes, geometry, or sparse occupancy make them worthwhile.

Specifically:

- **World partitioning:** Flat 2D region directory, with local 3D grids where necessary.
- **Entity neighbourhood queries:** CSR-style uniform grids.
- **GPU physics broad phase:** Sorted cell/entity arrays.
- **Morton codes:** Spatial ordering and locality optimization.
- **Streaming:** Direct cell-to-residency mappings.
- **Geometry:** Meshlet cluster hierarchies where adaptive detail is necessary.

A direct array lookup is O(1), but querying the entities in a cell still costs time proportional to how many relevant entries are present. In crowded cities, cell occupancy and processing load matter more than the lookup itself.

The most interesting follow-on optimization is **incremental GPU maintenance of the flat CSR index**. Instead of radix-sorting millions of entities every frame, we could track entities crossing cell boundaries and update only affected cell membership, periodically rebuilding or compacting when fragmentation becomes expensive.

That is the approach I'd benchmark against full GPU radix-sort rebuilding.

**One question that substantially changes our spatial architecture:** Are you envisioning a primarily terrain-based world with cities, interiors, caves and flying, or a genuinely volumetric world where players can move freely in all three dimensions?

  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

    <caption>GPU compute · Spatial queries · Broad phase · Active sets</caption>
  </box>
</box>

This preserves direct addressing within allocated regions without paying for empty fine-resolution cells across the entire world.

## 5. My recommendation for our MMO

I'd make **flat indexed spatial grids the primary world spatial infrastructure**, reserving BVHs or other hierarchies for workloads where variable object sizes, geometry, or sparse occupancy make them worthwhile.

Specifically:

- **World partitioning:** Flat 2D region directory, with local 3D grids where necessary.
- **Entity neighbourhood queries:** CSR-style uniform grids.
- **GPU physics broad phase:** Sorted cell/entity arrays.
- **Morton codes:** Spatial ordering and locality optimization.
- **Streaming:** Direct cell-to-residency mappings.
- **Geometry:** Meshlet cluster hierarchies where adaptive detail is necessary.

A direct array lookup is O(1), but querying the entities in a cell still costs time proportional to how many relevant entries are present. In crowded cities, cell occupancy and processing load matter more than the lookup itself.

The most interesting follow-on optimization is **incremental GPU maintenance of the flat CSR index**. Instead of radix-sorting millions of entities every frame, we could track entities crossing cell boundaries and update only affected cell membership, periodically rebuilding or compacting when fragmentation becomes expensive.

That is the approach I'd benchmark against full GPU radix-sort rebuilding.

**One question that substantially changes our spatial architecture:** Are you envisioning a primarily terrain-based world with cities, interiors, caves and flying, or a genuinely volumetric world where players can move freely in all three dimensions?

# Phase 06 — GPU-Native 2.5D Spatial Architecture

<badge color="success">Recommended direction</badge>

**Dense XY grid + sparse vertical layers + contiguous entity ranges + GPU spatial queries.**

The world is primarily addressed horizontally. Vertical complexity is introduced only where required.

## 1. The proposed spatial model

Each XY cell has direct array indexing.

\[
i = x + yN_x
\]

Its header identifies optional vertical subdivisions and the ranges of entities occupying that horizontal area.

For instance, a grassland cell may require only a ground index. A city cell may reference street-level entities, multiple floors, rooftops, and flight volumes.

**We allocate vertical indexing capacity only where the spatial complexity justifies it.**

## 2. Contiguous data structure

I would use a GPU-friendly structure resembling:

```rust
struct CellHeader {
    entity_start: u32,
    entity_count: u32,
    layer_start: u32,
    layer_count: u32,
}

struct VerticalLayer {
    min_height: f32,
    max_height: f32,
    entity_start: u32,
    entity_count: u32,
    space_id: u32,
}
```

These are conceptual structures; final GPU alignment and indexing types remain to be determined.

The buffers would be:

| Buffer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CellHeaders[]` | Direct-indexed XY cell metadata |
| `VerticalLayers[]` | Packed vertical intervals, only where needed |
| `CellEntityRefs[]` | Contiguous entity handles grouped by cell |
| `EntityBounds[]` | GPU AABBs or compact bounding data |
| `SpaceDescriptors[]` | Cave, building, interior and exterior space references |
| `SpatialUpdateQueue[]` | Entities requiring membership changes |

A pure CSR implementation can derive a cell's range from adjacent offsets. We could eliminate redundant `entity_count` fields where that proves worthwhile.

### Why this is fast

For ordinary ground-level nearby-entity queries:

1. Convert world XY position to cell index.
2. Read the corresponding cell header.
3. Fetch the contiguous entity range.
4. Process its contents in parallel.

No tree traversal is required.

For a cave or skyscraper, there is one additional layer-selection step.

The number of objects in the candidate cells still determines how much processing is necessary. This is especially relevant to crowds.

NVIDIA's GPU Gems documents GPU spatial subdivision using sorted cell/object identifiers and a cell-index table, which provides a useful foundation for our approach. <Cite ref="turn545314search0"/>

## 3. Four types of spatial indexing

I would not force one index to serve all vertical scenarios.

| Environment | Proposed index |
|---|---|
| Terrain and outdoor ground entities | Flat 2D grid + height bounds |
| Cities and multi-floor buildings | XY grid + per-cell vertical intervals |
| Interiors and caves | Local 3D grid plus portal/room connectivity |
| Open airspace | Coarser 3D grids with adaptive cell resolution |

For large flying objects, we can also register their bounding volumes across relevant vertical cells.

This avoids a major problem with pure 2D queries: a player on the ground should not need to scan every flying object thousands of metres above them.

## 4. Interiors and caves need spatial connectivity

For indoors and underground environments, I'd add **room/portal graphs** alongside the grid.

  </svg>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">Grid indexing answers where an entity is. Connectivity determines which spaces can be traversed or potentially seen through openings.</text>
</box>

The graph also helps streaming and occlusion decisions.

A door may change whether two spaces are visually connected, but it should not automatically change all networking interest or authoritative simulation rules.

## 5. Morton codes: where I'd use them

I'd retain Morton coding, but distinguish its uses.

- **World grid addressing:** Simple row-major indexing for direct cell lookup.
- **Locality and GPU batching:** Morton order for sorting spatial references.
- **Spatial maintenance:** Morton-keyed dirty lists.
- **Static geometry:** Morton codes as one option for constructing acceleration structures.
- **GPU physics:** Sorted uniform-grid references for broad-phase processing.

I would not use Morton codes universally merely because they're sophisticated. Row-major indexing is cheaper to calculate and naturally groups adjacent cells along one axis; Morton order can improve multidimensional locality for some access patterns.

We should benchmark both for the actual query and memory-access workloads.

## 6. Dynamic updates without full-grid sorting

Here's the interesting optimization for a living MMO.

Most entities don't cross spatial cells every frame. Even when characters move constantly, their **cell membership** can remain unchanged over many simulation steps.

I recommend two indexing tiers:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Base Spatial Index**
    <caption>Dense contiguous CSR ranges · Stable membership snapshot</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="plus" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Incremental Delta Index**
    <caption>New cell memberships · Removed entries · Dirty cells</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU Spatial Queries**
    <caption>Read base + delta, with stale base entries masked</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Budgeted Compaction**
    <caption>Rebuild affected cells or partitions when needed</caption>
  </box>
</box>

This can avoid sorting the entire resident population every frame.

But it adds query overhead and duplicate/stale-entry handling. A full parallel rebuild may actually be faster once a sufficiently large fraction of the population changes cells.

I would keep both approaches in the engine and dynamically select the better one using measured workload characteristics.

## 7. Proposed initial spatial configuration

We should treat cell dimensions as tuning parameters, not permanent engine constants.

## 2. Updated rendering pipeline

The notable improvement is the **flat-grid-driven coarse visibility stage**.

Rather than beginning with individual entities, the GPU can reject entire spatial cells before generating fine-grained work.

Task shaders remain valuable for meshlet-level amplification and culling; this is consistent with their intended Vulkan functionality. <Cite refs={["turn836581search0","turn836581search1"]}/>

## 3. Three refinements I would make

### A. Introduce spatially coherent render workgroups

Create GPU workgroups from cell ranges, then optionally group their contents by geometry and material.

This should improve work discovery when visible entities are spatially clustered.

However, do not force one task-shader invocation per world cell. Dense cities and nearly empty grasslands have radically different populations.

Use the grid to discover candidates, then compact them into GPU-friendly batches.

### B. Separate coarse world visibility from geometry visibility

We now have two distinct culling scales:

- **World-level culling:** Flat spatial cells, entity bounds, coarse occlusion.
- **Geometry-level culling:** Meshlet bounds, cones, hierarchical geometry LOD, fine occlusion.

The flat grid can efficiently reject irrelevant regions, but it cannot replace geometry-level culling.

A cell containing a skyscraper might overlap the camera frustum even though only a tiny section of that building is visible.

We still need fine-grained visibility tests.

### C. Let cell visibility influence GPU work scheduling

Our GPU ECS scheduler can use spatial activity to prioritise animation, environmental effects, procedural details, and rendering-related updates.

That potentially saves GPU work before the actual mesh/task rendering stages.

The crucial exception is authoritative simulation and gameplay-critical state: those cannot be disabled merely because an entity is not visible.

## 4. What I would specifically avoid

Three tempting optimizations could actually make the renderer worse:

- **One task shader per grid cell.** This risks excessive workgroups and poor occupancy in sparse areas.
- **Treating the flat grid as the geometry LOD structure.** Uniform world cells are not a substitute for hierarchical mesh clusters.
- **Using a single spatial index for every view.** Main-camera visibility, shadows, reflections, and world-space UI can have different candidate sets.

Instead, maintain shared world spatial data and generate view-specific work lists.

## Final architectural decision

**We keep the entire advanced rendering pipeline. We replace its initial world-object discovery stage with a flat-grid-driven, GPU-parallel spatial filtering system.**

That is a refinement rather than a redesign.

Our two central spatial structures become:

| World scale | Geometry scale |
|---|---|
| Flat 2.5D grids + contiguous ECS references | Hierarchical compressed meshlet clusters |
| Designed for entity discovery and locality | Designed for triangle efficiency and continuous LOD |
| Updated as objects move | Updated when geometry or its representation changes |

These two structures complement each other.

One additional opportunity I'd now investigate is **how to make the flat spatial grid produce visible ECS batches with the least possible sorting, compaction, and indirect-dispatch overhead**. That could be a significant architectural advantage for crowded MMO scenes.

Three tempting optimizations could actually make the renderer worse:

- **One task shader per grid cell.** This risks excessive workgroups and poor occupancy in sparse areas.
- **Treating the flat grid as the geometry LOD structure.** Uniform world cells are not a substitute for hierarchical mesh clusters.
- **Using a single spatial index for every view.** Main-camera visibility, shadows, reflections, and world-space UI can have different candidate sets.

Instead, maintain shared world spatial data and generate view-specific work lists.

## Final architectural decision

**We keep the entire advanced rendering pipeline. We replace its initial world-object discovery stage with a flat-grid-driven, GPU-parallel spatial filtering system.**

That is a refinement rather than a redesign.

Our two central spatial structures become:

| World scale | Geometry scale |
|---|---|
| Flat 2.5D grids + contiguous ECS references | Hierarchical compressed meshlet clusters |
| Designed for entity discovery and locality | Designed for triangle efficiency and continuous LOD |
| Updated as objects move | Updated when geometry or its representation changes |

These two structures complement each other.

One additional opportunity I'd now investigate is **how to make the flat spatial grid produce visible ECS batches with the least possible sorting, compaction, and indirect-dispatch overhead**. That could be a significant architectural advantage for crowded MMO scenes.

These are logical stages, not necessarily five separate full-frame dispatches. We should fuse compatible operations when doing so reduces memory traffic without introducing unsafe dependencies.

## 2. Don't scan the entire world grid

A flat grid gives us O(1) cell lookup. It does **not** automatically make discovering every visible cell O(1).

We should avoid dispatching one GPU workgroup for every world cell.

Instead, maintain a **resident-region directory** containing only potentially relevant chunks of the world.

At the beginning of each view's visibility cycle, the GPU processes resident regions, rejects those outside the view, and generates candidate cell ranges.

For a terrain-dominated world, we can also calculate conservative XY bounds for a camera's view and enumerate grid cells within those bounds.

For steep camera angles, flying, caves, and tall cities, region-level bounds and vertical-layer filtering become particularly important.

### Proposed broad-phase hierarchy

| Level | Data | Processing |
|---|---|---|
| Resident region | Bounds + active-cell directory | Reject entire regions |
| XY cell | Direct grid header + height bounds | Reject irrelevant cells |
| Vertical layer | Height interval + space reference | Select relevant floors / airspace |
| ECS entity | Instance bounds + flags | Object-level culling |
| Geometry cluster | Meshlet bounds + LOD error | Fine geometry selection |

Notice that the first three levels do not require pointer-based spatial trees.

We retain the advantages of direct indexing while allowing variable vertical complexity.

## 3. How to avoid sorting millions of entities

I'd use **CSR-preserved locality and GPU stream compaction** as the default.

Our spatial grid already groups entity references by cell. That is valuable spatial ordering established before rendering begins.

A view can consume cell ranges and produce tightly packed lists of entities that pass culling.

The visibility process does not need a new global Morton sort every frame.

### Recommended algorithm

    <row align="start" gap={3}>
      <box size="40px" radius="lg" background="surface-secondary" align="center" justify="center">
        <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{item.n}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{item.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{item.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

The next graphics pass consumes the generated buffers using indirect mesh/task draw commands.

Vulkan's `VK_EXT_mesh_shader` provides indirect mesh task draws with a device-supplied draw count, so the CPU does not have to retrieve the visible instance count first. <Cite ref="turn698375search0"/>

## 4. The most interesting optimization: skip global compaction when possible

A fully compacted visible-entity array isn't always the fastest solution.

Compaction requires reading candidates, producing counts, scanning offsets, and writing a new list. Sometimes it's cheaper to process the original spatial ranges directly.

I would implement **three GPU work-generation paths**.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row justify="between" align="center">
      **Path A — Direct cell processing**
      <badge>Low overhead</badge>
    </row>
    <text size="sm">Generate descriptors for relevant spatial chunks and let task shaders perform local entity/meshlet filtering.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Best candidate for coherent scenes with high visibility and relatively uniform cell populations.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Path B — Compact visible instances**

    <text size="sm">Compute shader culls entities and produces dense instance references before launching task/mesh shaders.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Best candidate for highly occluded scenes, irregular populations, or when several downstream passes reuse visibility results.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Path C — Hybrid chunk compaction**

    <text size="sm">Compact coarse work descriptors, but defer per-instance selection to task shaders or subsequent GPU passes.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">My preferred baseline for our MMO: fewer global memory writes while retaining efficient GPU workload generation.</text>
  </box>
</box>

The hybrid approach is particularly promising because a work descriptor might represent a small range of spatially related entities rather than a single entity.

## 5. GPU work descriptor architecture

I would introduce a compact, GPU-native *render work descriptor*.

Conceptually:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct RenderWork {
    entity_ref_start: u32,
    entity_count: u32,
    view_id: u32,
    flags: u32,
}
```

A descriptor identifies a range within a selected cell's entity-reference list. It doesn't copy the underlying ECS components.

Additional information—material family, geometry class, LOD policy—can be obtained from adjacent tables or encoded in specialized descriptors.

The benefits:

- No CPU-generated per-object draws.
- No unnecessary copying of transforms and mesh references.
- Spatial locality is preserved.
- Task shaders can filter and amplify geometry work.
- Multiple cameras can share the ECS while using different work lists.

The work descriptors should be grouped into bounded batches, not blindly map one descriptor to one task workgroup. A task shader has limited shared memory, payload size, and mesh-workgroup output limits. These are hardware-queryable through Vulkan. <Cite ref="turn698375search0"/>

## 6. Adaptive batching

This is where the system can become more efficient than a fixed batch size.

A grassland might contain hundreds of small vegetation instances in a cell. A city cell might contain thousands of characters, props, and buildings. Many distant cells might have no active entities at all.

The GPU scheduler can divide populated cell ranges into processing tiles and generate only as many work descriptors as needed.

{@body const [entities,setEntities] = DIL.useState(1024)}
{@body const [batch,setBatch] = DIL.useState(128)}
{@body const groups = Math.ceil(entities/batch)}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  **Work tile sizing — illustrative**
  <box gap={1}>

      <label>Candidate entities in region</label>

    </row>
    <slider min={0} max={4096} step={128} value={entities} onChange={setEntities}/>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Maximum entity references per work tile</label>
    <radio-group value={String(batch)} onChange={v=>setBatch(Number(v))}>
      <radio value="32">32</radio>
      <radio value="64">64</radio>
      <radio value="128">128</radio>
      <radio value="256">256</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
