    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Generated work tiles</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{groups}</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Last tile occupancy</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{groups===0?0:Math.round((entities-(groups-1)*batch)/batch*100)}%</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row gap="2px" wrap="wrap">
    {#each Array.from({length:Math.min(groups,24)},(_,i)=>i) as i}
      <box width="20px" height="20px" radius="2xs" background={i===groups-1?"#6A9F86":"#6298C3"}/>
    {/each}
    {#if groups>24}
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">+ {groups-24} more</text>
    {/if}
  </row>
  <caption>Tile count is not the number of meshlets or actual hardware task workgroups. This models only the initial entity-reference partitioning.</caption>
</box>

I'd use runtime profiling to determine whether different workload families should use 32-, 64-, 128-, or larger-reference tiles.

The optimum will vary with shader resource use, geometry density, subgroup size, and GPU architecture.

## 7. Visibility history: avoid unnecessary rework

Our renderer should maintain per-view visibility history and use it to improve temporal coherence.

For example, a building visible last frame is likely still visible if the camera moved only slightly.

I would explore:

- Previous-frame HZB for early occlusion rejection.
- Conservative treatment of newly visible and fast-moving entities.
- Temporal visibility confidence and periodic revalidation.
- Per-cell visibility history.
- Separate rules for small moving objects and large static geometry.

The key is avoiding persistent false negatives.

**Occlusion history must never become permission to permanently skip testing a cell.** Camera motion, moving occluders, disocclusion, and teleportation require conservative fallbacks or revalidation.

A useful geometry pipeline could perform an early pass based on previous-frame depth, generate current depth from accepted occluders, then retest uncertain candidates against an updated HZB.

This adds passes, so we should measure whether the saved geometry work justifies them.

## 8. Mesh/task shader integration

Our GPU scheduler ultimately needs to convert work descriptors into mesh/task workloads.

The Vulkan extension explicitly allows task shaders to generate varying numbers of mesh shader workgroups, which makes task amplification well suited to this pipeline. <Cite ref="turn698375search0"/>

I would split responsibilities as follows:

| Stage | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| GPU compute | Discover cells, form work tiles, compact workloads |
| Task shader | Coarse geometry-group culling, local LOD selection and amplification |
| Mesh shader | Decode geometry clusters, emit visible vertices/primitives |
| Fragment shader | Write visibility IDs and required surface data |
| Material resolve | Fetch attributes/materials and shade visible surfaces |

We should keep geometry residency validation before accessing cluster data. If the chosen detail isn't resident, the shader should select an available fallback or request missing pages through a controlled feedback mechanism.

### Sorting: only when the benefit outweighs the cost

We already have bindless materials and GPU-resident resource tables.

That reduces the need for traditional CPU material sorting and descriptor rebinding.

However, material coherence still matters for shader divergence and texture locality.

I'd investigate lightweight local grouping by material or geometry class, but avoid mandatory global material sorting.

The visibility-buffer resolve also gives us an opportunity to improve shading coherence independently of the original entity work ordering.

## 9. Synchronization strategy

The goal is a few well-defined GPU dependency boundaries rather than CPU waits.

<box gap={2}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text weight="medium">Candidate frame synchronization</text>
    {#each [{t:"Spatial/ECS writes → visibility",d:"Updated transforms, bounds and membership become readable."},{t:"Visibility counts → work descriptors",d:"Prefix scans consume completed counts."},{t:"Work descriptors → indirect rendering",d:"Task draws consume generated arguments and references."},{t:"Geometry pass → HZB / shading",d:"Depth and visibility outputs become available to consumers."}] as x,i}
      <row align="start" gap={2}>
        <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" size="30px" align="center" justify="center"><text size="xs">{i+1}</text></box>
        <box flex="1" gap={1}>
          **{x.t}**
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{x.d}</text>
        </box>
      </row>
    {/each}
  </box>
</box>

In Vulkan, compute-written indirect arguments and data must be made visible to their consuming stages with correctly scoped synchronization.

There is no need for the CPU to read back the work count.

And we should not assume that dispatching compute on an asynchronous queue automatically improves performance. The geometry pipeline and compute work may compete for memory bandwidth and hardware execution resources.

## 10. What I'd benchmark first

We should compare the three paths across representative MMO scenes.

| Benchmark | Primary stress |
|---|---|
| Open grasslands | High visibility, dense vegetation |
| Forest | High occlusion, many small instances |
| Crowded capital | Dense dynamic characters and props |
| Multi-floor city | Sparse vertical subdivisions |
| High-altitude flight | Huge horizontal view footprint |
| Cave network | Small connected spaces and portal visibility |
| Teleport into city | Cold residency and sudden visibility expansion |

Measure the complete cost of visibility plus rendering, not simply time spent in the culling kernel.

For every workload, we'd capture:

- Candidate cells and entities processed.
- GPU scan/compaction cost.
- Task and mesh shader invocations.
- Geometry emitted versus geometry surviving.
- Memory bytes read/written.
- HZB cost and occlusion effectiveness.
- GPU queue overlap and synchronization delays.
- Total frame critical-path time.

The winner may vary by scene. Our scheduler can select between direct, compacted, and hybrid paths using coarse scene statistics without complex CPU intervention.

## 11. Architecture decision

I'd lock the following as our **GPU render work-generation baseline**:

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{t:"Flat-grid region discovery",d:"Process resident regions and bounded candidate cell ranges, not the entire world."},{t:"CSR-preserved spatial locality",d:"Reuse spatially coherent entity lists instead of globally sorting every frame."},{t:"Hybrid work compaction",d:"Compact cell/chunk descriptors first; avoid unnecessary per-instance copying."},{t:"Adaptive GPU work tiles",d:"Generate bounded workloads based on occupancy and hardware characteristics."},{t:"Task-shader amplification",d:"Use task shaders for geometry-group culling and meshlet work generation."},{t:"GPU indirect submission",d:"Device-generated work counts without CPU readbacks."},{t:"Temporal and hierarchical visibility",d:"Combine region bounds, instance bounds, meshlet culling, and conservative HZB."},{t:"Benchmark-selected execution paths",d:"Retain direct and full-compaction paths for scenes where they outperform the hybrid baseline."}] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{x.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

### One additional architectural issue

We now need to distinguish **visible geometry**, **visible entities**, and **visible shading work**.

They are not the same thing.

A character might have a visible silhouette but hundreds of meshlets, only some of which survive occlusion. Meanwhile, its material may need expensive shading only for a small number of pixels.

That leads to what I'd investigate next:

**A unified GPU visibility-buffer architecture with virtualized meshlet geometry, material resolve, clustered lighting, and virtual shadow-map work generation.**

This will connect our flat-grid ECS discovery directly to final pixel cost—without undoing the GPU-first design or introducing CPU-generated rendering workloads.

      <radio value="256">256</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Generated work tiles</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{groups}</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Last tile occupancy</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{groups===0?0:Math.round((entities-(groups-1)*batch)/batch*100)}%</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row gap="2px" wrap="wrap">
    {#each Array.from({length:Math.min(groups,24)},(_,i)=>i) as i}
      <box width="20px" height="20px" radius="2xs" background={i===groups-1?"#6A9F86":"#6298C3"}/>
    {/each}
    {#if groups>24}
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">+ {groups-24} more</text>
    {/if}
  </row>
  <caption>Tile count is not the number of meshlets or actual hardware task workgroups. This models only the initial entity-reference partitioning.</caption>
</box>

I'd use runtime profiling to determine whether different workload families should use 32-, 64-, 128-, or larger-reference tiles.

The optimum will vary with shader resource use, geometry density, subgroup size, and GPU architecture.

## 7. Visibility history: avoid unnecessary rework

Our renderer should maintain per-view visibility history and use it to improve temporal coherence.

For example, a building visible last frame is likely still visible if the camera moved only slightly.

I would explore:

- Previous-frame HZB for early occlusion rejection.
- Conservative treatment of newly visible and fast-moving entities.
- Temporal visibility confidence and periodic revalidation.
- Per-cell visibility history.
- Separate rules for small moving objects and large static geometry.

The key is avoiding persistent false negatives.

**Occlusion history must never become permission to permanently skip testing a cell.** Camera motion, moving occluders, disocclusion, and teleportation require conservative fallbacks or revalidation.

A useful geometry pipeline could perform an early pass based on previous-frame depth, generate current depth from accepted occluders, then retest uncertain candidates against an updated HZB.

This adds passes, so we should measure whether the saved geometry work justifies them.

## 8. Mesh/task shader integration

Our GPU scheduler ultimately needs to convert work descriptors into mesh/task workloads.

The Vulkan extension explicitly allows task shaders to generate varying numbers of mesh shader workgroups, which makes task amplification well suited to this pipeline. <Cite ref="turn698375search0"/>

I would split responsibilities as follows:

| Stage | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| GPU compute | Discover cells, form work tiles, compact workloads |
| Task shader | Coarse geometry-group culling, local LOD selection and amplification |
| Mesh shader | Decode geometry clusters, emit visible vertices/primitives |
| Fragment shader | Write visibility IDs and required surface data |
| Material resolve | Fetch attributes/materials and shade visible surfaces |

We should keep geometry residency validation before accessing cluster data. If the chosen detail isn't resident, the shader should select an available fallback or request missing pages through a controlled feedback mechanism.

### Sorting: only when the benefit outweighs the cost

We already have bindless materials and GPU-resident resource tables.

That reduces the need for traditional CPU material sorting and descriptor rebinding.

However, material coherence still matters for shader divergence and texture locality.

I'd investigate lightweight local grouping by material or geometry class, but avoid mandatory global material sorting.

The visibility-buffer resolve also gives us an opportunity to improve shading coherence independently of the original entity work ordering.

## 9. Synchronization strategy

The goal is a few well-defined GPU dependency boundaries rather than CPU waits.

<box gap={2}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text weight="medium">Candidate frame synchronization</text>
    {#each [{t:"Spatial/ECS writes → visibility",d:"Updated transforms, bounds and membership become readable."},{t:"Visibility counts → work descriptors",d:"Prefix scans consume completed counts."},{t:"Work descriptors → indirect rendering",d:"Task draws consume generated arguments and references."},{t:"Geometry pass → HZB / shading",d:"Depth and visibility outputs become available to consumers."}] as x,i}
      <row align="start" gap={2}>
        <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" size="30px" align="center" justify="center"><text size="xs">{i+1}</text></box>
        <box flex="1" gap={1}>
          **{x.t}**
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{x.d}</text>
        </box>
      </row>
    {/each}
  </box>
</box>

In Vulkan, compute-written indirect arguments and data must be made visible to their consuming stages with correctly scoped synchronization.

There is no need for the CPU to read back the work count.

And we should not assume that dispatching compute on an asynchronous queue automatically improves performance. The geometry pipeline and compute work may compete for memory bandwidth and hardware execution resources.

## 10. What I'd benchmark first

We should compare the three paths across representative MMO scenes.

| Benchmark | Primary stress |
|---|---|
| Open grasslands | High visibility, dense vegetation |
| Forest | High occlusion, many small instances |
| Crowded capital | Dense dynamic characters and props |
| Multi-floor city | Sparse vertical subdivisions |
| High-altitude flight | Huge horizontal view footprint |
| Cave network | Small connected spaces and portal visibility |
| Teleport into city | Cold residency and sudden visibility expansion |

Measure the complete cost of visibility plus rendering, not simply time spent in the culling kernel.

For every workload, we'd capture:

- Candidate cells and entities processed.
- GPU scan/compaction cost.
- Task and mesh shader invocations.
- Geometry emitted versus geometry surviving.
- Memory bytes read/written.
- HZB cost and occlusion effectiveness.
- GPU queue overlap and synchronization delays.
- Total frame critical-path time.

The winner may vary by scene. Our scheduler can select between direct, compacted, and hybrid paths using coarse scene statistics without complex CPU intervention.

## 11. Architecture decision

I'd lock the following as our **GPU render work-generation baseline**:

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{t:"Flat-grid region discovery",d:"Process resident regions and bounded candidate cell ranges, not the entire world."},{t:"CSR-preserved spatial locality",d:"Reuse spatially coherent entity lists instead of globally sorting every frame."},{t:"Hybrid work compaction",d:"Compact cell/chunk descriptors first; avoid unnecessary per-instance copying."},{t:"Adaptive GPU work tiles",d:"Generate bounded workloads based on occupancy and hardware characteristics."},{t:"Task-shader amplification",d:"Use task shaders for geometry-group culling and meshlet work generation."},{t:"GPU indirect submission",d:"Device-generated work counts without CPU readbacks."},{t:"Temporal and hierarchical visibility",d:"Combine region bounds, instance bounds, meshlet culling, and conservative HZB."},{t:"Benchmark-selected execution paths",d:"Retain direct and full-compaction paths for scenes where they outperform the hybrid baseline."}] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{x.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

### One additional architectural issue

We now need to distinguish **visible geometry**, **visible entities**, and **visible shading work**.

They are not the same thing.

A character might have a visible silhouette but hundreds of meshlets, only some of which survive occlusion. Meanwhile, its material may need expensive shading only for a small number of pixels.

That leads to what I'd investigate next:

**A unified GPU visibility-buffer architecture with virtualized meshlet geometry, material resolve, clustered lighting, and virtual shadow-map work generation.**

This will connect our flat-grid ECS discovery directly to final pixel cost—without undoing the GPU-first design or introducing CPU-generated rendering workloads.

# Phase 08 — GPU Visibility Buffer, Virtualized Geometry & Lighting
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Advanced Rendering Architecture · October 2026</text>

We now have the foundation for a genuinely GPU-native renderer:

- GPU-primary ECS with contiguous SoA/AoSoA memory.
- Flat 2.5D spatial grids and sparse vertical indexing.
- GPU-generated render work from compact spatial ranges.
- Mesh and task shaders with GPU-selected geometry.
- Virtualized assets, streaming, and GPU-managed visual residency.
- GPU-rendered UI with direct Bézier-outline text.

The next architectural decision is how those systems produce the final image.

**My recommendation is a visibility-buffer renderer with deferred material evaluation, virtualized cluster geometry, clustered lighting, and GPU-managed virtual shadow maps.**

This is more appropriate for our world than a traditional renderer that shades materials while rasterizing every triangle.

## 1. The unified rendering pipeline

This is the logical processing architecture. The actual render graph should overlap independent work, reuse intermediate data, and eliminate redundant passes.

## 2. Visibility buffers instead of traditional G-buffers

In conventional deferred rendering, the rasterization stage writes several attributes for each visible pixel: normals, material parameters, perhaps albedo, roughness and more.

A visibility buffer instead records **which primitive produced each pixel**.

The material properties can then be reconstructed and evaluated after visibility is known.

<grid columns={2} gap={3}>
  <grid-item>
    <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
      **Traditional G-buffer**
      <svg viewBox="0 0 150 108" width="100%">
        {#each [{name:"Albedo",color:"#B98072"},{name:"Normals",color:"#7296C4"},{name:"Material",color:"#A594BB"},{name:"Depth",color:"#7E9C88"}] as a,i}
          <rect x="6" y={3+i*26} width="138" height="22" rx="3" fill={a.color} fillOpacity=".35"/>
          <text x="14" y={18+i*26} fontSize="11" fill="currentColor">{a.name}</text>
        {/each}
      </svg>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Stores several surface attributes directly in screen-space images.</text>
    </box>
  </grid-item>
  <grid-item>
    <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
      **Visibility buffer**
      <svg viewBox="0 0 150 108" width="100%">
        <rect x="6" y="16" width="138" height="32" rx="4" fill="#579F94" fillOpacity=".35"/>
        <text x="75" y="35" fontSize="11" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Primitive ID</text>
        <rect x="6" y="60" width="138" height="32" rx="4" fill="#7E9C88" fillOpacity=".35"/>
        <text x="75" y="79" fontSize="11" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Depth</text>
      </svg>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Stores compact identification. Surface attributes are fetched after rasterization.</text>
    </box>
  </grid-item>
</grid>

The potential advantages are significant:

- Less full-screen attribute storage.
- Material shading deferred until final visible surfaces are known.
- Better compatibility with compressed, GPU-addressable geometry.
- Easier separation of geometric complexity from material complexity.
- A useful source of primitive identity for material sorting and debugging.

But it introduces more random geometry fetches and complicated texture derivatives. We should not claim it universally beats a conventional G-buffer.

### Our proposed visibility record

I would investigate two formats:

| Format | Example | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Compact | 32-bit packed instance/cluster/primitive reference | Lower bandwidth, restricted addressable ranges |
| Extended | 64-bit logical primitive reference | Larger address space, higher bandwidth |

Crucially, these IDs would be **render-frame-local identifiers**, resolved through GPU tables, not persistent MMO entity IDs.

A 64-bit packed ID is not automatically sufficient for every possible combination of instance, cluster, primitive, generation and view. We must define the bit budget or use indirection.

The depth attachment remains separate.

Barycentric coordinates may be stored, recomputed during resolve, or reconstructed from projected triangle vertices. Vulkan provides `VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric` for direct fragment-stage barycentric access, but that feature does not automatically supply barycentrics to a later compute resolve pass. <Cite ref="turn522071search2"/>

That distinction is important for our shader architecture.

## 3. Material resolve entirely on GPU

After rasterization, each covered pixel can identify its geometry and material.

The GPU material resolver would:

1. Read the visibility ID and depth.
2. Resolve the corresponding instance, cluster, and triangle.
3. Fetch compressed vertex attributes.
4. Reconstruct or retrieve barycentric coordinates.
5. Interpolate UVs, normals, tangents, and other surface attributes.
6. Evaluate textures and material functions.
7. Output surface parameters or directly perform lighting.

The main technical challenge is **derivative reconstruction**.

Texture filtering and mip selection depend on screen-space gradients. A compute shader processing a visibility buffer cannot naively rely on neighbouring pixels belonging to the same triangle. Triangle boundaries, disocclusion, and divergent materials complicate gradient calculation.

For our engine, I'd investigate analytic derivatives based on projected triangle geometry, with appropriate edge handling and fallback sampling.

### GPU material organisation

We should keep materials in contiguous GPU tables, referencing bindless resources.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Visibility Primitive ID**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Geometry + Instance Tables**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Material Program / Parameter ID**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="xs">Bindless textures</text></box></grid-item>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="xs">Material parameters</text></box></grid-item>
  </grid>
</box>

I'd support material-family specialization instead of one enormous branch-heavy shader interpreting all possible materials.

For complicated scenes, a material-bin pass could group screen tiles or pixels by material family to improve coherence.

This is another benchmark decision: binning improves execution coherence but adds reads, writes, scans, and synchronization.

### Descriptor technology

Our original bindless decision remains correct, but there is a newer Vulkan option worth elevating.

Khronos now documents `VK_EXT_descriptor_heap`, a memory-oriented descriptor system intended to supersede descriptor-buffer workflows where available. Its Vulkan sample describes descriptor heaps as the preferred direction when supported. <Cite refs={["turn522071search9","turn522071search8"]}/>

I'd therefore define one resource-table abstraction with:

- Descriptor heap backend where supported.
- Descriptor indexing fallback.
- GPU buffer device addresses for suitable structured-data access.

We should not force the material system's logical resource IDs to depend on one descriptor implementation.

## 4. Virtualized geometry: hierarchical meshlets

Our flat 2.5D grid gets us to the relevant entities.

It doesn't tell us which triangles should be rasterized.

For that, we retain a separate **compressed geometry cluster hierarchy**.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Two independent selection systems</text>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={2} align="center">
        **Spatial grid**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Which world objects?</text>
        <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
        <text size="xs" textAlign="center">Visible entity references</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={2} align="center">
        **Geometry hierarchy**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Which triangles and detail?</text>
        <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
        <text size="xs" textAlign="center">Visible geometry clusters</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Mesh/Task Rendering**
  </box>
</box>

The cluster hierarchy should contain compressed geometry, conservative bounds, LOD error information, residency references, and material references.

Task shaders can filter and amplify mesh work. Mesh shaders decode and emit triangles.

### Hybrid hardware + software rasterization

This is one of the few advanced techniques I'd actively evaluate as a future foundational capability.

Hardware rasterization works well for triangles covering a meaningful screen area.

For extremely small triangles, however, hardware rasterization overhead can become disproportionate.

A hybrid renderer can choose between:

- **Hardware mesh shader rasterization** for ordinary geometry.
- **Compute-based software rasterization** for appropriately small projected triangles.

Both paths would write to a compatible visibility/depth representation with explicit cross-path depth ordering and race handling.

That last part is nontrivial. A compute shader cannot simply write a normal graphics depth attachment concurrently without a supported, correctly synchronized mechanism. A shared storage representation, ownership phases, or another deliberate merge strategy is required.

**I would design the visibility format to allow this hybrid path, but would not require software microtriangle rasterization for the first renderer milestone.**

## 5. GPU-driven virtual shadow maps

Our previous shadow recommendation remains, but we can now define how it connects to ECS and visibility.

Traditional shadow rendering can require substantial repeated geometry work, particularly with many shadow-casting lights.

I recommend **virtual shadow maps (VSMs)** based on demand-driven shadow-page allocation.

The basic idea is that lights have a large logical shadow-address space, while only the required pages are backed by physical GPU memory.

Epic documents virtual shadow maps as high-resolution shadowing intended for detailed geometry and large dynamic worlds. We would use the technique as a reference rather than adopt Unreal. <Cite ref="turn522071search18"/>

### Proposed shadow pipeline

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Visible Surfaces + Light Influence**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Shadow Page Demand**
    <caption>Which lights and shadow regions need resolution?</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Page Allocation + Cache Validation**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Shadow Caster Work Generation**
    <caption>Light-space culling · Geometry LOD · Mesh/task rendering</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Physical Shadow Page Atlas**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Shadow Sampling During Lighting**
  </box>
</box>

An important distinction: a visible receiver requesting a shadow page does not tell us every object that might cast a shadow onto it.

We still need **light-space caster discovery**, using suitable bounds and acceleration structures. Our flat-grid index can help discover casters, but the relevant geometry may lie outside the camera's visible cells.

### Cache invalidation

For an MMO, this is essential.

Static buildings and terrain should reuse cached shadow pages when valid. Moving characters, doors, destructible structures, and dynamic lights can invalidate parts of the cache.

I'd track conservative caster changes using dirty spatial ranges and light influence, then invalidate affected shadow pages.

Incorrect invalidation causes stale shadows. Overly broad invalidation destroys caching performance.

We should also reserve capacity for exceptional scenes rather than allow a crowded city to exhaust shadow pages uncontrollably.

<grid columns={2} gap={3}>
  <grid-item>
    <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
      **Traditional G-buffer**
      <svg viewBox="0 0 150 108" width="100%">
        {#each [{name:"Albedo",color:"#B98072"},{name:"Normals",color:"#7296C4"},{name:"Material",color:"#A594BB"},{name:"Depth",color:"#7E9C88"}] as a,i}
          <rect x="6" y={3+i*26} width="138" height="22" rx="3" fill={a.color} fillOpacity=".35"/>
          <text x="14" y={18+i*26} fontSize="11" fill="currentColor">{a.name}</text>
        {/each}
      </svg>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Stores several surface attributes directly in screen-space images.</text>
    </box>
  </grid-item>
  <grid-item>
    <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
      **Visibility buffer**
      <svg viewBox="0 0 150 108" width="100%">
        <rect x="6" y="16" width="138" height="32" rx="4" fill="#579F94" fillOpacity=".35"/>
        <text x="75" y="35" fontSize="11" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Primitive ID</text>
        <rect x="6" y="60" width="138" height="32" rx="4" fill="#7E9C88" fillOpacity=".35"/>
        <text x="75" y="79" fontSize="11" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Depth</text>
      </svg>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Stores compact identification. Surface attributes are fetched after rasterization.</text>
    </box>
  </grid-item>
</grid>

The potential advantages are significant:

- Less full-screen attribute storage.
- Material shading deferred until final visible surfaces are known.
- Better compatibility with compressed, GPU-addressable geometry.
- Easier separation of geometric complexity from material complexity.
- A useful source of primitive identity for material sorting and debugging.

But it introduces more random geometry fetches and complicated texture derivatives. We should not claim it universally beats a conventional G-buffer.

### Our proposed visibility record

I would investigate two formats:

| Format | Example | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Compact | 32-bit packed instance/cluster/primitive reference | Lower bandwidth, restricted addressable ranges |
| Extended | 64-bit logical primitive reference | Larger address space, higher bandwidth |

Crucially, these IDs would be **render-frame-local identifiers**, resolved through GPU tables, not persistent MMO entity IDs.

A 64-bit packed ID is not automatically sufficient for every possible combination of instance, cluster, primitive, generation and view. We must define the bit budget or use indirection.

The depth attachment remains separate.

Barycentric coordinates may be stored, recomputed during resolve, or reconstructed from projected triangle vertices. Vulkan provides `VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric` for direct fragment-stage barycentric access, but that feature does not automatically supply barycentrics to a later compute resolve pass. <Cite ref="turn522071search2"/>

That distinction is important for our shader architecture.

## 3. Material resolve entirely on GPU

After rasterization, each covered pixel can identify its geometry and material.

The GPU material resolver would:

1. Read the visibility ID and depth.
2. Resolve the corresponding instance, cluster, and triangle.
3. Fetch compressed vertex attributes.
4. Reconstruct or retrieve barycentric coordinates.
5. Interpolate UVs, normals, tangents, and other surface attributes.
6. Evaluate textures and material functions.
7. Output surface parameters or directly perform lighting.

The main technical challenge is **derivative reconstruction**.

Texture filtering and mip selection depend on screen-space gradients. A compute shader processing a visibility buffer cannot naively rely on neighbouring pixels belonging to the same triangle. Triangle boundaries, disocclusion, and divergent materials complicate gradient calculation.

For our engine, I'd investigate analytic derivatives based on projected triangle geometry, with appropriate edge handling and fallback sampling.

### GPU material organisation

We should keep materials in contiguous GPU tables, referencing bindless resources.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Visibility Primitive ID**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Geometry + Instance Tables**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Material Program / Parameter ID**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="xs">Bindless textures</text></box></grid-item>
    <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="md" align="center"><text size="xs">Material parameters</text></box></grid-item>
  </grid>
</box>

I'd support material-family specialization instead of one enormous branch-heavy shader interpreting all possible materials.

For complicated scenes, a material-bin pass could group screen tiles or pixels by material family to improve coherence.

This is another benchmark decision: binning improves execution coherence but adds reads, writes, scans, and synchronization.

### Descriptor technology

Our original bindless decision remains correct, but there is a newer Vulkan option worth elevating.

Khronos now documents `VK_EXT_descriptor_heap`, a memory-oriented descriptor system intended to supersede descriptor-buffer workflows where available. Its Vulkan sample describes descriptor heaps as the preferred direction when supported. <Cite refs={["turn522071search9","turn522071search8"]}/>

I'd therefore define one resource-table abstraction with:

- Descriptor heap backend where supported.
- Descriptor indexing fallback.
- GPU buffer device addresses for suitable structured-data access.

We should not force the material system's logical resource IDs to depend on one descriptor implementation.

## 4. Virtualized geometry: hierarchical meshlets

Our flat 2.5D grid gets us to the relevant entities.

It doesn't tell us which triangles should be rasterized.

For that, we retain a separate **compressed geometry cluster hierarchy**.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Two independent selection systems</text>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={2} align="center">
        **Spatial grid**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Which world objects?</text>
        <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
        <text size="xs" textAlign="center">Visible entity references</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={2} align="center">
        **Geometry hierarchy**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Which triangles and detail?</text>
        <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
        <text size="xs" textAlign="center">Visible geometry clusters</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Mesh/Task Rendering**
  </box>
</box>

The cluster hierarchy should contain compressed geometry, conservative bounds, LOD error information, residency references, and material references.

Task shaders can filter and amplify mesh work. Mesh shaders decode and emit triangles.

### Hybrid hardware + software rasterization

This is one of the few advanced techniques I'd actively evaluate as a future foundational capability.

Hardware rasterization works well for triangles covering a meaningful screen area.

For extremely small triangles, however, hardware rasterization overhead can become disproportionate.

A hybrid renderer can choose between:

- **Hardware mesh shader rasterization** for ordinary geometry.
- **Compute-based software rasterization** for appropriately small projected triangles.

Both paths would write to a compatible visibility/depth representation with explicit cross-path depth ordering and race handling.

That last part is nontrivial. A compute shader cannot simply write a normal graphics depth attachment concurrently without a supported, correctly synchronized mechanism. A shared storage representation, ownership phases, or another deliberate merge strategy is required.

**I would design the visibility format to allow this hybrid path, but would not require software microtriangle rasterization for the first renderer milestone.**

## 5. GPU-driven virtual shadow maps

Our previous shadow recommendation remains, but we can now define how it connects to ECS and visibility.

Traditional shadow rendering can require substantial repeated geometry work, particularly with many shadow-casting lights.

I recommend **virtual shadow maps (VSMs)** based on demand-driven shadow-page allocation.

The basic idea is that lights have a large logical shadow-address space, while only the required pages are backed by physical GPU memory.

Epic documents virtual shadow maps as high-resolution shadowing intended for detailed geometry and large dynamic worlds. We would use the technique as a reference rather than adopt Unreal. <Cite ref="turn522071search18"/>

### Proposed shadow pipeline

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Visible Surfaces + Light Influence**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Shadow Page Demand**
    <caption>Which lights and shadow regions need resolution?</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **GPU Page Allocation + Cache Validation**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Shadow Caster Work Generation**
    <caption>Light-space culling · Geometry LOD · Mesh/task rendering</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Physical Shadow Page Atlas**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Shadow Sampling During Lighting**
  </box>
</box>

An important distinction: a visible receiver requesting a shadow page does not tell us every object that might cast a shadow onto it.

We still need **light-space caster discovery**, using suitable bounds and acceleration structures. Our flat-grid index can help discover casters, but the relevant geometry may lie outside the camera's visible cells.

### Cache invalidation

For an MMO, this is essential.

Static buildings and terrain should reuse cached shadow pages when valid. Moving characters, doors, destructible structures, and dynamic lights can invalidate parts of the cache.

I'd track conservative caster changes using dirty spatial ranges and light influence, then invalidate affected shadow pages.

Incorrect invalidation causes stale shadows. Overly broad invalidation destroys caching performance.

We should also reserve capacity for exceptional scenes rather than allow a crowded city to exhaust shadow pages uncontrollably.

## 6. Clustered lighting with GPU-built light lists

With thousands of dynamic lights potentially present in a major MMO city, we should not evaluate every light against every pixel.

I recommend **clustered lighting**, with GPU-generated light membership lists.

Unlike our world grid, the lighting clusters live in camera/view space.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Illustrative screen-space light clusters</text>
  <svg viewBox="0 0 330 180" width="100%">
    {#each Array.from({length:5},(_,i)=>i) as y}
      {#each Array.from({length:9},(_,i)=>i) as x}
        <rect x={8+x*35} y={7+y*31} width="33" height="29" rx="2" fill={(x-4)**2+(y-2)**2<6?"#D3A34E":"#709EBF"} fillOpacity={(x-4)**2+(y-2)**2<6?".5":".19"} stroke="currentColor" strokeOpacity=".2"/>
      {/each}
    {/each}
    <circle cx="170" cy="83" r="35" stroke="#D3A34E" fill="none" strokeWidth="1.6" strokeDasharray="4 3"/>
    <circle cx="170" cy="83" r="5" fill="#D3A34E"/>
    <text x="165" y="178" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor" fontSize="10">Simplified 2D illustration; actual clusters include depth slices</text>
  </svg>
  <text size="sm" color="secondary">Each shading cluster references the lights potentially affecting its pixels, rather than the complete light collection.</text>
</box>

The GPU processes relevant lights, calculates cluster membership, compacts light references, and gives the material/lighting stage fast access to those lists.

Our flat 2.5D grid can accelerate broad-world light discovery, while view-space clustering provides efficient shading.

These structures are complementary.

### High-end lighting techniques

| Technique | Proposed role | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| Clustered lighting | Primary direct-light organization | Core |
| Physically based BRDF | Material lighting model | Core |
| Virtual shadow maps | High-detail shadowing | High |
| Reflection probes | Stable, economical reflection fallback | Core |
| Screen-space reflections | Reuse visible scene information | Optional |
| Ray queries / RT reflections | Higher-quality selective reflections | High-end |
| Probe-based GI / radiance caches | Scalable indirect lighting | High |
| ReSTIR DI/GI | Reuse lighting samples across pixels/frames | Research |
| Neural denoising / reconstruction | Improve ray-limited image quality | Research |

I would build a common lighting interface, so direct-light evaluation, shadowing, and indirect illumination can evolve independently.

One reason is hardware variability: a mesh-shader-capable GPU does not necessarily support every ray-tracing or advanced scheduling feature we may want.

## 7. Transparency, foliage, water, and particles

A visibility buffer is excellent for many opaque surfaces, but **it does not eliminate the need for specialised rendering paths**.

In particular, a single visibility ID per pixel cannot represent an arbitrary number of overlapping transparent surfaces.

| Content | Proposed rendering path |
|---|---|
| Opaque buildings, terrain, rocks | Visibility buffer |
| Opaque characters | Visibility buffer |
| Alpha-tested foliage | Visibility-compatible masked path, subject to performance |
| Glass | Dedicated transparency path |
| Water | Specialised surface + reflection/refraction |
| Smoke and fog | GPU volumetric/particle pipelines |
| Magical effects | GPU procedural/particle renderer |
| Hair and difficult translucency | Specialised rendering strategy |

For dense foliage, we'd benchmark alpha testing against suitable geometry or stochastic approaches.

For transparent surfaces, options include sorted rendering, weighted blended transparency, or more expensive order-independent methods.

I would not mandate one solution across the entire engine.

## 8. Multi-view rendering should share the GPU scene

An MMO can contain many views beyond the main camera:

- Main world camera.
- Shadow-map views.
- Mirrors and reflections.
- Portals.
- Character previews and inventory portraits.
- Minimap.
- In-world displays.

They should share the persistent GPU ECS and geometry resource tables.

But each view may need its own visibility and LOD work.

For the minimap, I would avoid rerendering the entire world at full geometric detail. A specialised terrain/map representation may be much cheaper.

Portal and reflection views need explicit recursion and GPU-work budgets.

## 9. GPU synchronization and execution layout

Our previous scheduler work still applies.

The critical dependencies now include:

| Dependency | Required result |
|---|---|
| ECS updates → visibility | Correct current transforms and bounds |
| Work generation → mesh rendering | Published descriptors and indirect counts |
| Visibility → material resolve | Completed primitive IDs and depth |
| Material resolve → lighting | Valid surface attributes |
| Shadow-page rendering → sampling | Completed shadow pages |
| Lighting → post-processing | Finished HDR scene colour |
| World post → UI | Correct UI composition target |

These are logical edges in the render graph.

We should aim for **a mostly precompiled Vulkan render graph with GPU-generated work sizes and a small number of explicit synchronization boundaries**.

Where hardware supports it and dependencies permit, independent compute jobs could overlap graphics work.

But multiple queues do not guarantee more performance. They may contend for the same compute units or bandwidth, and cross-queue dependencies introduce additional complexity.

### Important GPU ownership rule

The CPU can submit one or several reusable command-buffer sequences that orchestrate the frame.

That does not make the renderer CPU-driven.

The determining feature is whether the host generates individual entity draws, material batches, or per-object visibility decisions.

Ours should not.

## 10. Our architectural decisions

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {n:"Visibility-buffer-first opaque renderer",d:"Compact primitive identification, deferred material evaluation."},
    {n:"Mesh/task-shader geometry pipeline",d:"GPU-selected cluster LOD with compressed geometry decoding."},
    {n:"Hybrid microtriangle capability",d:"Architecture permits compute rasterization; implementation depends on benchmarks."},
    {n:"GPU-native material tables",d:"Bindless resources, specialised material families and optional coherent resolve."},
    {n:"GPU clustered direct lighting",d:"View-space light lists generated entirely on GPU."},
    {n:"GPU virtual shadow maps",d:"Demand-driven pages, caster discovery, conservative invalidation."},
    {n:"Pluggable indirect lighting",d:"Probe/radiance-cache baseline, optional RT and ReSTIR."},
    {n:"Separate transparency paths",d:"Do not force glass, water, or particles into opaque visibility records."},
    {n:"Shared scene, view-specific work",d:"Reuse GPU ECS and geometry while generating independent view visibility."},
    {n:"GPU-native UI after world reconstruction",d:"Maintain crisp Bézier text independent of world rendering resolution."}
  ] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{x.n}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. What I would prototype before freezing implementation

There are four areas where real GPU results matter more than theoretical elegance.

| Prototype | Critical question |
|---|---|
| Visibility buffer vs compact G-buffer | Is deferred attribute reconstruction cheaper for our material/geometry mix? |
| Direct task work vs precompacted meshlet lists | Which produces lower total visibility + geometry time? |
| Virtual shadow paging | Can we update dense-city dynamic shadows within a bounded GPU budget? |
| Material resolve with/without pixel binning | Does improved coherence justify binning overhead? |

We should test at least a forest, a crowded capital, a cave system, and a high-altitude flight scene.

I would set performance budgets in milliseconds for a defined GPU tier and resolution rather than rely on vague goals such as “millions of triangles.”

## 12. Next: temporal reconstruction and frame architecture

The next high-level layer is **how frames are assembled, reconstructed, and presented**.

This includes:

- Temporal antialiasing and supersampling.
- GPU-native motion-vector generation.
- Dynamic resolution and foveated shading.
- Spatiotemporal reuse of lighting and shadow information.
- Decoupled simulation/render frequencies.
- Frame pacing, latency, and GPU work budgets.
- Multiple in-flight ECS/render epochs.

The last item is particularly important: our GPU ECS, virtual shadow maps, temporal history, and resource residency must share a coherent notion of state lifetime without unnecessarily copying the entire world.

**I'd make temporal frame architecture our next topic**, then move into advanced GI, ray tracing, and neural rendering once the frame and synchronization model is settled.

# Phase 09 — Temporal Frame Architecture & GPU Synchronization
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Design · October 2026</text>

Our next objective is to make the GPU ECS, simulation, mesh/task renderer, visibility buffer, shadow maps, and GPU UI operate as **one coherent, low-latency frame system**.

I recommend:

**GPU-resident state epochs + a compiled Vulkan render graph + temporal reconstruction + independent simulation/presentation clocks + bounded frames in flight.**

We can make these decisions now without committing to advanced GI, ray tracing, neural rendering, or frame generation.

The underlying principle:

> **We should maximize useful GPU work overlap while minimizing the age of the information displayed to the player.**

High throughput alone isn't enough for an MMO. A renderer producing 200 FPS with unnecessarily delayed input or stale player positions is not performing well.

## 1. Separate the engine's clocks

Our engine should never assume that networking, simulation, GPU state processing, and display presentation all operate at the same frequency.

| Clock | Responsibility | Proposed policy |
|---|---|---|
| Server simulation | Authoritative gameplay and physics | Fixed timestep |
| Network replication | Deliver selected world changes | Independent, priority-driven |
| Client prediction | Responsive local gameplay where applicable | Fixed simulation steps |
| GPU ECS update | Apply deltas and run visual systems | Dependency-driven |
| Rendering | Generate the next visible frame | Display-paced, variable frequency |
| Streaming | Resource demand, loading and eviction | Asynchronous, budget-driven |
| UI | Input, layout and animations | Presentation-frequency with event-driven changes |

This is especially important for crowds and world simulation.

A distant character might receive fewer network updates than the client render rate. The GPU can interpolate its presentation state rather than requiring a new server packet for every displayed frame.

The client should maintain time-stamped authoritative samples and a defined presentation timeline rather than blindly interpolate between whichever two packets arrived most recently.

## 2. GPU state epochs — the foundation

I would make **state epochs first-class engine objects**.

An epoch represents a logically consistent published state of some part of the GPU ECS.

We do not need to copy the entire ECS every frame.

The key optimization is **selective versioning**.

| Data | Proposed lifetime strategy |
|---|---|
| Static meshlet geometry | Shared immutable, reference-counted residency |
| Static material parameters | Shared until modified |
| Dynamic transforms | Versioned where concurrent readers require it |
| Animation pose data | Ring-buffered or versioned per active character |
| GPU entity location table | Epoch-consistent publication |
| Spatial CSR index | Published base with controlled incremental updates |
| Visibility work buffers | Frame-local transient storage |
| Temporal images | Persistent history with explicit validity |
| UI state | Persistent retained representation with selective versioning |

Not every component needs two or three complete copies.

An important consequence: **ECS epoch, render frame, temporal-history frame, and server tick must be different identifiers.** They can advance independently.

## 3. Frames in flight: start with two

I'd initially design for **two CPU-submitted frames in flight**, with a configurable limit.

Three frames can help throughput on some hardware, but potentially increase input latency and memory pressure.

Frames in flight should be managed using GPU completion values and resource lifetimes, not by copying every state buffer into one slot per frame.

Vulkan timeline semaphores are suitable for queue progress tracking and safe resource reuse. Swapchain acquisition/presentation still requires attention to WSI synchronization, including binary semaphore lifecycle. <Cite refs={["turn604674search0","turn604674search10"]}/>

### An additional low-latency option

We should support delayed sampling of the latest input and late updates of camera-dependent data, provided they can be written safely before the consuming GPU work.

That may reduce perceived latency without changing authoritative simulation.

We must not allow such updates to race with rendering commands already reading the same data.

## 4. GPU-native motion vectors

Motion vectors are now a **foundational rendering requirement**, not an optional post-processing feature.

They allow temporal reconstruction to identify where currently visible surfaces appeared in a previous rendered frame.

Because our GPU ECS already owns transforms and animation, it is ideally positioned to produce them.

### What needs previous-frame information?

| Content | Required history |
|---|---|
| Static world geometry | Previous camera transform |
| Moving entities | Previous and current world transforms |
| Skeletal characters | Previous and current animated surface positions |
| Moving ships/platforms | Previous parent and child transformations |
| Procedural vegetation | Previous procedural deformation state |
| Terrain | Previous camera transform, unless terrain changes |
| Particles | Motion or specialized temporal treatment |
| GPU vector UI | Usually excluded from world reconstruction |

The difficult case is **deforming geometry**.

A character's root transform alone does not describe the motion of its arms, clothing, or animated silhouette.

Our GPU skinning/animation subsystem therefore needs a mechanism to reconstruct previous skinned positions.

I would investigate two variants:

- Store previous pose data and evaluate previous/current deformation when needed.
- Store previous deformed vertex positions for selected high-priority animated entities.

The first saves persistent memory but adds reconstruction work. The second reduces repeat deformation work but increases memory bandwidth and residency costs.

This becomes a benchmark decision, not a separate rendering architecture.

### Motion vector generation

For each visible surface position:

\[
\mathbf{v}=
\operatorname{Project}_{current}(\mathbf{p}_{current})
-
\operatorname{Project}_{previous}(\mathbf{p}_{previous})
\]

Both positions must be expressed in a consistent coordinate convention; projection jitter is handled explicitly.

Because our world uses large coordinates and camera-relative GPU rendering, we must ensure that origin rebasing does not create artificial motion.

We also need correctly defined behavior for newly spawned, teleported, destructed, or otherwise discontinuous objects.

## 5. Temporal reconstruction instead of relying on native resolution

My recommendation is to support **temporal antialiasing and temporal upscaling from the outset**.

That means the engine can render world geometry at a lower internal resolution and reconstruct a higher-resolution image using current and historical information.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>

  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

    <caption>Post processing · Tone mapping</caption>

    **Native-Resolution GPU UI**

    <caption>Sharp Bézier text · Vector controls · HUD composition</caption>
  </box>
</box>

I'd build a **backend-neutral temporal reconstruction interface**, rather than immediately implement every upscaling algorithm.

That interface should provide:

- Current scene colour, depth, and motion vectors.
- Camera jitter and render/output dimensions.
- Exposure and temporal reset flags.
- Reactive/transparency information when needed.
- Validity information for newly resident or changed content.

These inputs align with established temporal upscaling requirements. AMD's FSR documentation, for example, describes reactive masks for translucent or particle content that may not provide reliable depth or motion-vector footprints. <Cite ref="turn604674search9"/>

### Why this matters now

If temporal reconstruction is added late, animation, material rendering, transparency, and geometry LOD may all need substantial redesign.

By defining its inputs now, we preserve freedom to replace the reconstruction algorithm later.

## 6. Dynamic resolution and frame budgets

We should support GPU-driven adaptation of visual workload when the GPU is under pressure.

That doesn't mean changing internal resolution abruptly every frame. It means using measured GPU execution times to adjust quality smoothly.

For our MMO I would use several independent adaptive budgets:

| Budget | Adaptive control |
|---|---|
| Screen-space shading | Internal render resolution |
| Geometry | Meshlet LOD error and microtriangle thresholds |
| Shadows | Page-update budget and shadow detail |
| Distant animation | Frequency and pose-detail policy |
| Particles | Active count and simulation detail |
| Background GPU ECS | Work quota and dispatch frequency |
| Streaming | Upload, decompression, and residency quotas |

These should be coordinated, because reducing render resolution alone may not help when the bottleneck is geometry, streaming, or simulation.

A crowded MMO capital is likely to have a very different bottleneck profile from an open landscape.

This is a dependency illustration, not a promise that all branches can run concurrently. The compiler should determine actual overlap based on resources and hardware capabilities.

I'd use Vulkan Synchronization2 and timeline semaphores, with synchronization generated from pass dependencies and resource access.

The Khronos synchronization guidance explicitly emphasizes narrow dependencies and avoiding waits between work that can safely execute independently. <Cite ref="turn604674search2"/>

### Resource lifetime classifications

| Resource lifetime | Examples | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent | ECS arrays, meshlet data, material tables | Stable allocations |
| Epoch-versioned | Dynamic transforms, poses, selected metadata | Retire after reader completion |
| Frame-transient | Compaction lists, sorting scratch, temporary outputs | Alias where lifetimes do not overlap |
| Temporal-history | Previous colour, depth, visibility confidence | Preserve across frames |
| Streamed | Geometry/texture pages | Budgeted residency and deferred eviction |
| Swapchain | Presented images | Follow WSI acquisition/presentation rules |

Transient resource aliasing is particularly useful: mutually exclusive passes can reuse physical memory instead of holding every intermediate buffer simultaneously.

The frame graph must prove that lifetimes do not overlap before aliasing.

## 8. One critical challenge: temporal history invalidation

This is something we should design explicitly now.

An MMO has frequent events that break temporal continuity:

- Player teleports.
- Character respawns.
- New structures stream into view.
- Doors open.
- World geometry changes or is destroyed.
- Lighting or weather changes sharply.
- Camera cuts occur.
- Render resolution changes.

The renderer must know when historical data is no longer reliable.

I recommend a **temporal validity system**, with per-view invalidation flags and finer-grained per-object or per-pixel validity where beneficial.

For example:

| Event | Temporal response |
|---|---|
| Normal camera motion | Reproject history |
| Entity movement | Use motion vectors |
| Entity spawn | Reject history for newly covered regions |
| Teleport / camera cut | Reset affected view histories |
| Newly resident geometry | Mark newly revealed surfaces as history-unreliable |
| Shadow page change | Update shadow history validity as appropriate |
| Dynamic resolution change | Rescale or reset history, based on reconstruction backend |

This avoids ghosting and stale imagery without unnecessarily resetting all temporal data whenever one entity changes.

## 9. Important decision: late presentation updates

For low-latency input response, I'd reserve a **late-update stage** for camera and selected presentation transforms.

This allows an input sample taken closer to actual rendering to influence camera movement without rerunning the entire GPU ECS.

However, late camera changes affect frustum culling, occlusion, temporal reprojection, and motion vectors.

Therefore, we need a consistent camera snapshot for the parts of the frame that depend on it, or conservative visibility margins that accommodate a bounded late adjustment.

**Late camera updates cannot arbitrarily change the view after culling without risking missing geometry.**

I'd design the data interfaces now and implement aggressive late updating only after measuring end-to-end latency.

## 10. What we lock into the engine

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"Independent simulation and rendering clocks",d:"Fixed authoritative ticks, variable presentation rates and timestamped replication."},
    {t:"GPU ECS state epochs",d:"Consistent publication, selective versioning and safe memory retirement."},
    {t:"Two-frame initial submission limit",d:"Configurable frame pipeline with low-latency pacing."},
    {t:"First-class motion vectors",d:"Previous/current camera, entity and deforming geometry support."},
    {t:"Temporal reconstruction interface",d:"Backend-neutral upscaling, jitter, reactive masks and history management."},
    {t:"Dynamic resolution and adaptive GPU budgets",d:"Coordinate quality changes across shading, geometry, simulation and streaming."},
    {t:"Compiled Vulkan frame graph",d:"Resource dependencies, barriers, transient aliasing and asynchronous scheduling."},
    {t:"Temporal validity tracking",d:"Correct handling of teleportation, streaming, destruction and disocclusion."},
    {t:"Native-resolution GPU UI",d:"Bézier text and UI stay sharp independently of 3D render scale."},
    {t:"Optional late-view update architecture",d:"Preserve low-latency input improvements without unsafe camera changes."}
  ] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{x.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. Advanced GI / ray tracing — decisions we can defer

As requested, I would **not commit to ray tracing, ReSTIR, neural rendering or a specific advanced GI solution now**.

Only three architectural provisions are worth preserving:

1. **Keep geometry and material data GPU-addressable independently of rasterization.** Other lighting methods can consume it in the future.
2. **Keep lighting, shadowing and indirect illumination behind replaceable interfaces.** Do not bake one GI representation into every material.
3. **Make the render graph extensible to additional acceleration structures, persistent histories, and asynchronous passes.** No need to allocate or build these resources until an actual technique requires them.

None of those requires ray tracing or advanced GI in the baseline renderer.

## 12. Recommended next architectural phase

We've now defined the rendering and frame-processing architecture at a high level.

The next highest-impact topic is **GPU-native animation, character crowds, and simulation LOD**.

For an MMO, thousands of animated characters may become a greater problem than rendering static geometry. I'd investigate:

- GPU skeletal animation and hierarchical pose evaluation.
- Animation graph evaluation directly on GPU.
- Shared animation sampling for large crowds.
- Bone palette and compressed animation storage.
- GPU skinning versus mesh-shader skinning.
- Perceptual animation LOD and pose caching.
- Integration with ECS structural changes, motion vectors, and visibility.

This is the next area where decisions made now can materially affect our ECS layout, GPU memory architecture, and mesh/task rendering pipeline.

**My recommendation is to tackle animation next, before physics or advanced lighting.** It is one of the defining performance challenges of a large-scale MMO and directly tests whether our GPU-native ECS architecture delivers the scalability we're aiming for.

## 069 — Assistant

Message ID: `9d9d7a6f-7011-47eb-a21e-7a2b00b6b544` · 2026-10-08T03:58:20.734971+00:00

# Phase 09A — Low-Cost GI & Ray Tracing Opportunities

**Yes. Our existing architecture gives us several unusually good opportunities to add global illumination, ambient occlusion, and reflections without building a full ray-tracing renderer.**

The key is that we've already committed to most of the expensive *supporting infrastructure*:

- GPU-resident geometry and materials.
- Visibility buffer with depth.
- Hierarchical Z-buffer (HZB).
- GPU-generated work queues.
- Temporal history and motion vectors.
- Flat 2.5D spatial grid.
- GPU-resident world state and streaming.

I would prioritize techniques that reuse these systems, avoiding a second complete scene representation unless its visual benefit justifies the expense.

## 1. Best opportunities ranked

<text color="secondary" size="xs">Engineering estimates relative to our proposed renderer, not measured GPU costs.</text>

| Technique | Added implementation | Runtime cost | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GTAO / screen-space AO** | Low–medium | Low–medium | Implement |
| **Screen-space GI (SSGI)** | Medium | Medium | Implement as optional quality tier |
| **Screen-space reflections (SSR)** | Medium | Medium | Strong candidate |
| **Static baked indirect lighting** | Medium + content pipeline | Very low | Plan for it |
| **Probe-based indirect lighting** | Medium | Low–medium | Core fallback |
| **Screen-space contact shadows** | Low | Low–medium | Implement selectively |
| **Ray-query contact shadows** | High initially | Variable | Defer |
| **SDF / software-traced GI** | High | Medium–high | Preserve upgrade path |
| **Hardware RT GI / reflections** | High | High / variable | Defer |

The cheapest effects are not necessarily full global illumination. Ambient occlusion, contact shadows and reflection approximations can deliver substantial perceived lighting improvements with less new infrastructure.

## 2. Screen-space GI — highest reuse of our existing pipeline

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Existing Visibility Buffer + Material Resolve**
    <caption>Depth · Surface normals · Albedo · Direct lighting · Motion vectors</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Screen-space Ray Marching**
    <caption>Reuse HZB · Sample surrounding visible surfaces</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Temporal Accumulation + Denoising**
    <caption>Reuse motion vectors, depth validation, history management</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Indirect Diffuse Lighting**
    <caption>Approximate bounced radiance and colour bleeding</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Screen-space GI can trace through our already-rendered depth representation and sample the radiance of hit surfaces.

That gives us approximate effects such as sunlight reflecting from the ground onto surrounding objects and coloured walls contributing light to nearby surfaces.

It does not require hardware RT acceleration structures.

**The catch:** screen-space GI only knows about surfaces represented in its screen-space inputs. Hidden and offscreen geometry cannot contribute reliably. Temporal reuse improves stability but cannot recover information the system never observed. <Cite ref="turn980001search6"/>

For our MMO, I would run it at reduced resolution with bounded ray counts and reuse temporal history.

This is a worthwhile option, but not a complete world-space lighting solution.

## 3. GTAO — an easy visual improvement

Ground-truth ambient occlusion approximations use depth and surface geometry to estimate local occlusion.

They improve:

- Contact between characters and the ground.
- Rock formations and crevices.
- Architectural corners.
- Furniture and interior clutter.
- Layered vegetation.

This is particularly useful for our terrain, cities and caves.

We already generate depth and can obtain normals during material resolve. We'd need an AO pass, filtering and potentially temporal stabilization.

**I'd include GTAO in the core renderer**, with adjustable quality and a low-cost fallback.

It should supplement indirect lighting rather than be misrepresented as actual bounced light.

## 4. Screen-space reflections — strong value for the implementation cost

SSR is another natural addition.

<row align="start" gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="screen space reflections puddle wet cobblestone realistic video game graphics comparison reflection" aspectRatio="4:3" maxWidth="160px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **Reflections from existing scene information**

    SSR traces against screen-space depth and samples existing radiance. For wet streets, water-adjacent surfaces and glossy interiors, this can provide attractive reflections without a ray-tracing scene.
  </box>
</row>

AMD's FidelityFX Stochastic Screen Space Reflections demonstrates hierarchical depth traversal, ray classification, indirect dispatch and temporal/spatial denoising—the same types of GPU facilities our renderer already uses. <Cite ref="turn980001search1"/>

We would still need missing-hit fallbacks, typically reflection probes or environment maps.

SSR is a particularly good candidate for an optional high-quality setting because it shares much of its infrastructure with SSGI.

## 5. Static indirect lighting — potentially almost free at runtime

For our primarily terrain-based MMO, this is one of the strongest opportunities.

We can precompute indirect lighting for static environments and stream the resulting data alongside world content.

Examples include terrain bounce lighting, cave illumination, building interiors, and static architectural colour bleeding.

A compact representation might use:

- Irradiance probes.
- Spherical harmonics coefficients.
- Visibility or occlusion information.
- Region-local probe grids.
- Compressed lighting pages.

Our existing world streaming and GPU residency system can handle these as another resource family.

**The GPU cost of sampling precomputed probes can be relatively low.** The tradeoffs are offline baking, asset storage, updates after destruction, and incompatibility with fully dynamic lighting unless supplemented by another method.

I'd strongly consider static or slowly updated probes as the baseline GI system, supplemented by SSGI.

## 6. The intriguing option: GPU software-traced GI

This is the most interesting technique for our architecture, even though it's not free.

Our flat 2.5D grid already provides spatial indexing. We could extend selected resident cells with compact geometry occupancy or signed-distance data.

That creates a possible GPU software-ray-tracing structure:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Flat 2.5D World Grid**
  </box>

  </box>

  </box>

    **World-Space Indirect Light + Occlusion**
  </box>
</box>

AMD's <Entity category="software" value="FidelityFX Brixelizer GI"/> is a relevant reference. It uses a GPU-compute distance-field approach, screen probes, and radiance caching to produce diffuse and specular GI, without requiring the conventional hardware ray-tracing pipeline. It supports a Vulkan integration path. <Cite ref="turn980001search9"/>

However, **our flat grid does not automatically provide ray traversal**. We would still need to construct distance or occupancy representations, update dynamic geometry, handle missing data, and maintain radiance histories.

I'd preserve the capability to attach SDF bricks to world cells, but defer actually building the system.

## 7. Hardware ray queries — useful, but not free

Ray queries are less invasive than building a complete ray-tracing renderer because they can execute inside existing compute or graphics shaders.

For example, we could issue a selective ray query for a character's contact shadow, a reflection, or an occlusion test.

But Vulkan's `VK_KHR_ray_query` still requires `VK_KHR_acceleration_structure`, including construction and maintenance of BLAS/TLAS structures. <Cite ref="turn455669search0"/>

Our meshlet geometry representation also doesn't automatically serve as hardware RT acceleration data.

So hardware ray queries are a useful future extension, **not a nearly free addition**.

## 8. What I would actually integrate

## 9. Two decisions worth making now

**First: expose a compact resolved-surface buffer.**

Our visibility buffer stores primitive identity rather than normals, albedo, roughness and radiance directly.

Screen-space GI, AO and SSR need that information.

We should therefore support a **configurable GPU surface cache** generated by the material resolver, containing the attributes needed by enabled lighting effects.

This avoids repeatedly reconstructing the same surface data for every technique while preserving the visibility-buffer architecture.

**Second: support streamed lighting resources per world cell.**

Extend our existing resource directory with optional irradiance probes, compressed lighting coefficients and future distance-field bricks.

This costs little architectural complexity now and avoids forcing lighting to adopt an unrelated streaming system later.

Neither decision commits us to hardware RT.

## Final recommendation

I'd lock the following:

- **Core:** GPU probe lighting + GTAO/CACAO.
- **Enhanced:** SSGI and stochastic SSR using our existing HZB and temporal pipeline.
- **Architecture-only provision:** Sparse distance-field resources for future software GI.
- **Deferred:** Hardware RT, ReSTIR, full dynamic GI, neural GI.

This gives us meaningful lighting quality improvements with relatively little disruption to the engine's existing foundations.

The most important insight is that **our visibility buffer, HZB, GPU ECS and temporal infrastructure have already paid much of the architectural cost of screen-space lighting**. The additional effects still consume GPU time, but they don't require rethinking the renderer.

We can now return to **GPU-native animation and massive character crowds**, keeping these lightweight lighting capabilities integrated into the baseline.
