This should operate on contiguous ECS component streams, not individually allocated animation objects.

## 2. GPU animation ECS — contiguous storage

I'd divide animation data into specialized SoA streams rather than store a large animation object per character.

| GPU data stream | Contents |
|---|---|
| `AnimationState[]` | State machine ID, current states, transition flags |
| `AnimationParameters[]` | Speed, direction, action state, blend parameters |
| `ClipInstances[]` | Clip references, sample times, blend weights |
| `SkeletonReferences[]` | Skeleton IDs and bone hierarchy references |
| `PoseReferences[]` | Cached or unique pose locations |
| `BoneTransforms[]` | Contiguous transform palettes |
| `SkinningWork[]` | Active mesh deformation workloads |
| `AttachmentTransforms[]` | Weapons, armour, equipment, visual effects |
| `PreviousPose[]` | Motion-vector history where necessary |

Each stage processes only the component streams it needs.

For instance, determining that 2,000 distant characters are still walking should not require reading their vertex data or evaluating every bone.

### Separate three levels of computation

| Level | Operation | Sharing potential |
|---|---|---|
| Animation graph | Determine clips, transitions and parameters | Limited |
| Skeleton pose | Sample and combine bone transformations | High for similar characters |
| Vertex deformation | Skin actual character geometry | Depends on meshes and visibility |

This separation is crucial to making crowd animation scale.

## 3. Shared pose evaluation — our biggest opportunity

Imagine 5,000 humanoids in a city.

They may have different clothing and positions, but many will share skeleton definitions and animation clips.

We should avoid evaluating an identical skeletal pose thousands of times.

I propose a **GPU pose-sharing cache**.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **5,000 Character Animation Instances**

    <caption>Independent ECS animation state</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU Pose-Key Generation**

    <caption>Skeleton + clip + quantized time + blend state</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Unique Pose Workloads**

    <caption>Evaluate reusable poses once</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Instance → Pose References**

    <caption>Many characters reference the same bone palette</caption>
  </box>
</box>

### How sharing would work

The GPU constructs a pose key from compatible animation states, groups matching instances, and evaluates each unique pose.

We could quantize animation playback time for lower-detail characters to increase sharing.

For example, multiple NPCs using the same walking clip at approximately the same playback phase could reference one evaluated pose.

But this is not universally applicable.

A character with different upper-body attacks, aim direction, injuries, procedural adjustments or animation blending may require a distinct pose.

**We should never force important player characters to share poses when doing so creates visible animation errors.**

### Pose-sharing policies

| Character class | Policy |
|---|---|
| Local player | Unique high-quality pose |
| Nearby important characters | Unique or selectively shared |
| Nearby ordinary NPCs | Shared base pose with optional unique overlays |
| Distant crowds | Quantized playback and aggressive sharing |
| Very distant characters | Reduced bone sets, impostors or procedural approximation |

This lets us prioritize visible quality without duplicating work unnecessarily.

## 4. Mesh-shader skinning vs compute skinning

This is a decision worth making now because our renderer already requires mesh shaders.

There are two strong techniques.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Option A — Skin directly in mesh shaders**

    Mesh shaders fetch bind-pose geometry and bone transforms, then deform the emitted vertices.

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Best candidate for characters rendered once, when only visible geometry needs deformation and no other subsystem requires skinned vertex buffers.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Option B — Skin once using GPU compute**

    Compute shaders generate deformed vertex buffers, reused by rendering and other GPU systems.

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Best candidate for characters whose geometry is consumed repeatedly by shadow passes, multiple cameras, physics approximations, or other processing.</text>
  </box>
</box>

Khronos's current compute-skinning guidance explicitly describes persistent GPU-generated vertex buffers that subsequent passes can reuse, avoiding repeated skinning for different consumers. <Cite refs={["turn892999search1","turn892999search4"]}/>

### My recommendation: adaptive hybrid skinning

I would implement **both paths behind one animation interface**.

| Workload | Preferred starting path |
|---|---|
| Nearby player rendered in multiple passes | Compute skinning |
| Distant NPC visible in one view | Mesh-shader skinning |
| Repeated crowd instances | Shared pose + mesh-shader deformation |
| Characters with expensive cloth deformation | Compute where results are reused |
| Shadow-only distant characters | Lower-detail mesh-shader deformation |
| Character preview / multi-camera reuse | Compute skinning if total cost is lower |

For our virtualized geometry system, mesh-shader deformation should operate on LOD-selected meshlets, with bone palettes available through GPU resource tables.

However, we need to ensure shared vertices remain consistently deformed across meshlet boundaries.

### An important optimization

**Do not skin vertices that will never be needed.**

We should cull character instances and select geometry LOD before undertaking expensive mesh deformation where dependencies allow.

This is where our flat spatial grid and GPU task-shader architecture become valuable.

One caveat: precise animated bounds may depend on pose evaluation, so the early visibility pass should use conservative character bounds rather than require full skinning first.

## 5. Animation LOD needs its own system

Geometry LOD and animation LOD should be independent.

A distant character might require only 300 triangles, but it still wastes resources if we evaluate an elaborate 150-bone rig with numerous animation layers every frame.

I recommend **continuous or tiered skeletal-detail reduction**.

| Animation tier | Example processing |
|---|---|
| Tier 0 — Hero | Full bone set, animation layers, IK and secondary motion |
| Tier 1 — Near | Full primary skeleton, reduced secondary updates |
| Tier 2 — Medium | Reduced bone palette, simplified blending |
| Tier 3 — Far | Shared poses, quantized animation and reduced frequency |
| Tier 4 — Very far | Coarse skeletal transforms or animated impostors |

This is a proposed quality hierarchy, not fixed distance thresholds.

We would select tiers using projected character size, importance, visibility, animation complexity and performance budgets.

A raid boss might stay at high animation quality even when relatively far from the camera.

### Avoid visible animation snapping

When characters switch animation tiers, we must maintain phase continuity and blend compatible representations.

Reducing animation frequency does not mean rendering at that reduced rate. We can interpolate cached poses or analytically advance simplified animations for each displayed frame.

The player's current equipment, actions and important combat telegraphs must remain correct.

## 6. GPU animation scheduling and synchronisation

Animation integrates naturally with our GPU-native ECS scheduler.

I propose five major processing phases:

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {n:"1",t:"Classify animation workloads",d:"Use active sets, importance, projected size and current animation state."},
    {n:"2",t:"Evaluate animation graphs",d:"Select clips, transitions, blend parameters and required skeletal detail."},
    {n:"3",t:"Deduplicate pose requests",d:"Group compatible pose keys; create unique pose workloads."},
    {n:"4",t:"Generate poses and attachments",d:"Sample compressed clips, evaluate hierarchies, produce bone transforms."},
    {n:"5",t:"Deform and render",d:"Select compute skinning or mesh-shader deformation; update motion history."}
  ] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={3}>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" size="36px" align="center" justify="center">
        <text weight="medium">{x.n}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{x.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

We should process animation in large batches, using GPU-generated work counts.

A full global sort is not always justified. For small unique-pose populations, a compact hash/deduplication structure may be cheaper. For very large crowds, radix-sorted pose keys may offer better throughput.

The scheduler should support both.

## 7. Compressed animation data

A large MMO can contain enormous quantities of animations, skeletons and character variations.

We should treat animation clips as streamable GPU resources, similar to our virtualized geometry.

I'd investigate:

- Quantized bone rotations and translations.
- Variable-rate keyframes.
- Sparse per-track animation channels.
- Compressed clip blocks with GPU-friendly random access.
- Skeleton LOD mappings.
- Shared clip dictionaries.
- Bounded local decompression scratch memory.

For GPU execution, a compression scheme with slightly worse ratios but predictable parallel decoding may outperform a highly compressed format requiring serial processing.

The important optimization is reducing **total memory bandwidth plus decoding cost**, not maximizing compression ratio alone.

## 8. Integration with our locked SDF + radiance cache GI

Our new GI choice actually simplifies one difficult animation problem.

**We do not need every animated character's detailed skinned geometry inserted into the GI tracing representation every frame.**

Instead, I'd use contribution policies.

| Character/visual component | Dynamic GI policy |
|---|---|
| Terrain and static buildings | Full SDF contribution |
| Opening doors / moving architecture | Update local SDF regions |
| Large creatures | Optional simplified dynamic SDF proxy |
| Ordinary NPCs | Primarily receive GI |
| Player characters | Receive GI; selective coarse contribution |
| Weapons and small equipment | Generally excluded from world SDF |
| Emissive spell effects | Optional direct radiance injection, budgeted |

The GI system should not depend on full compute-skinned geometry for ordinary crowds.

A simplified capsule-based or low-resolution volumetric proxy may be sufficient for selected dynamic occlusion effects.

This avoids turning crowd animation into an expensive SDF-rebuilding workload.

AMD's Brixelizer GI documentation explicitly separates distance-field tracing from its radiance cache and discusses incorporating static and dynamic scene geometry. <Cite refs={["turn892999search6","turn892999search7"]}/>

Our policy would be more selective because MMO crowds can contain thousands of moving contributors.

## 9. How many animated characters could this support?

The architecture should be designed for thousands of independently represented characters, but a raw entity-count target is not enough to establish achievable performance.

The key is the number of **unique evaluated poses, deformed vertices, visible meshlets, and associated render passes**.

{@body const [group,setGroup]=DIL.useState(16)}
{@body const unique=Math.ceil(characters*(100-share)/100)}
{@body const shared=characters-unique}
{@body const poseJobs=unique+Math.ceil(shared/group)}

We should eventually benchmark:

| Scenario | Main stress factor |
|---|---|
| 10,000 marching NPCs | Maximum pose-sharing potential |
| 5,000 unique combatants | Highly divergent animation graphs |
| 2,000 heavily equipped characters | Different meshes, attachments and materials |
| 1,000 characters with cloth/hair | Secondary simulation and deformation |
| 500 giant creatures | Large skeletons and vertex workloads |
| Dense city with combat effects | Animation competing with GI and graphics |

These are stress-test workloads, not performance guarantees.

## 10. Decisions I would lock now

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"GPU-native animation graph processing",d:"Animation-state selection and transitions execute in batched compute workloads."},
    {t:"Shared GPU pose cache",d:"Deduplicate compatible skeleton and animation evaluations."},
    {t:"Adaptive skinning architecture",d:"Mesh-shader deformation by default where suitable, reusable compute skinning when worthwhile."},
    {t:"Independent animation LOD",d:"Bone counts, blend complexity and evaluation frequency adapt separately from geometry."},
    {t:"Compressed GPU animation resources",d:"Streamable clips, GPU-friendly decoding and shared skeleton definitions."},
    {t:"GPU-resident attachment transforms",d:"Equipment, weapon and effect placements derive from generated poses."},
    {t:"Temporal animation history",d:"Correct motion vectors for moving and deforming characters."},
    {t:"Selective SDF contribution",d:"Dynamic GI uses coarse or filtered character contributions, not mandatory full crowd geometry updates."}
  ] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{item.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{item.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. One important boundary: gameplay animation vs visual animation

We should not allow presentation animation to become the authoritative source of gameplay decisions.

A player attack, collision volume, movement constraint or combat hit must ultimately be determined by the server's authoritative simulation.

The GPU animation system can render the attack, interpolate its pose and provide cosmetic effects. The gameplay meaning of that action comes from authoritative state and approved prediction.

This matters because shared poses, reduced-frequency animation, and animation LOD are **visual optimizations**, not changes to gameplay rules.

## 12. Recommended next architecture phase

The natural next subsystem is **GPU-native physics and collision**, especially how to reuse our flat 2.5D grid for broad-phase queries.

This will answer several critical questions:

- How can millions of spatially indexed entities perform proximity queries without global sorting?
- Where should GPU collision detection and CPU/server authority meet?
- Can we use the same world SDF infrastructure for collision queries and dynamic GI?
- How do we support terrain, caves, interiors and flying movement?
- How do we handle ragdolls, rigid bodies and large character crowds without excessive GPU synchronization?

One critical caution: **our GI SDF representation is probably too approximate or asynchronously updated to serve as the authoritative collision representation**.

We can share spatial addressing, residency infrastructure and selected source geometry, but we should preserve separate accuracy and update requirements for gameplay collision.

That is the next high-level design I'd recommend tackling.

# Phase 11 — GPU-Native Physics & Collision Architecture
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Core Architecture · October 2026</text>

Our next major system is physics. Given everything we've locked in, I recommend:

**A GPU-native, data-oriented physics pipeline using our flat 2.5D spatial grid for broad-phase discovery, specialised collision geometry for narrow-phase tests, and parallel constraint solvers.**

But there's one extremely important MMO-specific distinction:

> **Authoritative gameplay physics and high-volume visual physics must share world semantics, not necessarily the same processor, solver, or update frequency.**

We want to push as much physics as suitable onto the GPU without turning every collision query into a CPU/GPU synchronization bottleneck.

## 1. Recommended physics architecture

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative World State / Client Inputs**
    <caption>Server rules · Replication · Predicted movement</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **GPU ECS Physics Components**

GPU broad-phase collision detection and rigid-body solvers are established techniques. ## 2. One spatial foundation, multiple query structures

Our flat 2.5D grid remains the primary *world addressing system*.

But I would introduce a distinct **physics spatial index** that shares cell coordinates with rendering without requiring identical cell occupancy lists.

| Spatial resource | Purpose |
|---|---|
| World XY cell directory | Direct-addressed coarse location |
| Physics cell index | Broad-phase collision candidate discovery |
| Rendering cell index | Visibility and mesh/task work generation |
| Sparse vertical layers | Separate floors, caves and airspace |
| Local static collision data | Terrain triangles, convex geometry and heightfields |
| Dynamic-body index | Moving objects, overlapping bounds and swept volumes |
| GI SDF bricks | Approximate world-space lighting traversal |

Why maintain separate membership lists?

A decorative grass mesh might be important to rendering but irrelevant to physics. A hidden collision barrier might have no visible geometry.

Using one universal candidate array would force each system to scan irrelevant objects.

**The spatial coordinate system is shared; membership and acceleration data are workload-specific.**

## 3. GPU flat-grid collision broad phase

The existing CSR cell index gives us an excellent baseline.

A broad-phase pipeline would:

1. Read dynamic-body AABBs and velocities.
2. Calculate overlapping 2.5D cells.
3. Generate cell/body references.
4. Group references by cell, preferably incrementally where profitable.
5. Generate potential collision pairs.
6. Deduplicate pairs.
7. Filter by collision layers, ownership and shape rules.

The output is a compact list of candidate pairs for narrow-phase processing.

### The dense-crowd problem

A cell containing 1,000 characters has up to 499,500 unordered pairs *within that cell alone*.

Even if most pairs can quickly be rejected, blindly enumerating them is wasteful.

We should therefore use:

- Bounded cell occupancy or local micro-bins.
- Vertical filtering before expensive pair tests.
- Collision-layer filtering.
- Swept bounds for fast-moving bodies.
- Specialized character-crowd interaction rules.
- Adaptive fallback for overloaded cells.

Our flat grid gets us to the correct neighbourhood very cheaply. It does not eliminate pairwise interaction complexity.

### Multicell objects

Large vehicles, giants, structures, and fast-moving objects can overlap numerous cells.

We should insert references into all relevant candidate cells, with a duplicate-pair suppression mechanism.

For extremely large objects, I'd use a separate coarse-body index rather than duplicating one object into thousands of fine cells.

The design must also handle objects crossing cell boundaries between physics steps.

## 4. Collision geometry: share sources, not necessarily SDFs

We've locked in sparse SDF tracing for dynamic GI.

Can physics use those same SDFs?

**Yes for certain approximate queries, but not as the universal collision representation.**

| Collision representation | Best application | GPU suitability |
|---|---|---|
| Terrain heightfields | Outdoor ground, slopes and landscapes | Excellent |
| Capsules / spheres | Characters and simple dynamic objects | Excellent |
| Boxes / oriented boxes | Props, buildings and triggers | Excellent |
| Convex hulls | Dynamic rigid bodies | Good |
| Triangle meshes | Static detailed collision | Good with acceleration |
| Local collision SDF | Soft contacts, procedural surfaces, approximations | Good |
| GI SDF | Approximate visual collision / effects | Not authoritative |

For example, a GI SDF might represent a thin doorway incorrectly or lag behind recent destruction because it updates under a lighting budget.

That is unacceptable for gameplay collision.

I recommend maintaining **separately versioned collision geometry**, even when the source asset is shared.

### Terrain and caves

For outdoor terrain, use a heightfield fast path. A character standing on open ground should not need a general-purpose triangle traversal.

For caves and interiors, use local collision meshes, convex decomposition, or spatially indexed triangle ranges.

For flying, use swept-volume testing and local 3D collision queries around relevant obstacles.

This keeps ordinary movement cheap while supporting complex environments.

## 5. Separate physics into three execution domains

This is the decision I consider most important.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Domain A — Authoritative gameplay physics**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Server-owned character movement, projectiles, hit validation, collision rules, interaction constraints and gameplay-relevant vehicles.</text>

    The server can use CPU or GPU acceleration, but must preserve correct authority, tick ordering and reconciliation semantics.
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Domain B — Client predictive physics**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Locally predicted movement, responsive collision, anticipated impacts and selected nearby interactions.</text>

    Must reconcile with authoritative state. GPU execution is preferred only where its latency characteristics support responsive gameplay.
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Domain C — GPU visual physics**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Ragdolls, cloth, hair, debris, cosmetic destruction, particles, environmental movement and secondary collisions.</text>

    Primarily GPU-owned, with aggressively scalable simulation detail and no routine CPU readback.
  </box>
</box>

We should not require all three domains to use an identical solver.

A particle, a player-character controller, and a stack of rigid-body crates have very different accuracy and performance requirements.

## 6. Parallel constraint solving

For visual rigid-body and deformable simulation, I would evaluate **Extended Position-Based Dynamics (XPBD)** alongside impulse-based rigid-body solvers.

XPBD is attractive for cloth, ropes, soft bodies and certain large-scale constraint problems because it supports a broad range of constraints with iterative solving.

For rigid-body stacks and frictional contacts, a purpose-built velocity/impulse solver may be a better starting point.

### GPU solver architecture

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Compact Contact + Constraint Arrays**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Island Discovery / Constraint Graph**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Parallel Independent Batches**
    <caption>Graph colouring, ownership partitioning or Jacobi-style updates</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Iterative GPU Solve**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Integrate + Publish ECS Changes**
  </box>
</box>

The major challenge is write contention: two constraints might attempt to modify the same body simultaneously.

We should investigate graph colouring for independent constraint batches, Jacobi-style solvers for suitable workloads, and island-based partitioning.

Large connected contact islands are especially difficult because they reduce parallel independence.

**More GPU cores do not automatically make one enormous rigid-body interaction graph fast.**

## 7. Physics scheduling and latency

Physics should have its own fixed simulation timestep.

The GPU renderer can interpolate presentation between completed simulation states, but we must not use render-frame delta time as the physics integration step.

For GPU-local visual physics, the scheduler could run several simulation substeps per frame where necessary.

For gameplay-critical prediction, we should preserve the option to perform a small amount of latency-sensitive collision work on the CPU.

A character-controller query that the CPU immediately needs for gameplay logic may be cheaper to execute locally than to dispatch to the GPU and synchronously read back.

The rule remains:

**Optimize total dependency latency, not merely GPU utilization.**

### Synchronization policy

| Dependency | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Position integration → broad phase | GPU pipeline dependency |
| Broad phase → narrow phase | Compacted candidate buffer |
| Narrow phase → solver | Published contact arrays |
| Solver iteration → next iteration | Explicit synchronization |
| Physics → animation | GPU buffer dependency |
| Physics → rendering | Completed transform epoch |
| GPU → server/host | Batched asynchronous events where suitable |

No CPU readback should be necessary for cosmetic ragdolls or cloth.

For authoritative decisions, however, the final answer must become available to the authoritative simulation at the required tick boundary. That requirement may change which processor is optimal.

**Optimize total dependency latency, not merely GPU utilization.**

### Synchronization policy

| Dependency | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Position integration → broad phase | GPU pipeline dependency |
| Broad phase → narrow phase | Compacted candidate buffer |
| Narrow phase → solver | Published contact arrays |
| Solver iteration → next iteration | Explicit synchronization |
| Physics → animation | GPU buffer dependency |
| Physics → rendering | Completed transform epoch |
| GPU → server/host | Batched asynchronous events where suitable |

No CPU readback should be necessary for cosmetic ragdolls or cloth.

For authoritative decisions, however, the final answer must become available to the authoritative simulation at the required tick boundary. That requirement may change which processor is optimal.

## 8. MMO-specific physics policies

The world must remain stable during situations such as 5,000 players occupying a town square.

I would not try to simulate those players as 5,000 fully interacting dynamic rigid bodies.

Instead, define interaction classes.

| Workload | Proposed simulation |
|---|---|
| Player locomotion | Kinematic character controller |
| NPC crowds | Kinematic movement + local avoidance |
| Flying characters | Swept-volume movement and obstacle queries |
| Vehicles | Dedicated vehicle controller + selective rigid-body dynamics |
| Combat projectiles | Analytic trajectories / continuous collision queries |
| Debris | GPU rigid bodies, cosmetic where possible |
| Clothing / capes | GPU XPBD with animation LOD |
| Ragdolls | GPU constraints with importance-based activation |
| Environmental particles | GPU simulation with simplified collision |

For crowds, **navigation and avoidance are not the same as rigid-body collision resolution**.

We should handle crowd movement primarily through navigation, local steering and controlled character separation, reserving rigid-body solving for systems that genuinely need it.

This can dramatically reduce contact generation and solver contention.

## 9. How physics affects our previous architecture

| Previous subsystem | Required change |
|---|---|
| Flat 2.5D grid | Add dedicated physics membership streams and overflow handling |
| GPU ECS | Add body, shape, contact and constraint component families |
| GPU scheduler | Support fixed substeps and iterative solver dependencies |
| Animation | Integrate kinematic targets, root motion and ragdoll transitions |
| Rendering | Consume physics-published transform epochs |
| Dynamic GI | Selectively invalidate SDF bricks for large moving geometry |
| Streaming | Treat collision residency as more urgent than visual detail |
| Networking | Support authoritative corrections and selective physics replication |
| Temporal system | Handle teleports and reconciliation in motion-vector history |

The key world-streaming rule is especially important:

**Gameplay collision must be resident and valid before a character can enter the corresponding area.**

Visual detail may stream in late and fall back to coarser representations. Required collision geometry cannot simply disappear while a player moves through the world.

## 10. Architecture decisions to lock

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"Flat-grid GPU broad phase",d:"Direct spatial addressing with CSR-style body membership and specialised dense-cell handling."},
    {t:"Independent physics collision resources",d:"Shared world coordinates, separate accuracy and residency from GI SDF."},
    {t:"GPU-native visual physics",d:"Cloth, ragdolls, debris, particles and secondary motion remain GPU-resident."},
    {t:"Hybrid authoritative execution",d:"Gameplay physics runs where correctness, determinism and dependency latency are best satisfied."},
    {t:"Specialised character controllers",d:"Kinematic movement and navigation instead of treating MMO crowds as rigid-body piles."},

## 11. The big question: deterministic simulation

Before we finalize physics implementation, there's one issue we should investigate carefully.

GPU floating-point operations, parallel reduction order, atomics, and constraint scheduling can produce different results across devices or even execution schedules.

That matters for authoritative simulation and client-side prediction.

I would therefore avoid requiring **bit-identical GPU physics across different vendors**.

Instead, design our network model around server-authoritative state, explicit prediction and reconciliation, and deterministic execution only in subsystems where it is genuinely required.

For cosmetic GPU simulation, reproducibility is much less important.

For competitive combat, projectile validation and authoritative movement, it may be essential to choose numerical representations and algorithms that produce controlled, testable outcomes.

### Next architectural phase

I recommend **Phase 12 — Networking, Authority, Replication & Server ECS**.

That will determine how our Rust/Go/Zig stack connects to the GPU-first client, including distributed world ownership, high-density interest management, delta-compressed ECS replication, client prediction, server reconciliation and server-side GPU acceleration.

It is the next major foundation before we move into detailed implementation.

| Flat 2.5D grid | Add dedicated physics membership streams and overflow handling |
| GPU ECS | Add body, shape, contact and constraint component families |
| GPU scheduler | Support fixed substeps and iterative solver dependencies |
| Animation | Integrate kinematic targets, root motion and ragdoll transitions |
| Rendering | Consume physics-published transform epochs |
| Dynamic GI | Selectively invalidate SDF bricks for large moving geometry |
| Streaming | Treat collision residency as more urgent than visual detail |
| Networking | Support authoritative corrections and selective physics replication |
| Temporal system | Handle teleports and reconciliation in motion-vector history |

The key world-streaming rule is especially important:

**Gameplay collision must be resident and valid before a character can enter the corresponding area.**

Visual detail may stream in late and fall back to coarser representations. Required collision geometry cannot simply disappear while a player moves through the world.

## 10. Architecture decisions to lock

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"Flat-grid GPU broad phase",d:"Direct spatial addressing with CSR-style body membership and specialised dense-cell handling."},
    {t:"Independent physics collision resources",d:"Shared world coordinates, separate accuracy and residency from GI SDF."},
    {t:"GPU-native visual physics",d:"Cloth, ragdolls, debris, particles and secondary motion remain GPU-resident."},
    {t:"Hybrid authoritative execution",d:"Gameplay physics runs where correctness, determinism and dependency latency are best satisfied."},
    {t:"Specialised character controllers",d:"Kinematic movement and navigation instead of treating MMO crowds as rigid-body piles."},
    {t:"Parallel solver architecture",d:"XPBD for suitable deformables; constraint/impulse solving for rigid bodies."},
    {t:"Fixed-step physics scheduling",d:"Independent of variable render rate, with GPU epoch publication."},
    {t:"Dedicated physics active sets",d:"Do not simulate every resident object on every physics tick."},
    {t:"Collision-first streaming",d:"Required collision data takes priority over cosmetic geometry and lighting pages."}
  ] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap="1px">
        **{x.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. The big question: deterministic simulation

Before we finalize physics implementation, there's one issue we should investigate carefully.

GPU floating-point operations, parallel reduction order, atomics, and constraint scheduling can produce different results across devices or even execution schedules.

That matters for authoritative simulation and client-side prediction.

I would therefore avoid requiring **bit-identical GPU physics across different vendors**.

Instead, design our network model around server-authoritative state, explicit prediction and reconciliation, and deterministic execution only in subsystems where it is genuinely required.

For cosmetic GPU simulation, reproducibility is much less important.

For competitive combat, projectile validation and authoritative movement, it may be essential to choose numerical representations and algorithms that produce controlled, testable outcomes.

### Next architectural phase

I recommend **Phase 12 — Networking, Authority, Replication & Server ECS**.

That will determine how our Rust/Go/Zig stack connects to the GPU-first client, including distributed world ownership, high-density interest management, delta-compressed ECS replication, client prediction, server reconciliation and server-side GPU acceleration.

It is the next major foundation before we move into detailed implementation.

## 099 — Assistant

Message ID: `eed80c1c-80ba-49e6-a0f1-3a034d88fa07` · 2026-10-08T04:45:50.030995+00:00

**Yes, you're correct. World of Warcraft generally allows players, monsters, and NPCs to move through one another without physical body blocking.** There are some exceptions for particular NPCs and scripted encounters, but ordinary characters do not behave like mutually colliding rigid bodies.

Players have explicitly discussed this behavior on Blizzard's forums, including how it prevents crowds from blocking vendors, mailboxes, doorways, and raid positioning. <Cite refs={["turn420208search0","turn420208search9"]}/>

And I think **we should adopt the same fundamental principle for our MMO engine**.

## 1. Separate physical collision from gameplay interaction

A character doesn't need a physically blocking collider to participate in combat, targeting, proximity detection, or interaction.

| Interaction | Recommended behaviour |
|---|---|
| Player ↔ Player | No physical blocking |
| Player ↔ Friendly NPC | No physical blocking |
| Player ↔ Vendor / Banker | No physical blocking |
| Player ↔ Monster | No physical blocking by default |
| Monster ↔ Monster | No physical blocking by default |
| Character ↔ Terrain | Physical collision |
| Character ↔ Buildings / Walls | Physical collision |
| Character ↔ Doors | Collision based on door state |
| Character ↔ Projectiles | Gameplay hit detection, not body blocking |
| Character ↔ Large boss | Configurable, encounter-specific |
| Character ↔ Vehicle | Configurable based on vehicle gameplay |

This is substantially simpler than simulating thousands of mutually colliding characters.

## 2. We should introduce independent collision channels

Rather than attaching one universal collider to every entity, I'd split collision functionality into distinct systems.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Character ECS Entity**

    <caption>Transform · Movement · Combat · Interaction</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{t:"World Collision",d:"Terrain, walls, obstacles"},{t:"Combat Hit Volumes",d:"Attacks, spells, projectiles"},{t:"Interaction Volumes",d:"Vendors, dialogue, proximity"},{t:"Navigation / Awareness",d:"Optional steering, aggro and crowd behaviour"}] as x}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} minHeight="89px">
          <text weight="medium" size="sm">{x.t}</text>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{x.d}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

These systems may use the same spatial grid but should have different query masks and semantics.

**No body blocking does not mean no collision detection.** Combat, targeting, spell areas, and interaction still need spatial queries.

## 3. This significantly improves our GPU architecture

Our previous physics design anticipated handling enormous amounts of dynamic body-to-body contact.

For ordinary MMO characters, we can eliminate much of that work.

| Physics workload | Effect of non-blocking characters |
|---|---|
| Character-character broad-phase pairs | Not needed for physical response |
| Contact manifold generation | Eliminated for ordinary character pairs |
| Character-character solver constraints | Eliminated |
| Dense-crowd physics islands | Largely avoided |
| Character-world collision | Still required |
| Combat proximity queries | Still required |
| NPC awareness / aggro | Still required |
| Character navigation | Still required |
| Cosmetic visual physics | Unchanged |

This is a meaningful performance and scalability improvement, particularly in major cities, auction houses, raids, and world events.

### Example: 5,000 players in a city

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <grid columns={2} gap={3}>
    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Potential unordered player pairs</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>12,497,500</title>
        <caption>Across all 5,000 players, before any spatial filtering</caption>
      </box>

    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Player-player physical contacts</text>
        <title size="xl" color="success" tabularNums>0</title>
        <caption>For standard non-blocking characters</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">This does not eliminate all spatial queries or 12.5 million actual processed contacts; the first number is only the theoretical all-pairs count. The gain is avoiding physical response between characters altogether.</text>
</box>

## 4. One thing I'd improve beyond WoW

Even without physical collision, other players can still visually obstruct vendors or interactable objects.

Warcraft's own community documentation notes that crowds can make interaction with objects difficult because they obscure the target. <Cite ref="turn420208search6"/>

For our GPU-rendered UI and interaction ECS, I'd implement:

- **Interaction priority:** Important interactable NPCs and objects can be selected even when other characters overlap them.
- **GPU hit-test filtering:** Clicking through non-targetable crowd members when appropriate.
- **Proximity interaction lists:** Show nearby vendors, bankers, quest NPCs, and other available interactions.
- **Optional character transparency:** Fade obstructing player models when viewing important interactive targets.

This eliminates both physical obstruction and much of the remaining interaction frustration.

## 5. Revised physics architecture decision

**I would lock this into Phase 11.** It lets us simplify character physics, reduce solver complexity, and devote more GPU time to our virtualized renderer, dynamic GI, animation, and visual simulation.

It also highlights a broader MMO design principle: **we should only pay for physically realistic behavior when it makes the gameplay better.** For crowded social hubs and large raids, non-blocking characters are often both the better gameplay choice and the more scalable technical solution.

## ADR-011 — Non-Blocking MMO Character Physics

**Status:** Approved — part of our Custom MMO Engine architecture.

We've established the following rules:

- **Player ↔ Player:** No physical blocking.
- **Player ↔ NPC / Monster:** No physical blocking by default.
- **Monster ↔ Monster:** No physical blocking by default.
- **Characters ↔ World:** Full terrain, building, obstacle and environmental collision.
- **Combat:** Independent hit volumes, targeting and spatial queries.
- **Interaction:** Independent proximity and selection systems.
- **Exceptions:** Large bosses, vehicles and special encounters may explicitly enable body blocking.
- **Crowd navigation:** Optional steering without mandatory physical separation.

### Architectural consequences

Our GPU physics engine no longer needs ordinary character-to-character contact generation or rigid-body constraint solving.

This reduces collision workloads in crowded cities, raids and large-scale battles.

We retain our **flat 2.5D spatial grid**, but use separate collision, combat and interaction query streams.

This decision is now part of our agreed working architecture, alongside GPU-native ECS, mesh/task rendering, and sparse SDF dynamic GI with a shared radiance cache.

**Next phase:** Networking, distributed server authority, ECS replication and client prediction—where we can capitalize on this simplified character movement model.

# Phase 12 — Distributed MMO Networking, Server Authority & ECS Replication
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Specification · October 2026</text>

This is one of the most consequential architectural phases. Everything we've designed so far—GPU-native ECS, contiguous arrays, flat 2.5D spatial indexing, non-blocking characters, world streaming, and GPU-driven presentation—needs to operate across a distributed multiplayer world.

My recommendation is:

**A server-authoritative, spatially partitioned MMO runtime using data-oriented Rust simulation workers, Go orchestration/services, and GPU-native client replication through compact, versioned ECS change streams.**

The networking system should transfer *state changes*, not render instructions or complete ECS snapshots every frame.

Our guiding principle:

> **The server decides what is true. The client GPU decides how to present it. The network delivers only what each client needs to know.**

## 1. Overall architecture

  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Persistent MMO World**
    <caption>Durable entities · World IDs · Accounts · Inventories · Economy</caption>
  </box>

  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>

      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>

        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Sessions, authentication, routing, orchestration, social services</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        <text weight="medium" size="sm">Rust Simulation Workers</text>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Authoritative ECS, movement, combat, AI, spatial queries</text>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Interest Management + ECS Replication**
    <caption>Spatial queries · Relevance · Delta compression · Bandwidth budgets</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Network Gateway / Session Transport**
    <caption>Authenticated connections · Message routing · Congestion control</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text weight="medium" textAlign="center">GPU-PRIMARY CLIENT</text>

      {#each ["Network receive bridge","GPU ECS delta application","Prediction + interpolation","Spatial index updates","Animation + visual physics","Mesh/task rendering"] as x}
        <grid-item>

            <text size="xs" textAlign="center">{x}</text>
          </box>
        </grid-item>
      {/each}
    </grid>
  </box>
</box>

### Language responsibilities

| Language | Primary responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Rust** | Authoritative simulation ECS, game networking hot path, engine core, Vulkan host and client runtime |
| **Go** | Distributed orchestration, service infrastructure, sessions, account/social services, persistence coordination |
| **Zig** | Low-level utilities, selected high-performance subsystems, tooling and native interoperability |
| **GPU shaders** | Client ECS processing, animation, visibility, rendering, visual simulation and presentation |

I would **not** force every network packet through Go simply because we use Go for server infrastructure.

For the latency-sensitive simulation path, Rust workers should be able to process authenticated game commands and produce replication records with minimal copying. Go can own the service layer without becoming a per-entity serialization bottleneck.

## 2. Server authority: divide responsibility by subsystem

The authoritative world is not one giant ECS living in one server process.

It is a collection of simulation and service domains with explicit ownership.

| Domain | Authority |
|---|---|
| Character position and movement | Simulation partition |
| Combat resolution and health | Authoritative combat/simulation worker |
| NPC behaviour | Simulation worker owning that NPC |
| World objects and doors | Owning simulation partition |
| Inventory and item transactions | Transactional inventory service |
| Currency and economic transactions | Durable transactional service |
| Parties, guilds and chat | Social services |
| Client visual animation | GPU presentation, derived from authoritative actions |
| Cosmetic effects | Client GPU where no gameplay authority is required |

A player's authoritative movement and inventory may therefore have different owners, consistency requirements and update paths.

This is intentional. **We should not impose the transactional consistency requirements of inventory transfers on ordinary character movement packets.**

### Ownership epochs

Every authoritative partition should have a versioned ownership record:

`Partition ID → Worker ID + Ownership Epoch`

If ownership moves from one worker to another, the epoch changes.

Commands from an old owner can then be rejected rather than accidentally modifying state after a migration.

The same mechanism supports recovery after worker failure, although failure recovery will also require durable checkpoints, journals or equivalent state-reconstruction mechanisms.

## 3. Spatial partitioning and load balancing

We've already selected a flat 2.5D spatial hierarchy.

We should reuse its addressing for simulation partitioning and interest discovery, but **not require one simulation worker per spatial cell**.

  <svg viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%">
    {#each Array.from({length:5},(_,i)=>i) as y}

      {/each}
    {/each}

    <text x="160" y="179" fontSize="10" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Worker territories need not match streaming cell boundaries</text>
  </svg>

    {#each [{name:"Worker A",c:"#488FB3"},{name:"Worker B",c:"#53A184"},{name:"Worker C",c:"#B396CD"},{name:"High-load area",c:"#C99038"}] as x}
      <row align="center" gap={1}>

      </row>
    {/each}
  </row>
</box>

For quiet areas, one worker might own many contiguous world cells. A busy city might justify more granular assignment.

However, dividing a city into dozens of workers isn't automatically beneficial. Cross-worker combat interactions, NPC ownership transfers, and shared environmental state introduce communication costs.

I'd use **load-aware ownership partitioning**, optimized for both CPU workload and cross-partition interaction frequency.

### Seamless partition handoff

When a character moves between authoritative partitions:

1. The current worker prepares its latest accepted state.
2. The destination worker receives and validates the transfer.
3. The authority directory advances the ownership epoch.
4. Inputs are routed to the new owner using sequence numbers.
5. Neighbouring clients continue receiving updates with stable world/entity IDs.

We should design the protocol to prevent duplicate authority. The handoff must have a clearly defined commit point.

A client should not need to unload or recreate the character's GPU ECS entity during an ordinary server partition crossing.

## 4. Networking transport: QUIC vs custom UDP

This is one area where I'd avoid locking an implementation too early.

Our protocol should distinguish:

| Traffic | Delivery semantics |
|---|---|
| Frequent character movement | Unreliable, sequenced; newer state supersedes older state |
| Player input commands | Sequenced, often redundantly included until acknowledged |
| Combat results | Reliable event or recoverable authoritative state |
| Entity creation/destruction | Reliable or explicitly repaired against lifecycle state |
| Inventory operations | Reliable, ordered, idempotent transactions |
| Chat/social messages | Reliable |
| World asset downloads | Separate reliable content streaming |
| High-volume state snapshots | Unreliable, priority-controlled |

### Candidate A — QUIC with datagrams

QUIC provides encrypted connections, multiplexed reliable streams, congestion control and optional unreliable datagrams.

RFC 9221 defines QUIC DATAGRAM frames, which can carry real-time state updates without transport-layer retransmission while sharing the connection's security context. <Cite ref="turn488836view0"/>

This is appealing because one authenticated session can support multiple delivery semantics.

### Candidate B — Custom UDP protocol

A custom encrypted UDP transport offers direct control over packet scheduling, reliability classes, packet packing and latency policies.

However, we would need to implement and maintain congestion control, loss recovery, secure session management, path-MTU handling and other difficult network infrastructure.

### My recommendation

**Prototype QUIC datagrams first, while keeping the game replication protocol transport-independent.**

We should benchmark it against a custom UDP implementation only if QUIC's transport behavior or overhead becomes a demonstrated limitation.

QUIC datagrams still follow congestion control and path-MTU constraints; unreliable delivery does not mean unlimited bandwidth or zero latency. <Cite ref="turn488836view0"/>

## 5. Network replication should operate on ECS component streams

This is where our contiguous ECS architecture becomes especially valuable.

We should not serialize complete object graphs or whole entities merely because one field changed.

Instead, our replication system should work with schema-defined component groups and packed state deltas.

### Proposed pipeline

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Authoritative ECS Component Changes**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Per-Client Interest Selection**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Replication Priority + Budget Allocation**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Delta Encoding + Bit Packing**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Network Transport**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Client State Decode + GPU Upload**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU ECS Apply / Structural Mutation**
  </box>
</box>

### Per-component replication policies

| Component family | Replication strategy |
|---|---|
| Transform and velocity | Quantized, prioritized updates |
| Animation state | Clip/state IDs, timestamps, relevant parameters |
| Character appearance | Reliable changes, then cached |
| Equipment | Reliable changes and attachment references |
| Health/resource values | Authoritative state updates plus important event notifications |
| NPC AI internals | Usually not replicated |
| Inventory | Owner-only transactional replication |
| Interactable state | Relevant nearby clients |
| Terrain/object destruction | Versioned world-state changes |
| Cosmetic GPU particles | Mostly locally generated, not individually replicated |

The server should transmit **what happened or what state changed**, allowing the client GPU to generate suitable presentation.

For instance, one authoritative spell-impact event could produce thousands of GPU particles without replicating those particles individually.

### Baseline-aware delta compression

I recommend maintaining acknowledged client baselines.

A delta refers to a known baseline snapshot or component version. If that baseline is unavailable, the server sends a replacement baseline or repair snapshot.

This prevents packet loss from permanently corrupting subsequent state interpretation.

Delta compression and snapshot interpolation are well-established approaches to reducing multiplayer state bandwidth, but each has tradeoffs around reliability, update frequency and jitter. <Cite refs={["turn693472search1","turn693472search6"]}/>

## 6. MMO interest management — more important than packet compression

For enormous MMO populations, the critical question isn't simply how efficiently we encode an entity.

It's **which entities need replication to each client, and how frequently**.

Our flat 2.5D spatial grid makes this particularly efficient.

I'd recommend a hybrid model with three kinds of interest:

| Interest class | Examples | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial | Nearby players, monsters, interactive objects | Distance, vertical layer and location |
| Semantic | Party members, combat targets, tracked objectives | Relevant even beyond ordinary spatial proximity |
| Visibility/presentation | Distant visual representations, streaming priorities | Coarse or aggregate updates as appropriate |

Interest also needs authorization. A client must not receive hidden or private state just because its entity happens to be nearby.

### GPU-native interest computation?

For the server, we have two paths:

**CPU SIMD spatial filtering:** Good for active authoritative workers, latency-sensitive queries, and workloads that already reside in CPU memory.

**GPU batch interest computation:** Attractive when generating thousands of similar client-interest queries over a very large resident ECS.

I would support a common spatial-query interface but **start server-side interest management on CPU**, using contiguous Rust ECS data and direct-addressed grids.

Moving it to a server GPU would be worthwhile only when batching and reduced CPU work outweigh data transfers, scheduling latency and GPU operating costs.

The client GPU still owns its rendering visibility and visual active sets.

### Network LOD

Just as geometry has LOD, replicated data should have levels of detail.

| Entity relevance | Replicated state |
|---|---|
| Local controlled character | Detailed authoritative corrections and relevant gameplay state |
| Nearby combatants | Frequent movement, actions, health and combat effects |
| Nearby social players | Movement, appearance, interaction state |
| Distant characters | Reduced-frequency motion and essential presentation |
| Distant crowd groups | Coarse/aggregate visual representation, where gameplay permits |
| Irrelevant entities | No active replication |

The server should not transmit a player's exact pose at 60 Hz simply because that player appears as a tiny figure on the horizon.

## 7. Bandwidth is a first-class scheduling budget

Let's use an illustrative example.

Suppose a player is in a crowded city with 2,000 relevant entities. Replicating all 2,000 at 20 updates per second, with an average of 24 bytes of application payload per entity update, would require approximately 960 KB/s before packet overhead, encryption, acknowledgments and other traffic.

That is far too expensive to treat as an unquestioned baseline.

{@body const [updates,setUpdates] = DIL.useState(10)}
{@body const [payload,setPayload] = DIL.useState(20)}
{@body const throughput = entities*updates*payload}

      <radio value="32">32 B</radio>
      <radio value="64">64 B</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>

    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Application payload</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{(throughput/1000).toFixed(1)} kB/s</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box gap={1}>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs">Payload bit rate</text>
        <title size="xl" tabularNums>{(throughput*8/1e6).toFixed(2)} Mbps</title>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <caption>Simplified bandwidth calculation, assuming every listed entity sends an update each cycle. Excludes transport overhead, headers, redundancy and unrelated traffic.</caption>
</box>

The real replication scheduler should assign per-entity priorities and produce as many updates as fit within each client's congestion-aware budget.

### Priority considerations

A nearby hostile spellcaster is more important than a stationary chair. A party member may deserve more frequent updates than an unrelated player at a similar distance.

I would use a priority score informed by proximity, relevance, state age, motion, action importance and eventual starvation prevention.

Important gameplay events should use appropriate reliable or repairable delivery, rather than merely receiving a higher unreliable priority.

## 8. Client prediction and reconciliation

We should distinguish the local player from remote entities.

### Local player

The client predicts permitted movement using local input, then reconciles against authoritative server state.

For responsive controls, this must not require synchronous GPU readback.

The server sends correction state with an acknowledged input sequence. The client reapplies subsequent inputs when necessary and smooths the resulting presentation correction where appropriate.

### Remote entities

Use time-stamped snapshot interpolation and limited extrapolation.

A remote player running across a field should look smooth even if their network updates arrive irregularly.

Gaffer on Games describes how snapshot interpolation trades some deliberate presentation delay for smoother playback under packet jitter and loss. <Cite ref="turn693472search6"/>

### GPU-primary prediction challenge

This is one area where I would be careful with our GPU-first principle.

A player movement system can run on the GPU. But network events and input arrive on the CPU, while authoritative correction may depend on a history of previous inputs and collision queries.

My proposed architecture is:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Host receives input + authoritative corrections**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Compact GPU Input/Correction Ring**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Prediction + Reconciliation**
    <caption>Replay bounded input history · Correct transforms</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU Animation + Presentation**
  </box>
</box>

This is our preferred GPU-primary research path.

However, I would retain a small host-side prediction option if testing shows that command submission, correction replay, or collision dependencies make GPU prediction too latent.

**Responsiveness is more important than achieving 100% GPU execution.**

Our non-blocking character physics decision helps enormously: the local player primarily needs static-world collision and selected interactive obstacles, not complex prediction of thousands of other player bodies.

# Phase 12 — Distributed MMO Networking, Server Authority & ECS Replication
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Specification · October 2026</text>

This is one of the most consequential architectural phases. Everything we've designed so far—GPU-native ECS, contiguous arrays, flat 2.5D spatial indexing, non-blocking characters, world streaming, and GPU-driven presentation—needs to operate across a distributed multiplayer world.

My recommendation is:

**A server-authoritative, spatially partitioned MMO runtime using data-oriented Rust simulation workers, Go orchestration/services, and GPU-native client replication through compact, versioned ECS change streams.**

The networking system should transfer *state changes*, not render instructions or complete ECS snapshots every frame.

Our guiding principle:

> **The server decides what is true. The client GPU decides how to present it. The network delivers only what each client needs to know.**

## 1. Overall architecture

### Language responsibilities

| Language | Primary responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Rust** | Authoritative simulation ECS, game networking hot path, engine core, Vulkan host and client runtime |
| **Go** | Distributed orchestration, service infrastructure, sessions, account/social services, persistence coordination |
| **Zig** | Low-level utilities, selected high-performance subsystems, tooling and native interoperability |
| **GPU shaders** | Client ECS processing, animation, visibility, rendering, visual simulation and presentation |

I would **not** force every network packet through Go simply because we use Go for server infrastructure.

For the latency-sensitive simulation path, Rust workers should be able to process authenticated game commands and produce replication records with minimal copying. Go can own the service layer without becoming a per-entity serialization bottleneck.

## 2. Server authority: divide responsibility by subsystem

The authoritative world is not one giant ECS living in one server process.

It is a collection of simulation and service domains with explicit ownership.

| Domain | Authority |
|---|---|
| Character position and movement | Simulation partition |
| Combat resolution and health | Authoritative combat/simulation worker |
| NPC behaviour | Simulation worker owning that NPC |
| World objects and doors | Owning simulation partition |
| Inventory and item transactions | Transactional inventory service |
| Currency and economic transactions | Durable transactional service |
| Parties, guilds and chat | Social services |
| Client visual animation | GPU presentation, derived from authoritative actions |
| Cosmetic effects | Client GPU where no gameplay authority is required |

A player's authoritative movement and inventory may therefore have different owners, consistency requirements and update paths.

This is intentional. **We should not impose the transactional consistency requirements of inventory transfers on ordinary character movement packets.**

### Ownership epochs

Every authoritative partition should have a versioned ownership record:

`Partition ID → Worker ID + Ownership Epoch`

If ownership moves from one worker to another, the epoch changes.

Commands from an old owner can then be rejected rather than accidentally modifying state after a migration.

The same mechanism supports recovery after worker failure, although failure recovery will also require durable checkpoints, journals or equivalent state-reconstruction mechanisms.

## 3. Spatial partitioning and load balancing

We've already selected a flat 2.5D spatial hierarchy.

We should reuse its addressing for simulation partitioning and interest discovery, but **not require one simulation worker per spatial cell**.

For quiet areas, one worker might own many contiguous world cells. A busy city might justify more granular assignment.

However, dividing a city into dozens of workers isn't automatically beneficial. Cross-worker combat interactions, NPC ownership transfers, and shared environmental state introduce communication costs.

I'd use **load-aware ownership partitioning**, optimized for both CPU workload and cross-partition interaction frequency.

### Seamless partition handoff

When a character moves between authoritative partitions:

1. The current worker prepares its latest accepted state.
2. The destination worker receives and validates the transfer.
3. The authority directory advances the ownership epoch.
4. Inputs are routed to the new owner using sequence numbers.
5. Neighbouring clients continue receiving updates with stable world/entity IDs.

We should design the protocol to prevent duplicate authority. The handoff must have a clearly defined commit point.

A client should not need to unload or recreate the character's GPU ECS entity during an ordinary server partition crossing.

## 4. Networking transport: QUIC vs custom UDP

This is one area where I'd avoid locking an implementation too early.

Our protocol should distinguish:

| Traffic | Delivery semantics |
|---|---|
| Frequent character movement | Unreliable, sequenced; newer state supersedes older state |
| Player input commands | Sequenced, often redundantly included until acknowledged |
| Combat results | Reliable event or recoverable authoritative state |
| Entity creation/destruction | Reliable or explicitly repaired against lifecycle state |
| Inventory operations | Reliable, ordered, idempotent transactions |
| Chat/social messages | Reliable |
| World asset downloads | Separate reliable content streaming |
| High-volume state snapshots | Unreliable, priority-controlled |

### Candidate A — QUIC with datagrams

QUIC provides encrypted connections, multiplexed reliable streams, congestion control and optional unreliable datagrams.

RFC 9221 defines QUIC DATAGRAM frames, which can carry real-time state updates without transport-layer retransmission while sharing the connection's security context. <Cite ref="turn488836view0"/>

This is appealing because one authenticated session can support multiple delivery semantics.

### Candidate B — Custom UDP protocol

A custom encrypted UDP transport offers direct control over packet scheduling, reliability classes, packet packing and latency policies.

However, we would need to implement and maintain congestion control, loss recovery, secure session management, path-MTU handling and other difficult network infrastructure.

### My recommendation

**Prototype QUIC datagrams first, while keeping the game replication protocol transport-independent.**

We should benchmark it against a custom UDP implementation only if QUIC's transport behavior or overhead becomes a demonstrated limitation.

QUIC datagrams still follow congestion control and path-MTU constraints; unreliable delivery does not mean unlimited bandwidth or zero latency. <Cite ref="turn488836view0"/>

## 5. Network replication should operate on ECS component streams

This is where our contiguous ECS architecture becomes especially valuable.

We should not serialize complete object graphs or whole entities merely because one field changed.

Instead, our replication system should work with schema-defined component groups and packed state deltas.

### Proposed pipeline

### Per-component replication policies

| Component family | Replication strategy |
|---|---|
| Transform and velocity | Quantized, prioritized updates |
| Animation state | Clip/state IDs, timestamps, relevant parameters |
| Character appearance | Reliable changes, then cached |
| Equipment | Reliable changes and attachment references |
| Health/resource values | Authoritative state updates plus important event notifications |
| NPC AI internals | Usually not replicated |
| Inventory | Owner-only transactional replication |
| Interactable state | Relevant nearby clients |
| Terrain/object destruction | Versioned world-state changes |
| Cosmetic GPU particles | Mostly locally generated, not individually replicated |

The server should transmit **what happened or what state changed**, allowing the client GPU to generate suitable presentation.

For instance, one authoritative spell-impact event could produce thousands of GPU particles without replicating those particles individually.

### Baseline-aware delta compression

I recommend maintaining acknowledged client baselines.

A delta refers to a known baseline snapshot or component version. If that baseline is unavailable, the server sends a replacement baseline or repair snapshot.

This prevents packet loss from permanently corrupting subsequent state interpretation.

Delta compression and snapshot interpolation are well-established approaches to reducing multiplayer state bandwidth, but each has tradeoffs around reliability, update frequency and jitter. <Cite refs={["turn693472search1","turn693472search6"]}/>

## 6. MMO interest management — more important than packet compression

For enormous MMO populations, the critical question isn't simply how efficiently we encode an entity.

It's **which entities need replication to each client, and how frequently**.

Our flat 2.5D spatial grid makes this particularly efficient.

I'd recommend a hybrid model with three kinds of interest:

| Interest class | Examples | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial | Nearby players, monsters, interactive objects | Distance, vertical layer and location |
| Semantic | Party members, combat targets, tracked objectives | Relevant even beyond ordinary spatial proximity |
| Visibility/presentation | Distant visual representations, streaming priorities | Coarse or aggregate updates as appropriate |

Interest also needs authorization. A client must not receive hidden or private state just because its entity happens to be nearby.

### GPU-native interest computation?

For the server, we have two paths:

**CPU SIMD spatial filtering:** Good for active authoritative workers, latency-sensitive queries, and workloads that already reside in CPU memory.

**GPU batch interest computation:** Attractive when generating thousands of similar client-interest queries over a very large resident ECS.

I would support a common spatial-query interface but **start server-side interest management on CPU**, using contiguous Rust ECS data and direct-addressed grids.

Moving it to a server GPU would be worthwhile only when batching and reduced CPU work outweigh data transfers, scheduling latency and GPU operating costs.

The client GPU still owns its rendering visibility and visual active sets.

### Network LOD

Just as geometry has LOD, replicated data should have levels of detail.

| Entity relevance | Replicated state |
|---|---|
| Local controlled character | Detailed authoritative corrections and relevant gameplay state |
| Nearby combatants | Frequent movement, actions, health and combat effects |
| Nearby social players | Movement, appearance, interaction state |
| Distant characters | Reduced-frequency motion and essential presentation |
| Distant crowd groups | Coarse/aggregate visual representation, where gameplay permits |
| Irrelevant entities | No active replication |

The server should not transmit a player's exact pose at 60 Hz simply because that player appears as a tiny figure on the horizon.

## 7. Bandwidth is a first-class scheduling budget

Let's use an illustrative example.

Suppose a player is in a crowded city with 2,000 relevant entities. Replicating all 2,000 at 20 updates per second, with an average of 24 bytes of application payload per entity update, would require approximately 960 KB/s before packet overhead, encryption, acknowledgments and other traffic.

That is far too expensive to treat as an unquestioned baseline.

## 8. Client prediction and reconciliation

We should distinguish the local player from remote entities.

### Local player

The client predicts permitted movement using local input, then reconciles against authoritative server state.

For responsive controls, this must not require synchronous GPU readback.

The server sends correction state with an acknowledged input sequence. The client reapplies subsequent inputs when necessary and smooths the resulting presentation correction where appropriate.

A remote player running across a field should look smooth even if their network updates arrive irregularly.

Gaffer on Games describes how snapshot interpolation trades some deliberate presentation delay for smoother playback under packet jitter and loss. <Cite ref="turn693472search6"/>

### GPU-primary prediction challenge

This is one area where I would be careful with our GPU-first principle.

A player movement system can run on the GPU. But network events and input arrive on the CPU, while authoritative correction may depend on a history of previous inputs and collision queries.

My proposed architecture is:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Host receives input + authoritative corrections**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

Our non-blocking character physics decision helps enormously: the local player primarily needs static-world collision and selected interactive obstacles, not complex prediction of thousands of other player bodies.

## 9. Durable state, transactions and persistence

The server ECS should not synchronously write gameplay state to a database for every movement tick.

Instead, separate high-frequency simulation from durable transactions.

| State type | Persistence strategy |
|---|---|
| Moment-to-moment movement | Periodic checkpoints, with recovery policy |
| Character progression | Durable commits at meaningful state changes |
| Inventory transfers | Transactional updates with idempotent operation IDs |
| Currency | Strong transactional consistency |
| Quest progress | Versioned durable state changes |
| World destruction | Versioned world event or state updates |
| Cosmetic particles | Not persisted |
| Temporary NPC visual state | Usually not persisted |

I recommend a **write-ahead event/journal mechanism for durable gameplay changes**, backed by periodic authoritative snapshots where appropriate.

This doesn't mean forcing full event sourcing onto every component.

The durability guarantees must match the data. Losing a few milliseconds of NPC walking is different from losing a valuable item after a trade.

### Critical transaction rule

An inventory trade must have a single authoritative commit outcome even if clients disconnect, retry or send duplicate requests.

That means idempotent commands and carefully designed ownership/transaction boundaries.

We should treat these as service architecture concerns, not ordinary unreliable ECS deltas.

## 10. Server-side GPU acceleration: optional, not mandatory

Our GPU-first client architecture should remain independent of whether a given authoritative server has a GPU.

Some server workloads could eventually benefit from GPU execution:

| Server workload | GPU potential |
|---|---|
| Large batches of spatial proximity queries | High |
| Crowd steering | High when sufficiently batched |
| Homogeneous NPC simulation | Potentially high |
| Parallel broad-phase queries | High |
| Irregular quest scripting | Low |
| Inventory transactions | Low |
| Cross-partition authority logic | Low |
| Small, latency-sensitive combat decisions | Workload-dependent |

The major issue is synchronization with authoritative CPU state.

If a Rust server worker performs combat logic on CPU but must wait for a GPU query to decide every attack, the GPU may make the system slower.

I would design an **optional GPU simulation backend** with coarse-grained asynchronous jobs, while keeping CPU execution as the server baseline.

This preserves deployment flexibility and avoids requiring an expensive GPU for every server worker.

## 11. Security and correctness requirements

The client is untrusted, regardless of how sophisticated its GPU ECS becomes.

We must never accept client-generated positions, hit outcomes, inventory changes or resource balances as authoritative facts.

The server should validate permitted input, movement constraints, action cooldowns, combat ranges and economic transactions.

The networking protocol should also account for:

- Packet replay and duplicate suppression.
- Per-client rate limits and bounded decode workloads.
- Entity generation/version checks.
- Schema compatibility and protocol version negotiation.
- Reliable entity lifecycle repair.
- Reconnection and resynchronization.
- Session migration and reconnect tokens.
- Congestion and backpressure.
- Server-side observability of suspicious state changes.

For an MMO, abuse resistance and resilience are part of the fundamental networking architecture—not features to bolt on later.

## 12. Architecture decisions I'd lock

    {t:"Go service and orchestration layer",d:"Authentication, sessions, routing, social systems and persistence coordination."},
