    {t:"Prediction and reconciliation",d:"Local responsiveness with server correction; remote entities use buffered interpolation."},
    {t:"Transactional persistence domains",d:"Inventory, currency and durable progression separated from high-frequency simulation."},

  ] as item}

## 13. What this means for our complete MMO engine

We now have a coherent architecture from persistence through GPU rendering.

| Layer | Primary architecture |
|---|---|
| Persistent world | Distributed authoritative data and transactional services |
| Server ECS | Chunked, data-oriented Rust simulation |
| World spatial structure | Flat 2.5D grid and sparse vertical indexing |
| Networking | Interest-filtered, quantized ECS deltas |
| Client ECS | GPU-primary persistent component stores |
| Client physics | Non-blocking characters, world collision and GPU visual physics |
| Animation | GPU animation graphs, shared poses and adaptive skinning |
| Rendering | GPU-driven mesh/task geometry and visibility buffer |
| Lighting | Sparse SDF software tracing with shared radiance cache |
| UI | GPU-resident vector UI and Bézier text |
| Frame management | Epoch-based synchronization and temporal reconstruction |

The largest open scalability problem is now **extreme multiplayer density**.

For example, 10,000 players occupying one visible battlefield stresses far more than the graphics pipeline. It stresses replication fan-out, authoritative combat interactions, server partitioning, animation diversity and the ability to present thousands of meaningful entities without overwhelming the player.

### Recommended next phase — Massive MMO Battles & Crowd Scalability

I would scope a reference workload of **10,000 players in one contiguous battlefield**, without assuming every player receives full-rate replication from every other player.

We can use that to derive concrete budgets for server tick processing, interest management, outgoing bandwidth, GPU ECS processing, meshlet rendering, animation, GI and frame-time stability.

That exercise will expose whether any of our current architectural decisions need modification *before* we start implementing the engine.

Message ID: `e435c986-9368-4e3e-bc12-823b4abb6a68` · 2026-10-08T04:53:09.504540+00:00

## 9. Durable state, transactions and persistence

The server ECS should not synchronously write gameplay state to a database for every movement tick.

Instead, separate high-frequency simulation from durable transactions.

| State type | Persistence strategy |
|---|---|
| Moment-to-moment movement | Periodic checkpoints, with recovery policy |
| Character progression | Durable commits at meaningful state changes |
| Inventory transfers | Transactional updates with idempotent operation IDs |
| Currency | Strong transactional consistency |
| Quest progress | Versioned durable state changes |
| World destruction | Versioned world event or state updates |
| Cosmetic particles | Not persisted |
| Temporary NPC visual state | Usually not persisted |

I recommend a **write-ahead event/journal mechanism for durable gameplay changes**, backed by periodic authoritative snapshots where appropriate.

This doesn't mean forcing full event sourcing onto every component.

The durability guarantees must match the data. Losing a few milliseconds of NPC walking is different from losing a valuable item after a trade.

### Critical transaction rule

An inventory trade must have a single authoritative commit outcome even if clients disconnect, retry or send duplicate requests.

That means idempotent commands and carefully designed ownership/transaction boundaries.

We should treat these as service architecture concerns, not ordinary unreliable ECS deltas.

## 10. Server-side GPU acceleration: optional, not mandatory

Our GPU-first client architecture should remain independent of whether a given authoritative server has a GPU.

Some server workloads could eventually benefit from GPU execution:

| Server workload | GPU potential |
|---|---|
| Large batches of spatial proximity queries | High |
| Crowd steering | High when sufficiently batched |
| Homogeneous NPC simulation | Potentially high |
| Parallel broad-phase queries | High |
| Irregular quest scripting | Low |
| Inventory transactions | Low |
| Cross-partition authority logic | Low |
| Small, latency-sensitive combat decisions | Workload-dependent |

The major issue is synchronization with authoritative CPU state.

If a Rust server worker performs combat logic on CPU but must wait for a GPU query to decide every attack, the GPU may make the system slower.

I would design an **optional GPU simulation backend** with coarse-grained asynchronous jobs, while keeping CPU execution as the server baseline.

This preserves deployment flexibility and avoids requiring an expensive GPU for every server worker.

## 11. Security and correctness requirements

The client is untrusted, regardless of how sophisticated its GPU ECS becomes.

We must never accept client-generated positions, hit outcomes, inventory changes or resource balances as authoritative facts.

The server should validate permitted input, movement constraints, action cooldowns, combat ranges and economic transactions.

The networking protocol should also account for:

- Packet replay and duplicate suppression.
- Per-client rate limits and bounded decode workloads.
- Entity generation/version checks.
- Schema compatibility and protocol version negotiation.
- Reliable entity lifecycle repair.
- Reconnection and resynchronization.
- Session migration and reconnect tokens.
- Congestion and backpressure.
- Server-side observability of suspicious state changes.

For an MMO, abuse resistance and resilience are part of the fundamental networking architecture—not features to bolt on later.

## 12. Architecture decisions I'd lock

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"Server-authoritative distributed ECS",d:"Versioned authority ownership across independent Rust simulation workers."},
    {t:"Go service and orchestration layer",d:"Authentication, sessions, routing, social systems and persistence coordination."},
    {t:"Transport-independent replication protocol",d:"QUIC datagrams as the initial transport candidate."},
    {t:"Component-level delta replication",d:"Quantized, schema-defined state changes with acknowledged baselines."},
    {t:"Hybrid spatial/semantic interest management",d:"Reuse the flat 2.5D index and apply authorization and relevance filtering."},
    {t:"Network LOD and bandwidth budgets",d:"Update cadence and payload fidelity scale with client relevance."},
    {t:"GPU-native client delta application",d:"Batched network state enters persistent GPU ECS storage without per-entity CPU scene updates."},
    {t:"Prediction and reconciliation",d:"Local responsiveness with server correction; remote entities use buffered interpolation."},
    {t:"Transactional persistence domains",d:"Inventory, currency and durable progression separated from high-frequency simulation."},
    {t:"Optional server GPU acceleration",d:"Only for batched workloads that benefit after accounting for synchronization costs."}
  ] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{item.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{item.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 13. What this means for our complete MMO engine

We now have a coherent architecture from persistence through GPU rendering.

| Layer | Primary architecture |
|---|---|
| Persistent world | Distributed authoritative data and transactional services |
| Server ECS | Chunked, data-oriented Rust simulation |
| World spatial structure | Flat 2.5D grid and sparse vertical indexing |
| Networking | Interest-filtered, quantized ECS deltas |
| Client ECS | GPU-primary persistent component stores |
| Client physics | Non-blocking characters, world collision and GPU visual physics |
| Animation | GPU animation graphs, shared poses and adaptive skinning |
| Rendering | GPU-driven mesh/task geometry and visibility buffer |
| Lighting | Sparse SDF software tracing with shared radiance cache |
| UI | GPU-resident vector UI and Bézier text |
| Frame management | Epoch-based synchronization and temporal reconstruction |

The largest open scalability problem is now **extreme multiplayer density**.

For example, 10,000 players occupying one visible battlefield stresses far more than the graphics pipeline. It stresses replication fan-out, authoritative combat interactions, server partitioning, animation diversity and the ability to present thousands of meaningful entities without overwhelming the player.

### Recommended next phase — Massive MMO Battles & Crowd Scalability

I would scope a reference workload of **10,000 players in one contiguous battlefield**, without assuming every player receives full-rate replication from every other player.

We can use that to derive concrete budgets for server tick processing, interest management, outgoing bandwidth, GPU ECS processing, meshlet rendering, animation, GI and frame-time stability.

That exercise will expose whether any of our current architectural decisions need modification *before* we start implementing the engine.

# Phase 12A — QUIC CPU Overhead & MMO Transport Architecture

**Your concern is justified. At MMO scale, QUIC can become a significant CPU bottleneck, particularly with large numbers of small, frequently transmitted packets.**

And given our engine's emphasis on contiguous memory, batched processing, and minimizing CPU overhead, I would reconsider making QUIC our default gameplay transport before benchmarking it.

There are two different costs to distinguish:

1. **Cryptographic cost:** Encrypting, authenticating, and decrypting network packets.
2. **Protocol processing cost:** Packet framing, connection state, acknowledgements, pacing, congestion control, memory allocation, and kernel I/O.

Both matter. Optimizing only the encryption algorithm may leave most of the networking bottleneck intact.

A 2024 research paper, *A Quantum of QUIC: Dissecting Cryptography with Post-Quantum Insights*, found substantial CPU cost associated with QUIC packet protection, with differences between AES and ChaCha20 implementations. <Cite ref="turn522788search46"/>

## 1. Why MMO networking is particularly demanding

Imagine an MMO gateway serving thousands of connected players. Most gameplay messages are relatively small, and they must be distributed frequently.

The critical metric becomes **packets processed per second**, not just gigabits per second.

{@body const packets=clients*pps}
{@body const cores=packets*Number(cost)/1000000}

## 2. Would custom UDP eliminate the crypto bottleneck?

**No—not if we want secure networking.**

QUIC uses TLS 1.3 negotiated authenticated encryption, including AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. It also protects parts of its packet headers. <Cite ref="turn522788search1"/>

A secure custom UDP protocol would still need authenticated encryption, nonce management, replay protection, secure key establishment, and key rotation.

What custom UDP *could* eliminate is some general-purpose QUIC protocol machinery that may not benefit our specific real-time replication workload.

| Operation | QUIC datagrams | Custom secure UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Authenticated encryption | Required | Required |
| Secure handshake | Built in | Must implement/integrate |
| Packet header protection | Required | Not necessarily |
| Packet numbering | Built in | Custom sequencing |
| Replay protection | Protocol-managed mechanisms | Must implement |
| Congestion control | Required | Must implement |
| Reliability streams | Available | Only what we implement |
| Datagram transmission | Supported | Native |
| Packet scheduling | QUIC connection rules | MMO-specific policies |
| Multi-message packet packing | Available | Customizable |
| Operational complexity | Lower | Higher |

QUIC datagrams are unreliable, but they are still encrypted and subject to QUIC congestion control. <Cite ref="turn522788search0"/>

A custom UDP stack therefore wins only if its workload-specific optimizations outweigh the cost of recreating secure transport infrastructure.

## 3. Hardware-accelerated cryptography changes the equation

On modern x86-64 servers, AES instructions and carry-less multiplication support can substantially accelerate AES-GCM.

On suitable ARM64 processors, hardware AES and polynomial multiplication instructions provide similar opportunities.

For our engine I'd prioritize **AES-128-GCM with hardware acceleration**, with ChaCha20-Poly1305 available where it performs better or where interoperability requires it.

But I would not implement either cipher ourselves. Use a mature, audited cryptographic implementation and configure the transport around it.

The remaining bottlenecks may be packet metadata processing, buffer allocation, syscall overhead, socket contention, cache locality, or replication fan-out.

That suggests a useful principle:

> **Minimize packet count and memory movement before attempting to accelerate encryption with exotic hardware.**

A GPU is especially unlikely to help with small, latency-sensitive packets if transfers and synchronization outweigh the cryptographic work.

## 4. The architecture that best fits our MMO

I would divide network responsibilities into two logical paths.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Authoritative Simulation ECS**

    <caption>Contiguous component deltas · Interest-filtered recipient lists</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Replication Encoder + Packet Scheduler**

    <caption>Quantization · Delta compression · Coalescing · Bandwidth budgeting</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="git-fork" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <text weight="medium" textAlign="center" size="sm">Real-Time Data Plane</text>
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Movement · Animation state · Frequent world snapshots</text>
        <box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="sm" align="center">
          <text size="xs" weight="medium">QUIC Datagram or Secure UDP</text>
        </box>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <text weight="medium" textAlign="center" size="sm">Reliable Control Plane</text>
        <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">Login · Inventory · Transactions · Lifecycle repair</text>
        <box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="sm" align="center">
          <text size="xs" weight="medium">QUIC Streams</text>
        </box>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authenticated Network Gateway**

    <caption>Session keys · Rate limiting · Packet batching · Congestion management</caption>
  </box>
</box>

This is a **logical separation** initially. We shouldn't immediately create two physical connections and duplicate transport infrastructure.

Start with a common application protocol and evaluate whether a single optimized QUIC connection is sufficient. Only separate the gameplay transport if measurements demonstrate a meaningful advantage.

### The really important optimization: batch packets

Our contiguous ECS naturally lends itself to building batches of replica updates.

Instead of producing one transport packet for every entity change, each client's replication scheduler builds a bounded packet payload containing multiple relevant changes.

On Linux, UDP Generic Segmentation Offload and Generic Receive Offload can also reduce packet-processing overhead in suitable workloads. They don't eliminate per-packet encryption, but can amortize portions of the I/O path. Recent UDP batching measurements illustrate how much implementation and syscall strategy can affect CPU utilization. <Cite ref="turn522788search7"/>

## 5. Compare transport strategies before locking one

| Candidate | CPU efficiency potential | Engineering risk | My assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Optimized Rust QUIC + datagrams | Good, hardware-dependent | Low–medium | Best initial baseline |
| Custom Rust secure UDP | Potentially excellent | High | Benchmark challenger |
| QUIC control + secure UDP gameplay | Potentially excellent | High | Only if justified |
| Unencrypted UDP gameplay | Avoids crypto | Unacceptable security tradeoff | Reject |
| GPU-offloaded packet crypto | Potential throughput benefit in specific bulk workloads | High latency/integration complexity | Not initially |

I would test Rust implementations such as <Entity category="software" value="Quinn" disambig="Rust QUIC transport library"/> and <Entity category="software" value="s2n-quic" disambig="Rust QUIC transport implementation"/>, alongside a narrowly scoped Rust secure-UDP prototype.

The benchmark must use **small, variable-sized gameplay packets, thousands of simultaneous sessions, and realistic network loss/jitter**, not just a single connection sending gigabytes of bulk data.

## 6. What we should benchmark

I'd collect:

| Metric | Why |
|---|---|
| Packets/sec/core | Actual packet-processing scalability |
| Encryption + authentication ns/packet | Is crypto really the bottleneck? |
| CPU cycles/byte | Bulk crypto efficiency |
| CPU cycles/packet | Fixed per-packet overhead |
| Allocations/packet | Detect avoidable allocator pressure |
| L1/L2/LLC misses | Verify cache-local transport state |
| p99 packet-processing latency | Detect gateway stalls |
| Maximum stable connections/core | Capacity planning |
| Bandwidth per client | Replication scaling |
| Loss and congestion behavior | Internet performance and fairness |

We should profile packet encryption, QUIC header processing, congestion bookkeeping, syscalls and application serialization separately.

That will tell us whether custom UDP is actually worth developing.

## 7. Architectural optimizations I would lock immediately

These benefit both QUIC and custom UDP.

- **Connection-sharded gateways:** Partition sessions across threads/cores to minimize cross-core synchronization.
- **Contiguous packet buffers:** Preallocated pools, batched serialization, and bounded payloads.
- **Hardware-accelerated AEAD:** Prefer efficient secure encryption rather than weakening security.
- **Packet coalescing:** Combine multiple ECS updates into an appropriate MTU-sized packet.
- **Zero or minimal copying:** Preserve contiguous encoded data where possible, but avoid complex scatter/gather arrangements that defeat encryption efficiency.
- **Dedicated networking threads:** Keep packet encryption and transmission off critical simulation threads.
- **Backpressure and prioritization:** Drop superseded movement updates before consuming unnecessary bandwidth.
- **Transport-independent replication:** Use the same ECS replication schema regardless of transport.

One nuance: cryptographic packet nonces and sequence numbers must be managed per connection with strict uniqueness requirements. Parallel packet generation cannot simply encrypt arbitrary chunks independently without coordinating those values.

## 8. Revised decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row justify="between" align="center">
    **ADR-012A — Transport Selection**
    <badge color="warning">Benchmark-gated</badge>
  </row>
  **Locked architecture:** transport-independent ECS replication, secure authenticated transport, batched packet generation, and dedicated gateway execution.

  **Not yet locked:** QUIC as the mandatory gameplay transport.

  **Baseline to benchmark:** Rust QUIC with datagrams and reliable streams.

  **Alternative:** Custom secure UDP for real-time replication, retaining QUIC for reliable operations if that separation demonstrates a material advantage.
</box>

My recommendation is to **withdraw our earlier provisional QUIC-first commitment as a final design decision**.

We should not build a custom UDP implementation merely because QUIC performs encryption—but neither should we choose QUIC without measuring how its full packet-processing pipeline scales to MMO populations.

For our custom engine, the best result may well be a **specialized secure UDP data plane with highly optimized batching and connection-sharded Rust gateways**. That remains a hypothesis until the benchmark confirms it.

The next architecture consideration I'd investigate is **whether networking gateways should perform replication encoding themselves, or receive pre-encoded, recipient-grouped packets from Rust simulation workers**. That decision could have an even larger CPU impact than QUIC versus custom UDP, especially in a 10,000-player battlefield.

| Optimized Rust QUIC + datagrams | Good, hardware-dependent | Low–medium | Best initial baseline |
| Custom Rust secure UDP | Potentially excellent | High | Benchmark challenger |
| QUIC control + secure UDP gameplay | Potentially excellent | High | Only if justified |
| Unencrypted UDP gameplay | Avoids crypto | Unacceptable security tradeoff | Reject |
| GPU-offloaded packet crypto | Potential throughput benefit in specific bulk workloads | High latency/integration complexity | Not initially |

I would test Rust implementations such as <Entity category="software" value="Quinn" disambig="Rust QUIC transport library"/> and <Entity category="software" value="s2n-quic" disambig="Rust QUIC transport implementation"/>, alongside a narrowly scoped Rust secure-UDP prototype.

The benchmark must use **small, variable-sized gameplay packets, thousands of simultaneous sessions, and realistic network loss/jitter**, not just a single connection sending gigabytes of bulk data.

## 6. What we should benchmark

I'd collect:

| Metric | Why |
|---|---|
| Packets/sec/core | Actual packet-processing scalability |
| Encryption + authentication ns/packet | Is crypto really the bottleneck? |
| CPU cycles/byte | Bulk crypto efficiency |
| CPU cycles/packet | Fixed per-packet overhead |
| Allocations/packet | Detect avoidable allocator pressure |
| L1/L2/LLC misses | Verify cache-local transport state |
| p99 packet-processing latency | Detect gateway stalls |
| Maximum stable connections/core | Capacity planning |
| Bandwidth per client | Replication scaling |
| Loss and congestion behavior | Internet performance and fairness |

We should profile packet encryption, QUIC header processing, congestion bookkeeping, syscalls and application serialization separately.

That will tell us whether custom UDP is actually worth developing.

## 7. Architectural optimizations I would lock immediately

These benefit both QUIC and custom UDP.

- **Connection-sharded gateways:** Partition sessions across threads/cores to minimize cross-core synchronization.
- **Contiguous packet buffers:** Preallocated pools, batched serialization, and bounded payloads.
- **Hardware-accelerated AEAD:** Prefer efficient secure encryption rather than weakening security.
- **Packet coalescing:** Combine multiple ECS updates into an appropriate MTU-sized packet.
- **Zero or minimal copying:** Preserve contiguous encoded data where possible, but avoid complex scatter/gather arrangements that defeat encryption efficiency.
- **Dedicated networking threads:** Keep packet encryption and transmission off critical simulation threads.
- **Backpressure and prioritization:** Drop superseded movement updates before consuming unnecessary bandwidth.
- **Transport-independent replication:** Use the same ECS replication schema regardless of transport.

One nuance: cryptographic packet nonces and sequence numbers must be managed per connection with strict uniqueness requirements. Parallel packet generation cannot simply encrypt arbitrary chunks independently without coordinating those values.

## 8. Revised decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row justify="between" align="center">
    **ADR-012A — Transport Selection**
    <badge color="warning">Benchmark-gated</badge>
  </row>
  **Locked architecture:** transport-independent ECS replication, secure authenticated transport, batched packet generation, and dedicated gateway execution.

  **Not yet locked:** QUIC as the mandatory gameplay transport.

  **Baseline to benchmark:** Rust QUIC with datagrams and reliable streams.

  **Alternative:** Custom secure UDP for real-time replication, retaining QUIC for reliable operations if that separation demonstrates a material advantage.
</box>

My recommendation is to **withdraw our earlier provisional QUIC-first commitment as a final design decision**.

We should not build a custom UDP implementation merely because QUIC performs encryption—but neither should we choose QUIC without measuring how its full packet-processing pipeline scales to MMO populations.

For our custom engine, the best result may well be a **specialized secure UDP data plane with highly optimized batching and connection-sharded Rust gateways**. That remains a hypothesis until the benchmark confirms it.

The next architecture consideration I'd investigate is **whether networking gateways should perform replication encoding themselves, or receive pre-encoded, recipient-grouped packets from Rust simulation workers**. That decision could have an even larger CPU impact than QUIC versus custom UDP, especially in a 10,000-player battlefield.

Message ID: `320b0130-716d-477f-8f31-115f9c5a82c7` · 2026-10-08T05:05:50.318000+00:00

**1. The Server-Side CPU Bottleneck**

MMORPG servers are bottlenecked by thread performance. They must calculate physics, spatial partitioning, AI, and pathfinding for thousands of concurrent players in a shared zone.

- **QUIC requires mandatory encryption** for every packet, including public headers. Handlings tens of thousands of real-time movement ticks through a QUIC crypto layer eats up massive amounts of CPU cycles compared to a barebones UDP socket. [[1](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/choosing-the-right-transport-protocol-tcp-vs-udp-vs-quic), [2](https://github.com/pgaijin66/Learn-QUIC-QUIC-ly)]
- Custom UDP lets the developer choose *not* to encrypt routine movement ticks, reserving cryptography solely for sensitive data like login tokens and item transactions.

**2. Strict Congestion Control Constraints**

QUIC datagrams are explicitly governed by QUIC’s internal **congestion control algorithms**. If a user experiencing a poor network connection suffers packet bursts, QUIC will **locally drop or throttle** your game's unreliable datagram frames before they even hit the wire.\
In an MMORPG, you want total sovereignty over your congestion control. If a player is lagging, you typically want to keep firing state updates to force state synchronization, or drop outdated packets at the application level rather than relying on a web-optimized throttling engine. [[1](http://www.aicassindra.com/blogs/bidi/quic_streams_for_real_time.html), [2](https://www.reddit.com/r/computerscience/comments/1jeeb97/why_do_games_use_udp_instead_of_tcp/), [3](https://daposto.medium.com/quic-for-gamenetworking-46cf23936228), [4](https://learn.lonelybinary.com/fundamentals/tcp-udp/choosing-and-quic)]

**3. Rigid Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) Limitations**

QUIC requires a minimum path MTU of 1200 bytes and **completely forbids IP fragmentation**. If you push a massive zone-load state or an item-burst update down an unreliable QUIC datagram frame that exceeds the path MTU, it will simply be discarded. Custom UDP frameworks circumvent this by writing proprietary fragmentation/reassembly routines tailored to the game's packet boundaries

- **Choose QUIC Datagrams if:** You are developing a **Mobile or Cross-Platform MMORPG** where players switch networks constantly, you want to launch quickly without inventing your own security/streaming protocol, or you are utilizing modern web stacks (e.g., [**WebTransport**](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebTransport_API) for browser-based client architectures). [[1](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/choosing-the-right-transport-protocol-tcp-vs-udp-vs-quic), [2](https://www.reddit.com/r/networking/comments/gjiohd/question_about_quic_viability_for_multiplayer/), [3](https://medium.com/@nishujangra27/why-quic-built-on-udp-over-tcp-e73efbcf8cf4), [4](https://medium.com/@massiverealm/the-foundation-of-realtime-multiplayer-part-2-data-transmission-protocols-33eb8e91242b), [5](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18518336)]
- **Choose Custom UDP if:** You are building a **Large-Scale, High-Density PC/Console MMORPG** where your primary objective is squeezing maximum player concurrency out of a single server core. The ability to avoid mandatory encryption on every tick and customize congestion logic gives you absolute dominion over server performance. [[1](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/choosing-the-right-transport-protocol-tcp-vs-udp-vs-quic)]

Thoughts?

# Phase 12B — QUIC vs Custom UDP: Architecture Review

I agree with the **direction of your argument**: for our high-density, PC/console-focused MMO, a specialized UDP transport deserves serious consideration, and QUIC should not be mandatory.

But I would challenge three assumptions before we lock the architecture:

1. Encryption may not be the dominant server CPU cost.
2. Custom congestion control is advantageous; sending without regard to congestion is not.
3. Custom UDP does not escape internet MTU limitations.

**My recommendation is to make a specialized Rust UDP data plane our preferred design candidate, but retain authenticated packet protection and congestion-aware scheduling.**

That preserves nearly all of the performance-control advantages you're seeking without taking on unnecessary security and networking failures.

## 1. Reviewing the three arguments

| Your argument | Assessment | My conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| QUIC encryption costs CPU | Correct | Benchmark packet protection separately from protocol overhead |
| Movement updates could be unencrypted | Technically possible | Not my recommended default |
| QUIC congestion control can throttle datagrams | Correct | Custom transport gives us useful scheduling control |
| We should keep transmitting at full rate under congestion | Risky | Prioritize fresh state while reducing expendable traffic |
| QUIC requires a 1200-byte minimum MTU | Partly correct | 1200 is a minimum supported UDP payload size, not the minimum size of every packet |
| Custom UDP supports fragmentation | Correct | Application-level fragmentation still has to respect path MTU |
| Custom UDP may maximize performance | Plausible | Requires measurement against optimized QUIC |

The protocol distinctions are defined by <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html" title="RFC 9000"/>, <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9221.html" title="RFC 9221"/> and <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085.html" title="RFC 8085"/>. <Cite refs={["turn669955view0","turn669955view2","turn553745search0"]}/>

## 117 — Assistant

Message ID: `eb9b7f95-1eb6-43b5-b46f-7871fb823f6a` · 2026-10-08T05:06:09.597979+00:00

# Phase 12B — QUIC vs Custom UDP: Architecture Review

I agree with the **direction of your argument**: for our high-density, PC/console-focused MMO, a specialized UDP transport deserves serious consideration, and QUIC should not be mandatory.

But I would challenge three assumptions before we lock the architecture:

1. Encryption may not be the dominant server CPU cost.
2. Custom congestion control is advantageous; sending without regard to congestion is not.
3. Custom UDP does not escape internet MTU limitations.

**My recommendation is to make a specialized Rust UDP data plane our preferred design candidate, but retain authenticated packet protection and congestion-aware scheduling.**

That preserves nearly all of the performance-control advantages you're seeking without taking on unnecessary security and networking failures.

## 1. Reviewing the three arguments

| Your argument | Assessment | My conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| QUIC encryption costs CPU | Correct | Benchmark packet protection separately from protocol overhead |
| Movement updates could be unencrypted | Technically possible | Not my recommended default |
| QUIC congestion control can throttle datagrams | Correct | Custom transport gives us useful scheduling control |
| We should keep transmitting at full rate under congestion | Risky | Prioritize fresh state while reducing expendable traffic |
| QUIC requires a 1200-byte minimum MTU | Partly correct | 1200 is a minimum supported UDP payload size, not the minimum size of every packet |
| Custom UDP supports fragmentation | Correct | Application-level fragmentation still has to respect path MTU |
| Custom UDP may maximize performance | Plausible | Requires measurement against optimized QUIC |

The protocol distinctions are defined by <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html" title="RFC 9000"/>, <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9221.html" title="RFC 9221"/> and <Link url="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085.html" title="RFC 8085"/>. <Cite refs={["turn669955view0","turn669955view2","turn553745search0"]}/>

## 2. Encryption: the real security/performance tradeoff

I would not make gameplay encryption optional by default.

Even when a movement packet contains no account credentials, leaving it unprotected exposes player locations, actions, movement patterns, and information that can be useful to cheating tools.

More importantly, **encryption and authentication are different security properties**.

We have three possible designs:

| Packet security | Confidentiality | Integrity/authentication | CPU cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain UDP | No | No | Lowest |
| Authenticated plaintext | No | Yes, with correctly designed MAC and replay protection | Low, implementation-dependent |
| AEAD-protected UDP | Yes | Yes | Low–moderate, hardware-dependent |

Authenticated plaintext is a legitimate technical option. It can prevent unauthorized packet modification without hiding packet contents, provided the protocol correctly implements sequence numbers, keys, replay windows, and authentication tags.

But we cannot assume it is significantly faster than hardware-accelerated AES-GCM. That is exactly what we should measure.

Also, QUIC does not encrypt every byte of its public header in the ordinary sense. It encrypts application payloads, authenticates the relevant header information, and separately protects selected header fields. <Cite ref="turn515069view1"/>

### My proposed security policy

**Use hardware-accelerated AEAD for normal client/server gameplay traffic**, but isolate crypto behind a replaceable packet-protection interface.

This means a custom UDP transport can remove unwanted QUIC machinery without sacrificing packet integrity or player privacy.

## 3. Congestion control: this is the strongest argument for custom UDP

Here I agree more strongly with your proposal.

QUIC DATAGRAM frames must follow the connection's congestion controller. They may be delayed or discarded before transmission when congestion prevents sending. <Cite ref="turn669955view2"/>

Our MMO should instead use an application-aware scheduler that understands the relative value of state updates.

Consider a player experiencing 200 ms of network congestion.

Sending four outdated positional snapshots is generally less useful than sending one fresh snapshot that supersedes them.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Proposed MMO congestion-aware packet scheduler</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **ECS Replication Events**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={2} align="center" gap={1}>
        **Critical**
        <caption>Combat, lifecycle, reliable changes</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={2} align="center" gap={1}>
        **Supersedable**
        <caption>Movement, velocity, cosmetic state</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Priority + Congestion Budget**
    <caption>Replace stale updates · Schedule reliable data · Pace packet output</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Custom UDP Transport**
  </box>
</box>

What we should avoid is treating unconstrained sending as a solution to packet loss.

Congested networks have finite capacity. Sending more packets into a saturated link can increase loss, queueing delay, and congestion collapse. The IETF's UDP guidance explicitly calls for congestion control even when applications build their own UDP protocols. <Cite ref="turn553745search0"/>

The advantage of custom UDP is that **we control how the application reduces traffic**, rather than surrendering all scheduling choices to a general-purpose transport implementation.

That could mean preserving critical gameplay state while aggressively reducing distant-character updates, optional cosmetic state, and superseded snapshots.

QUIC can also support application-level prioritization, but custom UDP gives us more direct control over transport scheduling.

## 4. MTU: a smaller advantage than it appears

QUIC's 1200-byte requirement is commonly misunderstood.

QUIC requires endpoints to support UDP payloads of at least 1200 bytes and applies minimum-size requirements to Initial packets. Normal gameplay packets do not all have to be 1200 bytes. <Cite ref="turn515069view0"/>

Custom UDP can fragment an application message into multiple smaller packets, but that is not unique to custom UDP as an application design technique.

For example, we could split a 10 KB zone-state message into individually identified fragments and reassemble them reliably.

The key is that each UDP packet must still respect the path MTU.

IP fragmentation is fragile on the public internet, and RFC 8900 recommends application-level solutions instead. <Cite ref="turn553745search3"/>

For our engine, I would favor:

- Small, MTU-safe gameplay packets.
- No reliance on IP fragmentation.
- Independent reliable chunks for large snapshots.
- Bounded reassembly memory and expiry.
- Separate asset delivery from gameplay-state bursts.

**Custom UDP gives us control over fragmentation semantics, not immunity from MTU limits.**

## 5. Revised network architecture

Given our established Rust/Go division, I would design the network layer as follows.

| Component | Preferred technology |
|---|---|
| Authentication and account services | Go |
| Simulation and replication ECS | Rust |
| Gameplay packet transport | Custom Rust UDP candidate |
| Encryption | Hardware-accelerated authenticated encryption |
| Congestion control | MMO-specific priority/pacing controller |
| Packet encoding | Zero/minimal-copy, contiguous bit-packed records |
| I/O | Batched UDP sockets, sharded across network threads |
| Asset delivery | HTTPS or reliable transport |
| Client GPU integration | Batched ECS deltas uploaded to GPU |
| Reliability | Separate ordered, unordered and supersedable delivery semantics |

I would also explicitly separate **connection-local packet processing** from **authoritative simulation**.

Crypto, pacing and network packet parsing should execute on dedicated gateway threads or services.

This doesn't make their total CPU cost disappear, but it keeps those operations off the simulation tick's critical path.

## 6. What would make custom UDP genuinely superior?

The benefit should come from more than skipping encryption.

Our custom transport could be built around the same data-oriented ideas as the rest of the engine:

- Fixed-capacity connection state arrays and cache-friendly packet queues.
- Thread/connection sharding to reduce locks and cross-core memory traffic.
- Batched UDP receive/send operations.
- Direct ECS delta encoding into reusable packet buffers.
- Reliable and unreliable payloads combined according to gameplay priority.
- Unreliable sequenced snapshots that replace stale data.
- Per-client adaptive update frequency.
- Application-aware congestion control.
- Hardware-assisted AEAD with no per-packet heap allocation.

The greatest potential savings may come from **reducing serialization, packet count, memory copies, and connection-state overhead**, not from removing encryption.

## 7. Architecture decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **ADR-012B — MMO Gameplay Transport**
    <badge color="info">Proposed revision</badge>
  </row>
  **Preferred implementation direction:** Custom Rust UDP data plane.

  **Security:** Authenticated packet protection by default.

  **Congestion:** Game-aware pacing, traffic prioritization and obsolete-state suppression.

  **Reliability:** Application-specific delivery classes and bounded fragmentation.

  **QUIC:** Retained as a benchmark reference and optional reliable/control transport, not a mandatory gameplay dependency.
</box>

I would make **custom UDP our primary prototype** rather than QUIC, given your target of maximizing high-density PC/console MMO concurrency.

But I would not lock *unencrypted gameplay traffic* or *unconstrained packet sending* into the engine. Those choices create risks without a demonstrated performance advantage large enough to justify them.

The critical experiment is straightforward: compare optimized secure UDP against QUIC datagrams under the same packet sizes, connection counts, encryption algorithms and simulated network conditions.

If custom UDP has a measurable advantage in CPU per delivered useful update and p99 latency, we can finalize it without changing our ECS replication architecture.

**One final point:** For a 10,000-player battlefield, replication fan-out and interest management are likely to be at least as important as the transport itself. The next optimization I would examine is **recipient-grouped replication, shared encoding, and multicast-like server fan-out**, which can avoid rebuilding similar state thousands of times for different clients.

I think that's the right decision for our engine. **We should use QUIC by default and only invest in custom UDP if measured performance demonstrates a substantial advantage.**

## ADR-012C — QUIC-First MMO Networking

<badge color="success">Recommended to lock</badge>

| Component | Decision |
|---|---|
| Primary gameplay transport | QUIC |
| Movement and snapshots | Unreliable QUIC DATAGRAM |
| Inventory, transactions and lifecycle events | Reliable QUIC streams |
| Congestion management | QUIC congestion control + application-level priority scheduling |
| Encryption | QUIC TLS 1.3 / hardware-accelerated AEAD |
| Replication | Custom data-oriented ECS replication |
| Packet generation | Batched, compact, allocation-conscious |
| Server implementation | Rust |
| Service orchestration | Go |
| Custom UDP | Only if benchmarks justify development |

This retains reliable and unreliable messaging under one authenticated connection. QUIC DATAGRAM is specifically designed for unreliable data that benefits from QUIC's shared security and congestion control. <Cite ref="turn531672search1"/>

## 1. QUIC already supports a useful MMO optimization

One detail in the current <Entity category="software" value="Quinn" disambig="Rust QUIC implementation"/> API is particularly relevant.

`send_datagram()` can discard older queued datagrams when new ones need buffer space. Its alternative, `send_datagram_wait()`, waits for space and effectively prioritizes older datagrams. <Cite ref="turn206805search0"/>

That aligns with our design:

**For supersedable movement snapshots, fresh information is usually more valuable than old unsent information.**

We still need our own replication scheduler to choose which entity updates enter each datagram. QUIC can't automatically understand which player, component, or gameplay event matters most.

But it already provides useful underlying delivery behavior.

## 2. Which Rust QUIC implementation?

## 3. Where I would invest our optimization effort

Rather than developing a custom UDP stack, I'd concentrate on these four areas.

**Connection-sharded packet processing.** Keep related QUIC connection state on consistent execution threads where practical, minimizing shared locks, cache misses, and cross-core traffic.

**Replication-aware datagram construction.** Group entity updates by client relevance and priority before they enter QUIC. Never encode and enqueue obsolete movement updates unnecessarily.

**Hardware-accelerated encryption and efficient I/O.** Benchmark cryptographic providers, packet batching and Linux UDP offload features on actual deployment hardware.

**Per-client adaptive network LOD.** When congestion increases, reduce optional data, distant-entity frequency and superseded state before sacrificing critical gameplay messages.

These techniques preserve our ability to optimize aggressively without maintaining an entire secure networking protocol.

## 4. When would custom UDP become justified?

I would establish a measurable escape criterion rather than revisit the question based on speculation.

A custom UDP prototype would only be warranted if optimized QUIC demonstrates a persistent limitation such as:

- An inability to meet p99 packet-processing latency targets at our required connection density.
- Excessive CPU cost after crypto, batching and connection sharding have been optimized.
- Congestion behavior that materially harms gameplay despite application-level prioritization.
- A protocol constraint that prevents a specific required gameplay feature.

As an initial decision gate, I'd investigate alternatives only if transport overhead alone consumes an unacceptable share of gateway CPU budget—for example, over 25% at target load—or if it demonstrably prevents us from meeting latency targets. That 25% is a proposed engineering threshold, not an industry standard.

## Final decision

**QUIC-first, Quinn-first, custom ECS replication on top.**

This gives us an established secure transport while keeping our networking architecture independent of its implementation.

The major performance opportunity now moves up one layer: **recipient-grouped ECS replication and server fan-out**.

For a 10,000-player battle, the cost of deciding who receives which entity updates—and repeatedly serializing nearly identical state—could outweigh the differences between QUIC and custom UDP.

That's where I would concentrate the next architecture phase.

**Yes. We can achieve nearly all of those optimizations while retaining QUIC.** In fact, I think the ideal architecture for our MMO is to use QUIC strictly as a secure transport layer and build our own highly optimized, data-oriented replication engine above it.

This gives us the best of both approaches:

- QUIC handles encryption, authentication, congestion control, connection management and packet delivery.
- Our engine controls serialization, component deltas, packet contents, update priorities, batching, memory layout and interest management.
- Rust manages network execution without requiring a custom transport protocol.

That is particularly interesting for our architecture.

# Phase 12D — Data-Oriented QUIC Networking

## 1. Which optimizations can we still achieve?

| Optimization | With QUIC? | Our approach |
|---|---|---|
| Zero-allocation ECS encoding | Yes | Preallocated serialization buffers |
| Component-level delta compression | Yes | Custom binary replication format |
| Shared serialization | Yes | Encode common state once |
| Packet coalescing | Yes | Batch entity updates before QUIC |
| Superseded state removal | Yes | Discard old movement snapshots |
| Contiguous packet memory | Yes | Pooled packet buffers |
| Batched socket I/O | Yes | QUIC implementation and UDP offload |
| Connection sharding | Yes | Partition network execution |
| Per-client bandwidth budgets | Yes | Application-aware replication |
| SIMD serialization | Yes | Vectorized quantization/packing |
| Minimal memory copies | Mostly | Reuse reference-counted buffers |
| Reduced connection-state overhead | Partially | Optimized lifecycle and runtime |
| Eliminate QUIC crypto overhead | No | Hardware-accelerated AEAD |

**The major restrictions are inside QUIC's transport state machine, cryptographic protection and congestion control—not in our ECS or replication architecture.**

## 3. Shared serialization — potentially our biggest saving

Imagine 5,000 players watching the same large battle.

Many of them need substantially overlapping world updates.

A naive design serializes the same character transform separately for every recipient.

Our ECS can avoid this.

### Two-stage encoding

**Stage A — Canonical component encoding**

Encode a changed transform once into a compact, client-independent representation.

For example:

```text
Entity 18427
    Component: Transform
    Quantized position: 6 bytes
    Rotation: 4 bytes
    Flags: 1 byte
```

These field sizes are illustrative, not our finalized network schema.

**Stage B — Per-client packet assembly**

Select the encoded records relevant to each client, apply client-specific IDs or delta baselines if needed, and pack them into QUIC datagrams.

This separates the expensive component serialization from the per-recipient delivery decision.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **One ECS change**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **One canonical encoded record**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={3} gap={2}>
    {#each ["Client A","Client B","Client C"] as x}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={2} align="center" gap={1}>
          <text size="xs" weight="medium">{x}</text>
          <caption>Own packet / baseline</caption>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

The same canonical data can be reused without repeating the entire encoding operation.

**Important limitation:** true delta encoding depends on each client's acknowledged baseline. We cannot always reuse an entire encoded delta across clients at different versions.

My recommendation is a tiered approach:

1. Share quantized, baseline-independent component values.
2. Reuse common delta encodings among clients with compatible baselines.
3. Perform only the necessary recipient-specific patching and packet assembly.

This also works with QUIC encryption. The plaintext component data may be shared, but each connection's packet protection still occurs separately.

## 4. Minimize memory copies

Our CPU-side replication buffers should be contiguous and pool-allocated, matching the broader data-oriented engine architecture.

I would design:

| Memory structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ChangedComponentRecords[]` | Compact list of changed component references |
| `EncodedStateBlocks[]` | Canonical reusable binary component records |
| `RecipientRanges[]` | Which clients need which encoded blocks |
| `PacketDescriptors[]` | Planned datagram payload ranges |
| `PacketBufferPool[]` | Reusable MTU-sized memory blocks |
| `ConnectionSendQueues[]` | Bounded per-client transmit scheduling |

The hot path should avoid allocating an object for every entity update.

However, **zero-copy needs a precise definition**.

Even if we pass an immutable `Bytes` buffer to Quinn, the QUIC implementation may still copy data into encrypted packet buffers or kernel-facing transmit storage.

Authenticated encryption operates on the final packet representation. We should not promise end-to-end zero-copy from ECS memory to the network interface.

What we can aim for is **zero per-entity heap allocation, minimal application-layer copies, and reusable packet buffers**.

## 5. Quinn has an especially interesting low-level architecture

The Quinn project consists of several layers:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| `quinn` | High-level asynchronous QUIC connections |
| `quinn-proto` | Transport state machine, independent of socket I/O |
| `quinn-udp` | UDP I/O utilities and platform-specific optimizations |

This separation is valuable because we don't necessarily need to accept the high-level runtime's scheduling and I/O model forever. <Cite ref="turn937145search9"/>

### Two implementation tiers

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Tier 1 — Standard Quinn**
      <badge color="success">Start here</badge>
    </row>
    <text size="sm">Use the high-level Quinn runtime with QUIC datagrams, reliable streams, pooled application buffers, and dedicated networking tasks.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Lowest engineering complexity. Provides our performance baseline.</text>
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **Tier 2 — Custom runtime over quinn-proto**

    <text size="sm">Build a tightly controlled I/O runtime around Quinn's QUIC protocol engine, potentially integrating connection sharding, batch scheduling, custom buffer pools and platform-specific socket handling.</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">We retain QUIC security and protocol behavior without writing our own UDP transport protocol. Requires more implementation and testing.</text>
  </box>
</box>

**This is likely our best escape hatch.**

If standard Quinn eventually becomes a bottleneck, we can optimize the runtime beneath our application protocol before considering custom UDP.

## 6. Packet batching and congestion management

Quinn already gives us several useful controls.

Its `send_datagram()` may discard older queued, unsent datagrams to make room for fresh ones, while `send_datagram_wait()` waits for buffer space. It also exposes the supported maximum datagram size and current send-buffer space. <Cite ref="turn937145search0"/>

For supersedable state such as movement snapshots, we should generally prioritize fresh data—but **discard stale state before handing it to Quinn**, rather than relying solely on the transport to decide what gets discarded.

For reliable operations, use streams with bounded queues and independent application-level sequencing.

Quinn also supports Generic Segmentation Offload where available, although its benefit depends on packet patterns and platform support. <Cite ref="turn937145search4"/>

### The correct batching strategy

I would not attempt to fill every packet to its maximum possible size.

Larger packets can be more efficient, but waiting too long to fill them increases gameplay latency.

Instead, build packets using:

- A maximum MTU-safe payload size.
- A maximum age for pending updates.
- An application priority budget.
- Current congestion and connection status.
- Explicit supersession rules for movement state.

For example, a packet scheduler could send a partially filled datagram immediately when latency-sensitive state reaches its deadline, rather than waiting for more NPC updates.

## 7. Connection-state overhead

This is the one area where QUIC imposes unavoidable costs compared with a minimal custom protocol.

Each connection needs cryptographic state, packet numbers, congestion tracking, loss detection, and related transport metadata.

However, we can still reduce surrounding overhead:

- Reuse established connections instead of reconnecting frequently.
- Avoid opening unnecessary streams per gameplay event.
- Keep application session state compact and contiguous.
- Shard connections across gateway workers.
- Limit pending reliable data and datagram buffers.
- Use connection pooling concepts only where semantically appropriate—not to combine independent players into one QUIC security session.

We cannot eliminate QUIC's per-connection protocol state, but we can avoid duplicating it unnecessarily in our application.

One further consideration: **our GPU-first principles do not require networking itself to run on the GPU**. Packet scheduling, AEAD and socket I/O are naturally host-side, latency-sensitive operations. GPU upload should happen after compact decoded state batches have been assembled.

## 8. Updated architecture decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **ADR-012D — Data-Oriented QUIC Networking**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  **Primary transport:** QUIC using Quinn.

  **Replication:** Custom contiguous, schema-driven ECS delta encoding.

  **Memory:** Pooled binary buffers, shared canonical encodings, bounded per-client queues.

  **Scheduling:** Recipient-aware batching, relevance priorities and superseded-state elimination.

  **Performance scaling:** Start with standard Quinn; move to `quinn-proto` and a specialized network runtime only if profiling justifies it.

  **Custom UDP:** Last-resort alternative, not part of the initial architecture.
</box>

## 9. Where I think the largest gains are

For our high-density MMO, I would prioritize optimization in this order:

| Priority | Optimization | Expected impact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Interest management and network LOD | Avoid sending unnecessary updates entirely |
| 2 | Shared canonical component encoding | Avoid repeating expensive serialization per recipient |
| 3 | Packet coalescing and stale-update suppression | Reduce packet count and wasted work |
| 4 | Contiguous buffers and pooled allocation | Reduce memory allocation and cache overhead |
| 5 | Connection sharding and optimized I/O | Improve multicore gateway scaling |
| 6 | Transport-specific tuning | Optimize QUIC after application-level inefficiencies are removed |

This ordering is a hypothesis to validate through profiling, but it is a sound starting point.

**So yes: we can retain QUIC and still pursue almost every major networking optimization we originally wanted from custom UDP.**

The next architecture step should be **shared ECS replication encoding and recipient-grouped fan-out**, especially for a scenario with 10,000 players in one battle.

That's where our custom engine could gain substantial scalability without needing to reinvent secure networking.

- Use connection pooling concepts only where semantically appropriate—not to combine independent players into one QUIC security session.

We cannot eliminate QUIC's per-connection protocol state, but we can avoid duplicating it unnecessarily in our application.

One further consideration: **our GPU-first principles do not require networking itself to run on the GPU**. Packet scheduling, AEAD and socket I/O are naturally host-side, latency-sensitive operations. GPU upload should happen after compact decoded state batches have been assembled.

## 8. Updated architecture decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **ADR-012D — Data-Oriented QUIC Networking**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  **Primary transport:** QUIC using Quinn.

  **Replication:** Custom contiguous, schema-driven ECS delta encoding.

  **Memory:** Pooled binary buffers, shared canonical encodings, bounded per-client queues.

  **Scheduling:** Recipient-aware batching, relevance priorities and superseded-state elimination.

  **Performance scaling:** Start with standard Quinn; move to `quinn-proto` and a specialized network runtime only if profiling justifies it.

  **Custom UDP:** Last-resort alternative, not part of the initial architecture.
</box>

## 9. Where I think the largest gains are

For our high-density MMO, I would prioritize optimization in this order:

| Priority | Optimization | Expected impact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Interest management and network LOD | Avoid sending unnecessary updates entirely |
| 2 | Shared canonical component encoding | Avoid repeating expensive serialization per recipient |
| 3 | Packet coalescing and stale-update suppression | Reduce packet count and wasted work |
| 4 | Contiguous buffers and pooled allocation | Reduce memory allocation and cache overhead |
| 5 | Connection sharding and optimized I/O | Improve multicore gateway scaling |
| 6 | Transport-specific tuning | Optimize QUIC after application-level inefficiencies are removed |

This ordering is a hypothesis to validate through profiling, but it is a sound starting point.

**So yes: we can retain QUIC and still pursue almost every major networking optimization we originally wanted from custom UDP.**

The next architecture step should be **shared ECS replication encoding and recipient-grouped fan-out**, especially for a scenario with 10,000 players in one battle.

That's where our custom engine could gain substantial scalability without needing to reinvent secure networking.

Message ID: `198a300b-6da7-4e10-9679-2ca93b031c40` · 2026-10-08T05:31:20.617000+00:00

The Direct Comparison

Feature	Quinn (QUIC)	Custom UDP (RUDP)
Delivery Modes	Streams (Reliable, ordered/unordered) + Datagrams (Unreliable).	Completely custom. You design exactly how packets are treated.
Head-of-Line Blocking	No across streams. If Stream A drops a packet, Stream B keeps moving.	No. Handled manually via sequence numbers and bitmasks.
Security	Built-in TLS 1.3 (Mandatory encryption and handshakes).	Manual. You must implement DTLS or custom encryption layer.
Connection Handshake	1-RTT / 0-RTT (Fast reconnections if mobile/wi-fi hops).	Fast, but you have to build the connection state machine yourself.
MTU / Fragmentation	Automated for streams. Manual for Datagram extensions.	Manual. You must fragment and reassemble large packets.
Server CPU Overhead	High (TLS encryption, intensive connection states).	Low (Lean, optimized purely for game byte-buffers).

1. Quinn (QUIC) Pros & Cons for MMOs

Historically, QUIC was seen as "just encrypted TCP over UDP". However, with modern features like Quinn's send_datagram (unreliable data), it is highly viable for games.

🚀 Why Quinn is great for MMOs:

• The "Hybrid" Data Model: MMOs require a mix of data types. Quinn gives you this out of the box.
	• Unreliable Datagrams: Use for rapid position updates, player rotation, or visual effects. If a packet drops, who cares? The next tick replaces it.
	• Reliable Streams: Create a stream for chat channels, inventory modifications, trade requests, or zoning data.
• Zero Head-of-Line Blocking: If a player downloads a massive chunk of data for a new map zone on Stream 1, it will not delay or block their urgent combat actions or chat messages on Stream 2.
• Connection Migration: Essential for mobile or laptop MMOs. If a player switches from Wi-Fi to 5G cellular, QUIC migrates the connection seamlessly without disconnecting them from the game world.

⚠️ The Quinn Catch:

• Server CPU Cost: QUIC mandates TLS 1.3. Encrypting and decrypting packets for thousands of concurrent MMO players will consume significant server CPU cycles.
• Lack of Game-Centric Packing: Quinn doesn't know about game ticks. It handles congestion control like a web protocol (BBR/Cubic), which can sometimes buffer bytes longer than a custom game loop would like.

2. Custom UDP (RUDP) Pros & Cons for MMOs

Building custom UDP means handling raw sockets (std::net::UdpSocket or tokio::net::UdpSocket) and implementing your own protocol rules on top.

🚀 Why Custom UDP is great for MMOs:

• Maximized Concurrency & Performance: You bypass all the web-centric overhead of QUIC. No strict TLS rules if you prefer lightweight custom encryption, and no bloated connection metadata. You can fit way more players on a single server core.
• Delta Compression & Bit-packing: You control every single bit. You can write custom algorithms where if packet #101 arrives before packet #100, packet #100 is automatically dropped and discarded because the data is stale.

⚠️ The Custom UDP Catch:

• The "Wheel-Revention" Trap: You will spend months implementing connection handshakes, NAT punch-through, packet fragmentation (splitting large inventory payloads across 1500-byte MTU limits), slide-window ACKs, and packet reordering.

Which one should you choose?

Choose Quinn if:
You want to build the actual game instead of writing network infrastructure for the next six months. If your MMO is a standard RPG, strategy game, or browser-based game where tick rates don't need to be sub-15ms, Quinn's developer ergonomics, built-in TLS, and stream-handling are unmatched.
Note: If you like the idea of Quinn/QUIC but use the Bevy engine, look at the bevy_quinnet plugin.
Choose Custom UDP if:
Your MMO is an action/survival MMO (like Rust or New World) requiring hyper-low latency, client-side prediction, and authoritative lag compensation. In this case, standard QUIC streams are too heavy, and you'll need absolute control over packet lifetimes.
Alternative Recommendation: Before building custom UDP from scratch, look at existing Rust game-networking crates like renet or naia. They give you custom, game-optimized Reliable/Unreliable UDP channels without forcing you to write raw socket bitmasks yourself.
To help tailor this, let me know:
• What sub-genre of MMO are you building (e.g., Tab-target RPG, fast-paced action, text/turn-based)?
• What is your target player count per server instance?

A wow like MMO

For a World of Warcraft-style MMO (tab-target combat, global cooldowns, heavy inventory management, instance zoning, and chat-heavy systems), Quinn (QUIC) is highly viable and an excellent choice, especially for a solo developer or small team.
WoW-like games run on a relatively slow simulation loop (historically 400ms world ticks for things like auctions and health regen, with network message loops around 20–50ms). This means you don't need the hyper-lean, frame-perfect performance of a first-person shooter. Instead, you need robust state synchronization, which Quinn makes much easier to manage.

How to map a WoW-like architecture onto Quinn

QUIC’s unique feature is that it allows multiple concurrent streams over a single connection. For a WoW clone, you can divide your game traffic like this:
• The Unreliable Datagram: Use Quinn’s send_datagram for movement updates and rotations of players and mobs. If a position update packet drops, it doesn't matter because a new one will arrive 50ms later.
• Stream 1 (The Combat & Action Channel): A reliable, ordered stream for spell casting, aura/buff applications, and damage events. You want to guarantee that a Cast Spell: Fireball request actually lands, and that damage is calculated in sequence.
• Stream 2 (The World & State Channel): A reliable stream for looting, inventory management, vendor buying, and quest progression. These actions must be 100% reliable but shouldn't clog up your combat packets.
• Stream 3 (The Chat Channel): A dedicated stream for Guild, General, and Party chat. If a player experiences minor lag during a massive boss fight, their chat messages might buffer, but it won't block incoming combat data (preventing Head-of-Line blocking).
• Ephemeral Streams: When a player crosses a boundary into a new zone or enters a dungeon, you can open a fresh, temporary stream to dump the bulk Map Data and NPC spawning states without stuttering their active connection.

The Reality Check: Quinn's Biggest Hurdle for a WoW-like MMO

While the architectural layout is perfect, you must design around Server CPU Overhead.
WoW-style games shine when hundreds of players gather in one spot (e.g., Orgrimmar/Stormwind or a 40-man outdoor raid boss). Because QUIC enforces mandatory TLS 1.3 encryption, your game server has to encrypt and decrypt every single packet for every single player.
If you have 500 players in a tight space all casting spells, the server is sending thousands of packets per second. With custom UDP, this is just raw bytes. With Quinn, it's a massive amount of cryptographic math. To mitigate this:
1. Use an architecture with separate proxy/gateway nodes. Have lightweight network servers handle the Quinn connections and TLS termination, then forward the raw, decrypted bytes to your actual simulation/world server thread.
2. Aggressively cull network updates. Don't send movement or spell updates to players who are too far away or behind walls.

The Verdict

• Start with Quinn if you want to get your prototype up and running quickly. It will save you months of work handling packet loss, connection dropouts, re-ordering, and security. It is more than fast enough for tab-target combat.
• If you want a middle ground, look at Renet. It is a Rust crate explicitly designed for games. It uses a custom, lightweight UDP protocol that gives you the same concepts (Reliable/Unreliable channels) but without the heavy TLS CPU overhead of QUIC.
Thoughts?

## 130 — Assistant

Message ID: `c8f6cf90-9da6-4fb4-8bf0-0904c5082138` · 2026-10-08T05:31:32.103613+00:00

# Quinn vs Custom UDP — Final Review for Our MMO

**I agree with the conclusion of the comparison: Quinn is the better starting point for our WoW-like MMO.** But I would not accept all of its technical reasoning.

Several statements overstate QUIC's cost, understate what Quinn lets us control, or attribute advantages to custom UDP that we can achieve equally well with QUIC.

Most importantly, **we don't need to choose between QUIC and a highly optimized custom MMO replication system. We can have both.**

## 1. Corrections to the comparison

| Claim | My assessment |
|---|---|
| QUIC offers reliable streams and unreliable datagrams | Correct |
| QUIC supports reliable unordered messages natively | Not quite. QUIC streams are ordered byte streams; unordered message delivery requires an application abstraction or implementation-specific read behavior |
| QUIC eliminates all head-of-line blocking | Partially. It eliminates cross-stream delivery HOL, but streams share congestion capacity and connection-level flow control |
| QUIC crypto creates massive server CPU overhead | Not established without profiling |
| Custom UDP permits bit packing and delta compression | True, but QUIC permits exactly the same optimizations |
| Custom UDP supports stale-packet rejection | True, but we can do this above QUIC DATAGRAM too |
| QUIC connection migration is automatic and seamless | Supported, but application/session recovery and path changes still need handling |
| WoW-like games don't require low latency | Misleading. Combat, interrupts and movement still benefit substantially from low latency |
| Renet removes the need for encryption | Encryption is not the reason to choose Renet; its transport/security configuration must still be reviewed |

The difference is that QUIC handles transport mechanics while we remain responsible for **gameplay semantics, replication and event prioritization**.

## 2. The most important misconception: QUIC streams and combat

The proposed mapping places all combat and spell events on one reliable ordered stream.

I would **not** implement it that way.

A reliable stream guarantees delivery and byte ordering, but a lost segment can delay subsequent data on that same stream.

That can be especially undesirable for real-time combat.

QUIC streams are independently ordered, while all streams still operate under connection-level resource constraints. <Cite refs={["turn890875search0","turn671469search12"]}/>

For our engine, we should separate commands, authoritative outcomes, and frequent combat-state snapshots according to their semantics.

### Revised traffic mapping

| Traffic | Preferred QUIC delivery | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Player movement input | DATAGRAM, sequenced, with short input redundancy | Fresh input matters; server checks sequence |
| Remote player movement | DATAGRAM | New snapshots replace older ones |
| Aim, facing and locomotion | DATAGRAM | Supersedable state |
| Cast spell request | Reliable message on a priority-controlled stream | Must have a definitive accepted/rejected outcome |
| Damage and combat events | Reliable events when required, plus snapshot repair | Important outcomes must not be permanently lost |
| Health, mana and resources | DATAGRAM snapshots with versioning; reliable repair as needed | Current state can supersede previous state |
| Buffs/debuffs | Reliable lifecycle changes plus periodic state repair | State transitions must eventually converge |
| Inventory and trades | Reliable, ordered, transactional | Correctness over throughput |
| Chat | Separate reliable stream | Independent ordering |
| Entity spawn/despawn | Reliable lifecycle events or versioned repair snapshots | Avoid ghost entities |
| Zone state | Chunked reliable transfer or snapshot streaming | Bounded resource use |
| Assets | Separate HTTPS/CDN or bulk delivery service | Avoid competing heavily with gameplay traffic |

The combat request is **not** made authoritative simply because it is reliable. We still need command IDs, server validation, idempotency, and acknowledged results.

The server should also tolerate retries without accidentally casting the same spell twice.

For input, a datagram carrying recent command sequences can survive occasional packet loss without waiting for retransmission.

### Revised traffic mapping

|---|---|---|

## 3. Head-of-line blocking: a subtle but important limitation

The comparison says that downloading a large zone over one stream won't affect urgent gameplay on another.

That's only partly true.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **One QUIC connection**
  <grid columns={3} gap={2}>
    {#each [{t:"Combat",d:"High priority"},{t:"Chat",d:"Normal priority"},{t:"Zone data",d:"Low priority"}] as x}
      <grid-item>
        <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={2} gap={1} minHeight="76px" justify="center">
          <text weight="medium" size="sm" textAlign="center">{x.t}</text>
          <text size="xs" color="secondary" textAlign="center">{x.d}</text>
        </box>

    {/each}
