        </row>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">ENGINE + SIMULATION</text>
        Engine host, Vulkan management, CPU ECS, authoritative gameplay simulation, physics, QUIC/Quinn, replication, persistence adapters.
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <row align="center" gap={2}>
          <box background="#49A9B6" radius="md" padding={2}>
            <icon name="server" color="#FFFFFF"/>
          </box>
          <title size="lg">Go</title>
        </row>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">DISTRIBUTED SERVICES</text>
        Authentication, accounts, sessions, social systems, cluster coordination, administration, service APIs and orchestration.
      </box>
    </grid-item>

        </row>

        Selected codecs, binary-processing utilities, asset transformations, native interoperability, and experimental optimized kernels.
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <row align="center" gap={2}>
          <box background="#8570CA" radius="md" padding={2}>
            <icon name="layers" color="#FFFFFF"/>
          </box>
          <title size="lg">Slang</title>
        </row>

        GPU ECS, compute scheduling, mesh/task shaders, animation, visibility, shading, GI, and GPU vector UI.
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
</box>

Slang is my preferred shader language because it supports modular shader development and SPIR-V compilation for Vulkan. Khronos's shader samples include Slang alongside GLSL and HLSL, although our specific mesh/task shader and GPU ECS capabilities must be validated against the chosen compiler and GPU drivers. <Cite refs={["turn243104search6","turn243104search10"]}/>

## 2. Ownership matrix

| Subsystem | Primary language | Supporting technology |
|---|---|---|
| Engine runtime and lifecycle | Rust | Platform libraries |
| Vulkan device and memory management | Rust | Slang shaders |
| GPU ECS storage and scheduling | Rust host + Slang | Vulkan compute |
| GPU structural mutations | Slang | Rust memory/resource management |
| Mesh/task renderer | Slang | Rust render graph |
| Virtualized geometry | Slang runtime | Rust/Zig offline tooling |
| SDF GI and radiance cache | Slang | Rust residency orchestration |
| GPU animation and visual physics | Slang | Rust component definitions |
| GPU vector UI / Bézier text | Slang | Rust platform/input bridge |
| Server simulation ECS | Rust | SIMD / optional GPU backend |
| Server networking | Rust | Quinn / QUIC |
| Replication, group replication, NetLOD | Rust | SoA encoding |
| Inventory and transactions | Rust or Go service ownership | Database |
| Account and social services | Go | Service APIs |
| Cluster administration | Go | Deployment infrastructure |
| Asset cooking / compression | Rust + selected Zig | Offline processing |
| Gameplay scripting | Undecided | Phase 18 |

One deliberate choice: **Zig should not become a compulsory layer between Rust and Vulkan**. We can use Rust's Vulkan ecosystem directly.

That keeps the GPU submission path short and avoids splitting GPU resource ownership across two host languages.

## 3. Keep the high-frequency execution paths within one language domain

I would enforce a rule:

**No cross-language FFI calls per entity, per component, per draw, or per GPU workgroup.**

That applies equally to Rust↔Zig, Rust↔Go, and host↔GPU interactions.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">EXECUTION AND COMMUNICATION BOUNDARIES</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Go Distributed Services**
    <caption>Accounts · Sessions · Social · Coordination</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Versioned service messages</text>
  </row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Authoritative Server**
    <caption>ECS · Simulation · Replication · Quinn</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">QUIC protocol + ECS deltas</text>
  </row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Client / Engine Host**
    <caption>Vulkan · Input · Networking · Streaming · Device resources</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Persistent GPU buffers + batched commands</text>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Slang GPU Runtime**
    <caption>ECS · Simulation · Animation · Rendering · UI · GI</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center" align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-left-right" color="secondary"/>
    <text size="xs" color="secondary">Zig utilities invoked through bulk interfaces or offline tools</text>
  </row>
</box>

### Rust ↔ Go

Use versioned service protocols rather than in-process FFI.

A Rust simulation worker should not cross into Go for every ability calculation, combat event, or position change.

Go is valuable for service orchestration and network-facing infrastructure, but we should avoid making the Go runtime part of our per-tick simulation critical path.

### Rust ↔ Zig

Use one of two approaches:

- **Build-time integration:** Zig executables process assets and generate binary outputs. No runtime ABI needed.
- **Native library integration:** Zig exports a small C-compatible ABI, with Rust passing bulk buffers and explicit lengths.

For example, processing 100,000 animation keys in one call may be reasonable; invoking Zig once per character per frame is unnecessary.

### Rust ↔ Slang

This is not conventional FFI. Rust submits Vulkan work; shaders operate on GPU resources.

The contract is binary buffer layout, shader resource binding, synchronization, and component schema compatibility.

The GPU should receive contiguous batches of updates and return compact result records, not participate in synchronous host function calls.

## 4. The most important shared technology: a schema compiler

We currently have many different representations of the same logical data:

- Rust authoritative ECS components.
- GPU SoA component columns.
- QUIC network messages.
- Persistent database records.
- Zig processing structures.
- Shader resource layouts.
- Scripting interfaces.

**I would not attempt to use one binary layout for all seven.**

Instead, define a canonical schema description and generate suitable representations for each domain.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Canonical Component / Message Schemas**
    <caption>Stable type IDs · Field IDs · Defaults · Version rules · Access policies</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{t:"Rust ECS types",d:"Simulation and component APIs"},{t:"Slang GPU layouts",d:"Aligned buffers and shader accessors"},{t:"Network codecs",d:"Quantization and delta encoding"},{t:"Persistence formats",d:"Durable versions and migrations"},{t:"Zig bindings",d:"Explicit native ABI structures"},{t:"Script bindings",d:"Capabilities and typed commands"}] as item}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={2} gap={1} minHeight="72px">
          <text weight="medium" size="sm">{item.t}</text>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{item.d}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
      {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

For instance, a canonical `Transform` component might generate:

| Representation | Data |
|---|---|
| Authoritative Rust | High-precision world position, rotation, version |
| GPU presentation | Camera-relative position, packed orientation, current/previous transforms |
| Network | Region-relative quantized position and packed rotation |
| Persistence | Stable world ID, full coordinate precision, schema version |
| Scripting | Readable position and validated movement commands |

The GPU layout prioritizes memory bandwidth. The network layout prioritizes bytes transmitted. Persistence prioritizes stability and recoverability.

These are different requirements.

### Schema rules I'd adopt

1. Stable numeric type and field identifiers.
2. Explicit compatibility and migration rules.
3. Distinct representations for each execution domain.
4. Generated serializers and GPU accessors.
5. GPU alignment and layout validation in automated tests.
6. No arbitrary runtime reflection in performance-critical loops.
7. Typed access permissions for scripts and network clients.

I'd build a small purpose-specific schema compiler rather than start with a huge general-purpose engine metadata framework.

        {#each ["Platform + Vulkan","GPU ECS Host","World Streaming","Render Graph","GPU Presentation","UI + Input Bridge"] as x}
          <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2}>
            <text size="xs">{x}</text>
          </box>
        {/each}
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU Shader Modules**
    <caption>Compute ECS · Spatial · Animation · Mesh/Task · Materials · GI · UI</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Offline Toolchain**
    <caption>Asset cooking · Schema generation · Shader compilation · World packaging</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Some proposed crate boundaries:

| Crate | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `engine-schema` | Component descriptors, type identifiers, generated contracts |
| `engine-math` | Coordinate systems and shared numerical conventions |
| `engine-ecs` | CPU-side archetypes, chunks, queries, scheduling |
| `engine-world` | Spatial addressing, scenes, residency metadata |
| `engine-gpu` | Vulkan device/resource abstraction |
| `engine-gpu-ecs` | GPU component pools, mutation control, epoch publication |
| `engine-render` | Render graph, pipelines, views and work scheduling |
| `engine-assets` | Content identity, streaming, decoding and residency |
| `engine-net` | Quinn integration and application protocol |
| `engine-replication` | Delta encoding, interest, group replication and NetLOD |
| `engine-server` | Authoritative simulation runtime |
| `engine-client` | Client application assembly and lifecycle |

Names are provisional.

I would **avoid generating dozens of tiny crates before actual code exists**. Start with a few coherent crates and split them when dependency boundaries become stable.

### Critical dependency rule

The renderer should depend on GPU ECS interfaces and scene data contracts.

The GPU ECS should not depend on the renderer.

Likewise, world persistence should not depend on Quinn or a particular network transport.

This keeps major systems replaceable without rewriting the entire engine.

## 6. Slang as our unified GPU programming language

I recommend making Slang the primary source language for GPU workloads.

The toolchain would be:

`Slang source → Slang compiler → SPIR-V → Vulkan shader module/pipeline`

Vulkan consumes SPIR-V, and Slang supports compilation to SPIR-V. <Cite refs={["turn243104search9","turn243104search10"]}/>

We should create separate shader modules for:

| Slang module | Work |
|---|---|
| `gpu_ecs` | Component access, mutation queues, active-set selection |
| `gpu_memory` | Chunk pools and suballocators |
| `gpu_spatial` | Flat-grid updates, sorting and compaction |
| `gpu_animation` | Graph processing, poses and skinning |
| `gpu_geometry` | Mesh/task shaders and geometry decoding |
| `gpu_visibility` | Culling and visibility-buffer output |
| `gpu_materials` | Material resolve and shading |
| `gpu_lighting` | Direct lights and virtual shadows |
| `gpu_gi` | Sparse SDF tracing and shared radiance cache |
| `gpu_ui` | Layout, vector geometry and Bézier text |

These can share utility modules, mathematical conventions, and generated GPU component structures.

We still need an explicit validation milestone for Slang's output across our required Vulkan compute, task and mesh shader features. Support for the shader language does not guarantee that every desired extension works correctly on every driver.

    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <row align="center" gap={2}>
          <box background="#D3A34F" radius="md" padding={2}>
            <icon name="wrench" color="#FFFFFF"/>
          </box>
          <title size="lg">Zig</title>
        </row>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">LOW-LEVEL NATIVE + TOOLS</text>
        Selected codecs, binary-processing utilities, asset transformations, native interoperability, and experimental optimized kernels.
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
        <row align="center" gap={2}>
          <box background="#8570CA" radius="md" padding={2}>
            <icon name="layers" color="#FFFFFF"/>
          </box>
          <title size="lg">Slang</title>
        </row>
        <text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">GPU EXECUTION</text>
        GPU ECS, compute scheduling, mesh/task shaders, animation, visibility, shading, GI, and GPU vector UI.
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
</box>

Slang is my preferred shader language because it supports modular shader development and SPIR-V compilation for Vulkan. Khronos's shader samples include Slang alongside GLSL and HLSL, although our specific mesh/task shader and GPU ECS capabilities must be validated against the chosen compiler and GPU drivers. <Cite refs={["turn243104search6","turn243104search10"]}/>

## 2. Ownership matrix

| Subsystem | Primary language | Supporting technology |
|---|---|---|
| Engine runtime and lifecycle | Rust | Platform libraries |
| Vulkan device and memory management | Rust | Slang shaders |
| GPU ECS storage and scheduling | Rust host + Slang | Vulkan compute |
| GPU structural mutations | Slang | Rust memory/resource management |
| Mesh/task renderer | Slang | Rust render graph |
| Virtualized geometry | Slang runtime | Rust/Zig offline tooling |
| SDF GI and radiance cache | Slang | Rust residency orchestration |
| GPU animation and visual physics | Slang | Rust component definitions |
| GPU vector UI / Bézier text | Slang | Rust platform/input bridge |
| Server simulation ECS | Rust | SIMD / optional GPU backend |
| Server networking | Rust | Quinn / QUIC |
| Replication, group replication, NetLOD | Rust | SoA encoding |
| Inventory and transactions | Rust or Go service ownership | Database |
| Account and social services | Go | Service APIs |
| Cluster administration | Go | Deployment infrastructure |
| Asset cooking / compression | Rust + selected Zig | Offline processing |
| Gameplay scripting | Undecided | Phase 18 |

One deliberate choice: **Zig should not become a compulsory layer between Rust and Vulkan**. We can use Rust's Vulkan ecosystem directly.

That keeps the GPU submission path short and avoids splitting GPU resource ownership across two host languages.

## 3. Keep the high-frequency execution paths within one language domain

I would enforce a rule:

**No cross-language FFI calls per entity, per component, per draw, or per GPU workgroup.**

That applies equally to Rust↔Zig, Rust↔Go, and host↔GPU interactions.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">EXECUTION AND COMMUNICATION BOUNDARIES</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Go Distributed Services**
    <caption>Accounts · Sessions · Social · Coordination</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Versioned service messages</text>
  </row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Authoritative Server**
    <caption>ECS · Simulation · Replication · Quinn</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">QUIC protocol + ECS deltas</text>
  </row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Client / Engine Host**
    <caption>Vulkan · Input · Networking · Streaming · Device resources</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Persistent GPU buffers + batched commands</text>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Slang GPU Runtime**
    <caption>ECS · Simulation · Animation · Rendering · UI · GI</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center" align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="arrow-left-right" color="secondary"/>
    <text size="xs" color="secondary">Zig utilities invoked through bulk interfaces or offline tools</text>
  </row>
</box>

### Rust ↔ Go

Use versioned service protocols rather than in-process FFI.

A Rust simulation worker should not cross into Go for every ability calculation, combat event, or position change.

Go is valuable for service orchestration and network-facing infrastructure, but we should avoid making the Go runtime part of our per-tick simulation critical path.

### Rust ↔ Zig

Use one of two approaches:

- **Build-time integration:** Zig executables process assets and generate binary outputs. No runtime ABI needed.
- **Native library integration:** Zig exports a small C-compatible ABI, with Rust passing bulk buffers and explicit lengths.

For example, processing 100,000 animation keys in one call may be reasonable; invoking Zig once per character per frame is unnecessary.

### Rust ↔ Slang

This is not conventional FFI. Rust submits Vulkan work; shaders operate on GPU resources.

The contract is binary buffer layout, shader resource binding, synchronization, and component schema compatibility.

The GPU should receive contiguous batches of updates and return compact result records, not participate in synchronous host function calls.

## 4. The most important shared technology: a schema compiler

We currently have many different representations of the same logical data:

- Rust authoritative ECS components.
- GPU SoA component columns.
- QUIC network messages.
- Persistent database records.
- Zig processing structures.
- Shader resource layouts.
- Scripting interfaces.

**I would not attempt to use one binary layout for all seven.**

Instead, define a canonical schema description and generate suitable representations for each domain.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Canonical Component / Message Schemas**
    <caption>Stable type IDs · Field IDs · Defaults · Version rules · Access policies</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{t:"Rust ECS types",d:"Simulation and component APIs"},{t:"Slang GPU layouts",d:"Aligned buffers and shader accessors"},{t:"Network codecs",d:"Quantization and delta encoding"},{t:"Persistence formats",d:"Durable versions and migrations"},{t:"Zig bindings",d:"Explicit native ABI structures"},{t:"Script bindings",d:"Capabilities and typed commands"}] as item}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={2} gap={1} minHeight="72px">
          <text weight="medium" size="sm">{item.t}</text>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{item.d}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
      {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

For instance, a canonical `Transform` component might generate:

| Representation | Data |
|---|---|
| Authoritative Rust | High-precision world position, rotation, version |
| GPU presentation | Camera-relative position, packed orientation, current/previous transforms |
| Network | Region-relative quantized position and packed rotation |
| Persistence | Stable world ID, full coordinate precision, schema version |
| Scripting | Readable position and validated movement commands |

The GPU layout prioritizes memory bandwidth. The network layout prioritizes bytes transmitted. Persistence prioritizes stability and recoverability.

These are different requirements.

### Schema rules I'd adopt

1. Stable numeric type and field identifiers.
2. Explicit compatibility and migration rules.
3. Distinct representations for each execution domain.
4. Generated serializers and GPU accessors.
5. GPU alignment and layout validation in automated tests.
6. No arbitrary runtime reflection in performance-critical loops.
7. Typed access permissions for scripts and network clients.

I'd build a small purpose-specific schema compiler rather than start with a huge general-purpose engine metadata framework.

## 5. Proposed engine module architecture

I'd use a Rust workspace with focused crates and explicit dependencies.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">CONCEPTUAL MODULE STRUCTURE</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Shared Engine Foundation**

  </box>

    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={2}>
        **Server Runtime**
        {#each ["CPU ECS","World Authority","Combat / Physics","Interest + NetLOD","Replication","Persistence Adapters"] as x}
          <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2}>
            <text size="xs">{x}</text>
          </box>
        {/each}
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={2}>
        **Client Runtime**
        {#each ["Platform + Vulkan","GPU ECS Host","World Streaming","Render Graph","GPU Presentation","UI + Input Bridge"] as x}
          <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2}>
            <text size="xs">{x}</text>
          </box>
        {/each}

  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

    <caption>Compute ECS · Spatial · Animation · Mesh/Task · Materials · GI · UI</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>

Some proposed crate boundaries:

| Crate | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `engine-schema` | Component descriptors, type identifiers, generated contracts |
| `engine-math` | Coordinate systems and shared numerical conventions |
| `engine-ecs` | CPU-side archetypes, chunks, queries, scheduling |
| `engine-world` | Spatial addressing, scenes, residency metadata |
| `engine-gpu` | Vulkan device/resource abstraction |
| `engine-gpu-ecs` | GPU component pools, mutation control, epoch publication |
| `engine-render` | Render graph, pipelines, views and work scheduling |
| `engine-assets` | Content identity, streaming, decoding and residency |
| `engine-net` | Quinn integration and application protocol |
| `engine-replication` | Delta encoding, interest, group replication and NetLOD |
| `engine-server` | Authoritative simulation runtime |
| `engine-client` | Client application assembly and lifecycle |

Names are provisional.

I would **avoid generating dozens of tiny crates before actual code exists**. Start with a few coherent crates and split them when dependency boundaries become stable.

### Critical dependency rule

The renderer should depend on GPU ECS interfaces and scene data contracts.

The GPU ECS should not depend on the renderer.

Likewise, world persistence should not depend on Quinn or a particular network transport.

This keeps major systems replaceable without rewriting the entire engine.

## 6. Slang as our unified GPU programming language

I recommend making Slang the primary source language for GPU workloads.

The toolchain would be:

`Slang source → Slang compiler → SPIR-V → Vulkan shader module/pipeline`

Vulkan consumes SPIR-V, and Slang supports compilation to SPIR-V. <Cite refs={["turn243104search9","turn243104search10"]}/>

We should create separate shader modules for:

| Slang module | Work |
|---|---|
| `gpu_ecs` | Component access, mutation queues, active-set selection |
| `gpu_memory` | Chunk pools and suballocators |
| `gpu_spatial` | Flat-grid updates, sorting and compaction |
| `gpu_animation` | Graph processing, poses and skinning |
| `gpu_geometry` | Mesh/task shaders and geometry decoding |
| `gpu_visibility` | Culling and visibility-buffer output |
| `gpu_materials` | Material resolve and shading |
| `gpu_lighting` | Direct lights and virtual shadows |
| `gpu_gi` | Sparse SDF tracing and shared radiance cache |
| `gpu_ui` | Layout, vector geometry and Bézier text |

These can share utility modules, mathematical conventions, and generated GPU component structures.

We still need an explicit validation milestone for Slang's output across our required Vulkan compute, task and mesh shader features. Support for the shader language does not guarantee that every desired extension works correctly on every driver.

## 7. Zig — where it adds value and where it doesn't

This deserves an important distinction.

We've chosen Zig as one of the engine languages, but we should not introduce Zig purely because it's low-level.

Rust already provides memory control, SIMD capabilities, explicit allocations, C interoperability and systems programming without garbage collection.

Zig becomes valuable where its compile-time facilities, explicit allocator conventions, cross-compilation workflow, or native binary processing offer a concrete benefit.

### My proposed Zig policy

| Use case | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Offline asset processing | Strong candidate |
| Specialized codecs | Strong candidate |
| Native binary tooling | Strong candidate |
| Platform-specific utilities | Evaluate individually |
| GPU memory management | Keep in Rust |
| Vulkan host and render graph | Keep in Rust |
| Main CPU ECS | Keep in Rust |
| Main network implementation | Keep in Rust |
| Gameplay scripting | Separate decision |
| Shader source language | Slang, not Zig |

There is one issue we must settle in Phase 18: **whether Zig is also intended to be our gameplay scripting language**.

You initially described using Rust, Go and Zig across server, engine, client and scripting.

If you want gameplay logic authored in Zig, we can investigate compiling Zig gameplay modules to a sandboxed target such as WebAssembly.

But Zig is a compiled systems programming language, not automatically a safe, hot-reloadable scripting runtime.

We would still need a module lifecycle, execution sandbox, ECS capability API, resource limits and state migration.

I would not let scripting call unrestricted native functions or mutate ECS memory without controls.

## 8. ABI and memory ownership contracts

We should define precise rules at language boundaries.

| Boundary | Contract |
|---|---|
| Rust ↔ Zig native | C ABI, explicit lengths and ownership |
| Rust ↔ Go services | Versioned network/service messages |
| Rust ↔ Slang | Generated GPU layouts and Vulkan resource contracts |
| Server ↔ Client | Schema-versioned QUIC application protocol |
| Engine ↔ Scripts | Capability-based typed interface |
| Engine ↔ Assets | Versioned packed binary asset formats |

For native Rust/Zig integration, I would require:

- No Rust-specific types crossing the ABI.
- No allocator ownership ambiguity.
- No untagged pointers with unspecified lifetime.
- Explicit error codes or tagged result structures.
- Fixed-width numeric types.
- Versioned public interfaces where independently updated modules require them.
- Bulk operations rather than fine-grained calls.

A particularly important rule for GPU resources: **Rust owns Vulkan device handles, allocation lifetimes, and synchronization.**

Zig utilities may generate data consumed by those resources, but they should not independently free or rebind allocations owned by Rust.

That avoids two different runtimes believing they own the same memory.

## 9. Build system and tooling

I recommend the following baseline.

| Area | Tooling direction |
|---|---|
| Rust workspace | Cargo |
| Rust formatting and linting | rustfmt + Clippy |
| Go services | Go modules |
| Zig tools | Zig build system |
| GPU shaders | Slang compiler |
| Vulkan validation | Vulkan SDK validation layers |
| SPIR-V validation | SPIRV-Tools |
| Shader interfaces | Generated schema bindings + reflection validation |
| Integration builds | CI orchestrating Cargo, Go, Zig and shader compilation |
| Automated tests | Unit, property, integration, GPU correctness and ABI tests |

For shader compilation, I would compile and validate production variants at build time, cache them by source/compiler/feature configuration, and support development hot reload.

The renderer should avoid unexpectedly compiling complex shaders during a latency-critical frame.

### No-C++ requirement

We should document precisely what **no C++** means:

**No C++ in our engine, server, client, scripting or custom tools source code.**

That is achievable with this design.

However, Vulkan drivers, operating systems, shader compilers, or third-party build tools may internally contain C or C++. Using a Slang compiler executable does not mean our game engine is written in C++.

If the requirement instead prohibits *any dependency implemented in C++*, we would need to reevaluate the shader/compiler toolchain and other external dependencies.

## 10. Final Phase 17 recommendations

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"Rust as the primary runtime language",d:"Engine host, client, authoritative ECS, networking, persistence integration."},
    {t:"Go for distributed services",d:"Long-lived service processes communicating through versioned protocols."},
    {t:"Zig for justified native/offline workloads",d:"No mandatory Zig layer inside the frame or simulation hot path."},
    {t:"Slang as preferred GPU language",d:"SPIR-V output with feature validation before final compiler commitment."},
    {t:"Canonical schema compiler",d:"Generate specialized ECS, GPU, network, persistence and scripting representations."},
    {t:"Explicit ABI and ownership boundaries",d:"Bulk interfaces, well-defined allocation ownership and no per-entity FFI."},
    {t:"Modular Rust workspace",d:"One engine foundation shared by distinct server/client runtimes."},
    {t:"Single Vulkan resource owner",d:"Rust GPU host manages resources, submission and synchronization."}
  ] as item}
    <row gap={2} align="start">
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{item.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{item.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. One decision before Phase 18

{@body const [script,setScript]=DIL.useState("zig-wasm")}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text weight="medium">Gameplay scripting direction</text>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">This determines how we implement abilities, quests, NPC behavior, encounters and hot-reloadable gameplay modules.</text>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={script} onChange={setScript}>
    <radio value="zig-wasm">
      **Zig-authored WebAssembly modules**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Keep Zig central to gameplay scripting, using a sandboxed runtime and generated ECS APIs.</text>
    </radio>
    <radio value="rust-wasm">
      **Rust-authored WebAssembly modules**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Simpler language reuse, while retaining sandboxing and module isolation.</text>
    </radio>
    <radio value="custom-vm">
      **Custom gameplay bytecode / scripting VM**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Maximum specialization and control, but substantially more compiler/runtime development.</text>
    </radio>
    <radio value="hybrid">
      **Hybrid: declarative gameplay + WASM modules**

      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Data-driven abilities and quests; compiled modules for exceptional logic.</text>
    </radio>
  </radio-group>
  <button block onClick={()=>GenUI.issueNewTurn("Proceed to Phase 18: scripting and gameplay architecture. Explore "+({ "zig-wasm":"Zig-authored WebAssembly modules with sandboxed ECS APIs", "rust-wasm":"Rust-authored WebAssembly modules with sandboxed ECS APIs", "custom-vm":"a custom gameplay bytecode/VM", "hybrid":"declarative gameplay plus WebAssembly modules"})[script]+". Evaluate runtime overhead, hot reloading, determinism, security, ECS integration, state migration, and MMO server scaling before locking the design.")}>Continue to scripting architecture <icon name="arrow-right" inline/></button>
</box>

My preference would be **a hybrid gameplay architecture with Zig-authored WASM modules as one supported extension mechanism**.

That preserves Zig's intended role while keeping high-frequency, homogeneous gameplay operations in native Rust ECS systems and declarative data—not thousands of separately invoked scripts.

It also gives us a sensible foundation for server-side modding, live gameplay updates, and safe scripting without compromising the performance goals we've established.

# ADR-017 — Simplified Technology Stack

<badge color="success">Decision Locked</badge>

Agreed. **We'll remove Zig from the engine architecture.** Rust already covers the low-level systems programming we need, and adding Zig would introduce another compiler, ABI boundary, toolchain and maintenance burden without a sufficiently compelling advantage.

For scripting, we'll adopt the **hybrid declarative + WebAssembly approach**, using Rust to author compiled gameplay modules.

This gives us a simpler architecture without abandoning performance, hot reloading or sandboxed gameplay logic.

## Updated technology stack

| Technology | Primary responsibility | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Rust** | Engine core, server simulation, client host, ECS, networking, asset tooling | Locked |
| **Go** | Distributed services, orchestration, accounts, social infrastructure | Locked |
| **Slang** | GPU ECS, compute, mesh/task shaders, rendering, animation and GI | Preferred; compiler validation pending |
| **Rust-authored WebAssembly** | Sandboxed gameplay extensions and complex scripted behaviours | Selected |
| **Declarative gameplay data** | Abilities, quests, status effects, encounters, configuration | Selected |

No C++ or Zig in our custom engine source.

Our previous architectural decisions—GPU-native ECS, flat 2.5D spatial indexing, mesh/task shaders, sparse SDF GI, Bézier UI and Quinn networking—remain unchanged.

## Phase 18 — Gameplay Scripting Architecture

I recommend three execution tiers rather than attempting to run every game rule through WebAssembly.

| Tier | Technology | Workloads |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Native systems** | Rust | Movement, combat calculations, spatial queries, inventory transactions, replication |
| **2. Declarative gameplay** | Schema-driven data + Rust evaluators | Ability definitions, buffs, cooldowns, quests, loot tables, NPC configurations |
| **3. Scripted extensions** | Rust → WASM | Boss encounters, quest events, unique NPC behaviour, complex world interactions |

This prevents thousands of individual script invocations from becoming a server CPU bottleneck.

### Execution architecture

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative Rust ECS**
    <caption>Entities · Components · Simulation clock · Change events</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Gameplay Event Scheduler**
    <caption>Tick events · Timers · Combat triggers · Quest events</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="git-branch" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Declarative Execution**
        <caption>Compiled abilities, rules and state machines</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **WASM Modules**
        <caption>Sandboxed exceptional gameplay logic</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Validated ECS Command Buffers**
    <caption>Damage · Spawn · Despawn · Quest state · Effects</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Authoritative Commit + Replication**
  </box>
</box>

For the WASM runtime, **Wasmtime is my initial candidate**. It supports embedding in Rust and typed interfaces through the WebAssembly Component Model and WIT-generated bindings. <Cite refs={["turn733461search0","turn733461search2"]}/>

Our scripts would receive restricted capabilities rather than direct mutable pointers into authoritative ECS memory.

### Hot reloading

I'd design for hot reload from the beginning:

1. Compile a new gameplay module or declarative definition.
2. Validate its schema, permissions and resource limits.
3. Instantiate the new version alongside the existing one.
4. Migrate persistent script state when required.
5. Activate the new version at a defined simulation boundary.
6. Retire the old version after outstanding work completes.

We also need version pinning so an encounter already in progress doesn't accidentally change behaviour halfway through a boss fight.

### Important performance rule

**No WASM call per entity per tick by default.**

Use native Rust for large homogeneous processing workloads and event-driven WASM for exceptional behaviour. Where scripts need to process many entities, expose batch-oriented APIs.

WASM is an isolation and extensibility mechanism, not an automatic performance improvement.

## Updated architecture decisions

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {name:"Remove Zig",desc:"Rust covers engine, native utilities, and asset tooling."},
    {name:"Keep Rust + Go",desc:"Rust for performance-critical runtimes; Go for distributed services."},
    {name:"Use Slang for GPU code",desc:"Subject to compiler and hardware validation."},
    {name:"Hybrid gameplay scripting",desc:"Declarative rules plus Rust-authored WASM extensions."},
    {name:"Wasmtime as initial runtime",desc:"Benchmark module calls, memory and execution budgets before finalizing."},
    {name:"Capability-controlled script APIs",desc:"No unrestricted mutation of ECS memory or authoritative state."},
    {name:"Versioned hot reloading",desc:"Safe module activation and gameplay-state migration."}
  ] as d}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{d.name}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{d.desc}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

One caveat worth recording: Rust-authored WASM is suitable for programmers, but less accessible for designers. Our declarative gameplay format and eventual visual tooling should handle common quest, ability, and encounter design without requiring Rust coding.

**Next architectural phase: asset processing and world authoring.** We need to specify how authored meshes, terrains, animations, collision geometry, textures and world scenes become our virtualized GPU-native formats. That should be settled before we perform the full architecture review.

|---|---|---|

| Native engine interoperability | Through defined WASM ABI | Through defined WASM ABI |

## Zig vs Rust for scripting

| Consideration | Zig → WASM | Rust → WASM |
|---|---|---|
| Compiled WebAssembly | Yes | Yes |
| Sandboxed execution | Yes, through runtime | Yes, through runtime |
| Native engine interoperability | Through defined WASM ABI | Through defined WASM ABI |
| Hot reload | Yes, with engine support | Yes, with engine support |
| ECS access | Generated bindings | Generated bindings |
| Runtime performance | Potentially comparable | Potentially comparable |
| Language ecosystem | Smaller | Larger |
| Toolchain maturity | More version-sensitive | Generally more established |
| Gameplay authoring ergonomics | Explicit, low-level | Strong typing, more language machinery |

Neither language automatically provides hot reloading, determinism or secure ECS access. Those are properties of the execution environment we build.

Zig's compiler supports WebAssembly targets, while Wasmtime supports running WebAssembly modules independently of their source language. <Cite refs={["turn0search0","turn0search1"]}/>

## My recommendation

**Bring Zig back, but exclusively for gameplay scripting.**

I'd use the following stack:

| Domain | Technology |
|---|---|
| Engine and client host | Rust |
| Authoritative server ECS | Rust |
| Networking | Quinn / QUIC |
| Distributed services | Go |
| GPU systems and rendering | Slang |
| Gameplay scripting | **Zig compiled to WASM** |
| Script execution | Wasmtime embedded in Rust |
| Standard abilities and quests | Declarative gameplay definitions |

For the initial implementation, I'd favor **Zig `wasm32-freestanding` modules with a narrow, versioned host ABI**. Zig explicitly supports this target. <Cite ref="turn871366search5"/>

We can define our gameplay interfaces using WIT where useful, but should validate Zig guest-side binding generation before committing to the WebAssembly Component Model. Wasmtime already supports WIT-driven Rust host bindings. <Cite ref="turn871366search0"/>

### Why I prefer this arrangement

Zig's lack of a garbage-collected runtime, explicit memory management and compile-time programming facilities make it attractive for technical gameplay scripting.

We would use Zig for authored logic, not for every high-frequency ECS operation. Standard combat calculations, spatial queries, replication and other bulk processing would remain native Rust.

Hot reload would work by replacing compiled WASM modules at safe simulation boundaries and migrating their explicitly serialized state.

**The crucial rule is that Zig scripts issue validated ECS commands rather than obtaining unrestricted pointers into server memory.**

That keeps the architecture fast, sandboxed and maintainable.

So I'd revise ADR-017 to:

**Rust + Go + Slang for the engine platform; Zig as the primary gameplay scripting language, compiled to WebAssembly.**

This retains your original preference for Zig without forcing it into subsystems where Rust already does the job.

# Phase 18 — Gameplay Scripting Architecture
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Rust vs Go · October 2026</text>

Given our WoW-like MMO and the architecture we've already agreed upon, I recommend **Rust for gameplay scripting, Go for distributed services, and Slang for GPU execution**.

We can remove Zig entirely.

The important decision is not simply Rust versus Go. It's **how we execute gameplay logic without adding unnecessary overhead to our authoritative ECS**.

## 1. Rust vs Go for gameplay scripting

| Capability | Rust → WASM | Go → WASM |
|---|---|---|
| Native integration with our Rust ECS | Excellent | Requires defined interfaces |
| Runtime overhead | Generally attractive | More variable, depending on runtime |
| Garbage collection | No GC required | Go/TinyGo runtime considerations |
| Sandboxed execution | Wasmtime | Wasmtime, with compatible compilation |
| Hot reloading | Yes, engine-managed | Yes, engine-managed |
| Deterministic execution | Possible with constraints | Possible with constraints |
| Compile-time type safety | Excellent | Strong |
| Developer simplicity | More complex | Generally simpler |
| Toolchain integration | Strong fit | Extra guest toolchain considerations |
| Shared engine types and schemas | Straightforward generation | Additional generated bindings |

Go isn't a bad scripting language. But because our authoritative ECS is already written in Rust, using Rust for gameplay modules reduces language fragmentation and lets us share tooling, schemas and domain models more easily.

We should still enforce isolation: a Rust script compiled to WASM doesn't automatically get unrestricted access to the native Rust ECS.

## 2. The scripting model I recommend

    **Validated ECS Command Buffers**
    <caption>Spawn · Apply effect · Damage · Modify quest · Trigger event</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Authoritative Commit + Replication**
  </box>
</box>

A standard fireball should not require invoking a separate WASM module for every player or target.

Instead, it might be defined declaratively:

```yaml
ability: fireball
cast_time_ms: 2000
resource_cost: 35
targeting: single_hostile
effects:
  - type: damage
    school: fire
    coefficient: 1.25
  - type: apply_status
    status: burning
    duration_ms: 6000
```

The actual validation, targeting and damage calculation would execute in native Rust ECS systems.

A complicated boss encounter with conditional phases, scripted behaviours and unusual mechanics would use a WASM extension.

## 3. Why Wasmtime?

<Entity category="software" value="Wasmtime" disambig="WebAssembly runtime by Bytecode Alliance"/> is a strong candidate because it embeds directly into our Rust server and provides WebAssembly isolation, resource controls and interruption mechanisms.

In particular, it supports fuel metering and epoch-based interruption. Fuel supports deterministic execution budgets, while epoch interruption is a lower-overhead, nondeterministic way to bound long-running execution. <Cite refs={["turn754778search0","turn754778search1"]}/>

I'd use one shared compiled module for a particular script version, with isolated or appropriately pooled execution state for its instances.

For example, 1,000 NPCs running the same behaviour should not require compiling that behaviour 1,000 times.

### Script performance rules

- No WASM invocation per entity per frame by default.
- Event-driven execution with batched ECS queries.
- No direct access to ECS memory pointers.
- No unrestricted filesystem or network access.
- Explicit memory and execution budgets.
- Versioned module interfaces.
- Hot reload at controlled simulation boundaries.

For very high-frequency AI decisions, native Rust batch systems are preferable.

## 4. Hot reload and live MMO updates

The scripting architecture should support updating gameplay without restarting every server.

The safe process is:

1. Compile the new Rust WASM module.
2. Validate its interface, permissions and limits.
3. Instantiate the new version alongside the previous version.
4. Migrate or reinitialize script-owned state.
5. Activate it at an authoritative simulation boundary.
6. Retire the previous module when no active execution depends on it.

We should also allow encounters to remain pinned to their original version until completion.

This avoids changing boss mechanics halfway through a fight because someone deployed a new script.

Wasmtime supports ahead-of-time component compilation and sharing compiled components across threads, which can help reduce repeated compilation overhead. <Cite ref="turn754778search4"/>

## 5. Revised language stack

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row justify="between" align="center">
    **ADR-018 — Engine Languages & Gameplay Scripting**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  <table>
    <table-row><table-cell>**Rust**</table-cell><table-cell>Engine, simulation, client, networking, scripting and asset tools</table-cell></table-row>
    <table-row><table-cell>**Go**</table-cell><table-cell>Accounts, services, orchestration and backend infrastructure</table-cell></table-row>
    <table-row><table-cell>**Slang**</table-cell><table-cell>GPU compute, ECS systems, mesh/task shaders, GI and UI</table-cell></table-row>
    <table-row><table-cell>**WebAssembly**</table-cell><table-cell>Sandboxed compiled gameplay extensions</table-cell></table-row>
    <table-row><table-cell>**Wasmtime**</table-cell><table-cell>WASM execution inside Rust server workers</table-cell></table-row>
  </table>
</box>

This leaves us with **three source languages rather than four**, and no custom scripting interpreter to maintain.

One further distinction: our GPU ECS will not execute WASM directly. Gameplay scripts run on the authoritative host and issue validated state changes, which the client receives and processes through its GPU ECS.

## 6. What comes next?

With the scripting decision settled, the next missing foundation is **Phase 19 — Asset Pipeline, Virtualized Content & World Authoring**.

That's where we define how models, terrain, textures, fonts, animations, collision meshes and SDF geometry become the GPU-native data formats our renderer requires.

I would make that our next discussion before the full architecture review.

However, you're raising a good architectural question: **Do we actually need WebAssembly at all?**

For our engine, the answer is **no, not necessarily**.

## 1. Why I originally suggested WebAssembly

WebAssembly can execute inside a native Rust server using a runtime such as Wasmtime.

For example:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Native Rust MMO Server**
    <caption>Authoritative ECS · Combat · AI · Networking</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Embedded Wasmtime Runtime**
    <caption>Executes sandboxed gameplay modules</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center" gap={1}>
    **Compiled Rust Gameplay Modules**
    <caption>Quest logic · Boss encounters · Scripted events</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The advantages are sandboxing, execution limits, controlled access to engine APIs, portable compiled modules and the possibility of hot-reloading gameplay logic.

But those advantages come with runtime integration, guest-host API, state-migration and maintenance costs.

And for **a custom MMO where we control all gameplay code**, those costs may not be justified initially.

## 2. Native Rust vs WebAssembly scripting

| Feature | Native Rust gameplay modules | Rust → WASM modules |
|---|---|---|
| Native PC client | Yes | Yes |
| Native server | Yes | Yes |
| Performance | Lowest overhead potential | Additional boundary/runtime overhead |
| Direct ECS integration | Excellent | Requires host APIs |
| Batch processing | Excellent | Possible |
| Sandbox isolation | No automatic isolation | Stronger isolation |
| Hot reload | Requires explicit design | Requires explicit design |
| Memory safety | Rust's normal guarantees | Rust plus WASM isolation |
| Runtime complexity | Lower | Higher |
| Modding/untrusted scripts | Less suitable | Better suited |
| Best use | Trusted, first-party gameplay | Isolated or untrusted extensions |

## 3. My revised recommendation for our MMO

Given your focus on performance and avoiding unnecessary technologies, **I would use native Rust for gameplay scripting initially, with declarative data for common gameplay rules.**

That produces a simpler architecture:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Native Rust MMO Server**
    <caption>ECS · Physics · Combat · AI · World Authority</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Native Gameplay Systems**
        <caption>Complex logic, boss mechanics, custom AI</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Declarative Gameplay Definitions**
        <caption>Abilities, quests, loot, buffs, configuration</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative ECS + Replication**
    <caption>Changes distributed through Quinn to native Rust clients</caption>
  </box>
</box>

For deployment and hot reloading, we have choices:

- **Statically linked Rust modules:** Fastest and simplest starting point, but gameplay code changes generally require rebuilding/redeploying the server.
- **Native dynamically loaded modules:** Potentially reload code without restarting, but require stable ABI boundaries, controlled memory ownership, safe unloading and state migration.
- **Declarative rules:** Can reload data definitions without replacing native executable code, provided we implement versioning and validation.

I would start with statically linked modules and declarative content. We can preserve a versioned module API for future dynamic loading without committing to its complexity today.

## 4. What happens to WebAssembly?

I'd move it from a required technology to an **optional future extension**.

It becomes useful if we later want community mods, third-party gameplay plugins, untrusted scripts, or a stronger isolation boundary for live-loaded code.

It is not required for native clients, GPU ECS, Rust gameplay logic, or our QUIC networking.

### Updated decision

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **ADR-018 — Native Gameplay Architecture**

  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <text weight="medium">Recommended revision</text>
    <badge color="success">Simplified</badge>
  </row>
  | Domain | Technology |
  |---|---|
  | Client | Native Rust + Vulkan |
  | Server simulation | Native Rust |
  | Gameplay logic | Native Rust |
  | Gameplay definitions | Declarative, schema-driven |
  | Distributed services | Go |
  | GPU systems | Slang |
  | WebAssembly | Optional, deferred |
  | Zig | Removed |
</box>

**This is what I'd choose for our engine.** We should not introduce a scripting virtual machine until we have a concrete requirement that justifies it.

One distinction worth remembering: Rust gameplay modules are compiled code, not interpreted scripts. We'd be using *scripting* to describe their role in authoring gameplay behaviour, not a separate language runtime.

The next decision I'd examine is whether we want **live gameplay hot reloading without server restarts**, because that determines whether native Rust modules alone will be sufficient or whether we need a more sophisticated module lifecycle.

## 186 — Assistant

Message ID: `e19a5246-512e-4556-8124-6764a8de313a` · 2026-10-09T04:27:05.996385+00:00

I agree with your preference. **We should design for minimal realm downtime and live gameplay updates, but avoid a complicated native hot-reloading system unless we actually need one.**

For our MMO, there's a better approach than trying to replace running Rust code inside a live server.

**Use hot-reloadable gameplay data for routine changes, and rolling server upgrades for actual code changes.**

This gives us most of the operational benefits of hot reload without introducing dynamic-library complexity into our authoritative ECS.

## 1. The four approaches

| Approach | Downtime | Complexity | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hot-reload declarative gameplay data | None intended | Low–medium | **Core feature** |
| Rolling updates across server workers | Potentially none | Medium | **Core architecture** |
| Native Rust dynamic-library hot swapping | Potentially none | High | Defer |
| WASM gameplay modules | Potentially none | Medium–high | Optional future extension |

Native dynamic libraries are particularly challenging because of ABI stability, shared allocations, executing code during unload, thread safety and state migration. Rust's dynamic-loading documentation explicitly warns about initialization and termination safety requirements. <Cite ref="turn424398search2"/>

We don't need that risk in our first engine implementation.

## 2. How live updates would work

### A. Gameplay data changes

Most routine MMO balancing work should require no native code changes.

Examples include spell damage coefficients, cooldowns, loot tables, NPC attributes, spawn schedules, quest requirements and configuration.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} align="center" radius="md">
    **Updated Gameplay Definition**
    <caption>Versioned declarative data</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} align="center" radius="md">
    **Validate + Compile Definitions**
    <caption>Schema checks · References · Gameplay constraints</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Publish at Simulation Tick Boundary**
    <caption>Atomic version switch; active operations use defined version policies</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} align="center" radius="md">
    **Replicate Relevant Changes**
    <caption>Clients receive compatible gameplay/content versions</caption>
  </box>
</box>

An active boss encounter could remain pinned to its original definition until completion. Newly started encounters use the updated version.

This is relatively straightforward compared with replacing arbitrary executable code.

### B. Actual Rust code changes

For engine logic, combat systems, ECS changes or networking fixes, we'd deploy a new server-worker version.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker V1**
        <caption>Currently authoritative</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker V2**
        <caption>Started and validated</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Versioned Authority Transfer**
    <caption>State snapshot · In-flight command sequence · Ownership epoch</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Worker V2 Becomes Authoritative**
    <caption>Old worker retires after successful handoff</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Rolling deployments are an established way to update services without taking everything offline; Kubernetes documents this for ordinary services. Our MMO still needs a custom *stateful simulation handoff*—container orchestration alone cannot guarantee uninterrupted gameplay. <Cite ref="turn424398search0"/>

Our earlier design for stable entity IDs, authority epochs, versioned schemas and distributed workers already supports this direction.

### An important Quinn consideration

QUIC connection migration is not automatically the same as moving a live connection between server processes.

I would keep player sessions at a stable gateway where practical, then transfer the authoritative simulation behind that gateway.

This allows the gateway to keep its Quinn connection while changing which Rust simulation worker receives the player's commands.

That simplifies rolling worker upgrades substantially.

## 3. What about a full realm restart?

Some changes may still require scheduled maintenance:

- Incompatible world-state or database migrations.
- Changes to foundational ECS schema semantics.
- Network protocol changes without backward compatibility.
- Major world repartitioning that cannot safely occur live.
- Updates to shared infrastructure that lack a safe handoff path.

We should aim to make these uncommon, but **promise zero downtime only for update classes we've explicitly designed and tested**.

A seamless world transition during a normal worker deployment is an engineering objective, not something guaranteed by choosing Rust or QUIC.

## 4. Proposed ADR-018A — Live Operations & Hot Reload

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Hybrid Live-Update Architecture**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  {#each [
    {t:"Native Rust gameplay systems",d:"Statically linked for speed, straightforward debugging and safe memory ownership."},
    {t:"Declarative gameplay hot reload",d:"Versioned definitions validated and published at safe tick boundaries."},
    {t:"Rolling simulation-worker upgrades",d:"Transfer authoritative state between server versions without realm-wide shutdown where compatible."},
    {t:"Stable Quinn gateways",d:"Keep client connections alive across simulation-worker changes."},
    {t:"Versioned schema compatibility",d:"Support controlled old/new server and client version overlap."},
    {t:"No native dynamic library hot swapping initially",d:"Avoid ABI, unload and state-migration hazards."},
    {t:"WASM deferred",d:"Revisit only for untrusted modules or more advanced hot-loaded executable gameplay."}
  ] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{item.t}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{item.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

This is the architecture I would choose.

It keeps our **Rust + Go + Slang** stack simple, preserves low-level ECS performance, and gives us a practical path toward live realm updates.

There is one additional benefit: designing simulation workers for graceful handoff also improves fault recovery, load balancing and server migration. We're building one useful mechanism rather than a special-purpose hot-reload framework.

**Next I'd move to Phase 19 — Asset Processing & World Authoring**, because we now have a sensible plan for how gameplay definitions and server code evolve while the realm is live.

## 189 — Assistant

Message ID: `167c25cf-c190-44df-b6dd-c79aa0ad7e1e` · 2026-10-09T04:30:50.824648+00:00

# Phase 19 — Asset Pipeline, Virtualized Content & World Authoring
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Pre-Implementation Architecture · October 2026</text>

We're now designing the system that turns raw game content into the highly optimized representations our engine expects.

This is a foundational subsystem. Our GPU-driven renderer, sparse SDF GI, GPU animation, world streaming, and contiguous ECS cannot reach their potential if assets are stored and loaded inefficiently.

**My recommendation: a content-addressed, incremental asset pipeline that builds immutable, GPU-native resource pages from editable source assets, with a separate versioned world-state layer for persistent changes.**

The key principle:

> **Perform expensive geometry processing, compression, validation, and packaging offline. The runtime should primarily stream, decode, upload, and reference preprocessed data.**

This matters particularly for a WoW-like MMO with enormous environments, repeatable dungeons, thousands of item appearances, and frequent world updates.

## 1. Separate authoring data from runtime data

We should never require the GPU renderer to consume Blender scenes, source FBX files, raw textures, or arbitrary authoring hierarchies directly.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Source Content / World Authoring**
    <caption>Models · Terrain · Materials · Animations · Fonts · Scenes · Gameplay definitions</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Asset Import & Validation**
    <caption>Normalize coordinates · Validate topology · Resolve references · Canonical intermediate data</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Offline Asset Cooking**
    <caption>Meshlets · LOD hierarchies · Virtual textures · Collision · Animation · SDF source data</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Content-Addressed Runtime Packages**
    <caption>Immutable compressed pages · Dependency manifests · Versioned asset IDs</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Streaming + GPU Residency**
    <caption>Request · Decode · Upload · Publish · Evict</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **GPU ECS + Mesh/Task Renderer**
    <caption>GPU-addressable geometry, textures, animation, spatial data and radiance resources</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The authoring format should prioritize editing and collaboration. The runtime format should prioritize predictable memory access and fast loading.

We should not compromise one to serve the other.

## 2. Asset formats and import strategy

I'd avoid inventing our own modelling format.

| Asset type | Authoring / interchange | Runtime representation |
|---|---|---|
| Static meshes | glTF 2.0 and optional USD import | Compressed meshlet clusters and hierarchical LOD |
| Characters | glTF / animation interchange | Skeleton tables, compressed clips, meshlet skinning data |
| Terrain | Heightfields and authored terrain layers | Tiled heightfields, geometry clusters, material pages |
| Textures | PNG, EXR, source texture formats | GPU-native compressed texture pages |
| Materials | Node/material definitions | Compiled Slang shader families + packed parameters |
| Collision | Cooked from authored geometry or explicit collision meshes | Heightfields, convexes, triangle pages |

## 6. SDF data for our locked dynamic GI

We've selected **sparse SDF software tracing with a shared GPU radiance cache**.

This has direct consequences for asset preparation.

The cooker should generate static tracing inputs for architecture, terrain and other suitable geometry.

Runtime GPU systems would then assemble or update local SDF bricks from those inputs and dynamic changes.

| Content | Proposed SDF processing |
|---|---|
| Terrain | Heightfield-derived distance/occupancy data |
| Static buildings | Precomputed local SDF source data |
| Caves | Precomputed volumetric SDF data |
| Doors | Dynamic SDF updates or simplified proxy representation |
| Large moving objects | Low-resolution transformable tracing proxies |
| Ordinary animated characters | Normally excluded from detailed world SDF |
| Destruction | Invalidate and rebuild affected local bricks |

We should separate **SDF geometry generation** from **radiance calculation**.

An unchanged wall geometry representation can remain valid even while sunlight direction, artificial lighting or emissive contributions change.

That allows us to update lighting without rebuilding geometry-derived SDF pages.

And the radiance cache must have its own resource versions and invalidation logic.

## 7. Animation and skeleton processing

The offline animation pipeline should produce GPU-friendly compressed streams.

I would split:

- Skeleton definition and hierarchy.
- Retargeting information.
- Animation clips.
- Animation graph definitions.
- Skinning metadata.
- Attachment points.
- Skeleton LOD variants.

This complements our approved shared-pose system.

The cooker can precompute compatible skeleton mappings, reduced-bone hierarchies and compressed animation segments.

At runtime, the GPU only needs to decompress, evaluate and blend relevant animation streams.

### Shared pose compatibility

Pose sharing requires more than two characters using the same animation name.

We should key compatibility by skeleton layout, clip identity, quantized phase, blend configuration and applicable procedural modifiers.

That's why the animation cooker should assign stable skeleton and clip identifiers and validate bone mapping.

## 8. Content-addressed resource storage

I strongly recommend **content-addressed assets**.

Instead of identifying an immutable resource solely by a filename such as:

`world/city/wall_01.mesh`

we generate a stable content digest for its cooked representation.

The engine uses two distinct identities:

| Identity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Logical Asset ID | Stable authoring/gameplay reference |
| Content Hash | Exact version of the cooked bytes |

A logical asset ID resolves to a specific version through a manifest.

### Why this matters for an MMO

It allows:

- Incremental content rebuilds.
- Deduplication of identical resources.
- Client caching.
- Content integrity verification.
- Versioned deployments.
- Rollback to earlier content releases.
- Distribution through CDN infrastructure.

When a wall model changes, its content hash changes. Assets that depend on it can be rebuilt according to a dependency graph, but unrelated content remains untouched.

I'd use a strong content hash and explicitly include relevant compiler/cooker versions, settings and target capabilities in build cache keys.

The output should also be deterministic where practical so that unchanged source inputs produce identical runtime artifacts.

## 9. Runtime packaging: pages, not giant monolithic archives

We should avoid treating every region as one enormous compressed file.

A large city may contain geometry, textures, collision, navigation, animation, GI inputs, and entity placement data with very different residency requirements.

I'd pack resources into independently addressable pages grouped by locality and access behaviour.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Proposed regional resource manifest</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
    **Region Manifest**
    <caption>Cell IDs · Versions · Dependencies · Residency priorities</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each ["Geometry pages","Texture pages","Collision pages","Navigation data","SDF source pages","Animation references"] as t}
      <grid-item>
        <box border radius="md" padding={2} justify="center" minHeight="45px">
          <text size="xs" textAlign="center">{t}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

**Asset page size should not automatically equal Vulkan sparse-memory page size or ECS chunk size.**

Those are three separate granularities serving three different purposes.

The asset page is an I/O and decompression unit. The physical residency page is a GPU allocation unit. The ECS chunk is a component-processing and mutation unit.

We should optimize each independently.

### Dependency-driven loading

A cell should declare dependencies such as:

- Required collision data.
- Coarse fallback geometry.
- Base material textures.
- Higher-detail geometry pages.
- Optional high-detail textures.
- Navigation data.
- SDF/GI pages.

The loader prioritizes required gameplay/collision data and minimum visual representations before optional detail.

This respects our earlier collision-first streaming decision.

## 11. Asset hot reload and realm uptime

Our previously agreed live-operations architecture applies to assets too.

For example, changing a building texture should not require a realm restart.

I'd use:

**Build new content version → validate → stage residency → publish updated manifest → retire old resources after GPU readers finish.**

Server-side world content changes may also require authority-side coordination.

Changing a decorative texture is relatively straightforward.

Changing terrain collision, dungeon geometry, or a destructible building's structure may require a controlled world-state transition, updated navigation/collision data, and safe handling of players occupying the modified area.

We should not automatically treat every asset hot reload as safe during live gameplay.

We also need to decide how we'll build and maintain the game world.

**I strongly agree. In fact, I'd revise Phase 19 to make established offline tooling our default, rather than developing custom asset-processing algorithms from scratch.**

Our goal is to build a cutting-edge MMO engine, **not to rebuild Blender, mesh optimizers, texture compressors, animation tools and geometry processors**.

The important distinction is:

> **Custom runtime architecture. Best-in-class existing offline tools. Custom asset formats and processing only where our engine has unique requirements.**

This should save substantial development effort without compromising our GPU-first design.

## 1. Recommended offline toolchain

Here is the stack I'd investigate first.

| Domain | Recommended tools | Our custom responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| 3D modelling and animation | <Entity category="software" value="Blender"/> | Import conventions, validation, runtime conversion |
| Complex scene interchange | <Entity category="software" value="OpenUSD"/> | World-cell packaging and runtime scene instantiation |
| Mesh optimization | <Entity category="software" value="meshoptimizer"/> | Hierarchical GPU geometry format and residency |
| Meshlet generation | meshoptimizer | Runtime cluster metadata and GPU decoding |
| Texture encoding | <Entity category="software" value="KTX-Software"/> / Basis Universal | Virtual texture page tables and residency |
| Texture formats | KTX2, BCn, ASTC where supported | Runtime format negotiation |
| Navigation mesh generation | <Entity category="software" value="Recast Navigation"/> | Streaming, server pathfinding integration |
| Shader compilation | <Entity category="software" value="Slang" disambig="GPU shader programming language and compiler"/> | Shader modules and pipeline management |
| SPIR-V validation | <Entity category="software" value="SPIRV-Tools"/> | Shader integration testing |
| Animation compression | <Entity category="software" value="Animation Compression Library" disambig="Skeletal animation compression library"/> | GPU animation decoding and shared pose scheduling |
| Font preparation | <Entity category="software" value="FontTools"/> | GPU Bézier curve packing and rendering |
| SDF generation | Evaluate existing voxel/SDF tools | Our sparse brick representation and updates |

Two particularly valuable examples:

**meshoptimizer** already provides meshlet construction, cluster partitioning, geometric simplification, boundary-preserving options, and functionality relevant to hierarchical LOD construction. We should use or benchmark those rather than begin by inventing a new mesh simplifier. <Cite ref="turn107255search0"/>

**KTX-Software** already provides texture conversion, Basis encoding, transcoding, and validation tools. We can build our virtual texture packaging around their outputs. <Cite ref="turn660857search2"/>

## 2. How our asset pipeline would work

  </box>
