    <caption>GPU ECS · Streaming · Mesh/task rendering · SDF GI · GPU animation</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The third stage is where we retain control over our unique engine architecture.

We shouldn't need to reinvent a mesh optimizer, but we *do* need to define how optimized clusters are addressed, compressed, streamed and decoded by our mesh shaders.

## 3. C++ tools are acceptable offline

I'd explicitly change our no-C++ policy to:

**No C++ required in our custom engine, client, authoritative server or gameplay code. External offline executables and tools may use C or C++.**

For example, meshoptimizer is implemented in C++, and Recast Navigation is also C++-based. Those are perfectly reasonable dependencies for offline content generation. <Cite refs={["turn107255search0","turn660857search0"]}/>

We have three integration approaches:

| Approach | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Invoke an external CLI executable | Preferred wherever practical |
| Use a mature library through FFI in a separate asset-builder process | Acceptable when no adequate CLI exists |
| Rewrite algorithms in Rust | Only for unique requirements, demonstrable bottlenecks, or unsuitable dependencies |

This keeps C++ out of our shipped application while letting us benefit from mature algorithms.

An additional benefit of separate asset-builder processes is isolation. If a third-party mesh processing tool crashes, it doesn't crash the game engine or live server.

## 4. What we should still build ourselves

There are several areas where our architecture genuinely differs from generic engines.

| Custom subsystem | Why we need ownership |
|---|---|
| GPU ECS component and memory formats | Closely tied to our contiguous GPU runtime |
| Hierarchical geometry residency format | Tailored to our mesh/task shaders and page allocation |
| GPU geometry decoders | Must match our shader-side cluster encoding |
| Flat 2.5D world cell packaging | Specific to our world partitioning model |
| Sparse SDF brick integration | Specific to our dynamic GI and radiance cache |
| Runtime resource page tables | Requires exact GPU memory and lifetime semantics |
| GPU-native Bézier text rendering | Core rendering decision |
| Content-addressed manifests | Required for updates, streaming and CDN distribution |

But even here, I would build on proven algorithms where possible. *Owning the runtime representation doesn't mean inventing every mathematical technique.*

## 5. One important refinement: don't build a full editor immediately

I'd also modify my earlier recommendation to develop a complete native Rust world editor.

**Initially, we should use Blender and other established authoring applications, with custom exporters, metadata schemas and asset-building scripts.**

Blender supports headless Python scripting, which makes it suitable for automated batch exports and asset preparation. <Cite ref="turn660857search8"/>

Only develop a dedicated MMO world editor when our requirements justify it—for example, editing persistent entity placement, streaming-cell boundaries, world-level simulation metadata or live realm state.

A full editor is an enormous project in its own right.

We can initially build smaller focused tools: a world-cell inspector, GPU residency viewer, terrain preview, and ECS debugging interface.

## 6. The one technical risk to watch

Our **Nanite-class virtualized geometry** requirement deserves special treatment.

meshoptimizer can provide many of the building blocks, including clustering and simplification. But that doesn't automatically give us a complete Nanite-equivalent hierarchy with crack-free continuous LOD, dependency-safe streaming, page residency and hybrid rasterization.

That runtime-specific integration remains one of our major custom engineering efforts.

Likewise, existing SDF generation tools won't automatically give us GPU-maintained dynamic bricks and a shared radiance cache.

We should explicitly distinguish **using established algorithms** from **having a production-ready implementation of our chosen architecture**.

Message ID: `7b3b51a6-e906-42dd-b4d8-ce5db57102d4` · 2026-10-09T04:49:38.442285+00:00

# Phase 20 — Persistence, Databases & World Consistency
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Server Architecture · October 2026</text>

We've now reached one of the most important parts of our MMO architecture: **how to maintain a persistent, evolving world without making database operations part of the real-time simulation bottleneck**.

My recommendation is a **hybrid persistence architecture**:

- **Rust ECS in memory** for authoritative, real-time simulation.
- **PostgreSQL** for transactional gameplay state.
- **Asynchronous journals and periodic snapshots** for persistent world simulation.
- **Object storage** for large world snapshots and immutable assets.
- **Versioned authority ownership** for worker recovery and migration.

I would not introduce a distributed database, Kafka cluster, or custom storage engine from the outset.

Our guiding principle:

> **The ECS is the live world. The database is its durable record. Neither should dictate the other's memory layout or execution schedule.**

## 1. Separate data by consistency requirements

Not all MMO data needs identical durability or update frequency.

| Data category | Examples | Persistence policy |
|---|---|---|
| **Transactional** | Currency, inventory, trades, auctions | Durable ACID transactions |
| **Durable progression** | Experience, quests, achievements | Versioned, reliably persisted |
| **Mutable world** | Buildings, destroyed structures, doors, resource nodes | Region snapshots + durable events where required |
| **Simulation state** | NPC positions, movement, transient combat state | Periodic checkpoints where necessary |
| **Ephemeral state** | Projectiles, particles, temporary visual effects | Usually not persisted |
| **Immutable content** | Geometry, textures, animations, authored world packages | Content-addressed object storage |

This distinction lets us optimize each workload separately.

For example, an ordinary NPC moving across a field should not generate dozens of database commits every second. But a completed player-to-player item trade must not be acknowledged as successful until its durable transaction has committed.

## 2. Proposed persistence architecture

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Authoritative ECS**
    <caption>Contiguous archetypes · Live world state · Simulation ticks</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Persistence Change Classification**
    <caption>Transactional · Journaled · Checkpointed · Ephemeral</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="git-branch" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} minHeight="108px">
        **Transactional Path**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary">Inventory, currency, trades, durable progression</text>
        <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2} align="center">
          <text size="xs" weight="medium">PostgreSQL</text>
        </box>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} minHeight="108px">
        **World Persistence Path**
        <text size="xs" color="secondary">Versioned change batches, journals, region checkpoints</text>
        <box background="surface-secondary" radius="sm" padding={2} align="center">
          <text size="xs" weight="medium">Journal + Snapshot Store</text>
        </box>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Recovery + Worker Migration**
    <caption>Restore checkpoint · Replay committed changes · Resume ownership</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The branches have different commit guarantees. We should not treat a buffered journal record as durable merely because it was enqueued.

## 3. Why PostgreSQL should be our initial database

I'd choose <Entity category="software" value="PostgreSQL" disambig="Relational database management system"/> for the transactional core.

It gives us mature transaction semantics, relational constraints, indexing, backup/recovery tooling, and a well-understood operational model.

PostgreSQL supports serializable transactions, although the application must handle serialization failures and retries. Its WAL durability settings also make the tradeoff between acknowledged durability and asynchronous commits explicit. <Cite refs={["turn461442search10","turn461442search3"]}/>

| Requirement | PostgreSQL suitability |
|---|---|
| Character accounts/profiles | Excellent |
| Inventory and item ownership | Excellent |
| Currency transfers | Excellent |
| Auction house | Excellent |
| Quest and achievement records | Good |
| Persistent world object metadata | Good |
| Per-tick NPC movement | Poor fit |
| Millions of frame-by-frame ECS component writes | Not recommended |

### What about distributed databases?

<Entity category="software" value="FoundationDB" disambig="Distributed transactional key-value database"/> is an interesting future candidate. It offers distributed ACID transactions with strict serializability, using optimistic concurrency and conflict retries. <Cite ref="turn461442search0"/>

However, a distributed transactional database introduces cluster operations, data modelling, consistency choices and failure handling that we don't need to adopt before we have demonstrated scale requirements.

I'd keep the persistence layer behind domain-level repository interfaces rather than hardwire SQL access throughout gameplay systems.

That permits future partitioning, sharding, or moving particular domains to another store without rewriting our ECS.

| Auction house | Excellent |
| Quest and achievement records | Good |
| Persistent world object metadata | Good |
| Per-tick NPC movement | Poor fit |
| Millions of frame-by-frame ECS component writes | Not recommended |

### What about distributed databases?

<Entity category="software" value="FoundationDB" disambig="Distributed transactional key-value database"/> is an interesting future candidate. It offers distributed ACID transactions with strict serializability, using optimistic concurrency and conflict retries. <Cite ref="turn461442search0"/>

However, a distributed transactional database introduces cluster operations, data modelling, consistency choices and failure handling that we don't need to adopt before we have demonstrated scale requirements.

I'd keep the persistence layer behind domain-level repository interfaces rather than hardwire SQL access throughout gameplay systems.

That permits future partitioning, sharding, or moving particular domains to another store without rewriting our ECS.

## 4. Inventory and currency must be transactionally correct

This deserves special treatment because item duplication and lost transactions can destroy an MMO economy.

Imagine Player A trading a rare sword to Player B for 1,000 gold.

We cannot safely implement this as two independent updates.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Atomic trade transaction</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Validate Transaction**
    <caption>Ownership · Balance · Restrictions · Idempotency key</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Single Database Transaction**
    <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
      <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="sm" align="center"><text size="xs">Transfer sword A → B</text></box></grid-item>
      <grid-item><box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="sm" align="center"><text size="xs">Transfer gold B → A</text></box></grid-item>
    </grid>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Commit + Durable Result**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Publish Updated ECS State**
    <caption>Then replicate the confirmed inventory and currency changes</caption>
  </box>
</box>

I'd establish these requirements:

- Every valuable item instance has a stable unique identity.
- Currency operations use atomic balance updates or a suitably designed ledger.
- Every transaction request has a unique, idempotent operation ID.
- Item ownership is enforced by database constraints and transaction logic.
- Database failures cannot result in a successful trade acknowledgement.
- The server must resolve ambiguous commit outcomes by checking the transaction ID before retrying effects.

For reliable publication of committed changes, we can use a **transactional outbox**: write the authoritative mutation and outgoing event in the same database transaction, then asynchronously deliver the event to the simulation and replication systems.

This avoids a dangerous case where a database transaction succeeds but the process crashes before notifying the rest of the world.

## 5. Mutable world state: snapshots plus journals

Our large terrain-based world has potentially millions of persistent objects.

Reconstructing the entire world from its original authored content on every server restart would be inefficient.

Instead, I recommend region-local state persistence.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Immutable Authored World**
    <caption>Geometry · Terrain · Default object placement</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="plus" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Latest Committed Region Snapshot**
    <caption>Persistent modified entity/components</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="plus" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Ordered Change Journal**
    <caption>Changes committed after the snapshot's sequence number</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Restored Authoritative ECS Region**
  </box>
</box>

A snapshot might record player-built houses, destroyed structures, persistent resource nodes, door states, and relevant NPC/encounter state.

The journal records subsequent durable changes.

### Important: snapshots must be consistent

We cannot simply copy ECS chunks while simulation threads modify them arbitrarily.

A snapshot must correspond to a defined simulation epoch, using either:

- A controlled snapshot barrier.
- Copy-on-write/versioned component data.
- A stable published snapshot assembled asynchronously.

The snapshot also records the journal sequence it includes.

On recovery, replay begins *after* that sequence, preventing already-snapshotted changes from being applied twice.

For ordinary transient movement, I'd allow a configured recovery point rather than journal every position update.

## 6. Separate durability levels

I recommend three explicit durability classes.

| Class | Examples | Acknowledgement policy |
|---|---|---|
| **Strict durable** | Trades, currency, purchases, important item ownership | Confirm durable commit before success |
| **Recoverable journaled** | Persistent building placement, major world changes, important progression | Commit to required durable journal before treating change as final |
| **Checkpointed** | Ordinary NPC locations, ambient world simulation | Accept a defined recovery window |

This should be declared in component or command schemas, not left to individual systems to improvise.

We should measure persistence queue depth and commit latency. If durable storage becomes unavailable, a worker must not keep acknowledging strict-durable operations indefinitely.

PostgreSQL's asynchronous-commit documentation specifically warns that recently acknowledged writes may be lost after a crash when synchronous durability is relaxed. <Cite ref="turn461442search3"/>

For valuable gameplay transactions, that is not an acceptable default.

## 7. Worker migration and realm uptime

This connects directly to our previously approved rolling-upgrade strategy.

A worker handoff must transfer more than ECS component data.

It needs:

- A stable partition identity and a new ownership epoch.
- A consistent simulation snapshot.
- Accepted and outstanding command sequence boundaries.
- Persistence journal position.
- Timers and scheduled gameplay events.
- Relevant authoritative script/definition versions.
- A clear single-writer cutover point.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker V1**
        <caption>Owns partition epoch 41</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker V2**
        <caption>Restores staged state</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Authoritative Cutover / Epoch 42**
    <caption>Fence old writes · Transfer input stream · Publish new owner</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Gateway Routes Commands to Worker V2**
  </box>
</box>

Our Quinn gateway remains connected to the player while the simulation partition changes ownership.

**The ownership epoch must be enforced by the systems that accept authoritative writes**, not merely stored in a routing directory. Otherwise, an old worker could continue committing stale actions.

Also, durable persistence is not the same as instant failover. After an unplanned crash, only committed or safely replicated state can be guaranteed recoverable.

## 8. Database scaling: avoid premature complexity

I would start with a small number of clearly owned persistence domains rather than one database per zone or one enormous shared table for everything.

| Domain | Initial storage direction |
|---|---|
| Accounts and identities | PostgreSQL |
| Characters and progression | PostgreSQL |
| Inventory and economy | PostgreSQL, transactionally isolated |
| Persistent world metadata | PostgreSQL initially |
| Large region snapshots | Object storage |
| Mutable world journals | Durable ordered journal mechanism, PostgreSQL-backed initially where suitable |
| Immutable assets | Content-addressed object storage/CDN |
| Live simulation ECS | Rust memory, not a database |

I would not add Redis or RocksDB automatically.

An embedded key-value database such as RocksDB can be useful for local caches or checkpoint staging, but its WAL and synchronization settings have explicit crash-durability tradeoffs, and it does not by itself solve distributed authority or cross-worker transactions. <Cite ref="turn461442search9"/>

We can introduce specialised storage when measurements justify it.

## 9. Versioned persistence schemas

This is one of the most important cross-system architectural contracts.

A persisted character created using server version 1 must remain loadable after the engine has evolved.

We should define:

**Logical component schema → persistence encoding → migration functions → current runtime ECS representation.**

Never persist raw in-memory archetype chunks and assume they'll remain compatible forever.

Those chunks are optimized for CPU cache locality and can change whenever we tune the ECS.

A durable world snapshot instead uses stable type identifiers, schema versions, field encodings and migration rules.

For rolling updates, the persistence format should support carefully controlled overlap between old and new worker versions.

This does not require every schema change to be backward-compatible indefinitely, but it does require explicit migration plans before deployment.

## 10. Architecture choices to record

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <row justify="between" align="center">
    **ADR-020 — Persistence & World Consistency**
    <badge>Proposed baseline</badge>
  </row>
  {#each [
    {t:"PostgreSQL transactional core",d:"Inventory, currency, progression and other durable domain state."},
    {t:"In-memory authoritative Rust ECS",d:"No database queries or writes in ordinary per-entity simulation loops."},
    {t:"Versioned region snapshots",d:"Restore mutable world state independently of immutable world content."},
    {t:"Durable change journals",d:"Replay committed changes following a snapshot's sequence boundary."},
    {t:"Explicit durability classes",d:"Strict, journaled and checkpointed changes have distinct guarantees."},
    {t:"Idempotent economy transactions",d:"Stable operation IDs, atomic ownership changes and durable outcomes."},
    {t:"Transactional outbox",d:"Reliable propagation of committed state changes."},
    {t:"Authority fencing and epochs",d:"Prevent stale workers from mutating transferred partitions."},
    {t:"Versioned persistence schemas",d:"Independent of physical ECS and GPU memory layouts."},
    {t:"Specialized databases deferred",d:"Add distributed KV stores or log infrastructure only for demonstrated needs."}
  ] as x}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{x.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{x.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. What this means for our engine

This approach preserves our existing performance decisions.

The CPU ECS remains contiguous and optimized for simulation. The client GPU ECS remains optimized for presentation. Neither needs to understand SQL, database transaction isolation, or object-storage protocols.

A separate persistence pipeline translates authoritative component events into durable representations.

For a WoW-like MMO, I'd consider **inventory correctness, progression recovery, and seamless worker handoff** more important initial requirements than exotic distributed databases.

We can scale database infrastructure incrementally without changing the core simulation architecture.

---

## Next — Phase 21: Navigation, Pathfinding & AI

This is the next substantial architectural gap.

Our flat 2.5D grid gives us extremely fast proximity queries, but it does not understand walkable routes, bridges, staircases, caves, doors, flying paths or obstacle avoidance.

The next discussion should cover:

- Hierarchical navigation meshes and region connectivity.
- Multilevel navigation through cities and caves.
- Flight and underwater navigation.
- GPU vs CPU pathfinding.
- Batched NPC navigation and behaviour scheduling.
- Dynamic navigation changes from doors, construction and destruction.
- Streaming navigation data alongside collision geometry.

**My recommendation is to reuse established offline navigation-building tools, then implement a data-oriented Rust navigation runtime with optional GPU acceleration for suitable batched queries.**

That keeps us aligned with our broader goal: reuse mature tooling, customize the performance-critical runtime, and avoid building complexity before we have a demonstrated need.

---

## 204 — Assistant

Message ID: `b71e570a-dd51-4305-9fde-87fce407b1c2` · 2026-10-09T04:56:57.660334+00:00

# Phase 21 — Navigation, Pathfinding & GPU-Assisted AI
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Specification · October 2026</text>

Our world is primarily terrain-based, with cities, interiors, caves, flying mounts, and non-blocking players and monsters.

This makes navigation considerably more interesting than simply implementing A* over a grid.

**My recommendation is a hierarchical, streamable navigation system with tiled navigation meshes, region-level routing, specialised flight navigation, and GPU-accelerated batch processing where it provides measurable benefits.**

We should continue using established offline tools rather than implementing navigation-mesh generation ourselves.

The central distinction:

> **Our flat 2.5D spatial grid tells us where things are. The navigation system tells us where they can travel and how to reach a destination.**

Both use the same world coordinates, but they serve different purposes.

## 1. Proposed navigation architecture

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative Rust ECS**
    <caption>NPC goals · Positions · Movement abilities · Navigation requests</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Hierarchical Navigation Graph**
    <caption>Regions · Connectivity · Portals · Transport links</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Tiled Navigation Meshes**
    <caption>Walkable terrain · City levels · Caves · Interiors</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Path Corridor Generation**
    <caption>Connected polygons · Waypoints · Movement constraints</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Movement Controllers**
    <caption>Ground locomotion · Flight · Swimming · Climbing · Special traversal</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Server ECS Movement + Client GPU Presentation**
    <caption>Authoritative transforms replicated through Quinn; client handles visual smoothing</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Navigation decisions remain authoritative for NPCs and gameplay movement. The client GPU may calculate visual smoothing or locally predicted paths, but doesn't get authority to decide whether a route is legally traversable.

## 2. Offline navigation generation: use Recast

<row align="start" gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="Recast Navigation navmesh tiled navigation mesh debug visualization polygons" aspectRatio="4:3" maxWidth="156px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Entity category="software" value="Recast Navigation" disambig="Open-source navigation mesh generation toolkit"/>**

    My recommended navigation-mesh cooker.

    Recast rasterizes source geometry, identifies walkable regions, and generates navigation polygons. It supports tiled navigation meshes, which are particularly useful for large worlds, streaming and local rebaking. <Cite ref="turn299487search2"/>
  </box>
</row>

Since we've agreed to permit C++ in offline tools, we can use Recast as an isolated offline executable or asset-build dependency without bringing C++ into our shipped server.

For runtime navigation, I'd initially build a Rust-native representation that consumes cooked polygons and connectivity data. We can benchmark existing Detour-style algorithms against our custom Rust runtime before deciding how much needs to be rewritten.

### Build profiles for different movement capabilities

Not every entity can traverse the same spaces.

| Agent type | Navigation requirements |
|---|---|
| Ordinary humanoid | Terrain, stairs, doors, shallow water |
| Large monster | Wider paths, larger clearances |
| Small creature | Narrow passages and smaller clearances |
| Flying creature | 3D movement with obstacle avoidance |
| Swimming creature | Water volumes and depth constraints |
| Vehicle / mount | Turning limits and traversal restrictions |

I would not bake a completely separate world navmesh for every creature type.

Instead, use a small number of clearance profiles plus runtime traversal filters for doors, hazards, factions, swimming abilities and special movement.

## 3. Hierarchical pathfinding — avoid world-scale A*

For a large MMO, a pathfinding query should not have to inspect thousands of local polygons simply to travel between two distant towns.

We should use two planning levels.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Hierarchical routing</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Long-distance route**
    <caption>Region A → Region B → Region C → Region D</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Local path corridor**
    <caption>Navmesh polygons and connection portals within active regions</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Local movement**
    <caption>Steering toward the next reachable corridor segment</caption>
  </box>
</box>

A distant navigation request first searches a much smaller region-connectivity graph.

Only the nearby or soon-to-be-needed sections of the route require detailed navmesh processing.

This also integrates with world streaming: a worker can plan a coarse route using metadata even when distant navmesh tiles are not fully resident.

### Algorithm candidates

| Navigation workload | Proposed approach |
|---|---|
| Local point-to-point | A* on navmesh polygons |
| Long-distance navigation | Hierarchical A* / abstract region graph |
| Shared destinations | Reusable reverse search / route cache |
| Large groups moving toward one objective | Flow fields where beneficial |
| Frequent small route changes | Incremental replanning and corridor repair |
| Flight | Coarse 3D volumes + specialised obstacle search |

These are complementary tools, not one universal algorithm.

I would use explicit traversal links for stairs, ladders, elevators, doors, jump points, cave entrances and transport connections.

Each link can declare eligibility, cost, capacity where relevant, and current traversability.

A closed door may make a route unavailable without requiring the entire surrounding navigation mesh to be rebuilt.

For elevators and other moving traversal mechanisms, the navigation service would coordinate boarding, movement and departure through gameplay-controlled transitions rather than treat the elevator as static ground.

## 5. Dynamic obstacles and world destruction

This is one of the areas that could affect our persistence and world-streaming architecture.

We have already decided that buildings, doors, terrain changes and constructed objects may modify the persistent world.

Those modifications need to influence navigation.

I would divide changes into three categories.

| Change type | Navigation response |
|---|---|
| Door opens/closes | Change traversal link state |
| Temporary hazard or obstruction | Overlay dynamic cost/blocking information |
| Building or terrain permanently changes | Rebuild affected navigation tiles asynchronously |

Not every dynamic object should cause a navmesh rebuild.

A large moving crate might be handled through local collision/avoidance. A newly constructed wall blocking a street may genuinely require new navigation polygons.

Recast/Detour's TileCache is a useful reference for localized rebuilding of affected tiles. <Cite ref="turn299487search2"/>

### Consistency with collision

**Navigation and collision must never disagree in a way that permits illegal movement.**

After a building is constructed, authoritative collision can become active before navigation tiles are rebuilt. During the transition, NPCs must validate movement against current collision and replan around blocked paths.

We should publish navigation versions independently from render geometry and GI SDF versions.

This gives us a controlled lifecycle:

`World change → authoritative collision update → navigation invalidation → rebuilt tiles → publication`

The visual SDF/radiance cache can update on its own budget without holding up authoritative movement.

## 6. Crowd navigation — simplified by non-blocking characters

Our earlier **ADR-011** eliminates ordinary player-player and monster-monster physical blocking.

That changes how much crowd avoidance we actually need.

Traditional crowd systems spend effort preventing agents from occupying the same physical space. Recast's DetourCrowd, for example, includes local neighbour avoidance and collision-oriented steering. <Cite ref="turn299487search1"/>

For our MMO, I would make character-character separation **optional visual behaviour**, not a gameplay physics requirement.

This gives us three navigation behaviours:

| Character class | Navigation policy |
|---|---|
| Player characters | No compulsory separation from other characters |
| Standard monsters/NPCs | World obstacle avoidance; optional soft separation |
| Cinematic crowds, patrols and formations | Flow/formation steering where useful |

A group of NPC guards could spread out naturally while walking, but a crowded banker or raid entrance must not become impassable because of their presence.

### Flow fields for large groups

When hundreds of NPCs share a destination, independent A* queries may repeat considerable work.

We could generate a shared flow field containing preferred movement directions toward that destination.

Message ID: `56536bbf-73a3-4e19-9a78-34dfbd067a41` · 2026-10-09T04:57:40.863317+00:00

## 7. GPU vs CPU pathfinding

Given our GPU-first philosophy, should we execute navigation on the GPU?

**For some workloads, absolutely. But I would not make GPU navigation mandatory for authoritative server pathfinding.**

Path searches can be irregular: different routes expand different numbers of nodes, with unpredictable control flow and memory accesses.

Those characteristics can be poorly matched to GPU execution, especially for individual low-latency requests.

| Navigation operation | Preferred execution |
|---|---|
| Offline navmesh generation | Established offline tools |
| Authoritative local path search | Rust CPU |
| Hierarchical long-range routing | Rust CPU |
| Batched independent path requests | GPU candidate, benchmark required |
| Dense flow-field generation | GPU candidate |
| NPC local steering | CPU SIMD or GPU batches |
| Client cosmetic crowd movement | GPU |
| Flight obstacle queries | CPU authoritative; GPU presentation support |
| Navigation visualization | GPU |

I would keep pathfinding behind a processor-independent interface.

That allows us to add a GPU pathfinding backend later without replacing navigation data formats.

### Avoid CPU/GPU ping-pong

The wrong architecture would be:

`CPU AI decision → GPU single-agent path search → CPU waits → movement decision`

Repeated across thousands of NPCs, this could perform worse than simply running batched CPU searches.

A better GPU workload would contain hundreds or thousands of independent requests, produce results asynchronously and consume those results in a later simulation phase.

For server authority, result availability must still respect tick correctness. If a result misses its deadline, the worker needs a defined continuation/retry policy.

## 8. AI architecture: separate decisions from navigation

Navigation is only one part of NPC AI.

We also need the system that decides *what an NPC wants to do*.

I'd use a data-oriented, event-driven AI architecture with three layers.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **High-Level AI**
    <caption>Goals · Threat · Combat decisions · Patrol schedules · Quests</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Planning / Navigation**
    <caption>Destination selection · Path queries · Traversal constraints</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Movement Execution**
    <caption>Character controller · World collision · Animation parameters</caption>
  </box>
</box>

For high-level AI, I'd favor **compiled behaviour/state graphs plus native Rust systems**.

Typical NPC behaviour can be declarative:

- Idle and patrol.
- Detect threat.
- Chase a target.
- Enter combat.
- Select an ability.
- Retreat or evade.
- Return to patrol.

A custom boss with unusual mechanics can use more specialized native Rust logic.

This avoids interpreting a complex behaviour tree for every NPC every frame.

### AI updates should be event-driven and scheduled

A stationary vendor should not evaluate an elaborate AI tree at the same rate as an actively fighting boss.

We should schedule AI updates according to relevance, recent events, timers and gameplay requirements.

| NPC state | Update model |
|---|---|
| In combat | High-frequency, bounded decision updates |
| Chasing a target | Movement-frequency updates; decisions less frequent |
| Patrolling | Scheduled or waypoint-triggered |
| Stationary vendor | Mostly event-driven |
| Distant ambient NPC | Coarse deterministic schedule or persisted state |
| Unloaded region | Defined world-simulation policy, not full active AI |

This ties into our server ECS active sets without requiring one AI update per entity per tick.

### AI memory layout

We should maintain contiguous streams for AI-related state, such as:

`BehaviourState[]`, `Goal[]`, `Target[]`, `ThreatReference[]`, `PathReference[]`, `NextDecisionTick[]`, and `AIEventQueue[]`.

Large, variable-length structures such as paths, threat lists and blackboards should use bounded arenas or explicit handles rather than placing enormous structures directly inside every entity row.

# Phase 21 — Navigation, Pathfinding & GPU-Assisted AI
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Architecture Specification · October 2026</text>

Our world is primarily terrain-based, with cities, interiors, caves, flying mounts, and non-blocking players and monsters.

This makes navigation considerably more interesting than simply implementing A* over a grid.

**My recommendation is a hierarchical, streamable navigation system with tiled navigation meshes, region-level routing, specialised flight navigation, and GPU-accelerated batch processing where it provides measurable benefits.**

We should continue using established offline tools rather than implementing navigation-mesh generation ourselves.

The central distinction:

> **Our flat 2.5D spatial grid tells us where things are. The navigation system tells us where they can travel and how to reach a destination.**

Both use the same world coordinates, but they serve different purposes.

Persistent changes—such as a constructed wall or destroyed bridge—belong to authoritative world state. They trigger navigation overlays or replacement cooked tiles.

This means a restarted simulation worker can reconstruct the correct navigable world from its authored navigation resources plus committed mutable-world changes.

For independently simulated regions, we also need boundary connectivity data available before requesting a route across worker ownership boundaries.

## 10. Architecture decisions

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **ADR-021 — Navigation & AI**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>

    {t:"Hierarchical region routing",d:"Route across the world without full fine-grained navmesh searches."},
    {t:"Layered multi-floor connectivity",d:"Explicit links for doors, stairs, caves, elevators and special traversal."},

        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{a.d}</text>

  {/each}
</box>

## 11. Does this affect earlier decisions?

Only a few refinements:

| Existing subsystem | Refinement |
|---|---|
| Flat 2.5D grid | Remains the primary spatial address and proximity-query structure |
| Collision | Navmesh is not a collision authority; movement still validates against collision |
| GPU ECS | Client navigation visuals and crowd behaviour may use GPU processing |
| Rust server ECS | Adds batched navigation/AI components and scheduling |
| World streaming | Navigation becomes a separate residency domain |
| Persistence | Dynamic navigation changes are driven from authoritative world state |
| Group replication | Server replicates NPC movement/results, not complete AI internals |
| SDF GI | No coupling required between navigation mesh and lighting SDF |

No changes are needed to mesh/task shaders, virtualized geometry, visibility-buffer shading or our radiance-cache GI architecture.

---

## 12. What's next before the full review?

We now have most of the core server-side and world-simulation architecture covered.

The remaining major phases are:

| Phase | Focus |
|---|---|
| **22** | Native client platform, Vulkan device tiers, windowing, input, audio and accessibility |
| **23** | Security, anti-cheat, tooling, observability, deployment and testing |
| **24** | Full architecture review, contradictions, risks and implementation sequencing |

**I'd move next to Phase 22 — Native Client Platform & Hardware Strategy.**

This is particularly important because we've mandated mesh/task shaders, GPU-native ECS, sparse SDF GI and GPU Bézier UI. We need to define our hardware capability baseline and fallback policy before implementation, or we risk building an engine that only works reliably on a narrow set of GPUs.

We should also settle Windows/Linux support, the Vulkan feature contract, HDR/VRR, input latency, audio and device-loss recovery.

## 211 — Assistant

# Architecture Revision — Static World Geometry
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Proposed ADR-022 · October 2026</text>

**I think this is an excellent simplification for our WoW-like MMO.** It could eliminate substantial engineering complexity without compromising our GPU-first rendering architecture.

If we adopt a **static authored world with dynamic characters, NPCs, combat, weather, lighting, and visual effects**, we can keep most of the visual sophistication we've planned while removing some of the hardest world-management problems.

The central architectural principle becomes:

> **The environment's physical geometry is immutable at runtime. The entities, gameplay state, lighting, animation, and effects within it remain dynamic.**

That doesn't mean the world must look static. We can still have day/night cycles, moving characters, animated foliage, weather, spell effects, elevators or decorative animations if desired. But these won't permanently modify the world's collision or navigation geometry.

## 1. What we can remove or significantly simplify

| System | Previous design | Static-world design | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terrain | Mutable heightfields, regional rebuilds | Immutable cooked heightfields | Major simplification |
| Buildings | Construction and destruction | Immutable authored structures | Major simplification |
| Navigation | Dynamic tile rebuilding | Offline baked navigation | Major simplification |
| World collision | Runtime collision topology changes | Immutable static collision | Major simplification |
| SDF GI | GPU rebuilds for destructible geometry | Precomputed static SDF bricks | Major simplification |
| Persistence | Mutable world geometry journals | Persistent gameplay state only | Major simplification |
| Asset streaming | Dynamic versions of changed structures | Immutable content-addressed pages | Simpler |
| Replication | World construction/destruction changes | Character and gameplay state changes | Less bandwidth |
| Server authority | Terrain/building mutation coordination | No geometry mutation authority | Simpler |
| GPU ECS | Dynamic world geometry mutation | Dynamic gameplay/visual entities only | Somewhat simpler |

**This removes entire classes of dependencies between physics, navigation, GI, streaming, persistence, and networking.**

For example, destroying a building previously meant coordinating new collision geometry, navigation routes, SDF updates, visual geometry, replication, and persistence.

Under the static-world model, that cross-system update problem disappears.

## 212 — Assistant

Message ID: `ed659980-faa3-4d0a-9bc3-ae2a939304a4` · 2026-10-09T05:05:15.909782+00:00

# Architecture Revision — Static World Geometry
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Proposed ADR-022 · October 2026</text>

**I think this is an excellent simplification for our WoW-like MMO.** It could eliminate substantial engineering complexity without compromising our GPU-first rendering architecture.

If we adopt a **static authored world with dynamic characters, NPCs, combat, weather, lighting, and visual effects**, we can keep most of the visual sophistication we've planned while removing some of the hardest world-management problems.

The central architectural principle becomes:

> **The environment's physical geometry is immutable at runtime. The entities, gameplay state, lighting, animation, and effects within it remain dynamic.**

That doesn't mean the world must look static. We can still have day/night cycles, moving characters, animated foliage, weather, spell effects, elevators or decorative animations if desired. But these won't permanently modify the world's collision or navigation geometry.

## 1. What we can remove or significantly simplify

| System | Previous design | Static-world design | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terrain | Mutable heightfields, regional rebuilds | Immutable cooked heightfields | Major simplification |
| Buildings | Construction and destruction | Immutable authored structures | Major simplification |
| Navigation | Dynamic tile rebuilding | Offline baked navigation | Major simplification |
| World collision | Runtime collision topology changes | Immutable static collision | Major simplification |
| SDF GI | GPU rebuilds for destructible geometry | Precomputed static SDF bricks | Major simplification |
| Persistence | Mutable world geometry journals | Persistent gameplay state only | Major simplification |
| Asset streaming | Dynamic versions of changed structures | Immutable content-addressed pages | Simpler |
| Replication | World construction/destruction changes | Character and gameplay state changes | Less bandwidth |
| Server authority | Terrain/building mutation coordination | No geometry mutation authority | Simpler |
| GPU ECS | Dynamic world geometry mutation | Dynamic gameplay/visual entities only | Somewhat simpler |

**This removes entire classes of dependencies between physics, navigation, GI, streaming, persistence, and networking.**

For example, destroying a building previously meant coordinating new collision geometry, navigation routes, SDF updates, visual geometry, replication, and persistence.

Under the static-world model, that cross-system update problem disappears.

## 2. What our simplified world would look like

I would distinguish **static physical geometry** from **dynamic gameplay entities**.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Immutable Environment**
    <caption>Terrain · Buildings · Caves · Floors · Walls · Bridges · Collision · Navmesh · Base SDF</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center"><icon name="plus" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Dynamic Gameplay ECS**
    <caption>Players · NPCs · Monsters · Items · Spawns · Combat · Quests · Interactions</caption>
  </box>
  <row align="center" justify="center"><icon name="plus" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} gap={1} align="center">
    **Dynamic Presentation**
    <caption>Day/night · Weather · Animation · Spell effects · Water · Vegetation movement</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Seamless MMO World**
  </box>
</box>

This preserves the dynamic elements that matter most to a WoW-style experience without requiring runtime world-geometry editing.

## 3. Significant benefits for our SDF dynamic GI

This may be the biggest rendering-related benefit.

Previously, we planned for:

`Geometry change → SDF brick update → Radiance invalidation → GI refresh`

With immutable environmental geometry:

**The SDF tracing representation can be precomputed offline, while the shared radiance cache remains fully dynamic.**

This is an excellent match for our previously selected asset toolchain.

| GI subsystem | Revised approach |
|---|---|
| Terrain SDF | Precompute offline |
| Building/cave SDF | Precompute offline |
| Sparse SDF brick hierarchy | Cook offline, stream at runtime |
| Geometry-driven SDF rebuilding | Remove from normal runtime |
| Radiance cache | GPU-updated dynamically |
| Day/night illumination | Dynamic |
| Spell/emissive lighting | Dynamic, budgeted |
| Dynamic characters contributing to GI | Optional coarse proxies |
| GI page residency | Still dynamic |

That distinction is supported by the architecture of existing sparse-SDF approaches such as FidelityFX Brixelizer GI, which separates static and dynamic geometry handling. <Cite ref="turn272560search6"/>

### What this means

We preserve **full dynamic lighting over static geometry**, but drastically reduce tracing-structure maintenance.

The sunlight can move, torches can flicker, spell effects can illuminate nearby walls, and indirect light can change—all without rebuilding the underlying static SDF geometry.

That is a particularly favorable tradeoff for a WoW-like MMO.

## 4. Navigation becomes substantially easier

We could make navigation meshes entirely offline-cooked for normal world geometry.

Our previous Recast-based toolchain becomes even more attractive. Recast explicitly supports generating navigation polygons from authored geometry and packaging them as tiled navigation meshes. <Cite ref="turn272560search0"/>

Our server would still handle pathfinding, flight navigation, NPC goals, patrol routes and gameplay-specific traversal restrictions.

However, we could eliminate the entire runtime navigation-mesh rebuilding system unless we later introduce genuine geometry modifications.

**No doors means no door-specific path-state handling.** We still need special traversal links for stairs, elevators or scripted transportation if we include them.

## 5. What doesn't change

Importantly, this decision does not make our advanced rendering architecture unnecessary.

| Previously agreed technology | Status |
|---|---|
| GPU-native ECS | Keep |
| Contiguous SoA/AoSoA storage | Keep |
| Flat 2.5D world grid | Keep |
| Mesh + task shaders | Keep |
| Virtualized geometry | Keep |
| GPU visibility buffer | Keep |
| GPU material resolve | Keep |
| Virtual textures | Keep |
| Virtual shadow maps | Keep |
| Sparse SDF GI + shared radiance cache | Keep, simpler |
| GPU animation and pose sharing | Keep |
| GPU Bézier UI | Keep |
| QUIC / Quinn | Keep |
| Group replication and NetLOD | Keep |
| Non-blocking characters | Keep |

Our flat spatial grid may become more efficient because static environment data can be cooked and indexed offline, while moving entities occupy separate dynamic spatial streams.

## 6. Server architecture benefits

Our previously discussed persistence system also gets simpler.

We no longer require persistence of arbitrary terrain edits, structure placement or destroyed world geometry.

Instead, authoritative persistent data mainly covers characters, progression, inventories, world-object state, quests, NPC schedules and world events.

The server still needs snapshots, journals, transactions and recovery—but not a generalized mutable-geometry database.

We can also eliminate construction/destruction replication and much of the coordination between world mutation, navigation, collision and rendering.

## 7. What I would lock

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **ADR-022 — Static Authored World**
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  {#each [
    "Terrain, buildings, caves, bridges and structural collision geometry are immutable during gameplay.",
    "No player-built structures or runtime terrain deformation.",
    "No generalized building destruction or dynamic structural navmesh rebuilding.",
    "No ordinary gameplay doors that change navigation connectivity.",
    "Static collision, navigation and SDF data are cooked offline and streamed as needed.",
    "Characters, monsters, items, spawns, spells and gameplay state remain dynamic.",
    "Day/night, weather, lighting, water and visual effects remain dynamic.",
    "Persistent world state remains supported for gameplay but not arbitrary geometry editing."
  ] as item}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="check-circle-2" color="success"/>
      <text size="sm">{item}</text>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

**My recommendation is to adopt this change.** It reduces technical risk more than almost any other simplification we've discussed.

It also lets us concentrate resources on the features that most distinguish our engine: enormous seamless environments, very high character counts, GPU-native ECS, sophisticated virtualized rendering, dynamic GI and large-scale networking.

The main design tradeoff is reduced support for player-driven environmental change. For a WoW-like theme-park MMO, that's a reasonable choice.

If we adopt it, I'd simplify Phases 19–21 accordingly and proceed to **Phase 22 — Client Platform & Hardware Strategy** before the full architecture review.

<badge color="success">Architecture Decision Locked</badge>

## ADR-022 — Static Authored World

**Status: Approved**

Our custom MMO engine will follow a **WoW-style static world architecture**, with immutable environmental geometry and fully dynamic gameplay, characters, lighting, and visual effects.

### Finalized decisions

| System | Decision |
|---|---|
| Terrain | Static, authored offline |
| Buildings and structures | Static, no player construction |
| Destructible environments | Not supported |
| Doors altering navigation | Not supported by default |
| World collision | Precomputed, immutable |
| Navigation meshes | Offline generated |
| Sparse SDF geometry | Precomputed offline |
| Shared radiance cache | Fully dynamic GPU updates |
| Day/night and weather | Dynamic |
| NPCs, monsters and players | Fully dynamic |
| Combat and spell effects | Dynamic GPU simulation |
| Persistent gameplay state | Retained |

### Architectural optimizations unlocked

This decision allows us to simplify five important subsystems:

1. **SDF GI:** Stream precomputed SDF bricks instead of rebuilding static geometry at runtime.
2. **Navigation:** Remove general-purpose runtime navmesh rebuilding.
3. **Collision:** Separate immutable world collision from dynamic entity queries.
4. **World persistence:** Eliminate terrain, construction, and destruction journals.
5. **Networking:** Eliminate replication of arbitrary structural world changes.

All previously agreed GPU-native ECS, mesh/task rendering, virtualized geometry, flat 2.5D indexing, Quinn networking, and group replication decisions remain intact.

**Next: Phase 22 — Native Client Platform & Hardware Strategy.**

We'll determine our minimum GPU capabilities, Vulkan requirements, Windows/Linux support, graphics feature tiers, input, display, and audio architecture before the full engine review.

# Phase 22 — Native Client Platform & Hardware Architecture
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Pre-Implementation Architecture · October 2026</text>

Now that we've locked the static authored world, GPU-native ECS, mesh/task rendering, sparse SDF GI, and Rust/Go/Slang stack, we need to define **what hardware our client targets and which platform features are mandatory**.

This matters because we're not building a conventional renderer with mesh shaders as an optional enhancement. Our entire geometry pipeline is designed around them.

My recommendation is:

**Native Windows and Linux clients, Vulkan 1.3 as the API baseline, mandatory mesh/task shader capability, and scalable quality tiers above that baseline.**

I'd rather establish a clean modern hardware requirement than spend years maintaining two completely different rendering architectures.

## 1. Proposed platform strategy

| Platform | Priority | Rendering backend |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 10/11, 64-bit | Primary | Vulkan 1.3 |
| Linux, 64-bit | First-class | Vulkan 1.3 |
| Steam Deck | Evaluate compatibility | Hardware feature gate |
| macOS | Deferred | Would need separate capability/backend evaluation |
| Consoles | Deferred | Platform-specific graphics backends and certification |
| Browser | Not targeted | None |
| Mobile | Not targeted | None |

Windows and Linux can share nearly all of our Rust engine code, GPU ECS design, Slang shader modules, networking and asset formats.

## 3. GPU quality tiers

I'd separate **hardware compatibility** from **graphics quality**.

Every supported GPU must execute our baseline GPU ECS and mesh/task renderer. Higher tiers unlock larger budgets and optional accelerators—not different gameplay semantics.

| Feature | G1 — Minimum | G2 — Recommended | G3 — Ultra |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mesh/task shaders | Required | Required | Required |
| GPU ECS | Full functionality | Full | Full |
| Geometry | Aggressive LOD | Higher detail | Maximum configured detail |
| Texture residency | Smaller budget | Larger budget | Highest budget |
| Sparse SDF GI | Reduced update budget | Full quality target | Higher tracing detail |
| Radiance cache | Coarse | Medium | High |
| Virtual shadows | Reduced page budget | Higher resolution | Maximum budget |
| Animation | Aggressive crowd LOD | Higher fidelity | Highest fidelity |
| World resolution | Temporal upscale | Balanced | High/near-native |
| RT hardware | Not required | Optional | Optional |

A critical design rule is that **gameplay entities, interaction ranges, hit validation and visibility permissions must not change based on graphics quality**.

We can simplify distant visual representation, but graphics settings must not change authoritative gameplay.

### Which GPUs actually qualify?

I would not publish a minimum GPU model yet.

NVIDIA, AMD and Intel devices must each pass a capability-probing and shader-correctness test suite. Supporting the extension does not guarantee identical performance or driver behaviour.

We should validate at least one GPU from each intended vendor before fixing the minimum specification.

Our baseline may exclude older but otherwise capable GPUs. That is a conscious tradeoff of our mesh/task-first architecture.

## 4. VRAM budgets and graceful degradation

Our renderer has several persistent memory consumers:

- GPU ECS component arrays.
- Meshlet geometry and hierarchy metadata.
- Virtual-texture pages.
- Sparse SDF GI bricks and the radiance cache.
- Virtual shadow-map pages.
- Animation pose storage.
- Visibility buffers and temporal histories.
- GPU UI state.
- Scratch and streaming buffers.

I would not assign each subsystem a permanently fixed percentage of VRAM.

Instead, use one engine-wide memory-budget controller with subsystem reservations, flexible allocations and protected minimums.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Proposed VRAM pressure response</text>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Monitor memory budget and residency**
    <caption>Allocations · Usage · Eviction pressure · Required headroom</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
    **Reduce optional resource demand**
    <caption>Texture mips · Distant geometry · GI cache detail · Shadow pages</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Preserve essential representation**
    <caption>Player state · UI · Required meshes · Safe fallback lighting</caption>
  </box>
</box>

If the engine encounters memory pressure, it should lower visual detail or evict optional pages instead of repeatedly allocating and freeing resources until a driver failure occurs.

The actual minimum VRAM requirement should emerge from a working representative scene, not an arbitrary number selected now.

## 5. Windowing and input

For our native Rust client, my initial recommendation is <Entity category="software" value="winit" disambig="Rust cross-platform windowing and event-loop library"/>.

It supports native window/event integration and exposes raw window/display handles suitable for Vulkan surface creation. Linux support includes Wayland and X11. <Cite ref="turn443427search0"/>

The architecture would be:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Operating System Input**
    <caption>Mouse · Keyboard · Gamepad · Text input</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Rust Platform / Input Layer**
    <caption>Event collection · Device mapping · Input timestamps</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Input Routing**
    <caption>Gameplay commands · UI interactions · Text editing</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **GPU ECS + GPU UI**
  </box>
</box>

Although we've committed to a GPU-rendered UI, the CPU still needs to handle OS input and text-input interfaces.

Our GPU can perform retained layout, visual interaction state and hit testing. But clipboard operations, keyboard input methods, accessibility integration and some cursor management require platform cooperation.

### Input latency

I'd support input timestamps and a configurable late-input path.

An important requirement is to maintain consistent input ordering between client prediction, UI interactions and network commands.

We should not send an authoritative action merely because the GPU's visual hit test indicated a particular entity without verifying the corresponding gameplay command against server rules.

## 6. Display, presentation and HDR

I would make the renderer internally **scene-linear HDR**, even on monitors that only support SDR.

This does not mean requiring an HDR monitor.

It means lighting and compositing operate in a high-dynamic-range working space before final tone mapping.

| Display feature | Decision |
|---|---|
| SDR | Mandatory |
| HDR10 output | Optional |
| ScRGB / higher-precision paths | Optional where available |
| Variable refresh rate | Support |
| VSync | Configurable |
| Borderless windowing | Support |
| Fullscreen | Platform appropriate |
| Dynamic resolution | Core |
| Temporal upscaling | Core |
| Native-resolution UI | Core |
| Ultra-wide / high-DPI | Support |

Vulkan's `VK_EXT_swapchain_colorspace` expands the available swapchain colour-space options, but output capabilities must still be queried against the OS, display and selected surface. <Cite ref="turn443427search6"/>

### GPU Bézier UI and HDR

Our UI should be composed in a well-defined colour space, not simply drawn into an arbitrary HDR buffer using SDR assumptions.

For example, a white chat message should remain readable regardless of whether a spell explosion produces very high scene luminance behind it.

I'd give the UI renderer an explicit paper-white/reference-luminance policy for HDR output.

This becomes especially relevant to accessibility and legibility.

# Phase 22 — Native Client Platform & Hardware Architecture
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Pre-Implementation Architecture · October 2026</text>

Now that we've locked the static authored world, GPU-native ECS, mesh/task rendering, sparse SDF GI, and Rust/Go/Slang stack, we need to define **what hardware our client targets and which platform features are mandatory**.

This matters because we're not building a conventional renderer with mesh shaders as an optional enhancement. Our entire geometry pipeline is designed around them.

My recommendation is:

**Native Windows and Linux clients, Vulkan 1.3 as the API baseline, mandatory mesh/task shader capability, and scalable quality tiers above that baseline.**

I'd rather establish a clean modern hardware requirement than spend years maintaining two completely different rendering architectures.

| Windows 10/11, 64-bit | Primary | Vulkan 1.3 |
| Linux, 64-bit | First-class | Vulkan 1.3 |
| Steam Deck | Evaluate compatibility | Hardware feature gate |
| macOS | Deferred | Would need separate capability/backend evaluation |
| Consoles | Deferred | Platform-specific graphics backends and certification |
| Browser | Not targeted | None |
| Mobile | Not targeted | None |

I'd give the UI renderer an explicit paper-white/reference-luminance policy for HDR output.

This becomes especially relevant to accessibility and legibility.

## 7. Audio — deliberately CPU-first

This is an area where I would depart from our GPU-first philosophy.

**Audio mixing, timing and device output should remain CPU-based initially.**

The GPU can optionally assist certain large-scale acoustic calculations later, but conventional game audio is often latency-sensitive and does not justify GPU synchronization overhead.

Our audio subsystem needs:

- Spatialized sound sources.
- Music and ambient sound streaming.
- Audio buses for music, voice, combat, UI and environment.
- Priority-based voice limits.
- Distance attenuation and occlusion.
- Dynamic mixing and ducking.
- Low-latency response to gameplay events.

My preferred initial candidates are <Entity category="software" value="Kira" disambig="Rust game audio library"/> for high-level sound control and <Entity category="software" value="CPAL" disambig="Rust cross-platform audio input/output library"/> for lower-level device access. Kira currently documents spatial audio, streaming sounds and flexible mixing, while CPAL exposes native audio backends including WASAPI and Linux audio systems. <Cite refs={["turn211909search1","turn211909search6"]}/>

I would benchmark their suitability before finalizing audio middleware.

### Audio and ECS

The GPU ECS can own visual positions, but audio shouldn't require synchronous GPU readback of every sound emitter.

We should maintain a compact, host-readable audio presentation state for relevant sources.

For ordinary character sounds, the client already receives authoritative or predicted movement data. The audio system can use that state directly.

For GPU-only particles, we can generate a limited number of asynchronous sound events rather than producing one sound for every particle.

## 8. Accessibility is a foundational UI concern

Our fully GPU-rendered UI must still support:

- Keyboard navigation and focus.
- Screen-reader semantics.
- Text selection and clipboard.
- Input methods for international languages.
- Scalable text and high-DPI layout.
- Colour-blind and high-contrast modes.
- Remappable inputs.
- Reduced motion and flashing controls.

**Rendering text from Bézier curves does not solve text shaping, accessibility or international input.**

I would maintain a semantic UI representation accessible to the host operating system, alongside the GPU's visual UI state.

That is one of the few cases where the CPU must maintain meaningful UI metadata even though drawing and layout are GPU-primary.

We should include this in the full architecture review so that GPU ownership doesn't accidentally make the interface inaccessible.

## 9. Device loss, graphics settings and recovery

A GPU-first engine has unusually substantial GPU-resident state.

If the Vulkan device is lost, we cannot assume the complete GPU ECS survives.

I would design:

**Recoverable presentation state, not an immortal GPU allocation.**

The client should retain or be able to reconstruct authoritative/replicated entities, graphics settings, resource manifests and important local state.

GPU-only cosmetic particles can be discarded. A character's inventory or authoritative position must not depend on surviving device memory.

Recovery options may include rebuilding the GPU device and scene, or safely terminating/restarting the client when the platform cannot support reliable in-process recovery.

We should not promise seamless device-loss recovery before testing actual drivers.

## Next — Phase 23: Development Tooling, Security & Operations

This is the final major gap before our consolidated architecture review.

I'd cover four areas:

1. **Developer diagnostics:** GPU ECS inspectors, frame-graph visualisation, resource residency, shader debugging and performance profiling.
2. **Security:** Server-authoritative gameplay, QUIC endpoint protection, anti-cheat, content integrity and script/data validation.
3. **Operations:** Realm orchestration, stable Quinn gateways, rolling worker upgrades, snapshots, recovery, observability and deployment.
4. **Testing:** Automated Vulkan correctness, GPU allocator stress, deterministic simulation checks, network loss simulation and asset validation.

After that, **Phase 24 should be a full architecture review**, where we resolve remaining contradictions, audit every locked technology against hardware constraints, and produce a staged implementation plan.

One important observation for that review: our architecture is deliberately advanced and depends on several custom subsystems working correctly together. We should validate it through small vertical slices before attempting the entire GPU-native feature set at once.

| Mesh/task workgroup sizes | GPU-dependent |
| Exact GI quality budgets | Requires GPU timings |
| Temporal upscaler implementation | Compare quality, latency and integration |
| Audio engine selection | Test latency, voice limits and integration |
| Steam Deck / handheld support | Depends on mandatory hardware features |
| Optional RT acceleration | No architectural dependency now |

---

## Next — Phase 23: Development Tooling, Security & Operations

This is the final major gap before our consolidated architecture review.

I'd cover four areas:

1. **Developer diagnostics:** GPU ECS inspectors, frame-graph visualisation, resource residency, shader debugging and performance profiling.
2. **Security:** Server-authoritative gameplay, QUIC endpoint protection, anti-cheat, content integrity and script/data validation.
3. **Operations:** Realm orchestration, stable Quinn gateways, rolling worker upgrades, snapshots, recovery, observability and deployment.
4. **Testing:** Automated Vulkan correctness, GPU allocator stress, deterministic simulation checks, network loss simulation and asset validation.

After that, **Phase 24 should be a full architecture review**, where we resolve remaining contradictions, audit every locked technology against hardware constraints, and produce a staged implementation plan.

One important observation for that review: our architecture is deliberately advanced and depends on several custom subsystems working correctly together. We should validate it through small vertical slices before attempting the entire GPU-native feature set at once.

## 222 — Assistant

Message ID: `18d31ca9-2120-4aea-aa0b-a05fff039fcc` · 2026-10-09T05:12:21.256934+00:00

Absolutely. **Linux becomes our primary development and target platform, with Windows retaining first-class support.**

This makes very little difference to our core engine architecture because we've already selected Rust, Vulkan, Slang, and cross-platform libraries.

In fact, Linux-first development aligns particularly well with our custom GPU-native engine.

## ADR-023A — Linux-First Platform Strategy

<badge color="success">Decision Locked</badge>

| Platform | Priority | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **Linux x86-64** | Primary | Main development, profiling, testing and optimization |
| **Windows 11 x86-64** | First-class | Supported, tested and maintained alongside Linux |
| Steam Deck | Evaluate | Subject to GPU feature and performance requirements |
| macOS | Deferred | Requires separate graphics backend considerations |
| Consoles | Deferred | Platform-specific backends |
| Mobile / Web | Not targeted | Outside initial scope |

### Linux-specific technology choices

| Subsystem | Preferred direction |
|---|---|
| Graphics | Vulkan 1.3 + mesh/task shaders |
| Windowing | winit |
| Display servers | Wayland primary, X11 supported |
| Audio | PipeWire, with ALSA compatibility where appropriate |
| Networking | Quinn over UDP |
| Network performance | `io_uring`, `sendmmsg`/`recvmmsg`, UDP GSO/GRO where beneficial |
| GPU profiling | RenderDoc, Tracy, vendor profilers |
| CPU profiling | Linux `perf`, flamegraphs |
| Memory | NUMA-aware allocation where beneficial |
| Shader compilation | Slang → SPIR-V |

The Linux-specific I/O optimizations are candidates to benchmark, not mandatory parts of our networking implementation.

## Does this change the renderer?

**No.** All the following remain unchanged:

- GPU-native ECS and scheduling
- Contiguous SoA/AoSoA storage
- Flat 2.5D spatial indexing
- Mesh + task shaders
- GPU visibility-buffer rendering
- Virtualized meshlet geometry
- Sparse SDF dynamic GI with shared radiance cache
- GPU Bézier UI
- GPU animation and physics
- Temporal reconstruction
- Vulkan render graph

The platform-specific differences sit primarily in window surfaces, input, audio, presentation, device handling and network I/O.

### One important requirement

We'll use **continuous integration on both Linux and Windows from the beginning**.

Linux-first should mean Linux is where we develop and optimize—not that Windows becomes an afterthought.

I'd also avoid Linux-specific assumptions in the engine core, keeping platform functionality behind narrow Rust interfaces.

**Updated platform policy: Linux-first, Windows first-class, Vulkan-first, native Rust client.**

This supersedes the platform ordering in Phase 22. We can now move to Phase 23—tooling, security, operations and testing—before the full architecture review.
