# Phase 23 — Developer Tooling, Security & Live Operations
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Final Architecture Phase Before Full Review · October 2026</text>

We've now covered most of our core technology architecture. Phase 23 is about making the engine **observable, debuggable, secure, recoverable, and practical to develop**.

For a conventional game engine, tooling is important. For our architecture—with GPU-native ECS allocation, scheduling, mesh/task shaders, persistent GPU scene data, and sparse SDF GI—it is essential.

My recommendation:

**Build lightweight diagnostics and automated correctness testing into the engine from the beginning, while postponing sophisticated developer applications and distributed infrastructure until they are needed.**

## 1. The architecture we're supporting

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Go Services / Operations**
    <caption>Authentication · Account services · Orchestration · Administration</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Rust Authoritative MMO Server**
    <caption>Contiguous ECS · AI · Combat · Physics · Persistence</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Quinn / QUIC Gateways**
    <caption>Secure connections · Group replication · Network LOD</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border={{size:2,color:"strong"}} radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <text weight="medium" textAlign="center">Linux-First Native Client</text>
    <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
      {#each ["GPU ECS + scheduler","Flat 2.5D spatial index","Mesh/task rendering","Sparse SDF + radiance cache","GPU animation / physics","GPU Bézier UI"] as t}
        <grid-item>
          <box background="surface-secondary" padding={2} radius="sm" minHeight="48px" justify="center">
            <text size="xs" textAlign="center">{t}</text>
          </box>
        </grid-item>
      {/each}
    </grid>
  </box>
</box>

We need tools that let us inspect both host-side state and GPU-resident state without introducing CPU readbacks into the normal production frame.

That distinction will guide the entire tooling architecture.

## 2. GPU debugging — our highest development-tooling priority

Traditional CPU debuggers are insufficient for much of our renderer.

A GPU allocator bug might corrupt an ECS component chunk. A stale epoch might cause a mesh shader to access reclaimed geometry. A missing resource barrier might produce intermittent errors on one GPU vendor.

We need three layers of diagnostics.

| Layer | Recommended tools | What they detect |
|---|---|---|
| Vulkan API correctness | Khronos Validation Layers | Invalid resource use, layout mistakes, synchronization hazards |
| Frame and shader inspection | RenderDoc + vendor GPU profilers | Workloads, graphics state, draw/dispatch behaviour |
| Engine-specific GPU invariants | Custom validation shaders and diagnostic buffers | Invalid ECS handles, pool corruption, stale generations, spatial-index inconsistencies |

Khronos's current validation tools include synchronization validation and GPU-assisted validation, which instruments shader execution to catch errors that ordinary CPU-side validation cannot see. GPU-assisted validation has meaningful overhead and should be used in diagnostic runs rather than performance measurements. <Cite refs={["turn971507search2","turn971507search4"]}/>

### Custom GPU ECS diagnostic tools

I'd make these first-class engine capabilities:

| Diagnostic | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Entity handle inspector | Resolve entity → generation → archetype/chunk/row |
| Chunk occupancy viewer | Visualize allocations, holes, density and fragmentation |
| Structural mutation trace | Show spawn/despawn/migration events by epoch |
| GPU allocation validation | Detect overlapping allocations and invalid free-list states |
| Component integrity checking | Validate known invariants after GPU systems execute |
| Spatial grid debugger | Display cell occupancy, active sets and stale references |
| GPU scheduler view | Show system dependencies, indirect counts and barriers |
| Residency viewer | Show geometry, texture, SDF and other resource pages |
| Radiance-cache debugger | Visualize sparse SDF bricks, cache updates and invalidation |

### How to avoid debugging stalls

Production frames should record lightweight counters and optional diagnostic events.

Full GPU memory dumps, comprehensive invariant scans and readbacks should be activated deliberately during debugging.

**Observability must not become a permanent source of GPU synchronization stalls.**

For particularly difficult bugs, we can capture selected buffer snapshots and replay them in a controlled test environment.

## 3. Profiling: measure complete system cost

Our GPU-first architecture needs performance measurements at multiple levels.

I recommend <Entity category="software" value="Tracy" disambig="Real-time CPU and GPU profiler"/> for detailed CPU timing and selected GPU instrumentation, alongside Vulkan timestamps and vendor profiling tools.

For Linux-first development, `perf` and flamegraphs are useful for server, networking and host-runtime analysis.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">Performance domains to instrument</text>
  {#each [
    {n:"GPU ECS",d:"Chunk traversal, work generation, mutation processing, compaction"},
    {n:"Rendering",d:"Visibility, mesh/task invocations, material resolve, shading"},
    {n:"Dynamic GI",d:"SDF traversal, radiance updates, denoising and memory residency"},
    {n:"Animation",d:"Unique poses, skinning workload, animation LOD"},
    {n:"Networking",d:"Useful updates/sec, encode cost, packet cost, congestion, queue age"},
    {n:"Simulation",d:"Tick critical path, ECS system timings, AI and combat"},
    {n:"Persistence",d:"Commit latency, journal lag, snapshot duration, recovery"}
  ] as a}
    <row align="start" gap={2}>
      <icon name="activity" color="secondary"/>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{a.n}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{a.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

An important measurement rule:

**Always measure the complete operation, not only its fastest kernel.**

For example, a GPU culling algorithm may run faster than its CPU equivalent but still lose overall after compaction, synchronization and subsequent rendering costs are included.

Likewise, shared encoding might dramatically reduce serialization CPU while total replication remains limited by bandwidth.

## 4. Automated GPU correctness testing

This is one of the areas I'd implement surprisingly early.

Our GPU ECS does not merely render triangles. It creates and destroys entities, moves component data, updates indirection tables, and performs parallel scheduling.

These systems require automated correctness tests.

### Proposed testing strategy

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Generate deterministic test workload**
    <caption>Known entities, component values, mutations, and random seeds</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
        **CPU Reference**
        <caption>Simple Rust implementation optimized for correctness</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
        **GPU Implementation**
        <caption>Slang compute kernels and GPU ECS storage</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Compare Outputs + Validate Invariants**
    <caption>Entity identity · Component results · Memory safety · Publication epochs</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Test cases should cover multiple GPU vendors where supported, including:

- Millions of entity spawn/despawn cycles.
- Compaction during heavy structural mutation.
- Entity generation reuse and stale references.
- Resource-pool exhaustion and recovery.
- Cross-chunk/archetype migration.
- Concurrent readers and deferred reclamation.
- Spatial-grid boundary crossing.
- Indirect dispatch argument correctness.
- GPU visibility and material resolve invariants.
- Sparse resource eviction and fallback behaviour.

Floating-point comparisons should use task-appropriate tolerances. Entity identity, allocator integrity and structural state should meet stronger exactness requirements.

For GPU scheduling and barriers, synchronization validation should be part of the test matrix. Khronos explicitly warns that incorrect Vulkan synchronization can cause hard-to-diagnose errors as well as unnecessary GPU idling. <Cite ref="turn971507search5"/>

## 5. Security architecture

Our server-authoritative design is already a strong foundation, but we should define the trust boundaries explicitly.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Untrusted Native Client**
    <caption>Input · Predicted state · Local GPU ECS · User-generated packets</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authenticated Quinn Gateway**
    <caption>Session validation · Rate limiting · Payload bounds · Replay handling</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative Command Validation**
    <caption>Movement · Ability legality · Timing · Interaction permissions</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Trusted World / Transaction Services**
    <caption>ECS commits · Inventory ownership · Progression · Persistence</caption>
  </box>
</box>

### Anti-cheat strategy

For our WoW-like MMO, I'd prioritize **server-side behavioral validation** rather than intrusive kernel-level anti-cheat.

| Threat | Primary defense |
|---|---|
| Speed/teleport hacks | Authoritative movement and collision validation |
| Invalid ability casting | Server-owned cooldowns, resources, targeting and timing |
| Item duplication | Idempotent transactional inventory operations |
| Packet replay | QUIC protection plus application command sequencing |
| Map/state exploits | Interest authorization and no replication of hidden information |
| Protocol fuzzing | Strict bounded decoding and schema validation |
| Resource exhaustion | Per-session and per-command quotas |
| Modified client assets | Content integrity controls where relevant; server never trusts them for gameplay authority |

One important point: **a custom GPU ECS client cannot be trusted merely because its internal implementation is difficult to modify**.

Cheaters can modify client memory or inject inputs. Our authoritative server needs to remain correct even when the client is completely compromised.

Client integrity and cheat-detection tools can be added later, but they cannot replace server validation.

### Privacy and telemetry

We should also limit diagnostic collection to what is operationally necessary.

Detailed packet captures, chat, player identities and account information should not be indiscriminately exported to profiling systems.

Development traces and production telemetry need distinct data-retention and access policies.

## 6. Live operations and deployment

We previously agreed to minimize realm downtime with hot-reloadable gameplay definitions and rolling Rust simulation-worker upgrades.

The operational architecture should support that, but we should not build a large orchestration platform before we have multiple servers.

### Proposed maturity stages

| Stage | Deployment model | Appropriate time |
|---|---|---|
| **Local development** | One machine, local Rust server and client, optional Go services | First implementation |
| **Integration environment** | Separate gateway, simulation and persistence processes | Multiplayer foundation |
| **Small hosted realm** | Managed processes with supervised restart and backups | Early online testing |
| **Multi-worker realm** | Authority routing, versioned handoff, coordinated deployment | When partitioning is implemented |
| **Large-scale operations** | Automated placement, scaling, failover and monitoring | After real load measurements |

I'd evaluate containers and Kubernetes for later service orchestration, but not require Kubernetes to launch a local test realm.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **Target live deployment model**

  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Stable Quinn Gateways**
    <caption>Maintain player sessions during simulation-worker upgrades</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker Version N**
        <caption>Current authority</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker Version N+1**
        <caption>Restored and validated</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Versioned Authority Cutover**
    <caption>Fence stale writes · Move input routing · Resume simulation</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The first implementation does not need seamless worker migration. But stable entity IDs, versioned state and clear authority boundaries should be designed so it can be added without rewriting gameplay systems.

## 7. Observability across Rust and Go

I'd standardize metrics, logs and distributed traces using **OpenTelemetry-compatible instrumentation**.

OpenTelemetry provides Rust and Go instrumentation, although their component maturity differs: its current documentation lists Rust traces, metrics and logs as beta, while Go traces and metrics are stable. <Cite refs={["turn971507search0","turn971507search1"]}/>

For our engine, that means keeping a thin telemetry abstraction rather than coupling critical runtime code directly to a particular exporter.

### Proposed operational dashboard

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">ILLUSTRATIVE REALM HEALTH DASHBOARD</text>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{v:"29.7 ms",t:"Simulation tick p99"},{v:"0.8 ms",t:"Replication encode p99"},{v:"42 ms",t:"Gateway RTT median"},{v:"8.4 ms",t:"Database commit p99"}] as a}
      <grid-item>
        <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
          <title size="xl" tabularNums>{a.v}</title>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{a.t}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
  <caption>Illustrative values only, not measurements from our engine.</caption>
</box>

I'd capture the following core metrics:

| Category | High-value metrics |
|---|---|
| Simulation | Tick p50/p95/p99, overrun count, ECS systems' critical path |
| Networking | RTT, loss, outgoing bytes, queue age, useful updates/sec, connection count |
| Replication | Cohort build time, encoding reuse, baseline repair, NetLOD changes |
| Persistence | Commit latency, durable journal lag, snapshot age |
| Authority | Ownership handoffs, stale-write rejection, worker recovery |
| Client GPU | Frame time, ECS kernel time, rendering passes, GI cost, VRAM pressure |

**Average latency alone is insufficient.** MMO problems often become visible as p99 spikes during combat bursts, zone transitions, or large numbers of simultaneous logins.

For GPU scheduling and barriers, synchronization validation should be part of the test matrix. Khronos explicitly warns that incorrect Vulkan synchronization can cause hard-to-diagnose errors as well as unnecessary GPU idling. <Cite ref="turn971507search5"/>

## 5. Security architecture

Our server-authoritative design is already a strong foundation, but we should define the trust boundaries explicitly.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Untrusted Native Client**
    <caption>Input · Predicted state · Local GPU ECS · User-generated packets</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authenticated Quinn Gateway**
    <caption>Session validation · Rate limiting · Payload bounds · Replay handling</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Authoritative Command Validation**
    <caption>Movement · Ability legality · Timing · Interaction permissions</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Trusted World / Transaction Services**
    <caption>ECS commits · Inventory ownership · Progression · Persistence</caption>
  </box>
</box>

### Anti-cheat strategy

For our WoW-like MMO, I'd prioritize **server-side behavioral validation** rather than intrusive kernel-level anti-cheat.

| Threat | Primary defense |
|---|---|
| Speed/teleport hacks | Authoritative movement and collision validation |
| Invalid ability casting | Server-owned cooldowns, resources, targeting and timing |
| Item duplication | Idempotent transactional inventory operations |
| Packet replay | QUIC protection plus application command sequencing |
| Map/state exploits | Interest authorization and no replication of hidden information |
| Protocol fuzzing | Strict bounded decoding and schema validation |
| Resource exhaustion | Per-session and per-command quotas |
| Modified client assets | Content integrity controls where relevant; server never trusts them for gameplay authority |

One important point: **a custom GPU ECS client cannot be trusted merely because its internal implementation is difficult to modify**.

Cheaters can modify client memory or inject inputs. Our authoritative server needs to remain correct even when the client is completely compromised.

Client integrity and cheat-detection tools can be added later, but they cannot replace server validation.

### Privacy and telemetry

We should also limit diagnostic collection to what is operationally necessary.

Detailed packet captures, chat, player identities and account information should not be indiscriminately exported to profiling systems.

Development traces and production telemetry need distinct data-retention and access policies.

## 6. Live operations and deployment

We previously agreed to minimize realm downtime with hot-reloadable gameplay definitions and rolling Rust simulation-worker upgrades.

The operational architecture should support that, but we should not build a large orchestration platform before we have multiple servers.

### Proposed maturity stages

| Stage | Deployment model | Appropriate time |
|---|---|---|
| **Local development** | One machine, local Rust server and client, optional Go services | First implementation |
| **Integration environment** | Separate gateway, simulation and persistence processes | Multiplayer foundation |
| **Small hosted realm** | Managed processes with supervised restart and backups | Early online testing |
| **Multi-worker realm** | Authority routing, versioned handoff, coordinated deployment | When partitioning is implemented |
| **Large-scale operations** | Automated placement, scaling, failover and monitoring | After real load measurements |

I'd evaluate containers and Kubernetes for later service orchestration, but not require Kubernetes to launch a local test realm.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **Target live deployment model**

  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Stable Quinn Gateways**
    <caption>Maintain player sessions during simulation-worker upgrades</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down-up" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker Version N**
        <caption>Current authority</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} gap={1}>
        **Worker Version N+1**
        <caption>Restored and validated</caption>
      </box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" align="center">
    **Versioned Authority Cutover**
    <caption>Fence stale writes · Move input routing · Resume simulation</caption>
  </box>
</box>

The first implementation does not need seamless worker migration. But stable entity IDs, versioned state and clear authority boundaries should be designed so it can be added without rewriting gameplay systems.

## 7. Observability across Rust and Go

I'd standardize metrics, logs and distributed traces using **OpenTelemetry-compatible instrumentation**.

OpenTelemetry provides Rust and Go instrumentation, although their component maturity differs: its current documentation lists Rust traces, metrics and logs as beta, while Go traces and metrics are stable. <Cite refs={["turn971507search0","turn971507search1"]}/>

For our engine, that means keeping a thin telemetry abstraction rather than coupling critical runtime code directly to a particular exporter.

### Proposed operational dashboard

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">ILLUSTRATIVE REALM HEALTH DASHBOARD</text>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    {#each [{v:"29.7 ms",t:"Simulation tick p99"},{v:"0.8 ms",t:"Replication encode p99"},{v:"42 ms",t:"Gateway RTT median"},{v:"8.4 ms",t:"Database commit p99"}] as a}
      <grid-item>
        <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="md" gap={1}>
          <title size="xl" tabularNums>{a.v}</title>
          <text color="secondary" size="xs">{a.t}</text>
        </box>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
  <caption>Illustrative values only, not measurements from our engine.</caption>
</box>

I'd capture the following core metrics:

| Category | High-value metrics |
|---|---|
| Simulation | Tick p50/p95/p99, overrun count, ECS systems' critical path |
| Networking | RTT, loss, outgoing bytes, queue age, useful updates/sec, connection count |
| Replication | Cohort build time, encoding reuse, baseline repair, NetLOD changes |
| Persistence | Commit latency, durable journal lag, snapshot age |
| Authority | Ownership handoffs, stale-write rejection, worker recovery |
| Client GPU | Frame time, ECS kernel time, rendering passes, GI cost, VRAM pressure |

**Average latency alone is insufficient.** MMO problems often become visible as p99 spikes during combat bursts, zone transitions, or large numbers of simultaneous logins.

## 8. Testing and continuous integration

Because Linux is our primary platform and Windows is first-class, I'd establish both testing environments from the beginning.

| Test level | What it verifies | Initial requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Rust unit/property tests | ECS logic, schemas, math, encoding | Required |
| Go service tests | Service protocols and transactions | When services exist |
| Shader compilation | Slang/SPIR-V validity | Required from first GPU milestone |
| Vulkan validation | API, resources and synchronization | Required |
| GPU reference tests | Compare CPU and GPU algorithms | Required for GPU ECS |
| Network simulation | Loss, jitter, duplication and reordering | Required for replication |
| Asset cooker tests | Deterministic builds, bounds, corruption, dependencies | Required when cooking begins |
| Persistence recovery | Restart, replay, idempotency, duplicate avoidance | Required when persistence begins |
| Cross-platform builds | Linux and Windows compatibility | Required |
| Large-scale stress | Thousands of simulated players | Later |

### Tests I'd prioritize before visual quality

Our first engineering milestones should prove:

- GPU memory allocation and reclamation are correct.
- Entity mutations produce consistent ECS state.
- GPU dependencies don't race.
- Scene loading and eviction don't access retired resources.
- Render work buffers cannot overflow silently.
- Network replication survives packet loss.
- Authoritative world state can recover after process termination.

A visually impressive renderer with nondeterministic GPU allocator corruption would be an extremely difficult foundation to build upon.

### Deterministic replay

I would also introduce a reproducible event-replay format early.

It should record relevant initial state, input sequences, random seeds, schema/content versions and authoritative events.

This would let us reproduce server-side combat bugs, compare algorithm implementations and investigate state divergence after a failure.

Not every GPU presentation effect needs deterministic replay. The authoritative simulation and transactional systems are the priority.

## 9. Security of our asset pipeline

Since we've agreed to use external offline tools—including C/C++ executables—we should isolate them from live runtime infrastructure.

I recommend:

- Version-pinned offline dependencies.
- Reproducible cooker inputs where possible.
- Content-hash verification.
- Asset validation before deployment.
- Resource limits for processing untrusted source content.
- CI isolation for external tools.
- Signed or authenticated release manifests where needed.

This is especially important for parsers processing large 3D scenes, textures, fonts, and other complex input formats.

Our asset cooker should not have unrestricted access to production database credentials or live server authority.

## 10. Decisions for the architecture register

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>

    **ADR-023B — Tooling, Security & Operations**
    <badge>Recommended</badge>
  </row>

    {t:"Quinn gateway protection",d:"Authenticated sessions, rate limits, bounded decoding and backpressure."},
    {t:"Progressive operational infrastructure",d:"Start with local processes; introduce orchestration when the scale warrants it."},

        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{a.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

## 11. We are now ready for Phase 24 — Full Architecture Review

At this point, the major systems have been scoped.

The next step should be a **critical technical review**, not another speculative subsystem expansion.

I would examine the architecture against five criteria:

| Review dimension | Central question |
|---|---|
| **Correctness** | Can GPU ECS mutation, streaming and multi-frame rendering coexist safely? |
| **Feasibility** | Are our chosen Vulkan/Slang features and data representations implementable on the intended GPUs? |
| **Performance** | Have we introduced redundant work, excessive data copies, barriers or avoidable cross-processor dependencies? |
| **Simplicity** | Can we remove components or reuse established implementations without weakening the design? |
| **Buildability** | What is the smallest vertical slice that proves the most important architectural assumptions? |

There are a few **specific decisions I want to challenge during that review**:

- Whether mandatory task shaders are worth requiring for all geometry workloads, even though mesh-only pipelines may be more efficient for some passes.
- Whether a GPU-primary ECS genuinely needs arbitrary archetype mutation, or whether selected fixed-layout streams would reduce complexity.
- Whether our visibility buffer remains the best choice across all material types.
- Whether sparse SDF GI plus a shared radiance cache can meet our frame budgets on the minimum GPU tier.
- Whether our CPU/GPU state-epoch design can avoid both extensive duplication and subtle synchronization hazards.
- Whether GPU text shaping is worth implementing immediately, rather than keeping shaping host-side while rendering Bézier glyphs on the GPU.

Those questions don't invalidate our previous decisions. They identify the highest-risk places where implementation measurements or hardware validation may require refinement.

**My recommendation: Phase 24 should produce our first consolidated Engine Architecture Specification v0.1**, with every previously agreed decision documented, open questions marked, and a realistic implementation sequence.

That is the appropriate point to move from exploratory architecture discussions toward the first Rust/Vulkan code.

# Phase 24 — Full Architecture Review v0.1
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Technical Architecture Audit · 9 October 2026</text>

We've reached the point where we should stop adding major technologies and examine whether everything we've selected forms a coherent, buildable engine.

**My overall assessment: the architecture is technically credible, but its greatest risk is integration complexity—not a fundamental lack of available hardware technology.**

Our approach is unusually ambitious because we aren't simply building a renderer or an ECS. We're combining a GPU-owned entity runtime, custom virtualized rendering, GPU vector UI, software-traced dynamic GI, and a distributed MMO backend.

Those systems can work together. But we must establish their ownership boundaries, memory contracts, and execution dependencies before implementation.

Message ID: `6926126c-bbb8-4e55-974a-391f4b985cfe` · 2026-10-09T05:17:38.865113+00:00

## 2. The ten architectural risks I would review

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Severity reflects potential redesign cost, not the likelihood of failure.</text>

| Area | Risk | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| GPU ECS | General-purpose dynamic archetypes, allocation and compaction are complex | High |
| GPU scheduler | Too many dependent dispatch stages and barriers | High |
| Meshlet geometry | Continuous LOD, crack prevention and page residency | High |
| Slang + Vulkan | Feature/compiler/driver compatibility | High |
| GPU UI | Text shaping, clipping, input latency and accessibility | High |
| Dynamic GI | SDF quality, radiance cache stability and memory cost | High |
| Animation | Unique character poses and skinning bandwidth | Medium–high |
| Multi-frame state | Safe mutations while older frames still read data | High |
| Distributed authority | State transfer and recovery under real combat load | High |
| Asset pipeline | Cooker/runtime representation incompatibilities | High |

This doesn't mean we should abandon any of these systems. It tells us what must be validated before we build layers on top of them.

## 3. Critical finding: our GPU ECS needs two storage policies

Our existing proposal focuses heavily on archetype chunks with GPU-native structural mutations.

That's appropriate for a general ECS, but it would be inefficient to force every GPU object through arbitrary archetype migration.

I recommend **two complementary GPU storage types**.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **A. General-purpose GPU ECS**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Dynamic entity composition, archetype chunks, component queries, generation handles and deferred structural mutations.</text>

    Best for gameplay replicas, animation state, presentation entities and general engine objects.
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **B. Specialized GPU data streams**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Fixed-layout, tightly packed buffers optimized for homogeneous workloads.</text>

    Best for particles, foliage instances, visibility candidates, meshlets, radiance probes, work queues and procedural detail.
  </box>
</box>

Both can participate in the same GPU scheduling system.

The distinction matters because a million particles shouldn't require the same metadata and structural operations as a million independently composable gameplay entities.

**Review decision:** Keep GPU-native archetype ECS, but explicitly permit specialized fixed-layout stores as first-class engine resources.

This is a refinement rather than a reversal.

## 4. Critical finding: task shaders should be available, not used indiscriminately

We agreed to a mesh/task-shader-based renderer.

That remains the correct architectural target. But there's a distinction between **requiring task-shader support from the device** and **requiring every geometry workload to execute a task stage**.

Vulkan explicitly allows mesh shaders to execute without a task shader. The task stage is an optional part of the mesh pipeline, intended for work amplification and coarse processing. <Cite refs={["turn262944search1","turn262944search2"]}/>

I recommend:

- Mesh shaders as our primary triangle-generation pipeline.
- Task shaders for meshlet group culling and workload amplification where profitable.
- Compute shaders for global compaction, sorting and work generation.
- Mesh-only passes where task amplification adds no value.

We can retain mandatory device capability for both stages without adding unnecessary task-stage execution.

## 5. Critical finding: Slang must pass an early qualification test

Slang is attractive for a modular GPU codebase. It supports Vulkan/SPIR-V generation and has the programming features we want.

However, Slang's current documentation still describes its mesh shader support as preliminary. <Cite refs={["turn262944search4","turn262944search5"]}/>

That is a genuine integration risk for an engine where mesh/task shaders are foundational.

Before writing the GPU ECS or geometry renderer, I would require a **shader toolchain qualification suite** covering:

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Compute shader | Correct storage-buffer access and subgroup operations |
| Task shader | Correct mesh workgroup amplification |
| Mesh shader | Correct primitive and vertex output |
| Indirect mesh dispatch | Correct device-generated work counts |
| GPU atomics | Required integer operations and memory ordering |
| Buffer device address | Correct alignment and addressing |
| SPIR-V validation | All required generated modules validate |
| Linux + Windows | Compilation and runtime shader compatibility |
| Multiple GPU vendors | Correct results on representative hardware |

If Slang fails a specific feature, our fallback should be **HLSL or GLSL for that shader module**, not immediately abandoning the entire rendering architecture.

The GPU buffer ABI and shader-module interfaces should therefore remain independent of the source language.

## 233 — Assistant

Message ID: `8d111ab6-8c7e-497e-843b-502046846891` · 2026-10-09T05:17:54.309323+00:00

## 6. Critical finding: GPU UI has a hidden platform cost

Our requirement is ambitious:

**All UI rendering on GPU, with glyphs represented by Bézier curves.**

We can keep that. But we should distinguish four responsibilities.

| Responsibility | Proposed execution |
|---|---|
| Glyph outline rendering | GPU |
| Vector shapes, panels, clipping | GPU |
| UI layout and animations | GPU-primary |
| Text shaping, text input and accessibility | Host bridge where required |

The difficult issue is full multilingual text shaping.

A glyph's Bézier curves tell us how to draw its outline. They don't tell us which glyphs belong in a shaped Arabic, Hindi or mixed-direction text run.

Implementing complete GPU-native Unicode shaping would become a project of its own.

**My recommended refinement is to start with host-side shaping and GPU Bézier rasterization**, while retaining the architecture for future GPU shaping.

That gives us the visual result we wanted without requiring us to write a complete GPU text-layout engine before rendering our first UI.

It also fits the CPU-as-state/orchestration principle: shaping is an occasional text-state transformation, not CPU-driven pixel rendering.

## 7. Critical finding: the static-world decision is particularly valuable

Our latest decision to eliminate runtime terrain destruction and player building substantially simplifies the architecture.

The biggest benefit is that we can now separate immutable spatial assets from dynamic runtime state.

| System | Revised architecture |
|---|---|
| World collision | Offline-cooked, immutable |
| Navigation | Offline-cooked tiled navigation meshes |
| SDF geometry | Precomputed static bricks |
| Geometry LOD | Offline-cooked hierarchies |
| World streaming | Immutable page manifests |
| Dynamic entities | GPU ECS / server ECS |
| Persistent world state | Gameplay objects and transactions |
| Radiance cache | Dynamic GPU updates |
| Dynamic shadows | Updated for moving characters and lights |

I would treat static environment geometry as **a separate, read-mostly scene database**, not insert every static triangle or decorative prop into the fully mutable GPU archetype ECS.

For static authored objects, ECS records should exist only where identity, interaction, animation or gameplay state requires them.

This may be one of our most significant memory and scheduling optimizations.

## 8. Critical finding: don't require complete GPU state snapshots per frame

Our epoch system is necessary for correctness.

But replicating every GPU ECS component for two or three frames would quickly become wasteful.

I recommend three lifetime classes:

- **Immutable shared:** Static scene geometry, cooked SDF bricks, material definitions.
- **Versioned mutable:** Transforms, poses, spatial membership and other data that can overlap readers/writers.
- **Frame-transient:** Visibility lists, indirect commands, material bins and scratch buffers.

We should also permit immutable components to be reused across epochs until their backing memory can safely be retired.

**The synchronization goal is not zero barriers. It is no unnecessary barriers and no routine host waits.**

This will influence our render graph, GPU allocator and ECS scheduler more than any exotic scheduling extension.

# Phase 24B — Implementation Roadmap

The most important outcome of this review is **not to implement all the agreed technologies simultaneously**.

We need a sequence of small, integrated milestones, each proving a dependency needed by the next.

## Recommended milestone sequence

<box gap={3}>
  {#each [
    {n:"M0",title:"Repository + GPU Toolchain",desc:"Rust workspace, Linux/Windows CI, Vulkan bootstrap, Slang compilation, validation and profiling.",exit:"Compute + mesh/task shader triangle displayed and validated."},
    {n:"M1",title:"GPU Memory + ECS Kernel",desc:"Dense buffers, entity handles, component chunks, allocation, mutation commands and simple GPU scheduling.",exit:"Entities mutate safely and match a CPU reference."},
    {n:"M2",title:"Spatial World + GPU Visibility",desc:"Flat 2.5D grid, CSR membership, spatial work tiles, frustum culling and indirect mesh/task dispatch.",exit:"GPU renders a dense instanced test scene without CPU-per-object draws."},
    {n:"M3",title:"Visibility Buffer + Materials",desc:"Primitive IDs, depth, GPU attribute resolve, bindless material tables and basic lighting.",exit:"A textured scene renders correctly with visibility-driven shading."},
    {n:"M4",title:"Virtualized World Content",desc:"Offline meshlet cooking, initial hierarchical LOD, geometry paging, texture streaming, immutable world cells.",exit:"Camera movement streams detailed terrain/buildings under a bounded VRAM budget."},
    {n:"M5",title:"SDF GI + Temporal Frame System",desc:"Stream static SDFs, build shared radiance cache, temporal reconstruction and GPU frame epochs.",exit:"Dynamic indirect lighting works with stable frame scheduling."},
    {n:"M6",title:"GPU Character + UI Runtime",desc:"Animation state, pose evaluation, adaptive skinning, retained GPU UI and Bézier text.",exit:"Animated characters and usable interface render without CPU-generated draw lists."},
    {n:"M7",title:"Local Authoritative Game Loop",desc:"Rust server ECS, navigation, world collision, gameplay commands, local client prediction.",exit:"A controllable character can move, interact and perform basic combat."},
    {n:"M8",title:"Networked MMO Vertical Slice",desc:"Quinn, ECS replication, persistence, authentication and basic multi-client world state.",exit:"Multiple real clients share a persistent authoritative world."},
    {n:"M9",title:"Scale and Operational Maturity",desc:"Cohort replication, NetLOD, worker ownership, streaming optimizations, rolling upgrades and load testing.",exit:"Measured scaling results against defined hardware and deployment targets."}
  ] as m,i}
    <row align="start" gap={3} key={i}>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" minWidth="47px" padding={2} align="center">
        <text weight="medium">{m.n}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{m.title}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{m.desc}</text>
        <text size="xs">**Exit criterion:** {m.exit}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

This is a **capability roadmap**, not a promise that each milestone should be entirely finished before beginning the next.

For example, the first local authoritative movement loop should be prototyped alongside the early renderer. We shouldn't wait until GI and Bézier UI are finished before testing whether networked player movement feels responsive.

### An important implementation adjustment

I'd maintain two parallel development tracks:

| GPU engine track | MMO gameplay/server track |
|---|---|
| Vulkan + Slang foundation | Rust ECS and simulation |
| GPU ECS + visibility | World collision and navigation |
| Materials + streaming | Basic gameplay rules |
| Meshlet geometry + GI | Quinn replication and persistence |
| Animation + vector UI | Multi-client integration |

The tracks should meet through a small vertical slice early, then grow independently.

This avoids a common failure mode: developing an impressive rendering laboratory that takes years to become a playable multiplayer engine.

# Phase 24 — Full Architecture Review v0.1
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Technical Architecture Audit · 9 October 2026</text>

We've reached the point where we should stop adding major technologies and examine whether everything we've selected forms a coherent, buildable engine.

**My overall assessment: the architecture is technically credible, but its greatest risk is integration complexity—not a fundamental lack of available hardware technology.**

Our approach is unusually ambitious because we aren't simply building a renderer or an ECS. We're combining a GPU-owned entity runtime, custom virtualized rendering, GPU vector UI, software-traced dynamic GI, and a distributed MMO backend.

Those systems can work together. But we must establish their ownership boundaries, memory contracts, and execution dependencies before implementation.

## 1. Consolidated technology stack

          </box>
        </grid-item>
      {/each}
    </grid>
  </box>

  </box>

| Domain | Selected architecture | Review status |
|---|---|---|
| Native engine | Rust | Locked |
| Backend services | Go | Locked |

| Database | PostgreSQL + snapshots/journals | Proposed baseline |
| Offline asset tools | Existing tools preferred | Locked policy |
| Target platforms | Linux primary, Windows first-class | Locked |

**Locked target** means we've agreed on the architecture, not that the implementation or performance has been proven.

## 2. The ten architectural risks I would review

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Severity reflects potential redesign cost, not the likelihood of failure.</text>

| Area | Risk | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| GPU ECS | General-purpose dynamic archetypes, allocation and compaction are complex | High |
| GPU scheduler | Too many dependent dispatch stages and barriers | High |
| Meshlet geometry | Continuous LOD, crack prevention and page residency | High |
| Slang + Vulkan | Feature/compiler/driver compatibility | High |
| GPU UI | Text shaping, clipping, input latency and accessibility | High |
| Dynamic GI | SDF quality, radiance cache stability and memory cost | High |
| Animation | Unique character poses and skinning bandwidth | Medium–high |
| Multi-frame state | Safe mutations while older frames still read data | High |
| Distributed authority | State transfer and recovery under real combat load | High |
| Asset pipeline | Cooker/runtime representation incompatibilities | High |

This doesn't mean we should abandon any of these systems. It tells us what must be validated before we build layers on top of them.

## 3. Critical finding: our GPU ECS needs two storage policies

Our existing proposal focuses heavily on archetype chunks with GPU-native structural mutations.

That's appropriate for a general ECS, but it would be inefficient to force every GPU object through arbitrary archetype migration.

I recommend **two complementary GPU storage types**.

<box gap={3}>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **A. General-purpose GPU ECS**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Dynamic entity composition, archetype chunks, component queries, generation handles and deferred structural mutations.</text>

    Best for gameplay replicas, animation state, presentation entities and general engine objects.
  </box>
  <box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    **B. Specialized GPU data streams**

    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Fixed-layout, tightly packed buffers optimized for homogeneous workloads.</text>

    Best for particles, foliage instances, visibility candidates, meshlets, radiance probes, work queues and procedural detail.
  </box>
</box>

Both can participate in the same GPU scheduling system.

The distinction matters because a million particles shouldn't require the same metadata and structural operations as a million independently composable gameplay entities.

**Review decision:** Keep GPU-native archetype ECS, but explicitly permit specialized fixed-layout stores as first-class engine resources.

This is a refinement rather than a reversal.

## 4. Critical finding: task shaders should be available, not used indiscriminately

We agreed to a mesh/task-shader-based renderer.

That remains the correct architectural target. But there's a distinction between **requiring task-shader support from the device** and **requiring every geometry workload to execute a task stage**.

Vulkan explicitly allows mesh shaders to execute without a task shader. The task stage is an optional part of the mesh pipeline, intended for work amplification and coarse processing. <Cite refs={["turn262944search1","turn262944search2"]}/>

I recommend:

- Mesh shaders as our primary triangle-generation pipeline.
- Task shaders for meshlet group culling and workload amplification where profitable.
- Compute shaders for global compaction, sorting and work generation.
- Mesh-only passes where task amplification adds no value.

We can retain mandatory device capability for both stages without adding unnecessary task-stage execution.

## 5. Critical finding: Slang must pass an early qualification test

Slang is attractive for a modular GPU codebase. It supports Vulkan/SPIR-V generation and has the programming features we want.

However, Slang's current documentation still describes its mesh shader support as preliminary. <Cite refs={["turn262944search4","turn262944search5"]}/>

That is a genuine integration risk for an engine where mesh/task shaders are foundational.

Before writing the GPU ECS or geometry renderer, I would require a **shader toolchain qualification suite** covering:

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Compute shader | Correct storage-buffer access and subgroup operations |
| Task shader | Correct mesh workgroup amplification |
| Mesh shader | Correct primitive and vertex output |
| Indirect mesh dispatch | Correct device-generated work counts |
| GPU atomics | Required integer operations and memory ordering |
| Buffer device address | Correct alignment and addressing |
| SPIR-V validation | All required generated modules validate |
| Linux + Windows | Compilation and runtime shader compatibility |
| Multiple GPU vendors | Correct results on representative hardware |

If Slang fails a specific feature, our fallback should be **HLSL or GLSL for that shader module**, not immediately abandoning the entire rendering architecture.

The GPU buffer ABI and shader-module interfaces should therefore remain independent of the source language.

## 6. Critical finding: GPU UI has a hidden platform cost

Our requirement is ambitious:

**All UI rendering on GPU, with glyphs represented by Bézier curves.**

We can keep that. But we should distinguish four responsibilities.

| Responsibility | Proposed execution |
|---|---|
| Glyph outline rendering | GPU |
| Vector shapes, panels, clipping | GPU |
| UI layout and animations | GPU-primary |
| Text shaping, text input and accessibility | Host bridge where required |

The difficult issue is full multilingual text shaping.

A glyph's Bézier curves tell us how to draw its outline. They don't tell us which glyphs belong in a shaped Arabic, Hindi or mixed-direction text run.

Implementing complete GPU-native Unicode shaping would become a project of its own.

**My recommended refinement is to start with host-side shaping and GPU Bézier rasterization**, while retaining the architecture for future GPU shaping.

That gives us the visual result we wanted without requiring us to write a complete GPU text-layout engine before rendering our first UI.

It also fits the CPU-as-state/orchestration principle: shaping is an occasional text-state transformation, not CPU-driven pixel rendering.

## 7. Critical finding: the static-world decision is particularly valuable

Our latest decision to eliminate runtime terrain destruction and player building substantially simplifies the architecture.

The biggest benefit is that we can now separate immutable spatial assets from dynamic runtime state.

| System | Revised architecture |
|---|---|
| World collision | Offline-cooked, immutable |
| Navigation | Offline-cooked tiled navigation meshes |
| SDF geometry | Precomputed static bricks |
| Geometry LOD | Offline-cooked hierarchies |
| World streaming | Immutable page manifests |
| Dynamic entities | GPU ECS / server ECS |
| Persistent world state | Gameplay objects and transactions |
| Radiance cache | Dynamic GPU updates |
| Dynamic shadows | Updated for moving characters and lights |

I would treat static environment geometry as **a separate, read-mostly scene database**, not insert every static triangle or decorative prop into the fully mutable GPU archetype ECS.

For static authored objects, ECS records should exist only where identity, interaction, animation or gameplay state requires them.

This may be one of our most significant memory and scheduling optimizations.

## 8. Critical finding: don't require complete GPU state snapshots per frame

But replicating every GPU ECS component for two or three frames would quickly become wasteful.

I recommend three lifetime classes:

- **Immutable shared:** Static scene geometry, cooked SDF bricks, material definitions.
- **Versioned mutable:** Transforms, poses, spatial membership and other data that can overlap readers/writers.
- **Frame-transient:** Visibility lists, indirect commands, material bins and scratch buffers.

**The synchronization goal is not zero barriers. It is no unnecessary barriers and no routine host waits.**

This will influence our render graph, GPU allocator and ECS scheduler more than any exotic scheduling extension.

    {n:"M3",title:"Visibility Buffer + Materials",desc:"Primitive IDs, depth, GPU attribute resolve, bindless material tables and basic lighting.",exit:"A textured scene renders correctly with visibility-driven shading."},
    {n:"M4",title:"Virtualized World Content",desc:"Offline meshlet cooking, initial hierarchical LOD, geometry paging, texture streaming, immutable world cells.",exit:"Camera movement streams detailed terrain/buildings under a bounded VRAM budget."},
    {n:"M5",title:"SDF GI + Temporal Frame System",desc:"Stream static SDFs, build shared radiance cache, temporal reconstruction and GPU frame epochs.",exit:"Dynamic indirect lighting works with stable frame scheduling."},
    {n:"M6",title:"GPU Character + UI Runtime",desc:"Animation state, pose evaluation, adaptive skinning, retained GPU UI and Bézier text.",exit:"Animated characters and usable interface render without CPU-generated draw lists."},
    {n:"M7",title:"Local Authoritative Game Loop",desc:"Rust server ECS, navigation, world collision, gameplay commands, local client prediction.",exit:"A controllable character can move, interact and perform basic combat."},
    {n:"M8",title:"Networked MMO Vertical Slice",desc:"Quinn, ECS replication, persistence, authentication and basic multi-client world state.",exit:"Multiple real clients share a persistent authoritative world."},
    {n:"M9",title:"Scale and Operational Maturity",desc:"Cohort replication, NetLOD, worker ownership, streaming optimizations, rolling upgrades and load testing.",exit:"Measured scaling results against defined hardware and deployment targets."}
  ] as m,i}
    <row align="start" gap={3} key={i}>
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" minWidth="47px" padding={2} align="center">
        <text weight="medium">{m.n}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{m.title}**
        <text size="sm" color="secondary">{m.desc}</text>
        <text size="xs">**Exit criterion:** {m.exit}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

This is a **capability roadmap**, not a promise that each milestone should be entirely finished before beginning the next.

For example, the first local authoritative movement loop should be prototyped alongside the early renderer. We shouldn't wait until GI and Bézier UI are finished before testing whether networked player movement feels responsive.

### An important implementation adjustment

I'd maintain two parallel development tracks:

| GPU engine track | MMO gameplay/server track |
|---|---|
| Vulkan + Slang foundation | Rust ECS and simulation |
| GPU ECS + visibility | World collision and navigation |
| Materials + streaming | Basic gameplay rules |
| Meshlet geometry + GI | Quinn replication and persistence |
| Animation + vector UI | Multi-client integration |

The tracks should meet through a small vertical slice early, then grow independently.

This avoids a common failure mode: developing an impressive rendering laboratory that takes years to become a playable multiplayer engine.

## 12. Proposed first vertical slice

I'd build one small environment specifically to validate the most difficult architectural interfaces.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text weight="medium">The first playable engine test</text>
  <AsyncImage query="minimal greybox fantasy game environment small terrain village buildings simple test scene game engine development" aspectRatio="16:9" width="100%"/>

          <icon name="check" color="secondary"/>
          <text size="sm">{x}</text>
        </row>
      </grid-item>
    {/each}
  </grid>
</box>

This environment is intentionally small.

It should exercise the complete path from input and authoritative server state to GPU ECS, spatial indexing, rendering and UI.

We can then replace its simple components with the more advanced systems we've selected, without losing a working end-to-end application.

## 13. Architecture review conclusions

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [
    {t:"The architecture is coherent",d:"No fundamental conflict requires abandoning the GPU-first approach."},
    {t:"Static world geometry was the right simplification",d:"It reduces collision, navigation, persistence and SDF-maintenance complexity."},
    {t:"Specialized GPU arrays should coexist with archetype ECS",d:"Avoid forcing homogeneous GPU workloads into general-purpose entity storage."},
    {t:"Task shaders should be selective",d:"Retain required capability but avoid unnecessary amplification stages."},
    {t:"GPU text rendering does not require GPU text shaping",d:"Use host shaping initially if it materially reduces development risk."},
    {t:"Shader/compiler and GPU memory correctness come first",d:"Validate these before building advanced geometry and GI systems."},
    {t:"Prototype gameplay integration early",d:"Keep the renderer and multiplayer engine connected throughout development."}
  ] as x}

      </box>

  {/each}
</box>

## 14. My recommendation for our next step

**Architecture v0.1 is ready to become an implementation specification**, but it is not yet a finished low-level design.

I would do one final engineering exercise before writing substantial runtime code:

**Define Milestone 0 in enough detail that we can create the repository, compile our first Slang shaders, create a Vulkan device, and verify mesh/task execution on Linux.**

That means specifying the initial Cargo workspace, library versions, GPU feature negotiation, shader compilation pipeline, Vulkan memory ownership, diagnostic setup and a very small test application.

We should also record the agreed architecture in versioned ADR files so later implementation decisions can be traced back to what we've chosen.

**The next deliverable should be Engine Foundation Specification v0.1 — the concrete blueprint for the first Rust/Vulkan implementation.**

That moves us out of exploratory architecture and into engineering, without prematurely attempting the full MMO engine.

# Phase 25 — Engine Foundation Specification v0.1
<text color="secondary" weight="medium">Custom MMO Engine · Milestone 0 · October 2026</text>

We're ready to move from architecture research into a concrete engineering blueprint.

**Milestone 0 will establish our native Rust/Vulkan engine foundation and verify that Slang, mesh/task shaders, GPU compute, memory transfers and synchronization work correctly on our target hardware.**

We will **not** implement the full GPU ECS, world renderer or MMO server yet. This milestone establishes the foundation those systems will depend upon.

## 1. Final technology baseline

| Layer | Technology | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Primary development OS | Linux | Locked |
| Secondary OS | Windows 11 | First-class |
| Engine implementation | Rust | Locked |
| GPU API | Vulkan 1.3 | Locked |
| Low-level Vulkan bindings | <Entity category="software" value="ash" disambig="Rust Vulkan bindings"/> | Recommended |
| Window/event management | <Entity category="software" value="winit" disambig="Rust windowing library"/> | Recommended |
| GPU shaders | <Entity category="software" value="Slang" disambig="GPU shader language"/> | Qualification required |
| Shader binary | SPIR-V | Locked |
| Validation | Khronos Validation Layers + SPIRV-Tools | Required |
| Server networking | Quinn / QUIC | Locked, not needed in M0 |
| Server/services | Rust + Go | Locked, later milestones |

I recommend `ash` rather than a higher-level graphics abstraction because we need explicit control over mesh/task shaders, GPU memory, command submission, feature chains and Vulkan synchronization. The current documented `ash` release is 0.38.0, with Vulkan 1.3 bindings. <Cite ref="turn608530search3"/>

We'll pin exact tool and dependency versions when creating the repository, rather than selecting them from memory or relying on floating versions.

## 2. First repository structure

I recommend a small Rust workspace, not dozens of crates.

### Module responsibilities

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `engine-core` | Result types, IDs, configuration, diagnostics and common utilities |
| `engine-vulkan` | Vulkan instance, device, queues, buffers, synchronization and swapchain |
| `engine-shaders` | Shader compilation, manifests, reflection and SPIR-V validation |
| `gpu-probe` | Enumerate hardware features and test device capabilities |
| `render-lab` | Minimal compute + mesh/task renderer used for experiments |

We won't introduce the full ECS until the Vulkan foundation is verified.

This keeps the initial codebase understandable and prevents premature abstractions.

## 3. GPU capability discovery comes first

Before creating a window or rendering anything, our `gpu-probe` application should enumerate Vulkan devices and report exactly what they support.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  **GPU initialization sequence**

  {#each [{n:"01",t:"Load Vulkan",d:"Find the Vulkan loader, enumerate instance extensions and API support."},{n:"02",t:"Enumerate physical GPUs",d:"Read vendor/device IDs, driver versions, memory heaps and queues."},{n:"03",t:"Query feature chains",d:"Vulkan 1.3 features, mesh/task capability, buffer addressing and resource indexing."},{n:"04",t:"Inspect GPU limits",d:"Workgroup sizes, task payload limits, mesh output limits, memory alignments."},{n:"05",t:"Build capability report",d:"List mandatory features, optional accelerators and missing requirements."},{n:"06",t:"Create logical device",d:"Enable only supported and explicitly required features."}] as a}
    <row gap={3} align="start">
      <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" size="34px" align="center" justify="center">
        <text weight="medium" size="xs">{a.n}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" gap={1}>
        **{a.t}**
        <text color="secondary" size="sm">{a.d}</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
</box>

Vulkan requires supported optional features to be explicitly enabled at logical-device creation. Querying `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` and its extension feature chain is therefore mandatory. <Cite refs={["turn608530search6","turn608530search8"]}/>

### Hardware capabilities to inspect

| Capability | Milestone 0 requirement |
|---|---|
| Vulkan 1.3 | Required |
| Mesh shader (`VK_EXT_mesh_shader`) | Required |
| Task shader | Required |
| Buffer device address | Required |
| Timeline semaphores | Required |
| Synchronization2 | Required |
| Dynamic rendering | Required |
| Required descriptor indexing features | Required |
| GPU compute queues | Required |
| Subgroup operations | Record exact supported operations |
| Storage image/buffer formats | Validate chosen test formats |
| Sparse residency | Report, optional in M0 |
| Hardware ray tracing | Report, not required |

We should also query the actual mesh/task shader limits. The extension provides device-specific limits and separate feature bits; simply detecting the extension name is insufficient. <Cite refs={["turn997491search0","turn608530search12"]}/>

**The engine should fail with a useful capability report, not crash or silently attempt unsupported GPU features.**

## 4. Slang shader qualification

This is our first major technology gate.

The latest Slang documentation supports Vulkan SPIR-V output and shows task/mesh shader syntax, but still describes mesh shader support as preliminary. That means we need functional validation rather than assuming compatibility. <Cite refs={["turn608530search7","turn608530search2"]}/>

I'd qualify four shader categories:

| Test | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Compute | Write and transform GPU buffer contents |
| Mesh-only | Generate triangle primitives without a vertex shader |
| Task + mesh | Task stage launches mesh workgroups |
| Indirect mesh/task | GPU-written dispatch count controls geometry workload |

We should build a small shader compilation pipeline with a manifest declaring entry points, stages, resources, and target capabilities.

An initial compute shader can use the documented Slang-to-SPIR-V workflow:

```bash
slangc shaders/compute/buffer_test.slang \
  -entry computeMain \
  -target spirv \
  -profile glsl_460 \
  -o build/shaders/buffer_test.spv

spirv-val build/shaders/buffer_test.spv
```

The compiler options follow Slang's documented CLI; we'd still configure the appropriate target Vulkan environment and additional capabilities for mesh/task shader modules. <Cite refs={["turn997491search4","turn997491search6"]}/>

I would require the build system to capture the compiler version, source dependencies, compilation diagnostics, and resulting SPIR-V hash.

If Slang fails a required mesh/task capability test, **we retain our rendering architecture and use a validated GLSL/HLSL shader for that specific path** until the issue is resolved.

## 5. Vulkan memory and resource ownership

For M0, I recommend a simple allocator—not our full GPU-native ECS allocator.

We need only:

- Device-local buffers.
- Host-visible staging buffers.
- Basic images and render targets.
- Alignment-aware suballocation.
- Explicit resource retirement.

The host must own every Vulkan object lifetime.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Rust Vulkan Device**
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Resource Registry**
    <caption>Buffers · Images · Pipelines · Shader modules</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center"><text size="sm">Device-local allocation arena</text></box>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <box border radius="md" padding={3} align="center"><text size="sm">Host staging and transfer arena</text></box>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Submission + Completion Tracking**
  </box>
</box>

I'd define opaque Rust handles for resources but avoid building a highly sophisticated allocator on day one.

We can reuse a mature Rust Vulkan allocation library if one passes our requirements, or start with a small explicit implementation for the test renderer.

The eventual ECS chunk allocator is a separate GPU-side suballocation system built on top of host-created backing buffers.

## 6. Synchronization: establish correct primitives now

I would use **Vulkan Synchronization2 and timeline semaphores** from the foundation milestone.

The first GPU dependency test should be:

`Host upload → GPU compute write → GPU mesh/task read → Graphics output`

Each transition must use correctly scoped resource-access dependencies.

A timeline semaphore can track submission completion and resource retirement, but isn't a substitute for every required buffer or image memory barrier.

Khronos highlights both hazards from missing synchronization and performance loss from overly broad dependencies. <Cite ref="turn997491search11"/>

### Two initial submission modes

| Mode | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Single graphics-capable queue | Simple correctness baseline |
| Separate transfer/compute queues | Experimental performance path |

**Start with one queue.**

That makes it easier to validate memory ordering and dependencies before introducing queue-family ownership transfers or cross-queue synchronization.

We can still execute compute and graphics on the same queue.

Later, independent work can migrate to asynchronous queues where profiling shows an advantage.
